items.title: LMCache MP GDS-L1 aborts in cuFileReadAsync with putStreamOp assertion during TP=4 hot retrieval
items.author: ekaynar
items.body_excerpt:
## Description

  LMCache MP native GDS-L1 crashes during the first hot KV-cache retrieval with TP=4 and DeepSeek V4 hybrid KV cache.

  The cold request successfully stores 8,192 tokens. Repeating the identical prompt finds all 32 GDS-L1 chunks, but the LMCache server aborts inside NVIDIA cuFile before completing the
  load.

  ## Error

  ```text
  [2026-08-16 07:32:46,757] LMCache INFO:
  Stored 8192 tokens in 0.642 seconds

  [2026-08-16 07:32:47,435] LMCache INFO:
  Prefetch request completed (L1+L2): 32/32 retained keys
  (32 L1, 0 L2) in 4.4 ms
  (external_request_id=chatcmpl-a1dc73801f7804a9-9b591ba6,
  prefetch_request_id=-1)

  [2026-08-16 07:32:47,451] LMCache INFO:
  AffinityThreadPool: affinity_key=-7117897118196929406 assigned to
  worker slot 0 of 1 (thread affinity-pool-0-0);
  2 distinct key(s) now bound

  [2026-08-16 07:32:47,451] LMCache WARNING:
  AffinityThreadPool: affinity_key=-7117897118196929406 wrapped onto
  worker slot 0 (only 1 workers), so it shares a thread with an earlier
  key and their tasks are serialized. Increase the worker count to give
  each client its own thread.

  [2026-08-16 07:32:47,452] LMCache INFO:
  AffinityThreadPool: affinity_key=-6742962413049701147 assigned to
  worker slot 0 of 1; 3 distinct key(s) now bound

  [2026-08-16 07:32:47,453] LMCache INFO:
  AffinityThreadPool: affinity_key=5784243743074828858 assigned to
  worker slot 0 of 1; 4 distinct key(s) now bound

  python3: cufile_async.h:107:
  void CUfileStream_s::putStreamOp(CUfileStreamInfo_t*):
  Assertion `tmp == sinfo' failed.
  ```

  This causes the LMCache process to abort rather than return a recoverable error.

  ## Secondary vLLM failure

  After the LMCache process aborts, vLLM enters the failed hybrid-cache-load path and exits with:

  ```text
  ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 1)

  File "vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py", line 2293,
  in _update_requests_with_invalid_blocks

  (req_block_ids,) = self.kv_cache_manager.get_block_ids(req_id)
  ```

  This appears secondary to the LMCache/cuFile process abort.

  ## LMCache configuration

  ```bash
  CUFILE_ENV_PATH_JSON=/etc/cufile.json \
  LMCACHE_LOG_LEVEL=INFO \
  LMCACHE_USE_EXPERIMENTAL=True \
  lmcache server \
    --host 127.0.0.1 \
    --port 5560 \
    --http-host 127.0.0.1 \
    --http-port 18080 \
    --prometheus-port 19090 \
    --enable-extra-logging \
    --l1-size-gb 200 \
    --gds-l1-path /mnt \
    --gds-l1-use-direct-io \
    --eviction-policy LRU
  ```

 No CPU L1 or NIXL L2 is configured. All four GPUs register successfully before the request.

  ## Reproduction

  1. Start LMCache MP with the native GDS-L1 configuration above.
  2. Start vLLM with TP=4 and `LMCacheMPConnector`.
  3. Send an 8K-token prompt once to populate GDS-L1.
  4. Send the identical prompt again.
  5. LMCache finds all `32/32` L1 chunks and then aborts in `CUfileStream_s::putStreamOp()`.

  ## Environment

  - LMCache: `0.5.4rc3.dev1 (g0373a573)`
  - vLLM: `0.23.0`
  - Python: `3.12.3`
  - PyTorch: `2.11.0+cu130`
  - PyTorch CUDA: `13.0`

items.title: [Perf][SM103] sparse MLA decode: bf16-dense-KV ABI doubles KV bytes vs FlashMLA's packed pages; mid-batch q=6 verify regression (B=3–12)
items.author: brandonfzhang
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

On DeepSeek-V4.1 sparse MLA (top-k 512, real captured indexer selections),
FlashInfer's SM103 path requires a **bf16 dense KV cache**, while FlashMLA reads a
584-byte/token packed fp8 page — ~2x KV bytes per decode step for FI. On the
call-count-weighted view over 3,819 real selections FlashMLA comes out ~1.2x ahead
(FI wins the expensive full-length prefills and net device time, so the verdict is
genuinely split). Inside the decode family there is a clean, shape-local regression:
at the production verify width (q=6, table width 640), FI is **1.5–1.6x ahead at
batch 1–2, then 1.04–1.43x behind for batch 3–12**, then ahead again at 13+.
The serving integration also pays a per-step index repack feeding the FI call
(~8% of FI attention time), which the packed-page rivals do not need.

## Environment

- NVIDIA GB300 (SM103); CUDA 13.0; FlashInfer 0.7.1rc5; rival: FlashMLA (vLLM build)
- Timing: CUPTI, 20 interleaved rounds, SM clock locked 2070 MHz, fp64 gates
- Workloads: real indexer selections captured from live serving of the published
  DeepSeek-V4.1 GB300 recipes and replayed verbatim (grid-synthetic selection
  patterns overstate FI's cost ~2x, so only real selections are used)

## Exact call parameters

Sparse MLA decode: `num_q_heads=16`, `head_dim=512` (+64 RoPE), q_len 6 per
sequence (speculative verify), selection table width 640 (top-k 512 + sliding
window 128), real captured per-sequence KV lengths 31k-108k; FI reads a bf16
dense KV pool (its SM103 ABI), FlashMLA reads its packed 584 B/token fp8 pages —
same selections replayed for both.

## Measurements — q=6 verify decode, table width 640 (µs)

| batch | FlashMLA | FI (trtllm-gen) | verdict |
|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 1 | 22.2 | 13.5 | FI 1.64x ahead |
| 2 | 22.2 | 15.2 | FI 1.46x ahead |
| 3 | 22.2 | 23.1 | FI 1.04x behind |
| 6 | 22.3 | 23.9 | FI 1.07x behind |
| 9 | 22.5 | 30.9 | FI 1.37x behind |
| 12 | 22.7 | 32.6 | FI 1.43x behind |
| 13 | 22.8 | 19.1 | FI 1.19x ahead |

FlashMLA is nearly flat in batch; FI's cost ramps from B=3 and drops back at B=13 —
it looks like a tiling/scheduling boundary. At the narrow table width (128) FI is
ahead across the board (the new `cake` backend takes several small-B classes).

## Ask

1. An fp8-packed KV page format for SM103 sparse MLA (it exists on SM120 only
   today) — the 2x KV-byte handicap is structural, and vLLM already defines a
   compatible 352-byte nvfp4 layout (#5716) and a 584-byte fp8 layout.
2. Fix the B=3–12 ramp at q=6/W=640 (the production verify regime: its weight is
   concentrated exactly at B=3–12 in our captures).

## Related

- #6301 (DSv4/4.1 sparse attention backend support, SM100/103/107)
- #5716 (nvfp4_ds_mla compressed KV layout)

	- Enable sharing of GPU-resident (L1) and host-resident (L2) KV caches across engines within the same super-node domain.
	- Add cache location awareness to the Router to coordinate request placement and KV transfers based on cache availability and engine load.
	- Extend HiCache linker integration to support GPU-to-GPU KV transfers over (NVLink @Shunkangz、AMD UALoE @TianDi101、SAIL's card-to-card interconnect @Vinsmoke86) and remote Grace DRAM access through EGM.
	- Optimize small KV-page transfers and NUMA placement; validate correctness, cache hit rate, and TTFT/TPOT on GB NVLink72、 AMD MI455X Helios Rack、and SAIL clusters.
- Build a KV cache orchestrator across the router and engine @ZhaiFeiyue @stmatengss 
	- Identify sessions, sub-agents, and tool calls, and expose `PREFETCH`, `DEMOTE`, and `PIN` hints for global cache scheduling. Align this work with the [[router roadmap](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/25760)](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/25760). 
	- Add session-aware scheduling to the router
- Enhance HiCache Linker Mode @hzh0425 @alphabetc1 @huangtingwei9988 
    - [[PR #40896](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40896)](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40896): Support fast failover and recovery.
    - [[PR #41343](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41343)](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41343): Extend support to hybrid models with Mamba and SWA.

    - [[PR #39727](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/39727)](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/39727): Add a page-unified host KV layout and topology-independent L3 keys.

- Extend the decode-side unified radix tree to fully support SWA, Mamba, and MTP.

items.title: [Bug] NVFP4 flashinfer_b12x MoE produces empty/garbage output under pipeline or tensor parallel on SM120 — regression between dev552 (06-29) and dev601 (06-30)
items.author: jhsmith409
items.body_excerpt:
**Title:** [Bug] NVFP4 `flashinfer_b12x` MoE produces empty/garbage output under pipeline or tensor parallel on SM120 — regression between dev552 (06-29) and dev601 (06-30)

## Summary

Serving `nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4` with `--moe-backend=flashinfer_b12x` (SM120 native FP4 MoE, PR #40082) produces **empty completions or degenerate repeated-token output** (`<|box_end|>` spam) as soon as the model is sharded across 2 GPUs — with **either** `--pipeline-parallel-size=2` **or** `--tensor-parallel-size=2`. The identical config on a **single GPU** (no sharding) works correctly.

We bisected this to a **49-commit window between two daily nightly builds**:
- `0.23.1rc1.dev552+g4559c43a9` (2026-06-29) — **works correctly**
- `0.23.1rc1.dev601+ga16dbd5b8` (2026-06-30) — **broken**

Compare: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/compare/4559c43a9...a16dbd5b8

## Environment

- GPU: 2× NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 Ti (16 GB), SM120 (Blackwell), no P2P between the two cards
- Driver: 610.43.02, CUDA 13.0 (torch 2.11.0+cu130)
- flashinfer-python: 0.6.12 (present in both the good dev552 and bad dev601/dev672 images — see note below)
- Docker images: `vllm/vllm-openai:nightly-<sha>` (official nightly builds)
- Model: `nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4` (ModelOpt `MIXED_PRECISION`: W4A16_NVFP4 experts + FP8 attn/KV, hybrid GDN/Mamba + attention, 256 experts / 8 active)

## Command used (identical across every test below)

```
vllm serve nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4 \
  --served-model-name qwen3.6-moe-nvfp4 --trust-remote-code \
  --moe-backend flashinfer_b12x --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --pipeline-parallel-size 2 --tensor-parallel-size 1 \
  --max-model-len 131072 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 \
  --max-num-seqs 8 --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \
  --reasoning-parser qwen3 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8005
```
(`flashinfer_b12x` correctly selected in all runs — confirmed via log line `Using 'FLASHINFER_B12X' NvFp4 MoE backend`. Attention backend auto-selects `FLASHINFER`.)

## Symptom

```
$ curl .../v1/completions -d '{"prompt":"The capital of France is","max_tokens":12,"temperature":0}'
{"choices":[{"text":""}]}          # on broken builds: empty
```
or, via chat completions:
```
"content": "<|box_end|><|box_end|><|box_end|>...<|box_end|>"   # repeated to max_tokens
```
No errors, warnings, or NaNs are logged. The server reports healthy and serves requests normally (200 OK) — the failure is purely in generation quality.

## Bisection (9 daily nightly images, 2026-06-22 → 2026-07-01)

| Date | Version | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| 06-22 | dev245 (`9037498c2`) | GOOD |
| 06-27 | dev515 (`68ee8300a`) | GOOD |
| 06-29 | dev552 (`4559c43a9`) | **GOOD** |
| 06-30 | dev601 (`a16dbd5b8`) | **BAD** |
| 07-01 | dev672 (`93d8f834d`, current `:nightly`) | BAD |

This pins the regression to the 49 commits merged between `4559c43a9` and `a16dbd5b8`:
https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/compare/4559c43a9...a16dbd5b8

## What we ruled out

1. **Attention backend** — tested both `FLASHINFER` (auto-selected) and `FLASH_ATTN` (forced by removing `--kv-cache-dtype fp8`, which reopened the backend choice). Both produce garbage under sharding on the broken builds.
2. **KV cache dtype** — tested both `fp8` and default (fp16/bf16). Both broken under sharding on bad builds.
3. **torch.compile / cudagraphs** — tested with `--enforce-eager`. Still broken. Not a compile/capture issue.
4. **Split strategy** — both `--pipeline-parallel-size=2` and `--tensor-parallel-size=2` (with `--pipeline-parallel-size=1`) are equally broken on bad builds. A same-vintage FP8/INT4 MoE model on the same hardware shards correctly via PP=2, so multi-GPU sharding itself is not broken in general — this looks specific to the NVFP4/b12x path.
5. **flashinfer-python version** — the bundled bump `4708292d4` "Bump flashinfer version to 0.6.13" (#46683) is *inside* our 49-commit window, but (a) its diff only touches `requirements/`, `docker/`, a gsm8k test threshold, and `kernel_warmup.py` — no changes to `nvfp4.py` / `flashinfer_fp4_moe.py`; and (b) we directly tested: took the broken `dev672` image and force-downgraded `flashinfer-python` to `0.6.12` (the good build's version) in-place — **still broken**, identical signature. Ruled out.
6. **Mamba hybrid "align" prefix-cache mode** (`61ab70ec3`, #42406) — our own boot log shows this experimental feature activating (`Mamba cache mode is set to 'align' ... when prefix caching is enabled`), and it's in-window. We re-tested the broken `dev601` (06-30) image with `--enable-prefix-caching` removed entirely (confirmed via the absence of that log line) — **still broken**. Ruled out.
7. **A separate known bug class** — #45741/#45739 (uninitialized `torch.empty` swizzled NVFP4 scale buffer in `create_fp4_scale_tensor`, causing NVFP4 decode degeneration on B300/GB300) looked suspicious given the symptom similarity, but: the originating regression (#42988) merged 2026-05-21, well before our known-good dev552 (06-29), and the fix (#45739) merged same-day as the bad dev601 build (06-30) — its presence/absence doesn't track our good/bad boundary. We also confirmed by grep that `flashinfer_fp4_moe.py` / `fused_moe/oracle/nvfp4.py` (the b12x MoE path) never call `create_fp4_scale_tensor` at all. Unrelated code path — ruled out.

## Remaining suspects (not yet isolated to a single commit)

Within the 49-commit window, these touch code closest to our path and haven't been individually tested:
- `43916891b` — "[GDN] Improve kkt kernel of CuteDSL prefill backend" (#46346) — this model's linear-attention mechanism is GDN
- `bc8481af0` — "[MoE Refactor] Standardize Humming MoE experts + utilities" (#43373)
- `5051698e4` — "Remove unnecessary `load_weights` methods" (#44589) — MoE weight loading
- `debec6440` — "Add MiniMax-M3 modelopt nvfp4 support" (#46756) — touches `modelopt.py`, our exact `modelopt_mixed` quant path

We stopped at the day-level bisection since going further requires building vLLM from source per-commit (no daily image exists

items.title: [Bug]: Speculative decoding with a hybrid draft model (LFM2/LFM2.5 short_conv) fails — drafter requires all draft layers in one KV cache group
items.author: qtris123
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

Speculative decoding with a **classical (separate) draft model that is itself hybrid** — e.g. `LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M` (short_conv + attention) drafting for the hybrid target `LiquidAI/LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct` — fails to initialize. The drafter code path assumes **all draft layers live in a single KV cache group** (one `AttentionMetadata`). A hybrid draft model has both attention and `short_conv` (Mamba-style) layers, which must occupy **different** KV cache groups, so initialization aborts with:

```
AssertionError: All drafting layers should belong to the same kv cache group
```

The two open PRs that make LFM2/LFM2.5 spec-decode almost work — #44296 (short_conv spec-decode correctness) and #35062 (separate speculator layers into a dedicated KV cache group) — are **necessary but not sufficient**: #35062 was designed for EAGLE-style drafters whose layers are all one uniform (attention) spec, and it collapses all drafter layers into a *single* dedicated group. That is invalid for a hybrid draft.

### Environment

- vLLM `0.23.1rc1.dev1271+gb6ff8a2f5` (image `vllm/vllm-openai:nightly`, commit `b6ff8a2f5`)
- 1× H200 (also reproduces on a MiG 1g.18gb slice)
- With PRs #44296 and #35062 cherry-picked on top of `b6ff8a2f5` (without them it fails even earlier, in `get_kv_cache_groups` / short_conv metadata).

### Reproduction

```
vllm serve LiquidAI/LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct \
  --quantization fp8 --enable-prefix-caching --max-model-len 32768 \
  --speculative-config '{"model": "LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M", "num_speculative_tokens": 3}'
```

`method` auto-infers to `draft_model`. The draft `LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M` is a 16-layer hybrid (≈6 attention + 10 short_conv), same architecture family as the target.

### Failure chain (with PRs #44296 + #35062 applied)

The path goes `get_kv_cache_groups` → `_get_kv_cache_groups_uniform_page_size` → drafter `initialize_attn_backend` → `validate_same_kv_cache_group`. Three distinct walls, each caused by the same "drafter is EAGLE-style / uniform" assumption:

1. **Drafter layers not detected for a *separate* draft model.** `_identify_speculator_layers` (added by #35062) detects drafter layers via the EAGLE convention `layer_idx >= target_num_layers`, plus a `"drafter"/"eagle"` name fallback. A classical draft model is loaded with `prefix="draft_model"` (`vllm/v1/spec_decode/draft_model.py`), so its layers are named `draft_model.*` with **local 0-based indices** and match neither rule → they are never isolated → `validate_same_kv_cache_group` fails.

2. **After fixing detection**, `_get_kv_cache_groups_uniform_page_size` collapses *all* drafter layers into one dedicated group, then `create_kv_cache_group_specs` → `FullAttentionSpec.merge` asserts:
   ```
   AssertionError: All attention layers in the same KV cache group must be FullAttentionSpec.
   ```
   because the hybrid draft's short_conv layers are not `FullAttentionSpec`.

3. **After splitting the dedicated drafter group per spec type** (attention group + short_conv group), we get `Separated 16 speculator layers into 2 dedicated KV cache group(s)` and `create_kv_cache_group_specs` succeeds — but the drafter runtime then fails at:
   ```
   File "vllm/v1/spec_decode/llm_base_proposer.py", validate_same_kv_cache_group
   AssertionError: All drafting layers should belong to the same kv cache group
   ```
   because `_draft_attn_layer_names` (all draft `AttentionLayerBase` layers *with a KV spec* — which includes short_conv) now legitimately spans **two** groups.

### Root cause

`validate_same_kv_cache_group` documents the assumption directly:

> Need this assumption to ensure all drafting layers can use the same AttentionMetadata. **May extend to multiple AttentionMetadata in the future.**

And `initialize_attn_backend` records a **single** `self.kv_cache_gid` (the first group any draft layer belongs to) and applies that one group's `kv_cache_spec` to every draft layer. There is already partial multi-group scaffolding (`self.draft_attn_groups` is a list; `build_per_group_and_layer_attn_metadata` builds per-group + per-layer metadata), but group/spec **discovery** and the single `common_attn_metadata` block table are hard-wired to one group. A hybrid draft needs per-layer group/spec resolution and per-group attention metadata (distinct block tables for the attention group vs. the conv/Mamba group).

### Partial workarounds (advance past walls 1–2, not a full fix)

These two changes let init progress from wall 1 → wall 3, which localizes the remaining work:

- In `_identify_speculator_layers` (`vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_utils.py`), also detect classical draft layers by the `draft_model` name prefix:
  ```python
  if "draft_model" in name:
      speculator_layers.add(name)
      continue
  ```
- In `_get_kv_cache_groups_uniform_page_size`, create one dedicated drafter group **per KV spec type** instead of a single mixed group (so the hybrid draft's attention and short_conv layers land in separate, spec-uniform groups).

### What a complete fix needs

Extend the drafter (`llm_base_proposer.py`) to support drafter layers spanning multiple KV cache groups / multiple `AttentionMetadata` — i.e. the "may extend to multiple AttentionMetadata in the future" work:
- Resolve each draft layer's own group id / `kv_cache_spec` in `initialize_attn_backend` instead of a single `self.kv_cache_gid`.
- Build and route per-group `common_attn_metadata` (distinct block tables) in the drafter forward/`propose` path, alongside the existing `build_per_group_and_layer_attn_metadata`.
- Ensure short_conv/Mamba draft state is managed correctly across the multi-token drafting loop (complementary to #44296's target-side conv-state rollback).

Happy to help test — I have a runtime-overlay setup that reproduces this end-to-end on H200.

items.title: [Performance]: FlashInfer NVFP4 KV cache causal prefill is ~1.7-1.8x slower than FP8 on SM120
items.author: lemonade1997
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

On NVIDIA consumer Blackwell (SM120), FlashInfer attention with an NVFP4 KV cache shows a significant causal prefill regression compared with an FP8 KV cache.

In a matched profiler segment with the same 48 causal paged-prefill kernel calls, the NVFP4 path took about **145.8 ms**, while the FP8 path took about **84.0 ms**. This makes NVFP4 prefill approximately **1.74x slower** (about 1.7-1.8x across measurements).

The profiler indicates that the current SM120 path uses BF16 Q with packed NVFP4 KV:

```text
NVFP4:
BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheKernel<
  ...,
  __nv_bfloat16,      # Q
  __nv_fp4x2_e2m1,    # KV
  __nv_bfloat16,      # output
  ...
>

FP8:
BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheKernel<
  ...,
  __nv_bfloat16,      # Q
  __nv_fp8_e4m3,      # KV
  __nv_bfloat16,      # output
  ...
>
```

The regression appears to come from the existing SM120 NVFP4 software unpack/dequant path: packed FP4 KV values and their FP8 block scales must be unpacked, converted, and scaled before the BF16 QK/PV computation. Prefill is compute-heavy, so the KV bandwidth reduction does not compensate for this per-element conversion overhead.

### Environment

```text
GPU: NVIDIA RTX PRO 5000 Blackwell, compute capability 12.0 (SM120)
PyTorch: 2.10.0+cu129
CUDA: 12.9
FlashInfer: 0.6.15
Attention backend: FLASHINFER
KV cache layout: HND
Model dtype / Q dtype on this path: BF16
KV cache modes compared: nvfp4 and fp8_e4m3
```

The vLLM code includes the recently added NVFP4 KV cache path. The NVFP4 cache is represented as packed E2M1 data plus one FP8 block-scale value per 16 head-dimension elements.

### Kernel-level profile

A comparable trace segment was selected from each profile. Both segments contain exactly 48 causal prefill calls:

| Metric | NVFP4 KV | FP8 KV | NVFP4 / FP8 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Causal paged-prefill calls | 48 | 48 | 1.00x |
| Causal paged-prefill total | 145.81 ms | 84.03 ms | 1.74x |
| Mean per call | 3.04 ms | 1.75 ms | 1.74x |
| CUTLASS GEMM total in the same segment | 93.61 ms | 96.69 ms | 0.97x |
| All GPU kernels in the segment | 297.73 ms | 238.45 ms | 1.25x |

The similar CUTLASS GEMM time suggests that the model's weight/MoE kernels are not the primary source of this difference. Most of the additional GPU time is inside `BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheKernel`.

### Decode and KV append observations

The same profiles show that NVFP4 is beneficial for decode:

| Kernel | NVFP4 KV | FP8 KV |
|---|---:|---:|
| Single-token/decode paged attention | ~9.63 us/call | ~12.35 us/call |
| KV append/write | ~8.39 us/call | ~3.01 us/call |

NVFP4 decode is about 22% faster in this workload because decode is more bandwidth-bound. The NVFP4 append kernel is about 2.8x slower because it performs quantization, packing, block-scale generation, and slot mapping, but its cumulative cost is only around 7 ms and is not the end-to-end bottleneck.

### End-to-end capacity stress result

With 30 concurrent requests:

| KV dtype | Completed | Preemptions | Peak running | Peak cache | Wall time |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| NVFP4 | 30/30 | 0 | 30 | 68.6% | 102.3 s |
| FP8 | 30/30 | 6 | 24 | 97.6% | 65.4 s |

NVFP4 provides the expected capacity benefit and avoids preemption, but the causal-prefill regression dominates this particular workload.

### Expected behavior / proposal

On SM120, the packed NVFP4 KV representation matches the hardware block-scaled FP4 MMA layout well. An optimized path could:

1. quantize Q to per-16-block NVFP4 on the fly;
2. execute QK directly with SM120 block-scaled NVFP4 MMA;
3. avoid expanding K through the FP4 -> FP16/BF16 conversion chain before QK;
4. retain the existing dequantized P x V path where the V-scale axis does not match the MMA reduction axis.

This is similar to the A4Q approach demonstrated for SM120/SM121, where an opt-in FlashInfer kernel uses FP4 Q x FP4 K block-scaled MMA.

Would the vLLM maintainers be interested in tracking or integrating an optimized FlashInfer A4Q-style path for NVFP4 KV prefill on SM120? At minimum, it would be useful to document that the current NVFP4 KV path trades substantial prefill performance for capacity/decode benefits on this architecture.

### Additional notes

- The NVFP4 cache itself is correctly compact: packed FP4 data plus FP8 scales uses about 56.25% of FP8 KV storage, giving an expected capacity ratio of about 1.78x.
- The two profiler JSON files contain more than one non-contiguous capture interval, so the comparison above uses matched segments instead of comparing total trace file size or total event counts.
- Full profiler JSON files can be provided if useful.
- Related NVFP4 KV integration discussion: #49011 and #32220.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Searched existing and past issues for NVFP4/FP4 KV prefill performance and unpack/dequant regressions.

items.title: [Bug]: Qwen3.5 family never loads checkpoint KV-cache scales — fp8 KV silently runs at scale 1.0 even for calibrated checkpoints
items.author: erdholion
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

vLLM v0.27.1 (`vllm/vllm-openai:v0.27.1`), RTX 5090 (SM_120), driver 595.58.03, TP=1. Also verified by code inspection on current main (`ae5b8e4a8`): the gap is still present.

Model: Qwen3.8-27B (hybrid GDN), NVFP4 checkpoints, `--kv-cache-dtype fp8`, FLASHINFER backend, MTP `num_speculative_tokens=3`.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

**The Qwen3.5 model family never loads checkpoint KV-cache scales.** A checkpoint that ships calibrated `k_scale`/`v_scale` tensors (e.g. `unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4`, which carries 32 such tensors — one pair per full-attention layer — and declares `kv_cache_scheme: {dynamic: false, num_bits: 8, type: float}`) boots with:

```
WARNING [kv_cache.py:151] Using KV cache scaling factor 1.0 for fp8_e4m3. If this is unintended, verify that k/v_scale scaling factors are properly set in the checkpoint.
```

and serves fp8 KV at scale 1.0 anyway. The scales are silently dropped. That checkpoint has 2.4M downloads, so every vLLM user running it with `--kv-cache-dtype fp8` is silently uncalibrated.

**Root cause** (three independent absences):

1. `vllm/model_executor/models/qwen3_5.py` — all `load_weights` implementations use bare `AutoWeightsLoader`; unlike `gemma4.py`, `gpt_oss.py`, `hunyuan_v1.py` etc., none of them call `maybe_remap_kv_scale_name`.
2. `AutoWeightsLoader` itself never calls `maybe_remap_kv_scale_name` (nothing in `models/utils.py` references it).
3. The ModelOpt quant config (`modelopt.py`) has no KV-scale name handling either.

So checkpoint names like `model.language_model.layers.11.self_attn.k_scale` have no route to the runtime parameter `...self_attn.attn.k_scale`, even though `maybe_remap_kv_scale_name`'s default pattern (`\.([qkv])_scale$` → `.attn.\1_scale`) handles exactly this rename.

**Proof by contrast:** taking the same checkpoint and renaming the 32 scale tensors to the vLLM parameter path (`...self_attn.attn.k_scale`) makes them load — `VLLM_LOGGING_LEVEL=DEBUG` shows `Loaded weight layers.N.self_attn.attn.k_scale with shape torch.Size([])` for all 32, and behavior changes measurably (below). With the stock naming, the same DEBUG log shows no scale loads and no complaint.

**A diagnosis trap worth noting:** the `kv_cache.py:151` warning is `warning_once`, and when MTP speculative decoding is enabled, the draft model's attention layer legitimately has no scales — so the warning fires **even when all target layers load their scales correctly**. The boot log cannot distinguish success from failure here; only DEBUG-level weight-load lines can.

**Measured impact** (GSM8K, greedy, n=300/arm unless noted, identical flags/image/seed, MTP k=3 on in all arms):

| KV config | accuracy |
|---|---|
| fp8, scale 1.0 (stock behavior) | 92.3% (reproduced exactly twice, different boots/ctx) |
| fp8, calibrated scales loaded (renamed tensors) | 93.7% |
| bf16 KV (control) | 94.5% (pooled n=600) |

The calibrated scale values for this model are ~1.06–1.63 (two independently published calibrations agree to 3–4 decimals), i.e. K/V amax runs past e4m3's ±448 on every full-attention layer, so scale 1.0 clips outliers.

**Proposed fix:** route scale-suffixed weight names through `maybe_remap_kv_scale_name` in `Qwen3_5Model.load_weights` before handing the iterable to `AutoWeightsLoader`, mirroring the existing pattern in `gemma4.py`. Happy to send the PR (one small loop, no behavior change for checkpoints without scales).

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Feature] Add configurable hash-based subdirectories to fs_native
items.author: cage-goat
items.body_excerpt:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

The `fs_native` L2 adapter currently stores all KV cache objects directly
under `base_path`. As the cache grows, this can create a large flat directory
and degrade metadata operations on some filesystems.

Supporting configurable hash-based subdirectories would distribute cache files
across directories and allow users to choose a layout appropriate for their
filesystem and workload.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Add an optional `hash_subdir_levels` setting to the `fs_native` adapter:

- `0` (default): `<base_path>/<filename>`
- `1`: `<base_path>/<hash[0:2]>/<filename>`
- `2`: `<base_path>/<hash[0:2]>/<hash[2:4]>/<filename>`

The default value should remain `0` for backward compatibility. Changing the
value for an existing cache directory would require clearing itscontents.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
A boolean option similar to NIXL dynamic's `shard_dirs` was considered, but it
would only support flat and fixed two-level layout. An explicit level provides
more flexibility while keeping the behavior predictable.

**Additional context**
I plan to submit a PR to implement this feature.

items.title: [RFC] Support VMM Allocations in lmcache-driven
items.author: bluayer
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

Serving processes may outlive their GPU allocations. A long-lived inference engine may release most of its HBM so another colocated workload can use it. When its KV remains reusable, LMCache can retain the logical KV in CPU or storage tiers and later restore it into a replacement GPU allocation. Colocated RL is one use of this pattern. Multi-model serving is another: an inactive engine can return HBM for another model server and later resume.

Engine-driven resolves the active GPU allocation in the inference worker for each transfer. lmcache-driven instead relies on an LMCache server registration of that allocation. That registration must be retired before the physical memory can be safely reclaimed and replaced before transfers resume. LMCache has no common lifecycle contract for this transition today, so choosing a virtual memory management (VMM) allocator can make lmcache-driven unavailable.

This RFC keeps both transfer modes available when an inference engine uses VMM allocations. It defines an engine-independent lifecycle contract that coordinates allocation replacement with LMCache registration retirement and re-registration. `vmm_fd` is the "experimental" registration transport to apply this contract to exportable same-node VMM allocations. `framework_ipc` remains the default, and engine-driven is unchanged.

## Terminology

- **Inference engine:** the vLLM or SGLang serving runtime, including its control components and execution workers. It coordinates scheduling and allocation-lifecycle transitions.
- **Inference worker:** an execution-side process or rank within the inference engine. It runs model execution, creates and holds its local active GPU KV allocation, and hosts the LMCache worker adapter.
- **LMCache server:** the separate LMCache MP process that manages cache storage and server-side transfer work.
- **Engine-driven:** the inference worker performs the GPU-side gather or scatter and exchanges CPU or shared-memory data with the LMCache server.
- **lmcache-driven:** the inference worker submits transfer metadata and synchronization events, while the LMCache server performs the GPU-side transfer against registered device memory.

The transfer-mode names identify where GPU-side KV movement runs. They do not identify allocation ownership. In both modes, each inference worker creates and holds its local active GPU KV allocation, while the inference engine coordinates the allocation lifecycle.

## Motivation

### Preserve transfer choice across GPU-memory handoff

An inference engine may return most of its HBM without exiting. In colocated RL, rollout yields memory to training. In multi-model serving, an inactive engine can yield memory to another model server and later resume. If KV from the same model version remains useful, LMCache can keep it in CPU or storage tiers until a replacement GPU allocation is ready.

Public inference-engine support for these allocation lifecycles is clearest today in colocated RL:

- The [vLLM Q3 2026 RL roadmap](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48314) models transitions between sleeping and awake, paused and running, old and new weights, and stale and fresh KV. Its [scheduler lifecycle RFC](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48311) covers drain, sleep, wake, weight update, and releasing only KV between rollout steps.
- [SGLang's RL integration](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/docs/advanced_features/sglang_for_rl.md) exposes tagged release and resume operations for `kv_cache` and `weights`. Releasing `kv_cache` flushes its logical contents, so these operations define the engine-side memory lifecycle but do not preserve reusable KV outside the released allocation.

These interfaces define when the inference engine releases and restores an allocation. They do not define whether logical KV remains valid or where it is stored while the GPU allocation is absent. Engine-driven already works with these lifecycle interfaces because no imported engine allocation survives in the LMCache server. The remaining compatibility gap is lmcache-driven, whose cross-process registration must be retired before the inference worker releases the physical memory.

The lifecycle boundary may support broader reusable-KV policies in the future, but those policies are outside this RFC.

### VMM breaks the current direct-access registration

The current lmcache-driven registration format cannot represent arbitrary VMM allocations held by an inference worker.

VMM separates the virtual address from the lifetime of the physical memory:

```text
allocation lifetime #1: pointer X -> physical allocation A
release:                pointer X -> unmapped
allocation lifetime #2: pointer X -> physical allocation B
```

The pointer can remain `X`, but an IPC registration for allocation A must not be used for allocation B. Supporting only initial VMM import would therefore be unsafe; LMCache must also drain, retire, and replace registrations as part of the inference worker's allocation lifecycle.

### What this proposal changes

The required interface has two ordering points: retire the current registration before allocator mutation, then register the replacement before transfer resumes. It also needs a unique identity for each allocation lifetime so a reused virtual address cannot resolve stale work to new physical memory.

The contract is defined around allocation retirement and replacement. `vmm_fd` applies it to exportable same-node VMM allocations; `framework_ipc` remains the default and engine-driven is unchanged.

## Proposal

The proposal has two parts:

1. An engine-independent lifecycle contract for retiring and replacing an LMCache-visible GPU allocation.
2. `vmm_fd`, an experimental same-node transport for registering POSIX-FD-exportable VMM allocations under this lifecycle contract.

The lifecycle contract is transport-independent. `vmm_fd` uses POSIX FDs on Linux, but a future transport could use CUDA Fabric or another pla

items.title: [Perf][MP] Opt-in grpc.aio server for more gRPC headroom per RPC
items.author: theminjunchoi
items.body_excerpt:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

While looking at gRPC performance, I noticed that the gRPC request server levels off at around 1.8k small RPCs/s on my machine, and its p99 climbs quickly as load goes up. When I profiled it under load, about half of the time was spent inside grpcio's sync server code (`grpc/_server.py`), and almost none in the LMCache handlers themselves.

This doesn't hurt anyone today. A single vLLM instance sends a few hundred RPCs/s. But since #4877 plans to make gRPC the default transport, I thought it might be worth having more headroom per RPC before that happens.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

I'd like to propose an opt-in `--grpc-server-mode aio`, with the default staying `sync`. It would serve the same generated services and handlers on `grpc.aio`, with one event loop receiving the calls. The handlers would keep their current meaning:

- `SYNC` handlers still run one at a time.
- Normal `BLOCKING` handlers still run on up to `max_cpu_workers` threads.
- Affinity handlers still go through the same `AffinityThreadPool`, so each client stays on one worker.
- Each server stream is still read on its own thread, as in the sync server.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

- #5260 removes the extra executor hop for normal handlers on the sync server. It's a nice improvement, but each call would still go through grpcio's sync request path, which is where most of the time went in my profile. As far as I can tell the two don't conflict.
- A long-lived bidi stream per client could go further, but it would change the protocol, so it felt like something for later if it's ever needed.

**Additional context**

I understand the gRPC server was kept simple on purpose so it could be made correct first, which is why this only adds an option and leaves the default alone. I have a working version with tests and will open a PR with the numbers shortly. I'd really appreciate any thoughts on whether this direction makes sense.

items.title: [Feature Request] Discuss optional CLOCK-FIFO eviction for MP L1
items.author: WyattJia
items.body_excerpt:
### Is your feature request related to a problem?

I'd like to discuss whether an optional CLOCK-FIFO eviction policy for the MP L1 cache would be useful before preparing a PR.

The goal is to reduce hit-path metadata work under frequent hot-prefix reuse mixed with one-time scans. Recording a reference bit instead of moving an entry on every hit may help, but this is a hypothesis, not a demonstrated end-to-end improvement.

### Describe the solution you'd like

An opt-in FIFO/second-chance eviction policy behind the existing policy interface. The exact queue and aging rules would be documented and agreed on before implementation. Existing LRU/ARC options and defaults would remain unchanged.

Could maintainers advise on:

1. **Acceptance:** Would you consider this addition alongside LRU and ARC, or prefer improvements to the existing policies?
2. **Required comparisons:** Which workloads, metrics, and validation gates would you require? Proposed comparisons against LRU and ARC include:
   - Stable hot prefixes with cold scans, shifting hot sets, all-hot/all-cold cases, and concurrent mixed reads/writes.
   - Effective prefix/token and byte hit rates, hit-path CPU cost, eviction p95/p99 latency, metadata memory, and real-engine TTFT/throughput.
   - Correctness across reservation/admission, pinned or in-flight keys, deletion confirmation, and multiple L1 instances.
3. **Review ownership:** Who would be willing to review the design and a subsequent focused PR?

### Describe alternatives you've considered

Use the existing LRU or ARC policies, or optimize their metadata paths if they address the same bottleneck. CLOCK-FIFO would need to demonstrate a useful trade-off against both; lower hit-path cost alone would not establish an overall improvement.

### Additional context

This issue asks for direction and evaluation criteria, not approval of a completed implementation. It does not propose changes to L2 placement or Mooncake's global eviction.

cc @YaoJiayi @hlin99 @zhengfeihe, listed owners of the eviction policy paths.

items.title: Performance comparison for dense shared prefix + block-diagonal local mask: custom mask in BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper vs MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper
items.author: catnanami
items.body_excerpt: I am trying to evaluate the best way to implement an attention pattern with a dense shared/global prefix plus a local block-diagonal suffix. The mask pattern is shown below: I am considering two implementations: BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper with a custom mask MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper Questions: 1. For this pattern, is cascade attention expected to be faster than paged prefill with a custom mask? 2. Or is this pattern better handled by a custom kernel/backend? My use case is speculative decoding, where all verification tokens share the same prefix KV, but each local block should only attend to its own block.

comments.author: VectorPeak
comments.body:
For the mask in the image - a dense shared prefix on the left plus independent block-diagonal local regions on the right - `MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper` is usually the better fit than `BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper` with one large custom mask.

The reason is that the custom-mask prefill path does not really exploit this structure as well: it still treats the problem like one masked attention problem over the full layout, so the block-diagonal sparsity mostly becomes masking overhead. Cascade attention lets you model this as:

- shared/global prefix KV: attended by all verification tokens
- local suffix KV: split into independent blocks/requests
- final result: merge prefix-attention state with each local block’s attention state

For speculative decoding, this is exactly the kind of case where cascade can help, especially when the shared prefix is large and the local verification blocks are relatively small. Each local block can be represented as a separate batch item sharing the same prefix. If the local part also needs causal masking inside each block, use the normal causal/local mask for that per-block suffix attention.

items.title: Misc. bug: UI Bug. Сhat message box grows above the top of the window on the empty chat screen (regression in b10824)
items.author: alexkhvlg
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

llama-server build **b11022** (commit `f172be756`), WebUI embedded in the binary, Windows 11 x64, browser Chromium/Chrome at desktop width.




### Operating systems

Windows

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

Other (Please specify in the next section)

### Command line

```shell

```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

On the **empty / new chat screen** ("Hello there"), pasting a long multi-line text into the message box makes the whole composer (message box + its toolbar) slide up **above the top edge of the window**. The top border of the box is clipped, the greeting is pushed out of the window, and that part cannot be reached by scrolling: the page is not scrollable at all.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Start `llama-server` (router mode works too) and open the WebUI at desktop width, e.g. a 1280x720 window.
2. **In Settings set "Paste long text to file length" to 0.**
3. **In Settings check "Copy text attachments as plain text".**
4. Stay on the empty chat screen, i.e. the one showing "Hello there" / "Type a message or upload files to get started".
5. Paste a long multi-line text (about 8+ lines is enough; more lines do not make it worse).
6. The composer's top edge is now above the top of the viewport. Measured geometry with the textarea at its `--max-message-height` cap:   * composer wrapper: top = **-132 px**, bottom = 456 px (588 px tall)   * textarea: top = **-15 px** (its top border is cut off), internally scrolled to the caret
5. There is no way to scroll the hidden part back into view: `html`/`body` are pinned to 100dvh with `overflow: visible`, `document.scrollingElement.scrollHeight == clientHeight` (720/720), `window.scrollTo(0, 100)` leaves `scrollY = 0`, and no ancestor has `overflow: auto/scroll`. The composer is also not a scroll container.
Measured values (viewport 1280x720, only the textarea content changes):


| text in the box | textarea height | composer height | composer top |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 line | 48 px | 252 px | +204 px (fine) |
| 5 lines | 240 px | 444 px | +12 px (almost touching) |
| 6 lines | 288 px | 492 px | -36 px |
| 8 or more lines | 384 px (cap) | 588 px | **-132 px** |


At a 1280x900 window the same threshold moves one row down (8 lines -> top = -42 px, 40 lines -> -42 px).
### Root cause
The composer wrapper in `tools/ui/src/lib/components/app/chat/ChatScreen/ChatScreen.svelte` is anchored to the bottom of the chat screen (`mt-auto`, `md:sticky`, `md:bottom-4`) and, **only while the chat is empty**, it is additionally lifted with a fixed translate:
```svelte
isEmpty ? 'md:translate-y-[calc(-50dvh+8rem)] 2xl:translate-y-[calc(-50dvh+5rem)]' : ''
```
Because `translate` is never clamped, the box can be moved outside both its containing block and the viewport. The lift keeps the composer's **bottom** edge pinned at `50dvh + 6rem` (456 px at a 720 px tall window, 546 px at 900 px), while the box itself only grows upwards, so as soon as the composer is taller than that value the top goes off-screen. The var that caps the textarea, `--max-message-height = max(24rem, min(80dvh, calc(100dvh - var(--chat-form-area-height) - 12rem)))` (384 px at 720 px height), accounts for the 24rem form area but not for the extra `50dvh - 8rem` lift, so the composer reaches 588 px and overflows by 132 px.




### First Bad Commit

`0afb805b1` - "ui: Improve Chat Messages rendering performance (#28460)", 2026-09-06, merged into master as build **b10824** (build number = `git rev-list --count HEAD`). The same patch also exists on the PR branch as `3d1da290f` "ui : smooth the chat navigation animations" (`origin/allozaur/ui/chat-perf`); `0afb805b1` is the squash of that PR, which is why the string shows up twice in `git log -S`.
```diff
- 'pointer-events-none md:sticky fixed  mt-auto transition-all duration-200',
+ 'pointer-events-none md:sticky fixed  mt-auto transition-transform duration-200',
...
- isEmpty ? 'md:bottom-[calc(50dvh-7rem)] 2xl:bottom-[calc(50dvh-4rem)]' : 'md:bottom-4'
+ 'md:bottom-4',
+ isEmpty ? 'md:translate-y-[calc(-50dvh+8rem)] 2xl:translate-y-[calc(-50dvh+5rem)]' : ''
```
Before that commit the empty-screen centering used a `bottom` offset on the same sticky element. Sticky offsets are clamped by the containing block, so an over-tall composer stopped at the top edge of the container instead of being pushed out of the window. I verified this by re-applying the old rule (`position: sticky` + `bottom: calc(50dvh - 7rem)`) through Custom CSS in the current build: with 40 lines of text the composer clamps to top = 0 (0...588) and the message box stays fully visible (117...501). The commit's own comment explains the motive for the change: animating the centered -> bottomed move with `transform` instead of a layout property keeps it on the compositor and avoids stutter while a long conversation loads.
### Suggested fix
Keep the transform animation, restore the clamp that `sticky` used to provide - clamp the lift by the element's own height:
```svelte
isEmpty
  ? 'md:translate-y-[max(calc(-50dvh+8rem),calc(100%-100dvh+2rem))] 2xl:translate-y-[max(calc(-50dvh+5rem),calc(100%-100dvh+2rem))]'
  : ''
```
Percentages in `translate` resolve against the element's own size, so `calc(100% - 100dvh + 2rem)` is exactly the lift at which the top of the composer would reach `y = 0` (`688px = 100dvh - 2rem` is the bottom anchor), and `max()` keeps the original centered position while there is enough room. Note that `translate` is a shorthand for `<x> <y>`, so a single value would move the box horizontally - the two-value form (or Tailwind's `translate-y-*`, which sets `--tw-translate-y`) must be used.
Verified in the browser through Settings -> Developer -> Custom CSS (`translate: 0 max(calc(-50dvh + 8rem), calc(100% - 100dvh + 2rem)) !important`):
| text in the box | composer top/bottom with the fix |
|---|---|
| 1 line | 204 ... 456 (same look as the current design intent) |
| 5 lines | 12 ... 456 |
| 8 and 40 lines

items.title: [Bug]: [Store] L4 (LOCAL_DISK offload) can serve another object's bytes: offload reports are matched by key alone
items.author: Juhyun-Kim-Memphis
items.body_excerpt:
### Bug Report

#### Summary

With SSD offload enabled (`enable_offload`, `FileStorage` with a bucket backend), a `Get` that is served from a LOCAL_DISK replica can return the bytes of a different object than the one currently stored under the key. No master restart is needed: it happens under ordinary remove / re-put churn. A master restart (or a store re-registering its disk tier for any other reason) makes it much more frequent.

All three root causes below have the same shape: the master registers a LOCAL_DISK replica from a report that does not say which offload it is the report of. `NotifyOffloadSuccess` carries only `(tenant, key, size)`, so the master matches it against whatever offload task the key has *now*, or, when the key has no task, creates the object or attaches the replica anyway.

#### Environment

- Unit tests: Mooncake `main` `1d97a1df`, Linux x86_64, gcc 13.3, Release, `-DBUILD_UNIT_TESTS=ON -DUSE_CUDA=OFF -DUSE_ETCD=OFF`.
- Load test numbers below: `main` as of `245e7106` with an unrelated change to the master's restart path. The offload report handling involved behaves the same on current `main` (#4562 moved the offload task onto the object record without changing how reports are matched).

#### Observed

Load test: one standalone `mooncake_master`, four CPU-only stores with L4 on a bucket backend, TCP, a churn load (put / get / remove / re-put of the same keys with the same sizes) whose reader checks every byte against an oracle, and a static key set larger than memory so that eviction and offload run all the time.

| phase | wrong reads |
| -- | -- |
| no restart (control) | about 2 per 1M gets |
| after a master restart in which every store re-registers its files | 33,209 in the first minutes |

Every wrong read was traced back (per-key history rebuilt from the load's seeded draws) to one of the three causes below; none was left unexplained.

#### Root causes

1. **A late offload completion brings a removed key back, or completes the task of a newer object.** A store takes an offload item (`OffloadObjectHeartbeat`), copies the bytes and reports `NotifyOffloadSuccess`. If the key was removed while the store was copying, the report arrives for a key without an object: `NotifyOffloadSuccess` falls through to `AddReplicaForRetainedClient`, which *creates* the object from the disk replica. The removed key is readable again with its old bytes, and the next `Put` of the key fails as already existing. If the key was re-put in the meantime, the new object has its own offload task and the late report is accepted as that task's completion: reads of the new object that fall back to L4 get the old object's bytes.

2. **A store's rescan re-registers old files.** On start, and after the master answers `SEGMENT_NOT_FOUND` (master restart, client expiry), the store calls `ScanMeta` and reports every file it holds through `NotifyOffloadSuccess`. `Remove` never deletes the store's file, so such a file can hold the bytes of a removed key or of an earlier object of the key. The master creates the removed keys again and attaches the old files to the current objects (and to their offload tasks when they have one). This is the dominant cause after a restart.

3. **The copy source can change during the copy.** The store copies from the first readable memory replica of the key in its own segments, looked up when the bucket is built; nothing keeps that replica alive while the bucket is written. If the key is removed (or the replica evicted) during the copy, the buffer can be freed and reused by another object before the bytes are read, and the file holds that object's bytes. The report is then registered through (1).

Promotion-on-hit has the same weakness: promotion calls are matched by key, so a late `Success` can publish a staged buffer that a newer promotion of the key is still writing into, and a late `Failure` can free it.

#### Reproduction on main

Unit tests that fail on `main` (`1d97a1df`) with only the test files changed (test-only patch, no production change):

- `MasterServiceSSDTest.LateCompletionDoesNotRecreateARemovedKey` (cause 1): put, the store drains the offload item, `Remove(force)`, then the completion arrives. On main the key exists again and a new `PutStart` of it fails.
- `MasterServiceSSDTest.ReRegistrationNeverRegistersADiskReplica` (cause 2): two keys are offloaded and removed, one is re-put with new bytes of the same size, then the store's rescan entries for both files arrive. On main the re-put object gets the old file as a LOCAL_DISK replica and the removed key is recreated.
- `FileStorageTest.OffloadWhoseSourceChangesDuringTheCopyIsNotRegistered` (cause 3, through the real `FileStorage` offload path and an in-process master): the key is removed and re-put (same size, other bytes) after the bucket is written and before it is reported. On main the new object gets a LOCAL_DISK replica that holds the old object's bytes.

```
master_service_ssd_test.cpp: Failure  (removed key exists again; PutStart refused)
[  FAILED  ] MasterServiceSSDTest.LateCompletionDoesNotRecreateARemovedKey
master_service_ssd_test.cpp: Failure  (re-put object has 2 replicas, expected 1)
[  FAILED  ] MasterServiceSSDTest.ReRegistrationNeverRegistersADiskReplica
file_storage_test.cpp: Failure        (new object has 1 LOCAL_DISK replica, expected 0)
[  FAILED  ] FileStorageTest.OffloadWhoseSourceChangesDuringTheCopyIsNotRegistered
```

All three pass with the fix.

#### Related issues

- #4487 reports the stale-rescan half of cause 2 (a re-put object can get the old file on rescan) and proposes carrying an object incarnation through the offload task. The fix below covers that half and the late completion / NACK cases listed there. It does not fix the other half of #4487 (a re-put key is never offloaded again while the backend still holds the old entry).
- #4479: the fix narrows what `NotifyOffloadSuccess` accepts (only the completion of a task the reporting client took, echoing that task's i

items.title: [Store] Offload completion can attach a stale LOCAL_DISK replica to a republished key
items.author: Aionw
items.body_excerpt:
An offload completion is matched to the key, not to the publication it was queued for. The offload task carries tenant, key and size; the completion carries where it wrote. The master's only link between them is `state.offloading_task`.

`EraseMetadata` clears that marker, but a store worker that has already drained the task keeps writing its SSD copy. If the key is erased and republished before the completion arrives, the completion finds no marker. `handled_existing_object` stays false, and the completion falls through to `AddReplicaForRetainedClient`, which attaches the LOCAL_DISK replica to whatever publication the key holds now. Nothing compares the object's size or content.

A plain `Remove` is enough to trigger it: the lease is already expired after `PutEnd`, and `Remove` does not check for an offload task. (`UpsertStart`, by contrast, refuses while a worker owns the task.)

Possible fixes:
- have the offload task carry a publication identity and the completion echo it back (a wire change), or
- have every erase path refuse, or leave a tombstone, while a worker owns the offload task.

Pre-existing on main. Found by @CAICAIIs in review of #4717.

items.title: [RFC]: Add an opt-in T-One RDMA performance regression gate
items.author: stmatengss
items.body_excerpt:
## Changes proposed

Extend the performance gate in #4639 with an opt-in T-One RDMA suite. GitHub-hosted runners do not provide a guaranteed RDMA hardware pair; Mooncake already uses T-One for eRDMA integration tests, but those tests do not compare native Transfer Engine performance against the PR base.

The implementation uses a fixed, exclusive two-host pair and the existing `tebench` JSONL output. Its initial workload is TENT DRAM read/write: 4 KiB batch-1 P99 latency and 1 MiB batch-16 throughput. GPU Direct, Store RPC, and serving benchmarks remain outside this scope.

### Execution and comparison

- The GitHub controller runs the reviewed base harness, submits full baseline/candidate/harness SHAs, and retrieves a machine-readable result envelope from T-One. Candidate code is built and executed only on the isolated pair.
- A dedicated `mooncake-rdma-perf` tone-cli functional suite reports Pass/Fail while retaining the performance data. Its installable adapter and example configuration live alongside the Mooncake harness so the contract can be reviewed in one PR; deployment into tone-cli/T-One is a separate operator step.
- Both hosts build both revisions in Release mode against the same frozen benchmark source and their provisioned RDMA userspace libraries. This avoids relying on `tebench` being packaged in a wheel. A small TENT-only `--dram_numa_node` benchmark option makes the DRAM placement explicit.
- An integrity smoke precedes measurement. Five paired repetitions alternate A/B and B/A; each measured invocation uses tebench's built-in warmup. Initial limits are 5% throughput loss and 10% P99 growth, with relative MAD rejecting unstable samples.
- GitHub independently verifies run/revision/policy/benchmark identity and recomputes the verdict. It publishes the comparison table, error annotations, and artifacts even on failure. Exit 0 is pass, 1 regression, and 2 invalid/incomplete/unstable execution. Completed jobs, missing reports, or stale successful reports cannot count as a pass.
- Per-host leases, owned-process cleanup, per-command/target watchdogs, and T-One stop requests bound overlapping or cancelled work.

### Rollout and validation boundary

Automatic PR execution stays off until the T-One template, fixed host/NIC/GID/NUMA configuration, matching dependencies, and reachable HTTPS result origin are commissioned. Use manual same-SHA A/A comparisons before selecting thresholds or making `RDMA Performance Gate` required. RXE/SIW, CPU fixtures, and a successful compile do not establish hardware RDMA performance. Fork PRs lack secrets and fail closed when the gate is enabled; reviewed manual comparisons do not automatically publish a required check on the fork PR.

Local validation covers the comparator, protocol fixtures, an injected 6% regression, stale/invalid provenance, missing results, timeouts, cancellation, exclusive leases, process cleanup, and template parsing. Actual T-One deployment and real-hardware A/A calibration remain pending; no new RDMA performance measurements are claimed.

### Existing work

This extends #4639's CPU gate and reuses the current native benchmark. Searches found no open PR implementing this T-One regression gate. #2607 concerns MoE/EP incast workloads; the open RDMA scheduling/feedback PRs change transport behavior rather than this CI integration.

## Before submitting a new issue

- [x] Searched relevant issues/PRs and read the contribution and existing T-One framework documentation.

AI assistance: Codex prepared the implementation and this RFC. Human review of the changed lines and infrastructure commissioning are still required.

items.title: RFC: Plugin Extension Points Needed for MetaX GPU Support
items.author: yangxin-mx
items.body_excerpt:
# Proposal: Generalize SGLang Hardware Plugin Interfaces for MetaX GPU Support

> Discussion draft based on a SGLang 0.5.19-derived codebase. The names below are proposed API shapes, not claims that they already exist on the latest `main` branch. If an equivalent upstream seam already exists, we would prefer to use or extend it. This is an umbrella discussion that can be split into smaller PRs.

SGLang already has useful foundations: hardware-platform entry points, `SRTPlatform.init_backend()`, an explicit OOT forward registry for fused ops, and MoE runner/fused-function registration. See the [plugin documentation](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/docs/docs/hardware-platforms/plugin.mdx) and [expert-parallelism documentation](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/docs/docs/advanced_features/expert_parallelism.mdx). When adapting another CUDA-compatible GPU, however, we still encounter framework call sites that select a built-in class, import a vendor implementation, or call a kernel through a module-level symbol before a platform plugin can participate.

Our goal is to make required hardware behavior expressible through platform methods and explicit, typed registries. We do **not** propose replacing module globals or monkey-patching framework functions. A missing optional platform implementation should preserve the current built-in behavior; a selected but unsupported implementation should fail with a clear capability error rather than silently run an incompatible kernel. The plugin owns its vendor kernels and package dependencies. The framework owns common algorithms, selection rules, lifecycle, and validation.

The Python snippets below illustrate **proposed interfaces and call sites, not complete, runnable code already present in the repository**. `ExampleGpuPlatform` and `vendor_ops` stand for any vendor plugin. Exact parameters should be settled against existing types and call paths in the corresponding PRs. Each section shows both where the framework would connect the extension point and how a plugin would use it.

## 1. JIT toolchain and cache identity

### Adaptation problem

In the 0.5.19-derived tree, JIT compilation derives the device compiler, architecture and flags through CUDA/ROCm-oriented paths in `kernels/jit/utils/compile/toolchain.py`. The build path (`ninja.py`) and cache path (`cache.py`) must agree on these values. A plugin cannot safely supply a different device compiler by changing only one path: the cache may reuse a binary built for another SDK or architecture.

### Plugin-oriented proposal

- Add an optional `SRTPlatform.get_jit_toolchain() -> JitToolchainSpec | None`. The immutable spec should include the host/device compilers, toolkit root, target architecture, include/link paths and flags, plus an explicit SDK/ABI cache identity.
- Resolve the spec lazily when compilation starts, and pass the **same resolved spec** to command generation and cache-key generation. `None` keeps the existing built-in toolchain logic.
- Let the vendor plugin package its AOT extensions itself. The common AOT setup need not import or name each vendor SDK.

On the framework side, add the optional method in `srt/platforms/interface.py` and have `kernels/jit/utils/compile/{toolchain,ninja,cache}.py` consume the same spec:

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class JitToolchainSpec:
    host_compiler: str
    device_compiler: str
    toolkit_root: str
    target_arch: str
    device_flags: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    include_dirs: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    link_flags: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    cache_identity: str = ""  # SDK/ABI version

class SRTPlatform(DeviceMixin):
    def get_jit_toolchain(self) -> JitToolchainSpec | None:
        return None

def compile_extension(source, **kwargs):
    spec = resolve_jit_toolchain(get_platform().get_jit_toolchain())
    cache_key = make_cache_key(source, spec=spec, **kwargs)
    return build_with_ninja(source, spec=spec, cache_key=cache_key, **kwargs)
```

The plugin only describes its own SDK; it does not modify global `CUDA_HOME` or framework compiler symbols:

```python
class ExampleGpuPlatform(SRTPlatform):
    def get_jit_toolchain(self) -> JitToolchainSpec:
        return JitToolchainSpec(
            host_compiler="/opt/example/bin/c++",
            device_compiler="/opt/example/bin/device-cc",
            toolkit_root="/opt/example",
            target_arch="example-arch",
            cache_identity="example-sdk-1:abi-1",
        )
```

## 2. Device properties and per-operator Triton tuning

### Adaptation problem

Several launch paths infer hardware behavior from CUDA properties or NVIDIA/AMD architecture names, while `num_stages`, warps, tile sizes and shared-memory limits are selected locally. A plugin may expose a CUDA-compatible device but still need different launch parameters; pretending to be a particular SM is not a sound capability contract.

### Plugin-oriented proposal

- Expose a read-only `DeviceKernelProfile` through the active platform, with architecture identifier, warp size, maximum shared-memory bytes and relevant device capabilities.
- Add an optional `tune_triton_launch(op, shape, dtype, default) -> TritonLaunchConfig`. Each caller first computes its present default, then asks the active platform for a per-operator override and validates it before launch. There should be no global change to Triton's defaults.
- Start with launch sites where hardware differences actually affect correctness or feasibility (MoE, quantization and attention), keeping other paths unchanged.

The framework could define device facts in `srt/platforms/device_mixin.py`/`interface.py` and consume the policy immediately before each Triton launch, keeping hardware facts separate from per-operator tuning:

```python

    arch: str
    warp_size: int
    max_shared_memory_bytes: int

@dataclass(frozen=

items.title: [Feature] Support pending external linker lookup at native prefill admission
items.author: feichai0017
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation

`UnifiedCacheLinker.lookup(rid, transfers)` currently returns a list of restorable boundaries. It cannot distinguish a query that is still pending from a completed miss. An asynchronous external cache must block the scheduler or add a private prefill-admission Hook to avoid immediately recomputing a pending hit.

Could the native linker contract represent pending and carry that state through prefix matching to prefill admission? Ready requests should continue while a pending request remains queued. Rank-local readiness should use the same reduction as sparse hit boundaries, so a ready rank cannot admit while a peer still waits.

### Proposed scope

- Allow `None` for pending and keep `[]` as a completed miss.
- Carry the current match state into `PrefillAdder.add_one_req` before budgets, locks or destination loads.
- Expose lookup-only cancellation for abort and superseded/session/HBM matches; retain existing accepted-load ownership and drain.
- Count only actually admitted requests in the native LoRA batch set, so a deferred lookup cannot occupy an adapter slot.
- Keep synchronous backends unchanged. Async backends own bounded waiting, input validation and stale-completion retirement.

A candidate implementation passes actual source CPU admission/linker/lifecycle tests. GPU, real rank collectives, cancellation during DMA and released-engine adoption still need separate validation. This proposal is independent of worker pre-graph preparation in #44856.

items.title: KernelLens: Deploying Triton Kernels to C++ Inference Engines (TensorRT & ONNX)
items.author: Just1truc
items.body_excerpt:
# Deploying OpenAI Triton Kernels to C++ Inference Runtimes (ONNX Runtime & TensorRT) with KernelLens

Hey Triton Community!

If you write custom `@triton.jit` kernels in Python for LLM operators (FlashAttention, Fused RMSNorm, SwiGLU, Selective Scans), you’ve probably hit the deployment bottleneck: How do you run your Python Triton kernels inside production C++ inference engines like NVIDIA TensorRT or Microsoft ONNX Runtime?

Traditionally, developers had two frustrating choices:
1. **Stay in Python PyTorch Eager/Dynamo**: Forfeiting TensorRT/ORT global graph optimizations across standard model layers.
2. **Manual C++/CUDA Rewrites**: Throw away Python Triton code and manually rewrite kernels in CUDA C++ (`__global__`) while authoring hundreds of lines of `OrtCustomOp` / `nvinfer1::IPluginV2DynamicExt` boilerplate.

To solve this, we created [**KernelLens**](https://github.com/Just1truc/kernel_lens), an open-source compiler framework from [Galiad Research](https://galiad-research.com) that automatically compiles PyTorch models containing Python `@triton.jit` kernels into native C++ plugins for ONNX Runtime and TensorRT in **1 line of Python**.

---

## Step-by-Step Guide to Run the Working Example

Follow these 3 simple steps to test KernelLens on any CUDA-enabled GPU machine:

### Step 1: Install Dependencies
```bash
pip install torch triton kernel-lens
```

### Step 2: Save the Python Script (`example.py`)
Save the following code into a file named `example.py`:

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import triton
import triton.language as tl
import kernel_lens as kl

# 1. Define a standard OpenAI Triton Kernel
@triton.jit
def add_kernel(x_ptr, y_ptr, out_ptr, n_elements, BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(axis=0)
    block_start = pid * BLOCK_SIZE
    offsets = block_start + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
    mask = offsets < n_elements
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask)
    y = tl.load(y_ptr + offsets, mask=mask)
    output = x + y
    tl.store(out_ptr + offsets, output, mask=mask)

# 2. Wrap the Triton Kernel inside a PyTorch Module
class VectorAddModule(nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor, y: torch.Tensor):
        out = torch.empty_like(x)
        n_elements = x.numel()
        grid = lambda meta: (triton.cdiv(n_elements, meta['BLOCK_SIZE']),)
        add_kernel[grid](<x, y, out, n_elements, BLOCK_SIZE=1024>)
        return out

if __name__ == '__main__':
    device = 'cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu'
    x = torch.randn(4096, device=device, dtype=torch.float32)
    y = torch.randn(4096, device=device, dtype=torch.float32)
    model = VectorAddModule().to(device)

    print("Compiling PyTorch + Triton Model with KernelLens...")
    
    # 3. Compile Model to C++ Plugins in 1 Line
    compiled_model = kl.compile(
        model, 
        (x, y), 
        name="simple_vector_add", 
        backends=["onnx", "tensorrt"]
    )
    
    print("Executing Zero-Copy Inference in ONNX Runtime...")
    ort_output = compiled_model.run((x, y), backend="onnx")
    
    print("Executing Zero-Copy Inference in TensorRT...")
    trt_output = compiled_model.run((x, y), backend="tensorrt")

    # 4. Verify Numerical Parity against PyTorch Result
    torch_expected = x + y
    max_diff_ort = (ort_output - torch_expected).abs().max().item()
    max_diff_trt = (trt_output - torch_expected).abs().max().item()

    print("Verification Complete!")
    print(f"ORT Max Floating-Point Difference: {max_diff_ort:.6e}")
    print(f"TRT Max Floating-Point Difference: {max_diff_trt:.6e}")
    print(f"Exact Numerical Match (ORT): {torch.allclose(ort_output, torch_expected)}")
    print(f"Exact Numerical Match (TRT): {torch.allclose(trt_output, torch_expected)}")
```

### Step 3: Execute the Test
```bash
python3 example.py
```

### Expected Terminal Output
```text
Compiling PyTorch + Triton Model with KernelLens...
Executing Zero-Copy Inference in ONNX Runtime...
Executing Zero-Copy Inference in TensorRT...
Verification Complete!
ORT Max Floating-Point Difference: 0.000000e+00
TRT Max Floating-Point Difference: 0.000000e+00
Exact Numerical Match (ORT): True
Exact Numerical Match (TRT): True
```

---

## How it Works Under the Hood 🛠️

1. **PTX & Metadata Extraction**: KernelLens intercepts `@triton.jit` launches, extracting compiled PTX assembly strings, dynamic shared memory bytes, and parameter bitwidths directly from Triton’s compiler cache.
2. **SymPy Grid Transpilation**: Triton grid functions (e.g., `grid = lambda META: (triton.cdiv(M, BLOCK_SIZE),)`) are parsed via AST inspection into pure C++ integer arithmetic, evaluated dynamically at inference time with $< 0.5 \ \mu\text{s}$ CPU overhead.
3. **C++/CUDA Plugin Synthesis**: Synthesizes production-ready C++ source files implementing `Ort::CustomOp` and `nvinfer1::IPluginV2DynamicExt`, executing the PTX assembly via CUDA Driver API (`cuModuleLoadData` & `cuLaunchKernel`).
4. **Zero-Copy VRAM Binding**: Directly maps PyTorch VRAM pointers (`data_ptr()`) to ONNX Runtime `IOBinding` and TensorRT `setTensorAddress()`.
5. **Hardware Hardening**: Automatically injects dynamic 16-byte address checks to prevent misaligned vector load crashes (`ld.global.v4.b32`), and applies PTX ISA version clamping (`.version 9.0`) for NVIDIA Blackwell (`sm_120a`) GPU driver compatibility.

---

## Benchmarks & Numerical Parity

Across LLaMA 3, Mistral, Qwen 2.5, and Liger-Kernel operators, KernelLens achieves **$3.4\times$ to $7.0\times$ speedups** over eager PyTorch execution while maintaining exact floating-point numerical parity ($\text{MaxDiff} = 0.00\text{e}+00$).

---

## Links & Resources

* 💻 **GitHub**: [Just1truc/kernel_lens](https://github.com/Just1truc/kernel_lens)
* 📦 **PyPI**: `pip install kernel-lens`
* 📄 **Technical Report (DOI)**: [10.5281/zenodo.23194523](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo

items.title: [RFC]: Support ViT Full CUDA Graph (Tracker)
items.author: shen-shanshan
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation.

Multimodal large language models (e.g., Qwen3-VL, Qwen3.5, GLM-V, Kimi K2.5) rely on a Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder to process visual inputs before feeding them into the language model backbone. In production serving scenarios, the ViT forward pass involves launching a large number of small CUDA kernels — including patch embedding, layer normalization, multi-head self-attention, and MLP projections — each of which incurs non-trivial kernel launch overhead on the host side.

Currently, vLLM supports CUDA graph capture for the decoder (LLM) portion of the model, which has proven effective at reducing kernel launch costs and improving throughput. However, the ViT encoder is still executed eagerly, meaning every forward pass re-launches all kernels from scratch. Extending full CUDA graph support to the ViT encoder would allow the entire encoder forward pass to be captured and replayed as a single graph, eliminating per-kernel launch overhead and enabling more consistent, low-latency inference for multimodal models.

### Proposed Change.

items.title: [Feature] Support box and ground decision primitives with GUI-Actor pointer-head models
items.author: ningyx25
items.body_excerpt:
# [Feature] Support `box` and `ground` decision primitives with GUI-Actor pointer-head models

## Motivation

The structured decisions API (`/v1/systemone`) answers questions about a state by
scoring a fixed set of options: `choice`, `noul`, `score`. That covers
classification and routing, but not what is often the next question about the
same input — **where** something is in an attached image.

GUI grounding models answer exactly that, and they do not do it by generating
text: a pointer head scores the image's visual patches against a query hidden
state and the answer is read off that distribution. There is no way to express
such a question through the current API, and no vLLM architecture serves these
checkpoints.

## Proposed API

Two new question types on `/v1/systemone`, matching the "System One" contract
(the reference serving layer's request shape):

```jsonc
{
  "state": "a screenshot of a checkout page",
  "images": ["https://example.com/shot.png"],
  "questions": {
    "pay":  {"type": "box",    "instructions": "the Pay button"},
    "cart": {"type": "ground", "instructions": "the cart icon"}
  }
}
```

| type | criteria | answer |
|---|---|---|
| `box` | `null`; the question needs one image | `box` (`left`, `right`, `top`, `bottom` as fractions of the image), `confidence` |
| `ground` | `null`; the question needs one image | `point` (`[x, y]` in 0–999), `confidence`, `topk_points` |

Neither carries `probabilities` — a spatial answer is a region, not a
distribution over options. `confidence` is the probability mass the predicted
region holds.

## Design notes worth reviewing

- **Pooler output is the raw patch distribution**, not a softmax. The decode
  applies the checkpoint's fitted temperature to the confidence afterwards, and
  a second softmax over an already-normalised row would move the geometry.
- **Chunked prefill and prefix caching must be off** for such a model: the
  answer is read from the image patches of the prompt's own prefill.
- **The model is identified by its weights** (`multi_patch_pointer_head.`
  tensors), not by a config field — a config can claim the pointer token ids
  without a trained head.
- **A question type a model cannot answer returns 501**, not 400, since a
  different model would accept the same request.

## Scope

- Serving `microsoft/GUI-Actor-{3B,7B}-Qwen2.5-VL` (Qwen2.5-VL backbones).
  Qwen3-VL / Qwen3.5 would be follow-ups.
- `/v1/decisions` keeps OpenAI's schema and does not gain these types.

## Implementation

Opening this issue to get a design read on the API surface before submitting an
implementation — in particular whether `box` / `ground` should be first-class question types
alongside `choice` / `noul` / `score`, and whether the reference-compatible
answer shape (edges as fractions, points as 0–999 integers) is the right one for
vLLM rather than, say, pixel coordinates.
