items.title: What is the first practical limit of persistent KV across Agent steps?
items.author: RyanX0198
items.body_excerpt:
Hi maintainers — I’m Rui from Psync.labs. Recent sampling and decode-interface work led me to a question about long-running local Agent workloads.

Persistent KV could reduce repeated prefill, but only if cache identity, layout, eviction and framework boundaries stay correct as models, adapters and stages change. Which condition is most likely to invalidate the idea in practice: layout incompatibility, model or tokenizer changes, fragmentation, eviction quality loss, scheduler interference, or missing cross-framework contracts?

One counterexample or minimum test would be especially useful. @yzh119

— Rui, Psync.labs

comments.author: eprogressing
comments.body:
For an agent that changes adapters or rewrites its prompt between steps, I would check **cache identity/correctness before fragmentation or scheduling**. That is a conditional priority, not a measured ranking of workloads.

A concrete counterexample is switching from adapter A to adapter B while retaining A's KV. If B changes the value projection (or earlier hidden states), identical token IDs and identical tensor shapes do not make those cached values valid for B. Similarly, editing earlier tool results breaks reuse past the unchanged token prefix in an ordinary causal transformer. Rendering the same conversation differently can also change that prefix.

I would start with this small integration test:

1. Under A, prefill a short token prefix P, then process suffix S using the cached prefix. Compare the next-token logits with a fresh A forward pass on P+S, within an appropriate numerical tolerance.
2. Use a distinct, nonzero B adapter that affects `v_proj`. Repeat with a fresh B prefill as the reference. Your cache manager should reject A's cache; forcibly reusing it is the negative control, which can expose a discrepancy.
3. Edit one early token in P and verify that cache lookup stops at the unchanged prefix. Check logits, rather than just generated text: argmax can hide a difference.

This is consistent with [vLLM's prefix-cache design](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/design/prefix_caching/), which keys blocks using the parent hash, block tokens and extra hashes such as LoRA IDs. Adapter IDs also need versioning/invalidation if their weights can change in place.

After that, check the storage contract separately: [FlashInfer's KV layout documentation](https://docs.flashinfer.ai/tutorials/kv_layout.html) specifies NHD/HND layouts and page metadata. Matching semantics alone does not make a buffer portable between frameworks.

Prepared with Codex assistance from the linked documentation. The integration test above was initially a proposal; the execution update below now supplies an actual mechanism test. Is your agent retaining one model/adapter with append-only history, or switching adapters and rewriting history?


---
**GPU experiment update (2026-10-11):** I ran the actual Transformers/PEFT forward path on an A100-SXM4-40GB, plus CPU controls: Torch 2.14.1+cu130, Transformers 5.19.0, PEFT 0.21.2. This is a random three-layer Llama (hidden 64, four attention heads/two KV heads), with rank-four v_proj LoRA; it does not exercise FlashInfer's attention kernel or a production agent cache manager.

Across seeds 0/1/2, CPU/CUDA and float32/float64, all 72 comparison expectations held. Correct same-adapter reuse, an adapter-name change with exactly zero update, and reuse limited to the two tokens preceding a prefix edit agreed with fresh forwarding (maximum absolute logit error <=1.49e-7; predeclared tolerances float32 1e-5 / float64 1e-10). Forcibly reusing A's KV with nonzero B produced max-absolute differences 0.2205–0.2727; retaining the old full prefix after the edit produced 0.1082–0.2622. Each stale-cache case changed argmax in only 4/12 trials, so comparing all logits matters. Each path used a newly created cache with asserted sequence lengths.

This supports the specific correctness counterexample, not a universal ranking against fragmentation/scheduling. It does not measure answer quality, throughput, cross-framework layout compatibility, or automatic rejection by a cache manager. [Reproduction scripts, full inputs/logits, versions and results](https://gist.github.com/eprogressing/84db3e068aabbe449f8629a3f362a6e5). Prepared with Codex assistance; these runs were actually executed.

items.title: Add support for Maple architecture (20B-A1B ternary MoE)
items.author: AlexGabbia
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation

Maple is a 20B-parameter MoE model with 1B active parameters (20B-A1B) using
ternary weights (TQ1_0/TQ2_0 quantization, ~2 bpw). It is released under MIT
license by DeepGrove (https://huggingface.co/deepgrove/maple-preview).

The model uses sliding-window attention (SWA-512) interleaved with global
attention at a 3:1 ratio, per-head Q/K RMS norms, and a MoE FFN with SiLU gate
clamped at +7 (DEEPSEEK4-style swiglu split). GGUF files are available at
https://huggingface.co/deepgrove/maple-preview-GGUF and currently run only on
the DeepGrove fork (https://github.com/deepgrove-ai/llama.cpp), not on
mainline llama.cpp.

### Proposed work

Add end-to-end support for the `maple` architecture:

- HF -> GGUF converter (`conversion/maple.py`) + GGUF tensor constants
- Architecture implementation (`src/models/maple.cpp`, arch registration,
  model mapping, rope type)
- One arch-gated line in `build_moe_ffn` (llama-graph.cpp) for the
  DEEPSEEK4-style swiglu clamp branch
- Test coverage in `test-llama-archs` (MoE-mandatory)

CPU-only support in the initial PR, consistent with the project guideline
("focus on CPU support only in the initial PR").

### Status

A working implementation exists on a fork of this repo (4 commits, based on
current master) and has been smoke-tested locally with the real GGUF
(TQ2_0-head-Q4_K, 5.5 GiB): coherent generation via llama-cli and
llama-server, ~120 tok/s decode on Apple M4 (CPU, 8 threads). The DeepGrove
maintainers were contacted about co-authoring
(https://github.com/deepgrove-ai/llama.cpp/issues/1) — no reply yet.

items.title: Add a way to clear the whole prompt cache (slots + host RAM)
items.author: yuya0408
items.body_excerpt:
I found that with the default settings, erasing all slots does not clear the host RAM cache. The next request loads the prompt back from it.

I want to clear the whole prompt cache of the server between benchmark runs, so that a run does not hit the cache of the previous run. Right now, the only ways to do this are: (1) restart the server, or (2) use `--cache-ram 0` and erase all slots.

Both have a problem. With (1), the server reloads the model on every restart, so the runs take longer. With (2), I can only measure with the host RAM cache turned off, but it is on by default. So I measure a setup that is different from what users normally run.

vLLM (`/reset_prefix_cache`) and SGLang (`/flush_cache`) have an endpoint to clear the cache, and their benchmark tools use it between runs.

So I propose one of these: (a) a new endpoint, or (b) an option for the existing erase action that also clears the host RAM cache.

My measurements:

```
Version: 0.7.0-dev (build 11716, commit 797de63b2), official Windows CPU build
Model: Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B-GGUF, Q8_0
Server: llama-server -m Qwen3-0.6B-Q8_0.gguf -c 8192 --slot-save-path ./slots

P, Q: two different prompts, about 1,300 tokens each
Steps: P -> Q -> erase all slots (POST /slots/{id}?action=erase) -> P
```

`timings.cache_n` of the last P (prompt = 1318 tokens):

| server options | cache_n |
|---|---|
| (default) | 1317 |
| `--parallel 2` | 1317 |
| `--cache-ram 0` | 0 |
| `--parallel 2 --cache-ram 0` | 0 |

Without Q in between (P -> erase all slots -> P), `cache_n` = 0 in all four cases.

items.title: [Track]: [Store] Land the tenant-first MasterService migration in staged PRs
items.author: Aionw
items.body_excerpt:
This issue tracks how the `MasterService` half of RFC #3670 lands in `main`. #4370 carries the whole migration as one PR (+7.3k/−6.6k), which is too large to review, so the work is split into 17 PRs. Each PR builds, passes the tests and is correct on its own, and the order below is the order they can merge in. The code for the whole series is already written. Each PR is cut from the finished end state, so reviewing it means reviewing that slice of a design that is already complete, not code still in progress. Review comments are welcome on any PR in the series, and on this issue for the overall plan. Anyone whose review suggestion is adopted is added as a co-author of the PR that takes it. ## Status Last updated 2026-10-16. In the dependency graph below, green is merged and yellow has an open PR. | Step | PR | State | |---|---|---| | 4. Tenant quota control plane | #4563 | Merged | | 1. Per-key `ObjectState` | #4562 | Merged | | 3. Dynamic replication controller | #4589 | Merged | | 2. Promotion candidate tracker | #4586 | Merged | | 5. Object route | #4585 | Merged | | 9. Accessor contract and write paths | #4717 | Open | | 6. Namespace layer | #4721 | Open | | everything else | — | Waiting on its dependencies | Phase 1 is complete and step 9 (#4717) is open; steps 10 to 14 wait on it. Step 5 is merged and step 6 (#4721) is open; steps 7 and 8 wait on it. ## Design ### Before: shard-level ownership ```mermaid flowchart TB MS["MasterService"] --> SH subgraph SH["1024 MetadataShards (hash of tenant and key, one lock each)"] TS["TenantState
one per shard and tenant"] TS --- MD["metadata map
ObjectMetadata + TenantQuotaLedger"] TS --- SM["7 per-key side maps
+ lease map"] end subgraph SIDE["Also inside MasterService"] GD["GroupDomain
all groups, one lock"] OL["ObjectOperationLock
4096 striped mutexes"] EV["BatchEvict · NoFBatchEvict
EvictTenantMemoryForQuota"] end SH -->|"census of every shard, every pass"| EV ``` - **Ownership.** A shard holds fragments of many tenants. Each `TenantState` in it keeps the object map plus seven separate per-key maps (processing keys, replication, offload and promotion tasks, promotion candidates, dynamic-replication pending records and cooldowns) and a map of dynamic-replication leases. Empty tenant states are erased by hand on about 55 paths. - **Locking.** One shard lock covers every object that hashes to it, so unrelated keys contend. Puts and upserts also take a striped `ObjectOperationLock`. Groups live in a separate single-lock `GroupDomain`. - **Background work.** Memory, NoF and tenant-quota eviction each run a census over all 1024 shards, and the expired-processing sweep walks every object. The eviction denominator depends on a per-shard `disk_object_count`. - **Quota.** Every path that changes replicas books or releases the tenant's charge through the ledger on the object, so correctness depends on each path doing it. - **Subsystems inline.** Dynamic replication, promotion retry, eviction and the quota control plane are all inside `master_service.cpp` (15.2k lines), reading and writing the shard maps directly. ### After: tenant-first namespaces with per-key locks ```mermaid flowchart TB MS["MasterService"] --> NT["NamespaceTable
tenant id → Namespace"] NT --> NS subgraph NS["Namespace (one per tenant)"] RT["ObjectRoute
1024 stripes"] --> KS["KeySlot (one per key)
lock · metadata · ObjectState"] RT --> GI["GroupIndex"] KS -->|"write lock released"| HOOK["write-release hook"] HOOK --> IF["In-flight list"] HOOK --> EI["EvictionIndex"] end subgraph SUB["Subsystems built on the core"] TASK["DynamicReplicationController
PromotionCandidateTracker"] QP["TenantQuotaPolicy
(a NamespacePolicy)"] EV["eviction::Evictor"] end KS <-.->|"ObjectState via *Locked"| TASK HOOK -->|"settle charge"| QP EI -->|"cursor, lowest rank first"| EV ``` - **`route::ObjectRoute`** owns one tenant's keys. Every key has a `KeySlot`: its lock, the object record when one is published, and the per-key `ObjectState` that replaces the side maps (the task in flight of each kind, the promotion candidate, the dynamic-replication pending record and cooldown). The lock belongs to the key, not to a publication, so a writer can lock a key that has no object yet and replace an object without a window in which the key is absent. - **Generations.** Each publication gets a `Generation`. Code that lets go of a key and comes back later (a scan that acts afterwards, a durable callback) holds an `ObjectRef{key, generation}` and acts only while that same publication is still there. - **Lock rules.** A stripe lock is held only to find, create or collect a slot, or across a cursor that only tries slot locks. A thread holds at most one slot lock at a time. The group index, the in-flight list, the eviction index and the policy's per-key state are leaves under a slot lock. - **`metadata::Namespace`** is the route plus what must stay in step with every write. As each write guard is released, the route reports it to the namespace. The namespace then updates the in-flight list (so the expiry sweep walks only keys with work in flight), refiles the key in the eviction index, and passes the release on to the policy. - **`metadata::NamespaceTable`** maps tenant ids to namespaces. Namespaces are created atomically, never move and are never deleted while the service runs, so a resolved reference needs no ownership. items.title: [RFC]: [TENT] Runtime-loadable transport plugins
items.author: xiaodouzi666
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

## Motivation

Every TENT transport is compiled into the core today. `transport_loader.cpp`
selects them with `#ifdef USE_*`, and `TransportType` is a closed enum. Adding
one transport means editing the core. #4425 (libfabric FABRIC) is a recent
example: it touched 12 existing files, including the enum and both name
functions, the C macro table, pybind, `forceTcp()`, the loader, three
default-transport chains, the staging lists, the selector whitelist, CMake and
tebench. It also means every build ships whichever vendor backends happened to
be enabled when it was compiled.

Roadmap #1058 ("Packaging & Usability: enable runtime dynamic loading")
describes the goal: package the TENT core once, and let each device, vendor or
environment supply its transports as plugins that are built, upgraded and
shipped separately. A missing, conflicting or incompatible plugin must be
diagnosed precisely and must never take the host process down.

## Design

**Unit.** A plugin is a shared object named `libtent_xport_<name>.so`. It
exports the C entry point `tent_transport_plugin_register`, which fills a
plain-C descriptor (`include/tent/transport_plugin.h`):

- the ABI version and an ABI fingerprint;
- the name and version;
- `builtin_type` (0 means a new transport);
- routing flags (same-machine-only, local-segment-only, host-staging, …);
- `declared_caps`, the most capabilities the transport may report;
- `probe`, `create`, `destroy` and `last_error`.

`create()` returns a `mooncake::tent::Transport*`. Built-in transports are
already `Transport` subclasses, so turning one into a plugin takes a one-line
entry file (`TENT_DEFINE_TRANSPORT_PLUGIN`). Mirroring the whole `Transport`
interface in C was rejected as too large a surface. The plugin follows the
style of the existing device-plugin ABI (`device_plugin.h`).

**Identity.** The 17 built-in enum values are unchanged. Eight plugin slots are
reserved after them (`kFirstPluginSlot` … `kNumTransportTypes`), so every
per-transport array grows by eight entries and no existing loop changes.
`transportTypeName()` and `parseTransportType()` fall back to a write-once,
lock-free slot table. As a result, policy files, `transport_hint`, Python
hints and metric labels accept plugin names with no other change.

Slots are local to the process. A segment descriptor never carries a plugin
slot as an integer. On export, plugin entries move to the new optional keys
`plugin_transports` and `plugin_transport_attrs`, keyed by name. On import,
names are mapped to this process's slots, and integers that are not built-in
transports are dropped. That second rule also closes an existing
out-of-bounds read in the legacy selection path when a newer peer advertises a
larger enum value.

**Loading.** Plugins are loaded only when `plugins/dir` (or
`MC_TENT_PLUGIN_DIR`) is set; it accepts a `:`-separated list of directories,
and the first directory that provides a name wins. An entry that starts with
`$ORIGIN` is relative to the directory of the file the core was loaded from,
as `/proc/self/maps` names it (symlinks resolved; TENT runs on Linux only):
the executable, `libtent_shared.so`, or the Python extension. `plugins/load`
(a list of names, or one name) is an allow-list applied per engine, and
`plugins/required` makes engine construction fail cleanly with
`PluginError` if a listed plugin is not installed in that engine. Malformed
lists fail closed (`load`: nothing is loaded; `required`: construction
fails). An engine without `plugins/dir` gets no plugin transports and treats
plugin names in its policies as unknown, whatever other engines of the
process loaded.

`MC_TENT_CONF` replaces the whole configuration: `Config::load` discards
whatever the application had set, and the engine restores only the keys the
caller passed for its identity (metadata, RPC, segment name, force-TCP, the
RDMA whitelist and three Ascend keys). Use it only when it carries the complete
configuration; to add a plugin directory to an otherwise programmatic
configuration (tebench, Python), set `MC_TENT_PLUGIN_DIR`, which is applied
after `MC_TENT_CONF`. The HP-TCP guide says the same about `MC_TENT_CONF` for
tebench.

Loading happens once per process and has three steps:

1. `ensureLoaded()` runs before the transport selector parses policies. It
   calls `dlopen` with `RTLD_LOCAL`, then checks the ABI version, the
   fingerprint, the name, and any conflict with a built-in. It then runs
   `probe()` and assigns a slot.
2. `instantiate()` runs at the end of `loadTransports()` and creates this
   engine's transport objects. Each engine gets its own objects.
3. `verifyInstalled()` runs after the install loop. It removes any transport
   whose `capabilities()` exceed `declared_caps`, or that reports
   notification or cancellation support without the matching flag. It also
   enforces `plugins/required` and returns this engine's plugin summary for
   the verbose banner.

Plugins are never unloaded.

**Symbols.** A plugin links no TENT library. Its TENT symbols are resolved
from the host process at load time, which guarantees a single copy of every
TENT singleton.

- If the host links TENT statically, it must export its symbols (`-rdynamic`).
- The loader looks up the core's own C symbol in the process's global scope
  (`dlsym` on the `dlopen(NULL)` handle). If the symbol is not there and the
  core is a shared object loaded with `RTLD_LOCAL`, such as the Python
  extension, the loader promotes the core to global scope and looks again.
  It does this only once the plugin directory has produced a candidate file.
- If the symbol then resolves to the core itself, plugins load. If it does
  not (another TENT copy is already global, or the executable was not linked
  with `-rdynamic`), every plugin is refused with one
  `host_symbols_not_exported` diagnostic instead of failing on an undefined
  symbol. A refused core is never promoted.

items.title: [RFC]: Add native MLU support to TENT
items.author: lhzds
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

Add native Cambricon MLU support to TENT using CNRT/CNDRV and the existing host-staging pipeline. The initial capability is synchronous local device/host copies plus cross-process or cross-host READ/WRITE over TCP and HP TCP.

Classic TE supports MLU, but TENT needs its own platform implementation and local-copy transport to register device memory and construct staging routes.

### Design

- Select `MluPlatform` with `USE_MLU`. Discover devices and host affinity; provide allocation, pointer/range validation, synchronous copies, and context restoration.
- Add a local-only MLU transport with device-to-host and host-to-device capabilities. Preserve existing transport enum values and expose the new value through C and Python.
- Use the staging planner for network transfers. Each network stage registers its own host buffer; raw MLU pointers must not reach a host-only transport. Preserve this route during retries and runtime-queued submission.
- Reject invalid allocation ranges, including out-of-bounds interior pointers. Callers retain allocation ownership and synchronize producer work before transfers.

```text
MLU A <-> host stage A <-> TCP / HP TCP <-> host stage B <-> MLU B
```

Staging admission and retry follow the existing TENT policy. Pool pressure can fail a request, and applications decide whether and when to resubmit. Failed transfers can have partially completed writes; callers keep buffers alive while physical operations remain in flight.

Implementation: #4691.

### Related work

- #4157 and #2733 establish local-stage transport support for XPU and TPU.
- #3380 defines deferred staging cleanup and in-flight resource ownership.

### Validation

#4691 reports the regression results and two-host TCP/HP TCP measurements on MLU590-M9DK. Tests cover SDK allocations, range checks, context restoration, routing, payload correctness, pool-pressure failure, caller resubmission and resource reclamation.

### Scope and compatibility

MLU device copies are synchronous. MLU direct RDMA, IPC/P2P, asynchronous copy overlap and serving-framework integration are outside this implementation. Peers using MLU metadata need an updated TENT build.

The two-host tests use one visible MLU per host; multiple-device configurations are not covered. Peer recovery uses a fresh segment identity and does not establish transparent same-identity restart or crash safety during partially completed writes.

AI assistance: OpenAI Codex assisted with implementation, validation and this description.

items.title: [RFC]: Rethinking the Master Global State Lock: Lifecycle Isolation and Finer-Grained Synchronization
items.author: Icedcoco
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

> **Status: discussion draft.** No implementation has been approved. This document is intentionally written to be challenged on GitHub.
>
> The purpose of this RFC is to review the remaining role of `snapshot_mutex_`, now named `master_state_mutex_`, after [PR #4406][pr4406] removed the legacy Master snapshot path. Please treat every proposed decomposition as a hypothesis: reviewers are encouraged to identify incorrect assumptions, missing call paths, unsafe interleavings, and simpler designs. The goal of this discussion is to improve the model before implementation begins.
>
> Audit baseline: local commit `db969643a00cb91f059acbccce34760ca0dabf23`. The main implementation files referenced here match the merged PR #4406 commit `342c8aeece6b4eefb76c6b8b31ccfac8dde07aa3`; source links therefore point to that merge commit. Function names and line numbers refer to this baseline and may move later.

## 1. Proposal and review goals

PR #4406 removed the legacy Master snapshot path, retained the OpLog-backed snapshot, and renamed `snapshot_mutex_` to `master_state_mutex_`. The old snapshot requirement for a global Master freeze is gone, but many guard sites remain. Some of those sites now protect unrelated lifecycle or metadata interactions that accumulated around the original barrier.

The direction proposed here is to give recovery, memory-segment remount, and LOCAL_DISK registration lifecycle explicit protocols; then gradually remove the global shared lock from ordinary RPCs and background scans; and finally decide whether the `master_state_mutex_` member can be removed entirely.

Here, “finer grained” means reducing the conflict domain. Unmounting one client's disk or remounting one segment should not automatically block every object operation in the Master. It does not primarily mean reducing the memory occupied by a mutex object or shortening one critical section in isolation.

The current preliminary assessment is deliberately open to correction:

- There is no evidence yet that one global `std::shared_mutex` must remain permanently.
- Removing all guard statements in one sweep would be unsafe with the current object-lifetime and publication model.
- The hardest issue is `ReMountSegment()` retaining metadata pointers after releasing shard locks. The next hardest issues are internal concurrency during restore and ordering between LOCAL_DISK deregistration and replica admission.
- A few narrow guard sites may be independently removable, but most metadata paths need the remount, readiness, and lifecycle questions resolved first.

The first questions for reviewers are:

1. Does production or embedded mode require restoring an already-serving Master, or can restore be startup-only?
2. What visibility and atomicity boundary does a multi-segment remount actually promise?
3. Can the same client UUID be registered again while an older LOCAL_DISK registration is being swept, or must registrations be generation-scoped?

Answers to these questions determine whether the eventual design is a small protocol split or a substantially broader state-publication change. Please also point out if this RFC overstates the protection provided by the current global lock, or if it misses callers that bypass it.

## 2. Background

### 2.1 From a snapshot freeze lock to a general state barrier

The old `snapshot_mutex_` was introduced with Master metadata persistence and recovery. The basic arrangement was shared locking for ordinary state access and exclusive locking for snapshot-like operations that needed to pause protocol participants. The historical entry point is described in [the Master persistence and recovery commit][history-persistence].

Over time, other workflows began relying on the same barrier:

- HA recovery and post-recovery segment remount coordinate metadata and allocator reconstruction.
- Explicit LOCAL_DISK unmount needs to prevent a registration admitted under the old state from landing after the owner sweep, as described in [PR #3316][history-local-disk].
- Client liveness and asynchronous offboarding introduced client-level lifecycle guards, as described in [PR #2991][history-liveness], while some paths continued to use the global shared lock.
- The graceful-unmount scheduler once formed an ABBA deadlock with this lock, as fixed in [PR #2486][history-deadlock].

Therefore, keeping the lock after #4406 does not by itself mean that legacy snapshots were incompletely removed. It means that the original snapshot barrier accumulated responsibilities beyond snapshots. The next cleanup should separate those responsibilities instead of assuming they have one common lifetime.

### 2.2 Relationship to the retained OpLog snapshot

The current batch OpLog snapshot captures state from the `HotStandbyService` metadata store. It checks cursor consistency at an applied durable-prefix boundary, pauses the standby replication loop, copies metadata in chunks, and releases the capture. That protocol has its own synchronization and lifetime rules and does not acquire the Master's global state lock; see [the standby capture path][source-oplog-capture]. It answers how an applied log state becomes a coherent snapshot. This RFC addresses how the recovered state is accessed at runtime after it has been installed in Master.

This RFC does not propose changing the OpLog snapshot format, replay order, durable prefix, or leadership fencing. Those persistence guarantees remain owned by the OpLog protocol.

The separation under discussion is **runtime synchronization for Master in-memory state**. The existence of an OpLog snapshot does not imply that the Master-wide lock is required. Conversely, removing the legacy snapshot path does not prove that every historical guard site is now unnecessary.

## 3. Current state: what the lock actually protects

items.title: [Bug]: Potential incorrect metadata removal for shared-address multi-protocol registrations
items.author: xp2001-coder
items.body_excerpt:
### Bug Report

## Description

I noticed a potential metadata consistency issue in the classic Mooncake Transfer Engine while investigating multi-protocol registration with the **MACA backend on MetaX GPUs**.

Under `ENABLE_MULTI_PROTOCOL`, multiple transport-specific `BufferDesc` entries may refer to the same memory address. However, `TransferMetadata::removeLocalMemoryBuffer()` currently identifies the descriptor to remove **only by its address, without considering the transport protocol**.

When multiple protocol descriptors share the same address, this may remove the wrong descriptor and potentially leave stale metadata for a transport that has already been unregistered.

### Environment

The preliminary reproduction was performed with the following configuration:

- **Mooncake commit:** `a9983dcd600270fcc5c0cc6df92906b1e1785f8c`
- **Transfer Engine:** Classic
- **Build options:** `USE_MACA=ON`, `ENABLE_MULTI_PROTOCOL=ON`
- **Hardware:** 2 × MetaX C600-A GPUs (single node)
- **MACA version:** 3.9.0.29
- **Driver version:** 3.9.6
- **OS:** Ubuntu 24.04

The observed metadata behavior was reproduced using synthetic buffer descriptors. A full hardware-backed same-address multi-protocol unregister scenario has not yet been validated.

### Relevant Code

The current removal logic in `TransferMetadata::removeLocalMemoryBuffer()` essentially performs:

```cpp
if (iter->addr == (uint64_t)addr) {
    new_segment_desc->buffers.erase(iter);
    break;
}
```

The removal interface does not accept a protocol identifier, so it cannot distinguish between descriptors belonging to different transports at the same address.

Additionally, `TransferEngineImpl` tracks local memory regions using an address-based index, while the multi-protocol unregister path invokes transport-specific unregister operations.

This raises a potential mismatch between **per-transport registration ownership** and **address-based metadata cleanup**.

### Preliminary Reproduction

A synthetic metadata test was constructed with two `BufferDesc` entries sharing the same address, ordered as `[tcp, maca]`.

The intended operation was to remove the MACA registration. However, the underlying metadata removal interface receives only the address, without any protocol information.

**Observed behavior:**

```text
Initial descriptors:   [tcp, maca]
Intended removal:      maca
Actual descriptors:    [maca]
Expected descriptors:  [tcp]
```

Because the removal logic selects the first descriptor matching the address, it removes the TCP descriptor while retaining the MACA descriptor.

This demonstrates that **address-only removal is insufficient to distinguish protocol-specific descriptors** in the constructed multi-protocol scenario.

The reproduction isolates metadata removal behavior; it does not establish that the complete hardware-backed unregister path necessarily exhibits the same outcome.

### Related Issues and Prior Work

I reviewed several related multi-protocol registration and unregister fixes:

- **#2724 / #2725:** Addressed incorrect transport-specific descriptor selection when the same GPU memory was registered under both HIP and RDMA. This demonstrates a real shared-address multi-protocol scenario, but the fix focuses on **transfer-time descriptor lookup**, rather than metadata removal during unregister.

- **#4240 / #4243:** Address partial unregister failures and recovery of per-transport registration state. PR #4243 introduces tracking of transport-specific registration and unregister progress, which is closely related to the ownership semantics discussed here. However, it does not explicitly establish protocol-aware `BufferDesc` removal as part of the reported fix.

- **#2962:** Improved best-effort unregister behavior by attempting unregister operations across transports even when an individual transport reports an error.

The concern reported here is specifically about **which protocol-specific metadata descriptor is removed when multiple descriptors share the same address**, rather than transfer-time selection or recovery from partial unregister failures.

It would also be useful to clarify whether the ongoing ownership-tracking work in #4243 is expected to address this metadata consistency concern.

### Questions for Maintainers

1. Is registering and publishing multiple transport-specific descriptors for the same memory address range an intended and supported use case across the available backends?
2. Should metadata removal identify the target descriptor using **(address, transport protocol)** rather than address alone?
3. Should `TransferEngineImpl` retain per-transport registration ownership in coordination with the metadata layer?
4. How should partial registration rollback and protocol-specific unregister operations maintain consistency with shared metadata, particularly in light of the ongoing work in #4243?

### Validation Scope

This finding is based on source inspection and a synthetic metadata reproduction performed while investigating MACA multi-protocol behavior.

End-to-end validation of the same-address MACA + RDMA registration/unregistration flow on real hardware has not yet been completed. Therefore, the impact on actual multi-protocol deployments remains to be confirmed.

I would like to clarify the intended registration ownership and metadata cleanup semantics before proposing changes to the Transfer Engine implementation.

items.title: [RFC]: [Store] HA: graceful leader shutdown on SIGTERM/SIGINT (release the lease before exit)
items.author: tensorcopy
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

### Summary

In HA mode, SIGTERM ends the master process with no cleanup. When that master is the leader, its etcd lease stays alive until it expires, and only then can a standby acquire leadership and begin its warmup. A planned restart (pod delete, rollout) therefore costs as much as a crash.

This RFC proposes that the HA master handle SIGTERM and SIGINT. It stops taking new work, waits for admitted admin handlers before the release and drains the healthy OpLog writer's ready queue (retaining today's failure behavior), revokes the leadership lease exactly once, and exits within a fixed deadline. A planned leader restart then costs about one warmup instead of lease expiry plus warmup. There are no data-plane changes, no new persistent state and no wire changes. The work is split into two PRs of about 520 and 440 lines (Section 9).

All code references are to `main` at `3aa0f716`. Related: #3808 (HA roadmap), #4559, #4666, #4706.

#4601, merged after `3aa0f716`, runs RPC handlers on a worker pool that the serving exit drains after the server future returns and before step 2 of 2.3; the ordered exit keeps that drain. It shifts later line numbers in `master_service_supervisor.cpp` and `master.cpp`.

### 1. Current behavior

- `main()` installs SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers only in the non-HA branch (`mooncake-store/src/master.cpp:1653-1658`). The HA branch builds a `MasterServiceSupervisor` and returns `supervisor.Start()` (`master.cpp:1612-1618`). In `mooncake-store/src` these are the only SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers on the master's path, so in HA mode SIGTERM takes its default action and ends the process without running destructors. The etcd backend's Go `c-shared` library does not install a SIGTERM handler either: Go installs handlers for asynchronous signals in that mode only when `signal.Notify` is called, and the wrapper does not call it.
- The supervisor loop (`mooncake-store/src/ha/leadership/master_service_supervisor.cpp:330`) has no stop condition. It leaves only through `return -1`: on a fatal backend error, or when the RPC listener fails to start (`:667-680`).
- The etcd coordinator grants the lease with `DEFAULT_MASTER_VIEW_LEASE_TTL_SEC` (5 s, `mooncake-store/include/types.h:101`) and creates the `master_view` key under that lease (`mooncake-store/src/ha/leadership/backends/etcd/etcd_leader_coordinator.cpp:216-228`), so a revoke deletes the key. For an acquired leadership session, normal cleanup revokes through `ReleaseLeadership` (`etcd_leader_coordinator.cpp:567-613`) or the destructor (`:155`, `:653-704`). SIGTERM's default termination does not run those cleanup paths.
- A new leader keeps renewing for one full lease TTL in warmup before it serves (`WarmupLeadership`, `master_service_supervisor.cpp:189-217`; the deadline is set at `:191`).
- A standby waits on an etcd watch of the `master_view` key (`etcd_leader_coordinator.cpp:436-531`), in 1 s slices (`master_service_supervisor.cpp:31`, `:392-393`, `:409-410`). It sees a delete at once (within one 1 s slice if the old leader was still warming up).

With lease TTL `T`, the two cases compare like this:

| | Leader killed (today) | Leader releases the lease (proposed) |
| -- | -- | -- |
| Successor can acquire | when the old lease expires, up to `T` after the kill | when the old leader revokes, at the end of its cleanup |
| Then | producer-view claim and catch-up/promotion, warmup `T`, then restore and serving startup | producer-view claim and catch-up/promotion, warmup `T`, then restore and serving startup |

The saving is up to `T` per planned leader restart. It grows with the TTL, which #4706 makes configurable up to 60 s.

### 2. Proposed behavior

#### 2.1 Signal intake

- `main()` installs SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers in the HA branch, before `supervisor.Start()`, so no lease can be acquired without them. If installation fails, the master refuses to start.
- The handler does one lock-free atomic exchange on a sticky "shutdown requested" flag (asserted lock-free at compile time). It does not log, lock or call a backend.
- The handlers are installed with `sigaction` and `SA_ONSTACK`. The etcd and k8s HA backends are Go `c-shared` libraries in the master process (`mooncake-common/etcd/CMakeLists.txt:3`, `CMakeLists.txt:83`), and Go requires `SA_ONSTACK` on any handler that non-Go code installs ([os/signal docs](https://pkg.go.dev/os/signal#hdr-Non_Go_programs_that_call_Go_code)). The `std::signal` calls in the non-HA branch (`master.cpp:1657-1658`) are not a model for this.
- A second signal calls `_exit(128 + signo)` (130 for SIGINT, 143 for SIGTERM), the convention the Transfer Engine watcher already follows (`graceful_shutdown.cpp:151`). This is the escape hatch for a shutdown that does not finish.
- The supervisor receives the request as a predicate (`std::function<bool()>`) that defaults to the process flag, so tests can inject their own.

The Transfer Engine already has a SIGTERM/SIGINT watcher that uses a self-pipe (`mooncake-transfer-engine/src/graceful_shutdown.cpp:146-167`, `:181-211`). The master's HA path does not construct a `TransferEngine` (in `mooncake-store/src`, only `client_service.cpp` does), and `mooncake_master` does not link `transfer_engine` (`mooncake-store/src/CMakeLists.txt:712-725`), so that watcher is not active here. Its design is a reference for open question 4.

#### 2.2 Supervisor: a shutdown request is handled like a lease loss, then the loop exits

The loop already has a release path for every phase after acquisition, because each failure calls `ReleaseLeadership` (`HandleLeadershipPhaseError`, `master_service_supervisor.cpp:179-187`, and the `LogLeadershipReleaseWarning` call sites). The change makes each phase notice the request and then leaves the loop instead of retrying.

| Phase | Today | With a shutdown request |
| -- | -- | -- |
| Outer loop and coordinator creation (`:330-338`) | retries every 1 s on error | checked at the top of each outer iteration; exits with no

items.title: [Bug][Store] Tenant-watermark eviction removes objects without an OpLog record and releases quota before durability
items.author: apex-mochen
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

With `enable_ha` + `enable_oplog` + `enable_multi_tenants`, the eviction thread's tenant pass (`EvictTenantsOverWatermark` → `EvictTenantMemoryForQuota`, on by default at `tenant_eviction_high_watermark_ratio = 0.90`) removes memory replicas, releases the tenant's committed quota and erases the metadata **without appending any OpLog entry**.

`BatchEvict` handles the same removal differently: `persist_evict_oplog_or_skip` marks the replicas `REMOVED`, appends `REMOVE` / `PUT_END` with a durable finalize, and frees the replicas and quota only in `FinalizeRemovedReplicasAfterDurable` ("HA strong-consistency: persist the post-eviction state before the helper mutates metadata"). The tenant pass has no equivalent step.

Checked on main `20fc0bc` and again on `129c961`.

### Reproduction (deterministic)

Regression test in `master_service_evict_scenario_test.cpp` (in the linked PR):
- HA config, `tenant-a` quota = 1 KiB, one completed, lease-expired 1 KiB object `cold`;
- no explicit eviction: wait 2 s so the tenant pass runs;
- `cold` no longer exists, but OpLog batch 3 never appears (`ETCD_KEY_NOT_EXIST`).

On unfixed main the test fails 5/5, both on `20fc0bc` and on `129c961`.

### Where it already shows up

- `MasterServiceEvictScenarioTest.OpLogDurabilityGatesTenantQuotaReclamation` fails intermittently: nightly run 37339233838, triaged in #4485; a PR run on 2026-09-15 is also mentioned in #4136.
- The failure always produces the same three messages:
  - `before-durable succeeded`
  - batch 3 `ETCD_KEY_NOT_EXIST`
  - `after-durable TENANT_QUOTA_EXCEEDED`
- With 32 CPU-burning processes (on `20fc0bc`), 33 of 50 repeats fail with exactly these messages; idle, 50/50 pass. No failing iteration contains `[EVICT-RESULT]`, so the explicit `EvictMemory` found nothing to evict, because the tenant pass had already removed `cold`.
- #4155 isolated two HA tests from the same interaction ("Background eviction can remove that object and release its quota before the tested operation, bypassing the blocked OpLog transaction"). It treated this as a test issue and left production unchanged.

### Possible consequence (not reproduced end to end)

A standby replays only the OpLog, so it would keep the evicted key with its old memory descriptor. If the primary later reuses that address, the standby could hold two live-looking descriptors for one range. That is the "overlapping memory descriptors" condition from #3760, where the maintainer note says overlap "is not expected during normal operation" and the source of the stale descriptor was still open. #3760's cluster ran with `-enable_multi_tenants=true`. I don't know whether a tenant quota was configured there, so I can't say this path caused it; it is one path that can produce the overlap.

### Proposed fix

Route the tenant pass through the same persist-before-mutate step as `BatchEvict` (shared helper), and leave quota release, metadata erase and the KV-removed publish to the durable finalize when the OpLog is on. I have this fix plus the regression test ready and will open a PR shortly.

items.title: [Inductor] Wrong gradient for bf16 conv -> log_softmax -> op under autocast
items.author: kamisli
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Under `torch.autocast("cuda", torch.bfloat16)`, `torch.compile` returns a wrong gradient
for `log_softmax(conv(x))` whenever any op follows the `log_softmax` inside the graph.

The repro compares two functions with identical backward by construction: `f2` only adds
a detached term (`q + (clamp_min(q, b) - q).detach()`). In eager their gradients agree
exactly. Compiled, they disagree, and the error grows with the magnitude of the logits.
A common offset on all logits changes nothing mathematically, since softmax is
shift-invariant.

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

torch.manual_seed(0)
conv = torch.nn.Conv2d(48, 48, 1).cuda()
h = torch.randn(8, 48, 16, 16, device="cuda")
w = torch.softmax(2 * torch.randn(8, 48, 16, 16, device="cuda"), dim=1)


def f1(t):
    return F.log_softmax(conv(t), dim=1)


def f2(t):  # same values up to a detached term, same gradient
    q = F.log_softmax(conv(t), dim=1)
    return q + (torch.clamp_min(q, -20.0) - q).detach()


def grad(f, compiled):
    torch._dynamo.reset()
    fn = torch.compile(f) if compiled else f
    t = h.clone().requires_grad_()
    with torch.autocast("cuda", torch.bfloat16):
        out = fn(t)
    (-(w * out.float()).sum()).backward()
    return t.grad


for offset in (0.0, 100.0, 1000.0):  # common logit offset: softmax-invariant
    with torch.no_grad():
        conv.weight.normal_(0, 0.6)
        conv.bias.fill_(-offset)
    for compiled in (False, True):
        g1, g2 = grad(f1, compiled), grad(f2, compiled)
        cos = F.cosine_similarity(g1.flatten(), g2.flatten(), dim=0).item()
        print(f"offset {offset:6.0f} compiled={compiled!s:5}: "
              f"cos(grad f1, grad f2) = {cos:.4f}, |g2|/|g1| = {(g2.norm() / g1.norm()).item():.3f}")
```

Output:

```
offset      0 compiled=False: cos(grad f1, grad f2) = 1.0000, |g2|/|g1| = 1.000
offset      0 compiled=True : cos(grad f1, grad f2) = 1.0000, |g2|/|g1| = 1.000
offset    100 compiled=False: cos(grad f1, grad f2) = 1.0000, |g2|/|g1| = 1.000
offset    100 compiled=True : cos(grad f1, grad f2) = 0.9919, |g2|/|g1| = 1.018
offset   1000 compiled=False: cos(grad f1, grad f2) = 1.0000, |g2|/|g1| = 1.000
offset   1000 compiled=True : cos(grad f1, grad f2) = 0.6943, |g2|/|g1| = 2.295
```

### What the generated code does

- The **forward kernel** adds the conv bias in fp32 and computes `amax` and log-sum-exp
  from these unrounded fp32 logits. It stores the logits into the conv's **bf16** output
  buffer, and saves that buffer for the backward together with `amax` and the log-sum-exp.
- The **backward kernel** recomputes `log_softmax` as `bf16_logits - amax - lse`, i.e. it
  mixes rounded logits with statistics of the unrounded ones. `exp()` of that is not the
  softmax the forward used, and the error is about `exp(bf16 rounding error of the logit)`.
- In `f1` the `log_softmax` output is a graph output, saved in fp32 and reused, so it is
  consistent. In `f2` it is an intermediate, so the backward recomputes it.
- `aot_eager` and `aot_eager_decomp_partition` give the correct gradient, so the problem is
  in Inductor's lowering, not in tracing or partitioning.
- `torch._inductor.config.emulate_precision_casts = True` fixes it.

In our model (a learned image codec trained with bf16 autocast, logits of a softmax-based
entropy model drifting to |x| ~ 8000), this made the gradients into upstream layers
nearly orthogonal to the correct ones (cosine 0.15), and training diverged. That also
happened on H100s.

### Possibly related

- #168126 (bf16 compile vs eager divergence) and its "Fix bf16 autocast precision
  barriers in Inductor" series: this looks like the same class, a bf16 cast that Inductor
  skips in the fused forward but not in the buffer it saves for the backward. Here,
  however, the *gradient* is wrong while the forward is fine. `aot_eager_decomp_partition`
  is correct, so decompositions are not involved, and `emulate_precision_casts=True`
  fixes it completely.
- #201017 (FlexAttention backward derives Delta from the rounded bf16 output): the same
  pattern, a backward computed from rounded stored values, but for `log_softmax` rather
  than attention.


### Error logs

No error is raised: the gradient is silently wrong. Output of the script above:

```
offset      0 compiled=False: cos(grad f1, grad f2) = 1.0000, |g2|/|g1| = 1.000
offset      0 compiled=True : cos(grad f1, grad f2) = 1.0000, |g2|/|g1| = 1.000
offset    100 compiled=False: cos(grad f1, grad f2) = 1.0000, |g2|/|g1| = 1.000
offset    100 compiled=True : cos(grad f1, grad f2) = 0.9919, |g2|/|g1| = 1.018
offset   1000 compiled=False: cos(grad f1, grad f2) = 1.0000, |g2|/|g1| = 1.000
offset   1000 compiled=True : cos(grad f1, grad f2) = 0.6943, |g2|/|g1| = 2.295
```


### Versions

Collecting environment information...
PyTorch version: 2.10.0+cu128

items.title: Block-wise Scatter-Reduce :  __getitem__ / __setitem__ errors
items.author: olivier-peltre
items.body_excerpt:
While trying to implement a scatter-add reduction inside a kernel, I get errors related to `tensor.__{get,set}item__`. 

As far as I understand, indexing features in triton are either limited or new and I'd like some advice on how to find a satisfactory workaround :slightly_smiling_face: 

Here is a sample code and descriptions of errors: 

```py
    ...
    # load indices and values
    idx = tl.load(idx_ptr + j + row)
    values = tl.load(values_ptr + begin + block)     
    # prepare output 
    out = tl.zeros((BLOCK_HEIGHT, OUT_WIDTH), values.dtype)
    mask = tl.full((OUT_WIDTH,), 0, tl.int1)

    # reduce on axis -1 in horizontal for-loop (FAILS) 
    offset = idx[0]
    for k in tl.static_range(BLOCK_WIDTH): 
        idx_k = idx[k] - offset
        mask[idx_k] = 1 
        out[:,idx_k] += values[:,k]
    
    # store output (atomic lock in case of small global height)
    tl.atomic_add(out_ptr + idx_0, out, mask) 
```
- when trying to access indices I get e.g.  line `offset = idx[0]` I get: 
    ```
    > `offset = idx[0]`
    ValueError("unsupported tensor index: constexpr[0]")
    ```
    is this intended?
    
    I can obviously replace this by `tl.load(idx_ptr + j (+k))`  as workaround
    
- I further get upon calling setitem:
    ```
    > mask[idx_k] = 1
    AssertionError()
    ```
    Overlooking the source, I guess this is because `tensor` doesn't have a `__setitem__` method, though throwing `AttributeError` would be more informative.
    
- I assume the following
  ```
  out[:, idx_k] += val[:,k]
  ```
  would fail for the same reason, though I could probably work around this with `tl.where`.  I'm also unsure whether the shared memory (?) accumulator `out` shouldn't be transposed for performance befor the final `store` instruction. 
  

But more generally, what would you recommend? Maybe this has been done somewhere else? 
Any form of advice greatly appreciated :pray: 

I'm tagging you here @apgoucher and @Mogball, as I wonder whether your recent #5262 PR could help on this subject. 


### Note

I'm looking into whether triton could help scale-up scatter-add kernels, after having noticed large runtime discrepancies between jax and torch implementations (torch ~4x faster) though both scale bad to large input sizes. I'm hoping that aligning loads to 128B sector sizes while putting more work on each warp (as opposed to a naive implementation relying solely on atomics) could improve the scaling in the large input size limit.

I'm also wondering whether leveraging cuda `__shfl_sync` semantics wouldn't be necessary to get satisfactory results on this (which would probably fall out of triton's scope). Though I'm still looking for a good triton implementation first!

items.title: Python 3.14t: C extension missing Py_MOD_GIL declaration causes GIL re-enable warning
items.author: kdt2014
items.body_excerpt:
### Description
Triton 3.5.0 provides binary wheels for Python 3.14t (free-threaded build), but the C extension module `triton._C.libtriton` does not declare GIL compatibility, causing Python to re-enable the GIL with a warning.

### Environment
- Python version: 3.14.0 free-threading build
- Triton version: 3.5.0
- Platform: Linux x86_64
- Installation: `pip install triton` (cp314t wheel)

### Current Behavior
When importing Triton in Python 3.14t:
```python
import triton._C.libtriton
```

Output:
```
RuntimeWarning: The global interpreter lock (GIL) has been enabled to load module 
'triton._C.libtriton', which has not declared that it can run safely without the GIL.
```

### Expected Behavior
The C extension should declare its GIL compatibility status using the `Py_mod_gil` slot in the module definition, as described in [PEP 703](https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/).

### Reproduction Steps
```bash
python3.14t -c "import triton._C.libtriton"
```

### Suggested Fix
Add the appropriate `Py_mod_gil` declaration in the C extension module initialization:
```c
static PyModuleDef_Slot module_slots[] = {
    {Py_mod_gil, Py_MOD_GIL_NOT_USED},  // or Py_MOD_GIL_USED if needed
    {0, NULL}
};
```

### Additional Context
- Since Triton already builds and distributes cp314t wheels, adding the GIL declaration would complete the free-threaded support
- This affects users trying to leverage true parallel execution in Python 3.14t
- The warning can be suppressed with `PYTHON_GIL=0`, but proper declaration is the correct solution

### References
- PEP 703: https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/
- Python 3.14 free-threading docs: https://docs.python.org/3.14/howto/free-threading-extensions.html
```

items.title: Floating-point `%` loses the sign of an exact zero remainder
items.author: merlinsun
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

For floating-point operands, Triton's `%` lowers through the floating remainder operation. On the tested build, the exact-zero result loses the sign of the dividend: `-0.0 % 3.0` is stored as `+0.0` for both f32 and f64. Other finite remainder values in the same probe matched the reference.

Minimal f32 reproducer:

```python
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def kernel(x_ptr, y_ptr, out_ptr):
    i = tl.arange(0, 2)
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + i)
    y = tl.load(y_ptr + i)
    tl.store(out_ptr + i, x % y)

x = torch.tensor([-0.0, 0.0], device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
y = torch.tensor([3.0, 3.0], device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
out = torch.empty_like(x)
kernel[(1,)](x, y, out)
torch.cuda.synchronize()
print(out, out.view(torch.int32))
```

Expected first result: `-0.0` (f32 bits `0x80000000`). Observed: `+0.0` (bits `0x00000000`). The same mismatch was observed for f64. `TRITON_INTERPRET=1` passes this isolated `%` test.

### Environment details

Triton https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/commit/4fd7cc5cfd0a84acfeb5dadb1578dffa409903fc on A800

## Release Cherry-Pick Criteria

After branch cut, we approach finalizing the release branch with clear criteria on what cherry picks are allowed in. Note: a cherry pick is a process to land a PR in the release branch after branch cut. These are typically limited to ensure that the team has sufficient time to complete a thorough round of testing on a stable code base.

* Regression fixes - that address functional/performance regression against the most recent release (e.g. 3.8 for 3.9.0 release)
* Critical fixes - critical fixes for severe issue such as silent incorrectness, backwards compatibility, crashes, deadlocks, (large) memory leaks
* Fixes to new features introduced in the most recent release (e.g. 3.8 for 3.9.0 release)
* Documentation improvements
* Release branch specific changes (e.g. change version identifiers or CI fixes)

Please note: **No feature work allowed for cherry picks**. All PRs that are considered for cherry-picks need to be merged on trunk, the only exception are Release branch specific changes. An issue is for tracking cherry-picks to the release branch is created after the branch cut. **Only issues that have 'cherry-picks' in the issue tracker will be considered for the release.**

## Cherry-Pick Process

1. Ensure your PR has landed in main. This does not apply for release-branch specific changes.

items.title: Compiler crash:LLVM AMDGPU MachineVerifier report "Virtual register defs don't dominate all uses"
items.author: O1iveira7
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

Compiling a legal, deterministic Triton GEMM kernel aborts the process during LLVM AMDGPU codegen: LLVM's post-RA MachineVerifier rejects the generated MIR and calls `abort()`. The same kernel compiles and runs correctly with `num_warps=2` or `num_stages=1/3`; the crash requires `num_warps=1, num_stages=2`.
**Likely cause**
`num_stages=2` enables software pipelining, which clones the A-tile address computation (`V_XOR_B32_e32 112, %3212`) into the prologue and the loop body. A late machine pass (register allocation / live-range splitting / COPY insertion) then makes both clones define the same virtual register `%9951`, without materializing one definition at a common dominator. The epilogue use is reachable from a path that bypasses each definition (bb.4 bypasses the loop-body def in bb.5; bb.1 bypasses the prologue def in bb.2), so no def dominates the use and MachineVerifier aborts. Correct behavior would be distinct vregs per path, or a single merged definition at the common dominator (bb.3).

**Error log excerpt**
Output before crash
REPRO_START M=31 N=63 K=33 BLOCK=128x128x32 num_warps=1 num_stages=2 grid=(1, 1)

LLVM MachineVerifier error (process SIGABRT, exit code 134)
*** Bad machine code: Virtual register defs don't dominate all uses. ***
- function:      gemm
- v. register:   %9951
LLVM ERROR: Found 1 machine code errors.

Definitions/uses of bad virtual register %9951
```
1952:  bb.2   %9951:vgpr_32 = COPY %9347:vgpr_32       def 1 (prologue path)
2254:  bb.5   %9951:vgpr_32 = COPY %9346:vgpr_32       def 2 (loop-body path)
3346:  bb.9   %9348:vgpr_32 = COPY %9951:vgpr_32       use 1 (inside loop; reachable only via bb.5)
4244:  bb.15  %9349:vgpr_32 = COPY %9951:vgpr_32       use 2 (epilogue; reachable via both bb.4/bb.5 paths)
```


Sources of the two definitions
(the same A-tile address computation was cloned twice by software pipelining)
1951:  %9347:vgpr_32 = V_XOR_B32_e32 112, %3212:vgpr_32, ...; 22_gemm_llvm_verifier_min_repro.py:56:18
2253:  %9346:vgpr_32 = V_XOR_B32_e32 112, %3212:vgpr_32

Dominance relationship (two incoming paths to bb.15)
```
bb.3 -> bb.5 -> (loop: bb.7..bb.9) -> bb.10 -> bb.6 -> ... -> bb.15
bb.3 -> bb.4 -> bb.6 -> ... -> bb.15
```
def 2 is in bb.5, but the bb.4 path bypasses bb.5; def 1 is in bb.2, but another path via bb.1 bypasses bb.2
=> the use in bb.15 has no dominating definition, so the verifier is correct to reject it

Exit code
134 (SIGABRT)

**Reproducer**
```
import os

import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def gemm(_fz_switch_ptr, _fz_switch_output_ptr, A, B, C, M, N, K, BLOCK_M: tl.constexpr, BLOCK_N: tl.constexpr, BLOCK_K: tl.constexpr):
    opaque_values = tl.load(_fz_switch_ptr + tl.arange(0, 2))
    opaque_zero, opaque_one = tl.split(opaque_values)
    opaque_true = opaque_zero < opaque_one
    n_id = tl.program_id(1)
    a_offset_m = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_M)
    acc = tl.zeros((BLOCK_M, BLOCK_N), dtype=tl.float32)
    for k in range(0, K, BLOCK_K):
        offset_k = k + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_K)
        a_tile = tl.load(A + a_offset_m[:, None] * K + offset_k[None, :], mask=(a_offset_m[:, None] < M) & (offset_k[None, :] < K), other=0.0)
        if opaque_true:
            tl.store(_fz_switch_output_ptr + tl.arange(0, 2), tl.min(tl.reshape(tl.arange(0, 4), (2, 2)) + opaque_one, axis=1) + opaque_values)
        b_tile = tl.load(B + (n_id * BLOCK_N + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_N))[None, :] + offset_k[:, None] * N, mask=((n_id * BLOCK_N + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_N))[None, :] < N) & (offset_k[:, None] < K), other=0.0)
        acc += tl.dot(a_tile, b_tile)
    if opaque_true:
        tl.store(C + a_offset_m[:, None] * N + (n_id * BLOCK_N + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_N))[None, :], acc.to(tl.float16), mask=(a_offset_m[:, None] < M) & ((n_id * BLOCK_N + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_N))[None, :] < N))


def _main() -> None:
    device = "cuda"  # ROCm uses the cuda namespace; no CPU fallback possible.
    M, N, K = 31, 63, 33
    num_warps = int(os.environ.get("NUM_WARPS", "1"))
    num_stages = int(os.environ.get("NUM_STAGES", "2"))
    BLOCK_M, BLOCK_N, BLOCK_K = 128, 128, 32

    torch.manual_seed(0)
    a = torch.rand(M, K, device=device, dtype=torch.float32)
    b = torch.rand(K, N, device=device, dtype=torch.float32)
    c = torch.rand(M, N, device=device, dtype=torch.float32)
    switch = torch.tensor([0, 1], dtype=torch.int32, device=device)
    scratch = torch.empty(2, dtype=torch.float32, device=device)

    grid = (triton.cdiv(M, BLOCK_M), triton.cdiv(N, BLOCK_N))
    print(
        f"REPRO_START M={M} N={N} K={K} BLOCK={BLOCK_M}x{BLOCK_N}x{BLOCK_K} "
        f"num_warps={num_warps} num_stages={num_stages} grid={grid}",
        flush=True,
    )
    gemm[grid](
        switch, scratch, a, b, c, M, N, K,
        BLOCK_M=BLOCK_M, BLOCK_N=BLOCK_N, BLOCK_K=BLOCK_K,
        num_warps=num_warps, num_stages=num_stages,
    )
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    print("REPRO_DONE (no crash; use NUM_WARPS=1 NUM_STAGES=2 to trigger)", flush=True)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    _main()

### Environment details

```
# Environment: 
- AMD MI308X (gfx942) 
- ROCm 7.2.3
- torch 2.14.0+rocm7.2
- triton-rocm 3.8.0.

items.title: [Gluon] Warp-specialized lowering emits different setmaxnreg instructions within one warpgroup
items.author: builtin-pb
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

When a warp-specialized kernel sets `worker_num_regs` and a warpgroup holds more than one partition, the warps of that warpgroup execute different `setmaxnreg` instructions. The partitions include the no-op padding partitions that `AllocateWarpGroups` adds, so a single 1-warp worker partition is enough to trigger this.

PTX ISA 9.4 §9.7.21.5 (`setmaxnreg`) requires all warps of a warpgroup to execute the same `setmaxnreg` instruction, and makes the behavior undefined otherwise. For the mandatory `.aligned` qualifier, it allows `setmaxnreg` in conditional code only when every thread of the warpgroup evaluates the condition identically. Here the instructions have the same text but are distinct instructions, reached by a branch whose condition differs across the warpgroup.

The pattern comes from the lowering (permalinks at main `0d4e0a0`):
- `padToMaxWarpGroups` pads the worker partitions to whole warpgroups ([AllocateWarpGroups.cpp L39–L87](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/0d4e0a0ceae18cecacf582b9c6f557847a772bdf/lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/AllocateWarpGroups.cpp#L39-L87)). Every partition in a warpgroup then gets the same count, the warpgroup's maximum ([L220–L242](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/0d4e0a0ceae18cecacf582b9c6f557847a772bdf/lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/AllocateWarpGroups.cpp#L220-L242), [L265–L272](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/0d4e0a0ceae18cecacf582b9c6f557847a772bdf/lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/AllocateWarpGroups.cpp#L265-L272)).
- `rewritePartitionRegions` calls the target's `reallocRegisters` at the start of each partition region and at each `warp_return` ([WarpSpecializeUtility.cpp L391–L393](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/0d4e0a0ceae18cecacf582b9c6f557847a772bdf/lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/WarpSpecializeUtility.cpp#L391-L393), [L423–L425](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/0d4e0a0ceae18cecacf582b9c6f557847a772bdf/lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/WarpSpecializeUtility.cpp#L423-L425)). On NVIDIA, that emits a `setmaxnreg` ([ConvertWarpSpecializeToLLVM.cpp L231–L238](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/0d4e0a0ceae18cecacf582b9c6f557847a772bdf/third_party/nvidia/lib/TritonNVIDIAGPUToLLVM/ConvertWarpSpecializeToLLVM.cpp#L231-L238)).

So partitions that share a warpgroup reach the same count through different instructions. The dispatcher chooses each warp's partition with a switch on a per-warp state byte; in the example below, that switch is a `brx.idx` jump table.

**Example.** Tutorial `python/tutorials/gluon/08-warp-specialization.py`, `elementwise_add_warp_specialized_kernel`, compiled with Triton 3.8.0 for sm_90a, using the wrapper's default arguments:
- `XBLOCK=32`, `YBLOCK=64`;
- 2 load and 2 store buffers;
- `num_warps=4`, `maxnreg=128`;
- worker partitions `[1, 1]` warps with `[24, 24]` registers.

Warps 0–3 run the default partition. Warps 4–7 form one warpgroup holding the 2-warp padding partition, the load partition and the store partition. The default warps store the selector word `0x01000202` (line 127, before the barrier at 128), so warps 4–7 read 2, 2, 0, 1. Excerpt of the generated PTX, with line numbers from our file:

```
127:  st.shared.b32   [global_smem+49376], 16777730;   // selectors 2,2,0,1 for warps 4..7
...
314:  setmaxnreg.dec.sync.aligned.u32   24;           // all of warps 4..7
316:  ld.shared.b8    %r14, [%r16+49372];              // %r16 = global_smem + warp index
321-325:  $L_brx_0: .branchtargets $L__BB0_5, $L__BB0_9, $L__BB0_13, $L__BB0_18;   // selector 3 = exit
326:  brx.idx         %r14, $L_brx_0;
327: $L__BB0_5:                                        // selector 0: warp 6 (load)
328:  setmaxnreg.inc.sync.aligned.u32   24;
...
426: $L__BB0_9:                                        // selector 1: warp 7 (store)
427:  setmaxnreg.inc.sync.aligned.u32   24;
...
303: $L__BB0_13:                                       // selector 2: warps 4, 5 (padding)
305:  setmaxnreg.inc.sync.aligned.u32   24;
```

Warps 4 and 5 execute the instruction at 305, warp 6 the one at 328, and warp 7 the one at 427, all within one warpgroup. The exits differ the same way: 308 for warps 4 and 5, 424 for warp 6, and 522 for warp 7.

The same holds in every warp-specialized kernel we compiled from the Gluon tutorials with Triton 3.8.0:
- tutorial 08: the add kernel with `num_warps=8` (warps 8–11 split the same way), and the matmul kernel for sm_100a;
- tutorial 10: `matmul_accumulate_kernel`, sm_100a;
- tutorial 11: `mma_scaled_warp_specialized_kernel`, sm_100a.

In the sm_100a kernels, the extra warps execute a common `setmaxnreg.inc 256` in the dispatcher. Each partition then executes its own `setmaxnreg.dec 24`.

**A second instance of the same rule.** PTX also requires all warps of the warpgroup to synchronize explicitly after a `setmaxnreg` before any of them executes the next one. Each partition's exit `setmaxnreg` branches straight back to the dispatcher's `setmaxnreg`, with no barrier in between: 424 → 314, 522 → 314 and 308 → 314. In the lowering, each `warp_return` becomes barrier, realloc, branch ([L420–L426](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/0d4e0a0ceae18cecacf582b9c6f557847a772bdf/lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/WarpSpecializeUtility.cpp#L420-L426)), and the switch loop starts with realloc, barrier ([L443–L445](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/0d4e0a0ceae18cecacf582b9c6f557847a772bdf/lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/WarpSpecializeUtility.cpp#L443-L445)). So warp 6 can execute 314 while warp 7 is still in the store partition.

**To reproduce.** On a Hopper GPU, run the tutorial's `test_elementwise_add_warp_specialized` with `num_warps=4`, then `grep -n setmaxnreg` the kernel's `.ptx` in the Triton cache.

We found this with a PTX-level checker on a Gluon GEMM of our own, and traced the tutorial PTX by hand. No GPU run.

**Expected behavior.** Every warp of a warpgroup executes the same `setmaxnreg` instruction, and the warpgroup synchronizes between

items.title: [FuseNestedLoops] flatten=True advances outer loop-carried indices on inner iterations
items.author: builtin-pb
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

With `tl.range(..., flatten=True)`, the kernel below returns wrong integers: a value carried from two outer iterations back is combined with the index from one iteration back. With `flatten=False` it matches the Python reference. This reproduces on Triton 3.5.1, 3.8.0 and main (`0d4e0a0c`).

### Reproducer

```python
import sys
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def flow_nested(X, Y, Z, Indices, Data, C, N, T, D, U, enabled,
                BLOCK: tl.constexpr, LOOP_STAGES: tl.constexpr,
                INNER_STAGES: tl.constexpr, FLATTEN: tl.constexpr,
                UNROLL: tl.constexpr, DISALLOW: tl.constexpr):
    pos = tl.program_id(0) * BLOCK + tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    valid = pos < N
    now = tl.zeros((BLOCK,), tl.int32)
    delayed_one = tl.zeros((BLOCK,), tl.int32)
    delayed_two = tl.zeros((BLOCK,), tl.int32)
    checksum = tl.zeros((BLOCK,), tl.int32)
    old_x = tl.zeros((BLOCK,), tl.int32)
    old_y = tl.zeros((BLOCK,), tl.int32)
    old_z = tl.zeros((BLOCK,), tl.int32)
    old_idx = tl.zeros((BLOCK,), tl.int32)
    old_valid = tl.full((BLOCK,), False, tl.int1)
    older_z = tl.zeros((BLOCK,), tl.int32)
    older_idx = tl.zeros((BLOCK,), tl.int32)
    older_valid = tl.full((BLOCK,), False, tl.int1)
    for t in tl.range(0, T, num_stages=LOOP_STAGES, flatten=FLATTEN,
                      loop_unroll_factor=UNROLL, disallow_acc_multi_buffer=DISALLOW):
        if enabled and t % 3 != 1:
            g1 = tl.load(Data + pos * D + old_idx,
                         old_valid & (old_idx >= 0) & (old_idx < D), other=0).to(tl.int32)
            delayed_one += tl.where(old_valid, (old_x * old_y + g1) * (t + 1), 0)
        if enabled and t % 2 == 0:
            g2 = tl.load(Data + pos * D + older_idx,
                         older_valid & (older_idx >= 0) & (older_idx < D), other=0).to(tl.int32)
            delayed_two += tl.where(older_valid, (2 * older_z + g2) * (t + 1), 0)
        x = tl.load(X + t * N + pos, valid, other=0).to(tl.int32)
        y = tl.load(Y + t * N + pos, valid, other=0).to(tl.int32)
        z = tl.load(Z + t * N + pos, valid, other=0).to(tl.int32)
        idx = tl.load(Indices + t * N + pos, valid, other=0)
        now += x * y + z * (t + 1)
        checksum += y * (pos + 1) + idx * (t + 1)
        inner_old = tl.zeros((BLOCK,), tl.int32)
        inner_valid = tl.full((BLOCK,), False, tl.int1)
        for s in tl.range(0, U, num_stages=INNER_STAGES, flatten=FLATTEN,
                          loop_unroll_factor=UNROLL, disallow_acc_multi_buffer=DISALLOW):
            neighbor = (pos + s + 1) % N
            inner_z = tl.load(Z + t * N + neighbor, valid, other=0).to(tl.int32)
            if enabled and (t + s) % 2 == 0:
                checksum += (inner_z + x * (s + 1)) * (t + 1) * (s + 1)
            if enabled and s % 2 == 1:
                checksum += tl.where(inner_valid, inner_old * (s + 1), 0)
            inner_old = inner_z
            inner_valid = valid
        older_z = old_z
        older_idx = old_idx
        older_valid = old_valid
        old_x = x
        old_y = y
        old_z = z
        old_idx = idx
        old_valid = valid
    tl.store(C + 4 * pos, now, valid)
    tl.store(C + 4 * pos + 1, delayed_one, valid)
    tl.store(C + 4 * pos + 2, delayed_two, valid)
    tl.store(C + 4 * pos + 3, checksum, valid)


def reference(X, Y, Z, I, Data, N, T, D, U):
    out = []
    for p in range(N):
        now = d1 = d2 = ck = 0
        old = older = None  # (x, y, z, idx) of the previous / second-previous outer iteration
        for t in range(T):
            if t % 3 != 1 and old:
                d1 += (old[0] * old[1] + Data[p * D + old[3]]) * (t + 1)
            if t % 2 == 0 and older:
                d2 += (2 * older[2] + Data[p * D + older[3]]) * (t + 1)
            x, y, z, idx = X[t * N + p], Y[t * N + p], Z[t * N + p], I[t * N + p]
            now += x * y + z * (t + 1)
            ck += y * (p + 1) + idx * (t + 1)
            inner_old = None
            for s in range(U):
                inner_z = Z[t * N + (p + s + 1) % N]
                if (t + s) % 2 == 0:
                    ck += (inner_z + x * (s + 1)) * (t + 1) * (s + 1)
                if s % 2 == 1 and inner_old is not None:
                    ck += inner_old * (s + 1)
                inner_old = inner_z
            older, old = old, (x, y, z, idx)
        out += [now, d1, d2, ck]
    return out


def main():
    print("torch", torch.__version__, "triton", triton.__version__, torch.cuda.get_device_name())
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(0)
    D, bad = 7, 0
    for flatten in (False, True):
        for N, T, U in ((129, 3, 2), (129, 4, 3), (256, 3, 2), (300, 5, 2), (64, 6, 3)):
            X, Y, Z = (torch.randint(-3, 4, (T * N,), generator=g, dtype=torch.int8) for _ in range(3))
            I = torch.randint(0, D, (T * N,), generator=g, dtype=torch.int32)
            Data = torch.randint(-3, 4, (N * D,), generator=g, dtype=torch.int8)
            C = torch.zeros(4 * N, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
            flow_nested[(triton.cdiv(N, 256),)](X.cuda(), Y.cuda(), Z.cuda(), I.cuda(), Data.cuda(), C, N, T, D, U, True,
                                                BLOCK=256, LOOP_STAGES=2, INNER_STAGES=3, FLATTEN=flatten,
                                                UNROLL=1, DISALLOW=False, num_warps=1, num_stages=2)
            want = reference(X.tolist(), Y.tolist(), Z.tolist(), I.tolist(), Data.tolist(), N, T, D, U)
            got = C.tolist()
            diff = [k for k in range(4 * N) if got[k] != want[k]]
            bad += bool(diff)
            first = f" first: element {diff[0]} (lane {diff[0] // 4}, output {diff[0] % 4}) got {got[diff[0]]} want {want[diff[0]]}" if diff else ""
            print(f"flatten={flatten} N={N} T={T} U={U}: {len(diff)} of {4 * N} wrong{first}")
    sys.exit(1 if bad else 0)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

items.title: Autotuner memoizes incorrectly on mixed-architecture setups
items.author: turboderp
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

`Autotuner.cache` is keyed only on key-arg values and dtypes. So a process using one decorated kernel on two devices of different capability uses the config from whichever device ran first, even if the second device is incompatible. `_bench()` drops configs that raise `OutOfResources`, but only on the device that ran the benchmark.

Miminal example is one kernel with two configs, where one config needs >64 kB smem, run on an Ampere GPU and then on a Turing GPU; nothing causes the autotuner to treat the two GPUs differently, so the second launch fails if autotuning picked the >64 kB config.

As far as I can tell it's fixable in [`Autotuner.run()`](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/3078daa76bbd55c1c3509f7ee8e899b1ed6a127e/python/triton/runtime/autotuner.py#L238) by appending e.g. `driver.active.get_current_target()` to the key, mirroring what the JIT compile cache already does.

### Environment details

Triton: Latest
GPU: Mixed setups

items.title: `ptr - x` with an unsigned offset moves the pointer forward by 2^k - x
items.author: shuyilinn
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

`ptr - x` with an unsigned offset `x` narrower than 64 bits moves the pointer forward instead of backward. The compiled kernel and the interpreter both read the wrong addresses; with `uint32` the address is about 2^32 elements past the pointer.

```python
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def kernel(X, Y):
    i = tl.arange(0, 64)
    tl.store(Y + i, tl.load(X + 300 - i.to(tl.uint8)))  # X[300 - i]


x = torch.arange(1024, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
y = torch.empty(64, device="cuda")
kernel[(1, )](x, y)
print(y[:5].tolist())
```

```
[300.0, 555.0, 554.0, 553.0, 552.0]
```

Expected `[300.0, 299.0, 298.0, 297.0, 296.0]`. The kernel reads `X[300 + 256 - i]`.

`semantic.sub` lowers `ptr - x` as `add(ptr, minus(x))`. `minus` computes `0 - x` in `x`'s unsigned type, which wraps to `2^k - x`, and `add` then zero-extends unsigned offsets to int64 (#5373), so the pointer moves by `+(2^k - x)`. `ptr + x` with an unsigned `x` is correct since #5373; only the subtraction is affected. Signed offsets and `uint64` are correct.

### Environment details

Triton: main @ 41846bc965
GPU: NVIDIA RTX 4090 (sm_89), driver 570 / CUDA 12.8. The bug is in the frontend; `TRITON_INTERPRET=1` reads the same wrong addresses.
score_reasons: 匹配 Serving 与评测、Kernel 与正确性

items.title: Casting between fp8e5 and fp8e4nv fails to compile: "Rounding mode must be specified for convertsions to fp8"
items.author: shuyilinn
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

Casting between the two fp8 formats (`float8e5` to `float8e4nv` and back) fails to compile on sm_89: the NVIDIA lowering hits an assertion (in a source build with assertions enabled). There is no workaround: `fp_downcast_rounding` is rejected for this cast. The interpreter accepts the cast.

```python
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def cast(X, Y):
    offs = tl.arange(0, 16)
    tl.store(Y + offs, tl.load(X + offs).to(Y.dtype.element_ty))


x = torch.full((16, ), 1.5, device="cuda").to(torch.float8_e5m2)
y = torch.zeros(16, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float8_e4m3fn)
cast[(1, )](x, y)
print(y.float()[0].item())
```

```
ElementwiseOpToLLVM.cpp:425: ... FpToFpOpConversion::createDestOps(...): Assertion `roundingMode.has_value() && "Rounding mode must be specified for convertsions to fp8"' failed.
...
RuntimeError: PassManager::run failed
```

Expected `1.5`.

`cast` in `python/triton/language/semantic.py` sets a default rounding mode only for casts to a narrower type, and raises if `fp_downcast_rounding` is passed for any other cast. The fp8 to fp8 `tt.fp_to_fp` therefore has no rounding mode, and `FpToFpOpConversion` (`third_party/nvidia/lib/TritonNVIDIAGPUToLLVM/ElementwiseOpToLLVM.cpp`) asserts that conversions to fp8 have one. Both directions can lose information (e5m2 to e4m3 can overflow, e4m3 to e5m2 drops a mantissa bit), so the cast does need a rounding mode.

### Environment details

Triton: main @ 41846bc965
GPU: NVIDIA RTX 4090 (sm_89), driver 570 / CUDA 12.8
Build: from source, with assertions enabled
score_reasons: 匹配 Serving 与评测、Kernel 与正确性
