items.title: [Performance]: Kimi K3 fused attention-residual epilogue is skipped for speculative verify steps (token ceiling defaults to 1)
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

In `modeling_kimi_linear.py`, `_apply_attn_res_add_and_rmsnorm()` / `_apply_attn_res_and_rmsnorm()` take the fused ops (`trtllm::attn_res_add_rmsnorm_fwd`, `trtllm::attn_res_rmsnorm_fwd`) only for `M <= _FUSED_ATTN_RES_MAX_TOKENS`. With the default `KIMI_K3_ATTN_RES_TOPOLOGY=per_token`, `_read_fused_attn_res_max_tokens()` resolves the ceiling to 1, so only single-token decode steps are fused. A speculative-decoding verify step (e.g. 1 + 7 draft tokens, M = 8 per rank) and any decode batch of more than one request fall back to torch add + `attn_res_fwd` + RMSNorm at every layer: in an nsys trace of one Kimi K3 + DSpark verify step that is about 186 `attn_res` + 188 RMSNorm + ~270 add kernels. Under `split`, the same per-token kernels are already used up to 32 tokens ("the top of the measured range").

Measured on SM107 (single GPU, model helper functions in a CUDA graph, M = 8, N = 2..12 snapshots):

| op | unfused | fused |
|---|---|---|
| add + attn_res + RMSNorm | 6.6-9.0 us | 3.4-4.3 us |
| attn_res + RMSNorm | 5.3-7.7 us | 3.0-4.2 us |

M = 16 is the same. The updated prefix is bit-identical; the normalized output differs from the unfused chain by 2-25 bf16 ulps (max abs 0.016-0.031 at |x| ~ 4), the same as the fused path that M = 1 decode already uses by default.

End to end (Kimi K3 + DSpark, 7 drafts, 8 GPUs over 2 nodes, SM107, single request) with `KIMI_K3_FUSED_ATTN_RES_MAX_TOKENS=32`, together with a small unrelated double-add fusion worth about 0.1 ms: decode step -0.59 ms at 2K context, -0.53 ms at 32K and 128K. Speculative acceptance unchanged over ~825 requests; our quality checks unchanged apart from one numerics-sensitive item that also flips between cold starts.

items.title: Speedup build cu files
items.author: lexasub
items.body_excerpt:
Compiling llama.cpp can be an extremely slow process, primarily due to the .cu files. These CUDA source files often take a significant amount of time to compile, and it’s unclear whether all of them need to be compiled for every specific build configuration. Ideally, if it’s possible to avoid compiling unnecessary .cu files based on conditional features or specific hardware capabilities, it would be great to have an option to easily disable unused components during the build process.

Unfortunately, we have no control over NVIDIA’s compiler (nvcc), which is a major factor in this bottleneck. However, there might be some ways to optimize the build process:

Splitting .cu Files: If the .cu files are large and contain multiple independent parts, breaking them into smaller chunks could potentially speed up the compilation process. This approach would allow the compiler to handle smaller units of work, which could reduce memory usage and improve parallelism during compilation.

Selective Compilation: Introducing build flags or configuration options to exclude unnecessary .cu files for specific builds could save time and resources. For example, if certain features or hardware-specific optimizations are not required, those parts of the code could be skipped during compilation.

Precompiled Objects: If certain .cu files don’t change often, precompiling them into object files and reusing them across builds could reduce compilation time.

Parallel Compilation: Ensuring that the build process takes full advantage of all available CPU cores (e.g., using ninja -j with an appropriate number of jobs) can help speed up the process, especially on multi-core systems.

That said, on lower-end hardware, such as dual-core CPUs, the compilation process will inevitably be slower(30m-1h compilation), and the memory usage during the build can be significant. While it’s tempting to try and optimize the .cu files further, this can be a risky and unstable path, as it may introduce bugs or compatibility issues.

For now, the best approach might be to explore splitting or modularizing the .cu files and adding build options for conditional compilation. If anyone has additional ideas or proven methods to improve the performance of CUDA file compilation, they would be highly valuable for the community.

items.title: json-schema-to-grammar: `enum`/`const` discard sibling constraints, so the grammar admits enum members the schema rejects
items.author: amitabhsh
items.body_excerpt:
### What happens

When a subschema has `enum` (or `const`) next to other constraints, the grammar
admits every enum member, including members those other constraints rule out.
JSON Schema requires a value to satisfy *all* keywords in a subschema, so those
members are invalid.

```json
{"type": "string", "pattern": "^[A-Z]{3}$", "enum": ["ABC", "abc"]}
```

Generated grammar:

```
root ::= ("\"ABC\"" | "\"abc\"")
```

The grammar accepts `"abc"`, which the schema rejects because it fails the
`pattern`. The same thing happens with numeric bounds:

```json
{"type": "integer", "minimum": 0, "maximum": 100, "enum": [5, 500]}
```

```
root ::= ("5" | "500")
```

The grammar accepts `500`, which breaks `maximum: 100`.

### Why

`visit()` dispatches on `schema.kind()`. A subschema with `enum` becomes
`KIND_ENUM`, and one with `const` becomes `KIND_CONST`. Those branches emit an
alternation of the literal values and return, so the `pattern`, length and bound
fields of that same subschema never take part (master `eb1e1f495f`, lines
888–896). No warning is emitted.

### Suggested fix

This one is cheap to fix exactly. The enum is a finite list, so filter it: keep
only the members that validate against the rest of the subschema, which means
the `type`, `pattern`, length, bounds and `multipleOf` checks the converter
already knows how to read. If no members are left, the schema is
unsatisfiable, and that can be reported as an error. The `const` case is the
same with a one-element list.

### How common it is

Enums with a sibling `pattern` or `maxLength` are common in hand-written and
generated schemas, where an enum is often added to an existing string field.
In a fuzzed corpus of 200 schemas, a grammar-constrained `qwen2.5:1.5b` emitted
a sibling-violating enum member on 13 of 90 such instances. On constraints the
grammar did encode, it produced zero violations.

### Environment

- llama.cpp `common/json-schema-to-grammar.cpp` at `eb1e1f495f` (read
  2026-10-17). Reproduced on the llama-server vendored in Ollama 0.40.5.
- XGrammar 0.2.8 and outlines-core 0.2.14 have the same behaviour. llguidance
  1.9.1 filters correctly.

items.title: [RFC] Review MC_USE_TENT=1 gaps for classic TE callers
items.author: staryxchen
items.body_excerpt:
## How this list was produced

Started as a static pass over:

- the C++ shim (`mooncake-transfer-engine/src/transfer_engine.cpp`, `use_tent_` branches)
- the Python wrapper (`mooncake-integration/transfer_engine/transfer_engine_py.cpp`)
- inference-engine call sites that use `mooncake.engine.TransferEngine`

Local runtime (2026-09-10, installed TENT wheel, 1P1D PD) then confirmed
some items and left others unverified. Status below is as of **2026-09-17**
(`origin/main` `c4d632888b`). Please still reproduce on your tree before
treating a remaining item as confirmed.

## Why the compatibility layer

We are wiring inference engines to TENT's **native** APIs, but that work is
not finished. Until it is, we use the classic TE compatibility layer
(`MC_USE_TENT=1`) to validate TENT **runtime** stability against existing
callers (PD disaggregation and others). This RFC tracks gaps in that layer.
It is not the native-API migration itself.

## Summary

`MC_USE_TENT=1` (and `MC_USE_TEV1=1`) is meant to run existing
`mooncake::TransferEngine` / `mooncake.engine.TransferEngine` code on the TENT
runtime. Register + sync submit/poll are wired up enough for PD KV transfer.

PD happy path **works** under `MC_USE_TENT=1` (local 1P1D Qwen3-4B
`/generate` 200). This RFC is not a claim that PD is broken today.

Most of the original P0/P1/P2 shim holes now have merged PRs. What is still
open is protocol pinning for `efa`/`ascend`, Python sync/poll semantics, and
`installTransport()` returning `nullptr` for classic C/Go/EFA callers.

If you find a **new** compatibility-layer issue, please report it on this
issue. We will add it to the work-item list.

## Non-goals

- Landing inference-engine (or Mooncake Store) native-API migration in this RFC
  (that work is separate and in progress, e.g. #4070).
- Teaching applications to `installTransport` under TENT. Making the shim
  honor the classic `Transport*` contract so existing callers do not treat a
  successful TENT init as failure **is** in scope (`P1-install-transport`).
- Changing TENT runtime scheduling / failover policy.

## Work items

Priority is "if the reading holds, impact is high" — not "already on fire".

| ID | Problem | Difficulty | PR | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P0-send_probe | Python `send_probe` SIGSEGV (`getMetadata()` is null) | M | #4081, follow-up #4115 | **done** |
| P0-stale-handle | Transfer failure may keep a dead peer's cached handle (`CheckSegmentStatus` was always OK) | M | #4109 | **partial** |
| P0-device-filter | `initialize(device=...)` still opened all HCAs | M | #4028 | **done** |
| P0-force-tcp | `MC_FORCE_TCP=1` / `protocol=tcp` may still select RDMA | M | #4027, follow-up #4113 | **done** |
| P0-efa-ascend | `protocol=efa\|ascend` may no-op or look successful without that transport | H | — | **open** |
| P1-sync-status | Python `transferSync` retry / `CANCELED` handling may not match TENT failover | S–M | — | **open** |
| P1-error-codes | Shim returned TENT `Status::Code` (non-negative); classic callers expect `ERR_*` | M | #4139 | **done** |
| P1-request-options | `priority` / `remote_accessible` were dropped at the shim | M | #4114 | **done** |
| P2-first-buffer | `getFirstBufferAddress` also called `getMetadata()` (same null deref as `send_probe`) | S | #4138 | **done** |
| P1-install-transport | TENT `installTransport()` returns `nullptr`; classic C/Go/EFA callers treat that as install failure | M | — | **open** |

### Residuals on landed items

These do not reopen the row, but they are not "the original hole is gone with no leftover":

- **P0-send_probe.** Python no longer dereferences `getMetadata()`. #4081 closed the segment after probing, which invalidated a handle already stored in Python `handle_map_`; #4115 stopped closing it. C++ `getMetadata()` is still `nullptr` under TENT — any remaining `getMetadata()->sendProbe` caller will still crash.
- **P0-stale-handle.** `CheckSegmentStatus` now probes via `probePeerAliveByID`. Python only calls it when **`submitTransfer` fails**. Peer death that shows up as `getTransferStatus` `FAILED` / `TIMEOUT` still leaves `handle_map_` intact. That leftover belongs with **P1-sync-status**. The unit test covers an never-opened handle, not a still-mapped handle whose RPC probe fails.
- **P0-force-tcp.** #4113 makes `forceTcp()` disable HP TCP so a config with both enabled does not fail init.
- **P1-error-codes.** Integer-returning APIs go through `tentToClassicError()`. `submitTransfer` still wraps TENT failures as `Status::Context(...)`. No in-tree test that failed on main and passed after (#4139 checklist).
- **P1-request-options.** Shim forwards `remote_accessible` → TENT perms and `TransferRequest::priority` on submit. Python `transferSync` does not set `priority` (default MEDIUM). No in-tree red/green test (#4114 checklist).

### Still open

- **P0-efa-ascend.** `init(..., protocol)` is now forwarded, but the TENT branch only special-cases `"tcp"`. `"efa"` / `"ascend"` do not pin those transports. On `USE_EFA` / `USE_CXI` Python builds, `initialize` still calls `installTransport()` after init; under TENT that returns `nullptr` and `initialize` returns `-1`. #4122 is classic TE Ascend Direct selection, not this shim item.
- **P1-sync-status.** `transferSync` still retries `numContexts()+1` times; under TENT `numContexts()` is hardcoded `1`. The poll loop handles `COMPLETED` / `FAILED` / `TIMEOUT` only — not `CANCELED` — and does not evict the cached handle on poll failure.
- **P1-install-transport.** Added from @chlins (2026-09-14). The TENT branch logs `"installTransport not used by TENT"` and returns `nullptr`. Classic contract: `nullptr` means install failed. Store already skips this via `isUsingTent()` (#2596). C / Go (`transfer_engine_c.h`) and EFA/CXI Python do not. Proposed fix A (TENT returns a non-null sentinel; in-tree callers only null-check) is preferred over gating every caller (B) or fixing only the C shim (C). Waiting on TENT owners (@alogfans) before a PR. R

items.title: torch.special.bessel_j0 / bessel_j1 / bessel_y0 lose ~9 significant digits in float64: the Cephes p1evl denominators drop their implied leading 1
items.author: the-Shallow
items.body_excerpt:
Description

The CPU implementations of `torch.special.bessel_j0`, `bessel_j1` and `bessel_y0` are ports of Cephes
`j0.c`, `j1.c`, `y0.c`. Cephes evaluates the rational approximations' denominators with `p1evl`, which
treats the coefficient array as a monic polynomial (an implied leading coefficient of 1). The ports
evaluate those denominators with a plain Horner loop seeded at 0, i.e. one degree too low. The results
are wrong by up to ~1e-6 relative in float64 (about 9 lost digits), and the functions jump at the internal
branch point x = 5.

### Steps to reproduce

```python
import mpmath, torch
mpmath.mp.dps = 40
for f, ref, x in [(torch.special.bessel_y0, lambda v: mpmath.bessely(0, v), 5.004),
                  (torch.special.bessel_j1, lambda v: mpmath.besselj(1, v), 7.0),
                  (torch.special.bessel_j0, lambda v: mpmath.besselj(0, v), 5.01)]:
    got = f(torch.tensor(x, dtype=torch.float64)).item()
    want = float(ref(mpmath.mpf(x)))
    print(f.__name__, x, got, want, abs(got - want) / abs(want))
# relative errors ~7e-7, 6e-6, 2e-6 instead of ~1e-15
```

Expected

Relative error near double-precision rounding (~1e-15), as Cephes and `scipy.special.j0/j1/y0` give.



### Versions

Environment

PyTorch 2.14.0 (the latest release, CPU wheel) and 2.12.0, Python 3.12, Ubuntu 24.04, x86_64

cc @mruberry @kshitij12345

items.title: [Bug]: Grouped MLA generation kernels read out of bounds at batch > 1: the MLA generation path never sets cumSeqLensQPtr / cumSeqLensKvPtr
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

SM107, TensorRT-LLM main (C++ attention op, trtllm-gen FMHA, BF16 MLA generation with HQk 576 / HV 512, paged KV with 32 tokens per page).

### Who can help?

@farazkh80 (#15009) @pengbowang-nv

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [x] My own modified scripts

### Reproduction

`AttentionOp` fills `TllmGenFmhaRunnerParams` for MLA generation (`cpp/tensorrt_llm/common/attentionOp.cpp`, the trtllm-gen MLA generation branch) with `seqLensKvPtr = params.cache_seq_lens`, but it never sets `cumSeqLensQPtr` or `cumSeqLensKvPtr`. The `SwapsAbForGen` kernels selected today do not read them, so nothing fails on main.

The grouped tokens x heads MLA generation kernels (`...VarSeqQ64Kv128{Static,Persistent}GroupedKeepsAbForGen`, selected when `FmhaOptions::mSelectsGroupedMla` is set, as #15009 proposed) do read them. With `mSelectsGroupedMla = true` and the runner parameters exactly as `AttentionOp` builds them:

- In a standalone `TllmGenFmhaRunner` microbenchmark (Kimi K3 MLA decode shape with MTP, KV length 64): batch 1 output is correct, but batch 4 and batch 16 are wrong (output sums -209.5 and -218.6, expected -243.7). Passing correct `cumSeqLensQ = [0, T, 2T, ...]` and `cumSeqLensKv = prefix sum of seqLensKv` makes all batch sizes match the non-grouped kernel.
- In serving (Kimi K3 with MTP, CUDA graphs), capture of the batch-4 graph fails with `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_ADDRESS` right after the grouped cubin is loaded. Captures of batches 5..16 happened to succeed.

#15009 only measured batch 1, where the offsets are never needed, which may be why this did not show up there.

### Expected behavior

Every kernel that the MLA generation path can select gets the metadata it reads. Either `AttentionOp` provides `cumSeqLensQPtr` / `cumSeqLensKvPtr` whenever a grouped MLA generation kernel can be selected, or the selection refuses grouped kernels when they are absent.

### actual behavior

With grouped selection enabled, batch > 1 MLA generation reads past the end of its offsets: the output is silently wrong or there is an illegal address.

### additional notes

Workaround we validated on SM107 (Kimi K3 serving, all graph batch sizes 1..16, unchanged accuracy): when grouped selection is enabled and batch > 1, `AttentionOp` launches a one-CTA kernel per MLA generation call. That kernel writes `cumSeqLensQ[i] = i * maxSeqLenQ` and `cumSeqLensKv` = the prefix sum of `cache_seq_lens` into a device buffer that is allocated before graph capture, and passes both pointers to the runner. Batch 1 skips the kernel. I can turn this into a PR together with whatever change enables grouped MLA selection, or separately behind the same switch, whichever maintainers prefer.

Related: the grouped MLA generation cubins are also registered with a mask type that does not match their names (#20376), the NVRTC fallback fails for these kernels on SM107 (#20377), and with FP8 KV the grouped E4M3 cubins hang when heads per rank do not divide 64 (#20382).

items.title: [Performance] CuTe DSL MLA FP8-KV decode kernel slower at long KV after #19338
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

Since #19338 (9257aaefbb, "Upgrade Blackwell cuteDSL MLA kernel for packed q heads and compact input"), the CuTe DSL
FP8-KV MLA decode kernel (`mla_decode_fp8.py`, used by `trtllm::cute_dsl_mla_decode_fp8_blackwell`) is **10–30% slower at
long KV** for a small number of heads per rank, whenever the split-KV grid fills the GPU. The output is unchanged
(bit-identical for the same split plan). The BF16 kernel (`mla_decode_fp16.py`) has no such regression, and the
packed-q target of #19338 (H 96, q 8) does get faster.

## Setup

- Blackwell (SM10x) GPU, CUDA graphs.
- Before: bcdc2d5aaf (its `mla_decode_fp8.py` is byte-identical to 9257aaefbb~1). After: e88d19ca3b (current main).
- MLA decode geometry: latent 512 + rope 64, page size 32, FP8 E4M3 KV / Q, BF16 output, 12 heads per rank (TP8 of a
  96-head model like the one in #19338), q = 1 and q = 8 (MTP verify), KV 128K and 1M tokens, batch 1–16.

## Repro 1: kernel only, the module's own benchmark `run()`

Same arguments on both builds: q = 1 (no folding / packing involved), uniform `split_kv` so that `B * split_kv` is about
one wave of 2-CTA clusters, `CUTEDSL_BENCH_CUDA_GRAPH=1`, `skip_ref_check`.

<details><summary>fp8_standalone.py</summary>

```python
import inspect, os
import cutlass
from tensorrt_llm._torch.cute_dsl_kernels.blackwell.attention.mla import mla_decode_fp8 as k

os.environ.setdefault("CUTEDSL_BENCH_CUDA_GRAPH", "1")
params = inspect.signature(k.run).parameters
for L in (131072, 1048576):
    for B, split in [(1, 32), (2, 32), (4, 25), (8, 12), (16, 6)]:
        kw = dict(batch_size=B, seq_len_q=1, seq_len_k=L, num_heads=12, latent_dim=512, rope_dim=64,
                  in_dtype=cutlass.Float8E4M3FN, out_dtype=cutlass.BFloat16, acc_dtype=cutlass.Float32,
                  lse_dtype=cutlass.Float32, mma_qk_tiler_mn=(128, 128), mma_pv_tiler_mn=(128, 256),
                  split_kv=split, is_persistent=False, is_var_seq=False, is_var_split_kv=False, page_size=32,
                  softmax_scale=0.0722, output_scale=1.0, skip_correction_threshold=0.0, tolerance=1e-2,
                  warmup_iterations=5, iterations=30, skip_ref_check=True, use_cold_l2=False)
        # arguments added after #19338
        for n, d in dict(is_var_q=False, query_lens=None, emit_softmax_stats=False, kv_bounds=None).items():
            if n in params:
                kw[n] = d
        print(f"B{B} L{L} split{split}: {k.run(**kw):.1f} us")
```
</details>

H 12, q 1 (mean of 2 runs, µs):

| KV | B (split) | before | after | |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 128K | 1 (32) | 41.2 | 39.5 | −4% |
| 128K | 2 (32) | 43.7 | 43.8 | 0% |
| 128K | 4 (25) | 54.2 | 59.1 | +9% |
| 128K | 8 (12) | 86.4 | 97.0 | +12% |
| 128K | 16 (6) | 151.7 | 170.8 | +13% |
| 1M | 1 (32) | 199.1 | 200.8 | +1% |
| 1M | 2 (32) | 201.4 | 204.9 | +2% |
| 1M | 4 (25) | 286.5 | 334.7 | +17% |
| 1M | 8 (12) | 555.8 | 591.7 | +6% |
| 1M | 16 (6) | 1095.5 | 1342.8 | +23% |

With 32–64 clusters (B 1–2, split 32) the two kernels are on par; with about one full wave the new kernel is slower.

## Repro 2: same runner, same plan, only the kernel swapped

On current main, through `CuteDSLNVMlaDecodeBlackwellRunner` with a per-request split plan (`block_split_kvs` from

items.title: [Bug]: trtllm-gen FMHA JIT requires /usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc (ignores CUDA_HOME / PATH) even with NVRTC, failing MLA generation and executor warmup when the toolkit lives elsewhere
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- TensorRT-LLM main @ e88d19ca3b, PyTorch backend, `TrtllmAttention`
- Any container or host where the CUDA toolkit is not at `/usr/local/cuda`, for example conda/pixi environments. `CUDA_HOME` is set, and `nvcc` is on `PATH`.
- Seen on SM107. The code path (trtllm-gen FMHA NVRTC JIT) is not architecture-specific.

### Who can help?

Same module as #20507 (`fmha/lib/<arch>/libTrtLlmGen.a`, the prebuilt trtllm-gen archive). Related: #12612 (trtllm-gen FMHA JIT), #14851 (JIT warmup).

### Reproduction

Any configuration where a trtllm-gen FMHA kernel takes the NVRTC path, for example MLA generation. The unit test is enough:

```bash
# In a TensorRT-LLM container built from main, as root: move the toolkit away from /usr/local/cuda
mv /usr/local/cuda /usr/local/cuda-real
export CUDA_HOME=/usr/local/cuda-real
export PATH=$CUDA_HOME/bin:$PATH
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=${LD_LIBRARY_PATH//\/usr\/local\/cuda/$CUDA_HOME}
which nvcc && nvcc --version | tail -1          # nvcc is found
cd tests/unittest && pytest -q _torch/attention/test_attention_mla.py
```

Result: 28 failed, 68 passed. Each failure is:

```
[E] [GenCtx.cpp:68]: Cannot parse NVCC version from /usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc. Output:
sh: 1: /usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc: not found
[E] [FmhaInterface.cpp:426]: Error parsing configs: Cannot parse NVCC version from /usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc. Output:
...
RuntimeError: Error parsing configs: Cannot parse NVCC version from /usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc.
```

The printed kernel config has `"usesNvRtc": true`.

In serving, the same error comes from the trtllm-gen FMHA JIT warmup (`Running TRTLLM-Gen FMHA JIT warmup`). The first MLA generation warmup step fails on every rank, and executor creation fails with `Failed to initialize executor on rank 0: Error parsing configs: Cannot parse NVCC version from /usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc`.

### Expected behavior

The JIT uses the toolkit the environment points to (`CUDA_HOME`, or `nvcc` on `PATH`). Better, it does not need `nvcc` at all when it compiles with NVRTC.

### Actual behavior

`libTrtLlmGen.a` (`GenCtx.cpp`) runs `/usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc --version` and parses `release X.Y` from the output. That path is the default of the `GenCfg` `nvccPath` field, and TensorRT-LLM's generated config (`populateJsonConfig` in `fmha/fmhaKernels.h`) does not set it. The version query does not consult `CUDA_HOME`, `CUDA_PATH` or `PATH`: `GenCtx.cpp.o` in the archive does not call `getenv` and contains none of those names. This happens with `usesNvRtc: true`, so it applies even though the kernel is compiled by NVRTC.

I checked what the JIT actually needs from `nvcc`, on the same test file, with `CUDA_HOME` set and the toolkit outside `/usr/local/cuda` in all three runs:

| `/usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc` | result |
|---|---|
| absent | 28 failed, 68 passed (140 × `nvcc: not found`) |
| symlink to the real `nvcc` | 96 passed |
| stub that answers only `--version` (via the real `nvcc`), logs every call, and fails on anything else | 96 passed; the stub was called once, with `--version` only |

So `nvcc` is needed only for the version query. All compilation goes through NVRTC.

### Additional notes

Suggested fix, in the trtllm-gen archive (`GenCtx`), in order of preference:

1. When `usesNvRtc` is set, take the version from NVRTC (`nvrtcVersion`, which the archive already references) and do not require `nvcc`.
2. Otherwise resolve `nvcc` in this order: an explicit `nvccPath`, then `$CUDA_HOME/bin/nvcc`, then `$CUDA_PATH/bin/nvcc`, then `nvcc` on `PATH`, and only then `/usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc`. Report the path that was tried in the error.

Possible TensorRT-LLM-side stopgap until the archive is refreshed: emit `"nvccPath"` in `populateJsonConfig`, resolved as in item 2. I have not verified that the archive honors the field when it is set from the generated config; I only see the field name next to its default in the archive's string table.

Workaround for affected environments: provide `/usr/local/cuda/bin/nvcc`, for example a symlink to the real toolkit.

What is verified: the table above, on SM107 with a build of main at e88d19ca3b in a container whose toolkit is not under `/usr/local/cuda`. I have not run the "rename `/usr/local/cuda`" variant in an official image, but it recreates the same condition.

Cross-reference #20507: the serving warmup goes through `warmupOneKernel`, and the config printed with this error there has `"smVersion": "107a"`. That is the path #20507 describes, which hands `Sm107a` to the archive without the `Sm100f` rewrite that `run()` applies. The unit-test failures above go through `run()` and print `"smVersion": "100f"`.

items.title: KV event decoder drops group_idx/medium/lora_name, breaking prefix matching for hybrid and multi-tier models
items.author: Jeffwan
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

Our ZMQ decoder reads only the first four positional fields of vLLM's `BlockStored` (block_hashes, parent_block_hash, token_ids, block_size) and drops the rest. Upstream `BlockStored` (`vllm/distributed/kv_events.py`) now also carries `medium`, `lora_name`, `extra_keys`, and `group_idx`. Two of these affect correctness:

- `group_idx`: hybrid-attention models (sliding-window + full layers — Gemma, Ministral, Llama-4) hash the same token range into different KV-cache groups. Collapsing all groups into one hash space can produce false prefix matches.
- `medium`: with KV offloading, blocks live on CPU/remote tiers, but we count every block as a GPU hit, so prefix routing over-credits pods that only hold the prefix on a slower tier.

`lora_name` is also the canonical adapter id (`lora_id` is deprecated upstream); `prefix_cache.go` currently passes `loraID=-1` everywhere, so adapters aren't isolated in the index.

Relevant: `pkg/cache/kvcache/msgpack_decoder.go` (`parseEventArray`), `pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/prefix_cache.go`.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Serve a hybrid-attention model (e.g. `google/gemma-2-9b-it`) with `--kv-events-config` enabled.
2. Send shared-prefix traffic across ≥2 replicas with the kv-event prefix router.
3. Observe requests routed to pods that don't actually have a GPU prefix hit.

### Expected behavior

Decoder parses `group_idx`/`medium`/`lora_name`; the index keys prefix entries by `(model, lora_name, group_idx)` and scores non-GPU mediums lower.

### Environment

AIBrix: main · vLLM: main (kv-events enabled).

items.title: [Feature]: Support NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 ASR Streaming (nemotron-3.5-asr-streaming-0.6b)
items.author: robin-bially
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

NVIDIA recently released **Nemotron 3.5 ASR Streaming** ([nemotron-3.5-asr-streaming-0.6b](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/nemotron-3.5-asr-streaming-0.6b)), a 600M-parameter multilingual streaming ASR model under the OpenMDW-1.1 license.

Key features:
- **Native streaming architecture** with Cache-Aware FastConformer-RNNT, supporting configurable chunk sizes from 80ms to 1120ms
- **35 languages** (19 transcription-ready + 13 broad-coverage + 8 adaptation-ready), including German, English, French, Spanish, Japanese, Korean, etc.
- **Automatic language detection** via `target_lang=auto`
- **Punctuation & capitalization** built-in
- On a single H100: **240 concurrent streams at 80ms chunk**, ~17x more than Parakeet RNNT 1.1B

This would be a great addition to vLLM's supported ASR models, complementing the existing Voxtral Realtime and Qwen3-ASR support. The model is already available in HuggingFace Transformers (`AutoModelForRNNT`) and NVIDIA NeMo.

### Alternatives

Currently, the only open-source streaming ASR options in vLLM are:
- **Voxtral Realtime (4B)** — high VRAM due to persistent encoder KV-cache, limiting concurrent streams
- **Qwen3-ASR (0.6B/1.7B)** — segment-based (5s chunks), higher latency

Nemotron 3.5 would fill the gap for a lightweight, truly native streaming model with low latency and high throughput.

### Additional context

- HuggingFace: https://huggingface.co/nvidia/nemotron-3.5-asr-streaming-0.6b
- Architecture: FastConformer-CacheAware-RNNT with language-ID prompt conditioning
- Primary framework: NeMo, with Transformers support added
- Release date: June 4, 2026

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the documentation page, which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Bug]: Breakable prefill CUDA graphs replay corrupted outputs for some buckets: the shared output buffer is only weakly referenced
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- TensorRT-LLM main @ acb83ac268, PyTorch backend, breakable prefill CUDA graphs (BCG, `BreakableCUDAGraphRunner`)
- Reproduced on an SM107 GPU, with torch 2.14. The bug is in Python-side memory ownership and does not depend on the model or the GPU.

### Who can help?

Authors and reviewers of #16609 (BCG in prefill).

### Reproduction

`BreakableCUDAGraphRunner.capture_output()` routes every bucket's body output through the largest bucket's output buffer. The first (largest) capture returns its output as `_shared_output`, and every later capture adds `self._shared_output[:num_tokens].copy_(output[:num_tokens])` to its graph. However, `_shared_output` is stored as `make_weak_ref(output)`, and nothing else holds that tensor: `_outputs[n]` is a weak ref too, and the original tensor goes out of scope after the capture. Its blocks are therefore free in the shared graph memory pool, so a later capture can allocate its own temporaries and body output on them.

When a later bucket's body output lands at an offset inside `_shared_output`, its final `copy_` reads and writes overlapping memory. The tensors have different storages, so PyTorch's overlap check does not catch this. Every replay of that bucket then returns a corrupted hidden state, while eager execution of the same inputs is correct.

Minimal reproduction: no model is needed. Each bucket is captured in descending order, then replayed and compared bitwise with eager:

```python
import torch
from torch import nn
from tensorrt_llm._torch.pyexecutor.breakable_cuda_graph_runner import BreakableCUDAGraphRunner

hidden, narrow, buckets = 1024, 256, (2048, 1536, 1024, 512)

class Body(nn.Module):
    def forward(self, value):
        scaled = value[:, :narrow] * 2   # narrow temporary allocated before the output
        output = value * 3
        output[:, :narrow] += scaled
        return output

body = Body().cuda()
runner = BreakableCUDAGraphRunner(body)
static_input = torch.zeros(max(buckets), hidden, device="cuda")
active = {}

def engine_forward():
    value = static_input[: active["n"]]
    if runner.is_capturing:
        return runner.capture_model_body(lambda: body(value))
    return body(value)

for n in buckets:
    active["n"] = n
    runner.capture(n, engine_forward)

for n in buckets:
    static_input.normal_()
    expected = body(static_input[:n])
    active["n"] = n
    replayed = runner.execute(n, engine_forward)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    print(n, torch.equal(replayed, expected), (replayed - expected).abs().max().item())
```

On main, buckets 1536 and 1024 replay wrong on every replay; buckets 2048 and 512 are correct. Logging the pointers shows that the body outputs of 1536 and 1024 start 0.5 MiB and 2 MiB below `_shared_output` and overlap it. The output of 512 ends exactly where `_shared_output` begins. I also ran the same pattern with other shapes and with bf16, three processes each and three replay rounds per process. Every bucket whose output overlapped failed on every replay, and no other bucket failed.

We first saw this on a real model with the default prefill bucket list up to 8192 tokens. One large bucket (7168, or 6144 under a different capture order) overlapped the shared output by tens of MiB. Every replay of that bucket returned a wrong hidden state: the max |diff| against eager was the size of the largest reference value. All other buckets were bitwise exact. Whether a bucket overlaps depends on allocation order, so smaller bucket lists may or may not be affected.

### Expected behavior

Every captured bucket replays bitwise identical to eager execution with the same padded inputs.

### Actual behavior

Buckets whose body output is placed on the shared output buffer return corrupted outputs on every replay. Nothing reports an error.

### Additional notes

Fix: keep a strong reference to the first capture's output in `capture_output()`, i.e. `self._shared_output = output` instead of `make_weak_ref(output)`. `clear()` and the failure path of the first capture already reset it. The extra memory is one output tensor of the largest bucket, which stays allocated for the life of the graphs. In our case that was about 0.11 GiB for an 8192-token bucket and about 7 MiB for a 512-token bucket. With that change, the reproduction above and our model-level check, which compares all 24 buckets bitwise and runs a 300-step random replay soak, show no mismatch.

I have a branch with the fix and a unit test, which captures several buckets and compares each replay with eager, bitwise, in `tests/unittest/_torch/executor/test_breakable_cuda_graph.py`. On main the new test fails for both of its parametrizations; with the fix both pass. I will open the PR when I can.

items.title: [Roadmap]Fast Engine Recovery: Weight Cache Daemon
items.author: liusy58
items.body_excerpt:
# [Roadmap] Fast Engine Recovery: Weight Cache Daemon 
@liusy58 @QiuMike @alexnails 
Phase 1 landed in #27139 — a per-rank daemon holds post-quantized weights and serves them over CUDA IPC; weight load drops from ~306–327s to <1s on Qwen3-235B FP8 ([blog](https://www.lmsys.org/blog/2026-08-21-sglang-fast-recovery)). This issue tracks the next steps. Contributions and feedback are welcome.

Related: #27052 (Fast Recovery framework), #27310 (GPU Memory Service / VMM)

Goals: <10s cold restart and <1s warm standby switch; broaden model & quant coverage; make the cache outlive the daemon; make resident weights usable beyond the one GPU they sit on.

Where Phase 1 stands: TP + PP, single-node and multi-node launch (each node spawns its share of ranks and joins one dist group), zero-copy IPC per GPU, unquantized + block-wise FP8. Not yet: cross-node daemon coordination / failover, DP & EP shard keying, spec-decoding draft models, weight update / sleep-wake, cache surviving daemon death.

## Model & quantization coverage

- [ ] parity harness — disk-load vs daemon-load `state_dict` diff (names / shape / dtype / stride / byte hash) + short GSM8K gate; required evidence for every new allowlist entry
- [ ] carry post-processing metadata in the manifest (final shape/stride, layout tag, whitelisted module attrs) instead of reproducing `process_weights_after_loading` on a meta-init model — this is what blocks most quant methods today
- [ ] quant methods: per-tensor fp8 / w8a8 int8 / mxfp8 / nvfp4 / compressed-tensors / awq / gptq-marlin #32398 
- [ ] archs: MoE (DeepSeek V3/V4, Ling, Kimi K3) / hybrid linear attention / multimodal (vision tower + projector) / LoRA base weights https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/33684
- [ ] MTP & EAGLE draft models (per-rank draft daemon), removing the `--speculative-algorithm` rejection in `server_args.py` #32744
- [ ] generic post-map rebuild hook to replace the hardcoded `_rebuild_stale_views`; make tied storages, param→buffer flips and non-persistent buffers explicit in the manifest
- [ ] publish the support matrix in docs; unsupported combinations keep hard-erroring (no silent wrong numerics)

## Transport: CUDA VMM shareable handles (#27310 §4.2)



- [ ] `vmm_fd` backend (skeleton already in `weight_cache/transport.py`): `cuMemCreate` + FD handles over `SCM_RIGHTS`, VA reservation on import, `torch_ipc` stays the fallback, `--weight-cache-transport {auto,torch_ipc,vmm_fd}` #33279
- [ ] `mooncake` backend https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/36293


## Weight update without reload

- [ ] epoch handoff on stable VAs: readers unmap → writer commits → readers remap at the same VAs, so captured CUDA graphs stay valid
- [ ] daemon as the weight delivery agent for trainer pushes (NCCL/RDMA); un-gate the `update_weights_*` rejections in `weight_updater.py`
- [ ] colocated RL: engine itself takes the writer role, same protocol, no daemon in the loop

## Multi-instance & cross-GPU sharing

- [ ] key the cache by physical GPU UUID + config fingerprint (plus optional `--weight-cache-namespace`) under a configurable runtime dir. Today the socket is `/tmp/sglang_weight_cache_rank{global_rank}.sock`, so 2× tp=4 on one 8-GPU node collide and rank 0 of the second instance attaches to the GPU 0 daemon
- [ ] discovery: replace static socket paths with a lightweight registry (file-based dir, optionally etcd) so an engine rank selects a daemon by `CacheConfig` match rather than by process rank, and locates daemons across nodes without a manual `--weight-cache-socket`
- [ ] `--weight-cache-peer-copy` — when no daemon holds the shard on the local GPU, `cudaMemcpyPeerAsync` it from a peer-GPU daemon (NVLink-domain check, chunked on a low-priority stream, bandwidth cap so a serving neighbour is not disturbed). 1× memory per instance, sub-second over NVLink vs ~300s from disk
- [ ] preference order local zero-copy > peer copy > disk, reported per rank
- [ ] fleet fill: a daemon fills itself from a peer daemon instead of disk (P2P on-node, NCCL/RDMA cross-node), so a fleet cold start pays one disk read per shard group — the real bottleneck for 1T+ models on shared FS; align with the checkpoint-engine broadcast path
- [ ] out of scope for now: resharding across TP/EP topologies (tp=4 daemon → tp=8 engine)

## Multi-node, DP & EP

- [ ] primary–secondary daemon coordination for multi-node TP (e.g. TP=16 = 2 nodes × 8 GPUs): primary orchestrates daemon startup, cross-node NCCL process-group formation and readiness signalling; secondaries load their local shards in parallel and serve IPC handles to engines on their own node. Basic multi-node launch already works via `--nnodes/--node-rank/--dist-init-method`; what is missing is the cluster state machine
- [ ] cross-node daemon lifecycle: primary tracks which secondaries are alive, triggers coordinated restarts, signals engines on a dead secondary's node to fall back to disk; promote a secondary when the primary dies
- [ ] DP support: every DP rank on a GPU maps the same daemon's handles, so a model is read from disk and quantized exactly once per GPU regardless of DP degree (today each DP rank disk-loads independently). This is about supporting SGLang's DP deployment model, not cross-GPU sharing
- [ ] EP support: expert shards differ per EP rank, so cache and key them by `ep_rank`; handle partial expert loading when a rank owns a subset of experts
- [ ] `CacheConfig`: add `ep_rank`, `dp_rank` and `node_rank` for correct shard identification under EP and multi-node (`dp_size`/`ep_size` are already there)

## Ops & reliability

- [ ] `daemon status` command + Prometheus metrics (resident bytes, attached clients, load time, hit / mismatch / fallback), and an engine endpoint reporting how each rank got its weights
- [ ] runtime dir with owner-only permissions + `SO_PEERCRED` check before handing out handles (no world-writable `/tmp` sockets)
- [ ] `protocol_version` in the handshake with a documented skew policy (the env stamp alrea

items.title: [NVIDIA] ProxyFenceInsertion: no fence between tcgen05 async-proxy reads and later generic writes to a reused buffer
items.author: builtin-pb
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

`ProxyFenceInsertion` (`lib/Dialect/TritonNvidiaGPU/Transforms/ProxyFenceInsertion.cpp`) inserts `fence.proxy.async` when a generic shared-memory access is followed by an async-proxy access to an overlapping buffer. It checks async accesses only against earlier generic ones, so it never fences an async-proxy access followed by a generic access. For `cp.async.bulk` and `wgmma` that direction needs no fence: PTX says their completion "is followed by an implicit generic-async proxy fence" (PTX ISA 9.4 §9.7.10.28.2 and §9.7.17.4). ConSan relies on the same reading (#10668: "for all relevant accesses ptx spec claims that after such wait no fence is required").

`tcgen05` is the exception. §9.7.18.6.5 says the shared-memory accesses of `tcgen05.mma` and `tcgen05.cp` "are performed asynchronously and via the asynchronous proxy" and that "Accessing the same memory location across multiple proxies needs a cross-proxy fence". The `tcgen05` chapter states no implicit fence at their completion (`tcgen05.commit` and an mbarrier wait).

Example: in the Gluon tutorial `06-tcgen05.py`, `blocked_matmul_kernel` allocates `c_smem` after the K loop, and the allocator places it at offset 0, over `a_smem`. In the PTX (sm_100a, Triton 3.8, c01b677), `a_smem` and `c_smem` are both at `%r5 = global_smem`:
- the A-tile TMA load writes `[%r5]`;
- the epilogue's `st.shared` writes `[%r5 + %r132]`;
- the TMA store reads `[%r5]`.

The MMAs read A through the async proxy. Each K iteration ends with `mbarrier.try_wait.parity` on the MMA barrier (line 192 in the peeled first iteration, 224 in the loop). The epilogue then runs `tcgen05.ld` (323) and writes `c_smem` with four `st.shared::cta.v4.b32` (422–443), with no `fence.proxy.async` in between. The only fence in the kernel (447) is the tutorial's own `fence_async_shared()` before the TMA store. The overlap is made by the allocator, so the user cannot see it and has no reason to fence there.

The PTX is Triton 3.8's output for the tutorial, as published in a public corpus (gpu-verifier/sentryward, `corpus/tritongluon-06-tcgen05-blocked-matmul.ptx`). On main (2122e24), `ProxyFenceInsertion` still has the same structure ("Async-proxy accesses are retained only while they can still conflict with generic accesses preceding the current function").

Expected, one of:
- the pass also fences when bytes last accessed through the async proxy by a `tcgen05` op (`tcgen05.mma`, `tcgen05.cp`) are next accessed by generic ops, with the fence after the completion wait and before the generic access;
- or NVIDIA confirms that `tcgen05` completion carries the same implicit generic-async proxy fence as `wgmma` and bulk copies, in which case only the PTX text is missing it.

This is latent: it is a read followed by an overwrite, very likely ordered on current hardware, and we have not seen a failure. It affects any kernel in which the allocator reuses a `tcgen05` operand buffer for generic accesses with no fence in between, such as this tutorial. We found it by checking the PTX against the ISA.

#12340 fixes the other direction at the Tensor Memory base-address slot, which `tcgen05.alloc` writes at offset 0 and a TMA load then overwrites.

### Environment details

Triton main 2122e24 (source reading; we have compiled and run nothing). PTX for sm_100a from Triton 3.8 (c01b677), from the corpus named above.

comments.author: Rachit23110261
comments.body:
Hi @builtin-pb,

I'm looking into this. I have a minimal MLIR reproducer for the tcgen05 async-read → completion wait → overlapping generic-write case, and confirmed that `ProxyFenceInsertion` currently doesn't insert `ttng.fence_async_shared` between the wait and the generic access.

I'm investigating the completion/barrier tracking now and will work on a fix.

items.title: CUTLASS 4.8.0
items.author: Junkai-Wu
items.body_excerpt:
### CuTe DSL
* New features
  - Initial Rubin support to accelerate dense GEMMs. The following features are available:  
    - CuTe DSL and CuTe extensions
      - Support for higher-throughput FP8 (MMA_K=64) and FP4 (MMA_K=128) Tensor Core MMA instructions
      - B collector reuse 
      - Extended TMEM size from 512 COL to 576 COL
      - Larger shared memory allocations (328KB)
      - Enhanced mixed precision throughput (FP8/FP4)
      - Softmax acceleration related features
    - Primitives
      - Support for higher-throughput FP8 (MMA_K=64) and FP4 (MMA_K=128) Tensor Core MMA instructions
      - B collector reuse
      - Extended TMEM size from 512 COL to 576 COL
      - Larger shared memory allocations (328KB)
      - Enhanced mixed precision throughput (FP8/FP4)
      - Softmax acceleration related feature
      - 2:4 sparsity support for FP4

  - CuTe DSL extensions has several new features:
    - CTA-V maps are now inferred automatically for `cute_ext` TMA load, store, multicast, and reduce-store operations. Explicit CTA-V maps remain supported as overrides.
    - Added asynchronous atomic TMA reduce-store and sparse MMA operations.
    - Added reusable `cute_ext` GEMM mainloop and TMA epilogue helpers.
    - Added opt-in TMEM accumulator-buffer planning, including overlapping ping-pong storage for capacity-constrained kernels.
    - Improved device-side TMA descriptor updates and grouped GEMM performance through SMEM-staged updates, workspace reuse, and reduced prologue and synchronization overhead.
  - This release includes an opt-in preview of the CuTe DSL extensions (`cute_ext`) compiler pipeline for ordinary Cute DSL kernels. This pipeline lets user mix `cute_ext` APIs directly into `@cute.jit` and `@cute.kernel` code and is required for kernels that mix the two API surfaces. You may test this feature with the following:
  `CUTE_DSL_USE_EXTENSION_COMPILER=1 python your_program.py`
The pipeline is expected to preserve program behavior and performance, but generated PTX/SASS may differ.  Note that this pipeline will become the default in the future, no earlier than 4.10.
  - Added examples for better control over Primitives' compiler warnings/errors introduced in 4.7.0.  See the `CuTeDSL/experimental/compiler_diagnostic/` directory.
  - IKET Profiler Tool
    - Rubin kernels (sm107) can now be profiled.
    - It is now possible to only dump timing data for a specific cluster to reduce profiling overhead.  Previously all clusters were profiled.
    - Task Scheduling can instrument the schedule with IKET ranges when constructing TaskManager objects (`iket_enable_profiling=True`).  Task execution will generate an IKET range and individual pipeline stages in a schedule may generate separate ranges (`iket_profiling_stages`).
  - A number of new examples were added in this release:
    - Rubin (CuTe):
      - Dense GEMM for legacy data type with B collector reuse as applicable
      - Grouped GEMM with B collector reuse
      - Dense blockscaled GEMM with FP4/FP6/FP8 mixed precision and UE5M3 / block-32 scale-factor support
      - Grouped blockscaled GEMM with B collector reuse as applicable
      - Blockwise GEMM
    - Rubin (CuTe extension):
      - Support for higher-throughput FP8 (MMA_K=64) and FP4 (MMA_K=128) blockscaled GEMM with UE5M3 scale-factor
      - Grouped GEMM with B collector reuse
    - Blackwell (CuTe extension):
      - Dense GEMMs
        - Back-to-back GEMM
        - Blockscaled GEMM
        - Persistent GEMM with alpha/beta scaling
        - CLC scheduler/dynamic persistent GEMM
        - GLU GEMM
        - Mixed input GEMM
        - Planar complex GEMM
        - Input transform GEMM
        - GeForce pingpong dense GEMM
        - Blackwell Ultra blockscaled GEMM
      - Dense Convolutions
        - Implicit-Gemm Fprop Conv
        - Blocksclaed Implicit-Gemm Fprop Conv
        - GeForce Implicit-Gemm Fprop Conv
        - GeForce Blockscaled Implicit-Gemm Fporp Conv 
      - Attention
        - GQA Decode
      - Grouped GEMM
        - Unscaled and blockscaled grouped GEMM
      - Top-K
    - Ampere (CuTe extension):
      - SIMT GEMM
  - CuTe DSL now supports x86_64 Windows
  - CuTe DSL AoT now supports new host target: QNX8.0 
  - Notebooks are restructured under examples/python/CuTeDSL/cute/notebooks and new notebooks for primitives will be added under examples/python/CuTeDSL/notebooks 
  - Numpy is now not a default dependency

* Bug fixes and improvements:
  - `nvidia-cuda-nvdisasm` is now an optional dependency of `nvidia-cutlass-dsl` via the optional `[sass]` extra. SASS dumping (`CUTE_DSL_KEEP=sass` / KeepSASS) now resolves `nvdisasm` from the bundled wheel (recommended since its version matches the DSL toolchain) or from a local CUDA Toolkit (`CUDA_HOME`/`CUDA_PATH`). A locally-provided `nvdisasm` must come from a CUDA Toolkit at least as new as the toolchain that produced the CUBIN. Installations that never dump SASS are unaffected.
  - Reduced the protobuf version requirement of IKET profiler from 6.30 to 4.21.  This should make protobuf an easier requirement to satisfy in preparation for transioning IKET to an optional extra.
  - Improved JAX PyTree input/output aliasing for `cutlass.jax.cutlass_call`
  - Fixed a regression from 4.6.0 where `cute.autovec_copy` emitted per-element instead of

items.title: [cake deslop] cake_fmha round 2: fix unwritten LSE, fold ~194K lines of clones, drop dead metadata, decide exact-shape members
items.author: yyihuang
items.body_excerpt:
**Background.** `csrc/cake_fmha` (imported in #4980) is the Cake-generated paged-attention backend for sm_100a/sm_103a. It serves `trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache(backend="cake")` / `cake_batch_decode_with_kv_cache`, `trtllm_batch_context_with_kv_cache(backend="cake")`, DCP spec decode (`causal_seqlens_kv_global` → `cake_dcp.run_dcp_spec_decode`) and request-ordered decode (sm_103a with exactly 152 SMs). It is JIT-only: AOT (`flashinfer/aot.py:684-686`) packages only `compat_v1`. The first round closed three sub-issues. #5801 was closed by #5933 (−98,111: 16 unreachable sources deleted, 19 one-line arch pairs merged). #5802 was closed by #5934 (request-ordered; manifest 12,627 → 714 lines). #5803 was closed by #6043 (DCP static, one program per split variant). #5932 split the registry per component. Those PRs deferred the flag/page clones, the exact-shape members and the per-arch context_bf16/decode_native_bf16/quant_fp8 pairs. Around and after that round, #5750 (+109,530: balanced DCP bf16/fp8/d256), #5855, #5887, #6061 and #5913 added material. #5913 re-introduced `dcp_spec_bf16_fp8_balanced/kernel_eight_slice_fold1.cu` (4,431 lines, 0/+17 vs fold0) and `decode_balanced_bf16_hd64_g16/default.cu` (2,652 lines, 105/133 vs hd64). The tree went from 189 files / 378K lines to 150 / 278K, and is now 204 files / 350,221 lines at 3184bbea. A loader table names all 122 kernel sources, so every source is compiled. The excess is clones, exact-shape members, unread metadata and duplicated host code.

**Findings**
- **Unwritten LSE (latent correctness bug).** None of the 8 exact `decode_native_bf16` members (b4, b128 ×5 incl. per-arch, b256 ×2) ever writes LSE: `LSE_ptr` appears only in the kernel signature. Generic members do store it (e.g. `has_sink0_has_window0_retain_kv_l21_use_scale_ptr0.cu:1172-1192`). `_resolve_decode_native_bf16_selector` (`flashinfer/jit/cake_fmha.py:240-278`) tries the exact member first. `flashinfer/cake_fmha.py` guards a caller `lse` only for (b256, sink), via `exact_sink_no_lse` (945-957). `flashinfer/decode.py:4426` allocates `lse` for `return_lse=True` and passes it at :4556. As a result, (b4|b128, hq32, hkv4, q1, bf16 HND page16 hd128, no sink/window) with `return_lse=True` or a caller `lse` returns an unwritten buffer. No test covers this; `test_cake_fmha_exact_sink_no_lse_member_falls_back_for_caller_lse` checks b256 only. The bug is source-confirmed; the symptom still needs one GPU run.
- **Decode flag clones.** `decode_native_bf16` (11 generic files), `decode_native_fp16_nhd` (16) and `decode_native_fp16_hd512` (8) total 35 files / 88,464 lines. Normalized pair diffs: use_scale_ptr 1/7, has_sink 7/22, retain_kv_l2 9/41 (65/321 for hd512), has_window 1/67. The loader already passes `-DCAKE_FMHA_HAS_SINK/HAS_WINDOW/USE_SCALE_PTR/RETAIN_KV_L2` (`flashinfer/jit/cake_fmha.py:1129,1591`), but 0 kernels read them; each file hard-codes its own `#define`. Folding removes 80,020 lines. It also serves the 5 bf16 flag combos that currently fall to `compat_v1`; for example, (sink=1, window=0, retain=0, scale=0) is served only at the exact b256 shape.
- **Context clones and per-arch pairs.** context_bf16 generic (12 files, 35,242) and context_fp8 (6, 21,812) differ by sink 1/8, lse 1/10 and causal 12/74. `-DCAKE_FMHA_CONTEXT_IS_CAUSAL/RETURN_LSE/ENABLE_SINK` are passed (`flashinfer/jit/cake_fmha.py:531,665,793`) but unused, so 50,411 lines are removable. The 6 context_bf16 sm_100a/sm_103a pairs differ by 209/212 lines in 39 hunks. The only semantic difference is the row max: a fused `tcgen05.ld.red…x64.max.f32` on sm_103a vs two x32 loads + `row_max_x32_accum` on sm_100a. The sm_103a text already carries `__CUDA_ARCH__ == 1000` guards (lines 1645/1653). Larger per-arch pairs: decode_quant_fp8 page16 (110/355 in 67 hunks) and DCP fp8_d256 split1 (544/352, inline-asm MMA vs the `tcgen05_mma` helper).
- **Balanced, small-M and quant clones.** The 14 `decode_balanced_*/default.cu` files (40,331 lines) reduce to 6, removing 23,241 lines. Pair diffs: mtp_n32/n64 10/10, bf16/fp16 75/75, hd256 p32/p64 16/16, bf16q/fp16q 35/43, hd64/hd64_g16 108/136. The adapters already pass `-DCAKE_FMHA_BALANCED_N_ROWS/_FP16/_PAGE_SIZE`, which the kernels do not use. Small-M hd256 goes 6 → 1 (8,664 removable). The bf16q/nvfp4/fp8 page16 vs page32 pairs differ by 28/1, 6/1 and 16/1 lines (10,582 lines in the four `page_size32` files).
- **DCP static programs and bindings.** The 14 static kernels (25,346 lines) are split/retain clones: fp8_d128 retain 4/16 and split 6/121–6/135, bf16_v1 retain 7/31, bf16_v4 38/52, fp8_d256 8/161 per arch. #6043 moved NUM_SPLIT to the compile line but kept one program per split class and retain flag. Going 14 → 5 removes 16,455 lines. The 14 tvm-ffi bindings form 4 groups (6×332, 4×356, 2×350, 2×335). Within a group, files differ only in 4 hash-bearing lines (kernel symbol, namespace, error string), so 3,413 lines are removable.
- **Duplicated host code.**
  - The 209-line `TmaDeviceArena` block is copied in 8 JIT adapters, `CheckSameDevice` in 16 and `ScalarScale` in 11 (1,603 removable).
  - The 4 request-ordered exact bindings (2,794 lines) differ from `*_fallback_binding.cpp` only in cubin ident, kernel symbol, smem (142208/173824), cluster dims (1/2/4), a scheduling-policy launch attribute and a grid-divisibility check.
  - The two `sink_peer_clc` bindings differ in 2 host lines (smem 178176 vs 210944).
  - `cuda/dcp_spec/cake_cake_fmha_dcp_spec_host_common.cuh` is byte-identical to 13 other Cake families' copies (52 × 14 = 676 lines repo-wide).
- **Dead declarations and unread metadata.**
  - `include/cake_fmha.h:694-764` declares `cake_fmha_launch_dcp_spec_bf16`, `_bf16_v4` and `_bf16_fp8`, none of which is defined (71 lines).
  - In `dcp_spec/registry.json`, `pass_through` (14 lines, naming files that do not exist) and `programs[*].arg_plan` (1,204) have no reader.
  - In `registry.json`, the loader does not read `parameters` (2,921), `parametric_axes` (659),

items.title: [Feature]: b12x MoE: inline NVFP4-CSF scales for the micro W4A16 decode path (GB10)
items.author: zengjiajun0623
items.body_excerpt:
### Before submitting

- [x] I have searched existing issues and this request has not been filed yet.

### Problem

On DGX Spark (GB10, SM121), single-stream decode of `nvidia/GLM-5.3-Flash-FP4-Local` spends about 5.8% of GPU busy time in the standalone NVFP4-CSF scale expansion kernel (`nvfp4_csf` `Pair`), which runs before every routed-expert MoE layer and is not overlapped with other work.

Setup: 2x DGX Spark, TP=2, `eugr/spark-vllm-b12x:latest` (2026-10-15 build, flashinfer 0.7.1 with b12x), the published recipe (`--moe-backend b12x`, `VLLM_B12X_MOE_FP4_FORCE_A16=1`, MTP with 3 speculative tokens, CUDA graphs on). Decode therefore runs the `micro` implementation with `quant_mode == "w4a16"`.

What the torch profiler shows for a decode window (CUDA graphs, rank 0):

| | value |
|---|---|
| CSF expansion kernel time | 325.8 ms over 2562 launches (about 104 to 129 us per MoE layer per step) |
| of which overlapped with other kernels | 73.4 ms (23%) |
| exposed (serial) CSF time | 252.4 ms = **5.8% of GPU busy time** |
| launch stream | the main stream for 2478 of 2562 launches |

`VLLM_B12X_CSF_SCALE_PREFETCH` does not help here, since per its comment it applies to eager prefill calls only.

For context, the weight-streaming kernels in the same trace are already close to the memory roofline (device copy measured at 218 GB/s on GB10): the W4A16 fused MoE kernel reaches roughly 215 GB/s and the FP8 dense GEMMs 188 to 200 GB/s. That makes the scale expansion one of the few remaining overheads in the decode step that is not set by weight bandwidth.

In current `main`, `_impl.py` already has an inline path (`nvfp4_inline_scales` via `experts.nvfp4_csf.inline_scales`), but it is gated on `binding.implementation == "dynamic"` and `quant_mode == "nvfp4"`, so the `micro` / W4A16 decode path still calls `experts.nvfp4_csf.decode(...)` into scratch before the MoE kernel reads the expanded scales.

### Requested outcome

Let the `micro` W4A16 decode path read NVFP4-CSF scales inline (or fuse the routed expansion into the MoE kernel prologue), as the `dynamic` NVFP4 path already can, so the scale expansion no longer costs a separate serial kernel per MoE layer during decode. If that is not practical, overlapping the expansion with the preceding attention on a side stream in CUDA-graph decode (as `VLLM_B12X_CSF_SCALE_PREFETCH` does for eager prefill) would recover most of the same time.

Expected upper bound on GB10 for this model: about 5 to 6% faster single-stream decode, with no change in numerics (the format is lossless).

### Target hardware

SM121 (DGX Spark / GB10). Likely also SM120 (RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, RTX 5090) with the same checkpoint.

### Additional context

- Model: https://huggingface.co/nvidia/GLM-5.3-Flash-FP4-Local
- Recipe: https://github.com/eugr/spark-vllm-docker (`recipes/glm-5.3-flash.yaml`)
- I have not built current `main` to re-measure; the gating above is from reading `flashinfer/experimental/b12x/moe/fused_moe/_impl.py` on `main`. Happy to re-run the profile against a newer build if that is useful.

items.title: [Bug]: ModelClaim engine crashes with IndexError in kvcached get_new_blocks after the controller raises its KV limit above the engine's initial block pool
items.author: Jeffwan
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

A vLLM engine started by the ModelClaim runtime (kvcached-patched) crashes with `IndexError` after the controller raises its KV limit above the KV block pool the engine allocated at startup. EngineCore exits, the runtime restarts the engine (`restart_count` +1), and every request to that model fails until it is back (about 40 s for an 8B model).

```
File ".../vllm/v1/core/single_type_kv_cache_manager.py", line 399, in allocate_new_blocks
    new_blocks = self.block_pool.get_new_blocks(num_new_blocks)
File ".../kvcached/integration/vllm/patches.py", line 1003, in get_new_blocks
    block = self.kv_block_pool[bid]
IndexError: list index out of range
EngineCore encountered a fatal error.
```

What we observed:

1. vLLM sizes the block table once, at engine start: `self.kv_block_pool = [KVCacheBlockClass(i) for i in range(num_gpu_blocks)]`. For a single Qwen3-8B-FP8 engine on an A100-40GB this is 26.2 GiB of blocks (kvcached log: `Using kvcached process-local KV capacity: ... available=28173858448 bytes`).
2. When that engine is alone on the card, `planKVLimits` gives it the engine's held KV plus the whole remaining card, 29.0 GiB. Nothing caps the limit at the engine's initial pool ([kvplan.go#L114-L127](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/main/pkg/controller/modelclaim/kvplan.go#L114-L127)). The event reads `KV limit set to 29.0 GiB, from 26.2 GiB`.
3. kvcached then hands out block ids up to the new limit. An id at or above `num_gpu_blocks` indexes past `kv_block_pool`.

We hit the crash 4 times in one benchmark run:

- **History captured:** in the two crashes whose limit history we captured, the engine had been raised above its initial pool. One of them crashed 4 minutes after its limit had been lowered from 29.0 GiB back to 9.2 GiB, when a second engine was placed. Lowering the limit afterwards did not prevent the crash.
- **History not captured:** the other two engines ran in the same setup, alone on the card first.
- **Never above the pool:** engines whose limit never exceeded their initial pool never crashed, across dozens of KV-saturating runs. These include engines placed next to an existing engine and engines started in pairs or groups.
- **Above the pool, no crash:** two engines were raised above their pool briefly and did not crash: a 0.6B engine at concurrency 1 (36.7 vs 34.9 GiB), and an 8B engine under load for 90 s. Exceeding the pool is necessary but not sufficient; the crash depends on how many blocks get allocated afterwards.
- **Prefix caching and reset:** prefix caching makes it trigger sooner, but it is not required: one crash happened with `--no-enable-prefix-caching`. `/reset_prefix_cache` is not required either.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Deploy a warm pool with one GPU (`samples/modelclaim/warm-runtime-pool.yaml`, 1× A100-40GB) and no pool policy annotation.
2. Apply one ModelClaim alone on that pod:
   ```yaml
   spec:
     modelName: qwen3-8b-z
     artifactURL: huggingface://Qwen/Qwen3-8B-FP8
     engine: vllm
     perGPU:
       maximumFootprint: 10752Mi
       kvFloor: 2Gi
     engineConfig:
       args:
         --max-model-len: "8192"
         --max-num-seqs: "32"
         --max-num-batched-tokens: "2048"
   ```
3. Check the event `KV limit set to 29.0 GiB, from 26.2 GiB` (runtime snapshot `kv_capacity_bytes: 31132614656`).
4. Send RAG-shaped load directly to the engine port. Repeat with `--seed 1`, `2`, `3`:
   ```bash
   vllm bench serve --backend openai-chat --base-url http://<pod-ip>:<engine-port> \
     --endpoint /v1/chat/completions --model qwen3-8b-z --tokenizer Qwen/Qwen3-8B-FP8 \
     --dataset-name random --random-input-len 1024 --random-output-len 128 \
     --num-prompts 300 --request-rate 32 --max-concurrency 16 --ignore-eos --seed 1
   ```
   Runs 1 and 2 complete 300/300. Run 3 crashed after 144 requests, and the snapshot showed `restart_count: 1`.

### Expected behavior

- The controller never sets an engine's KV limit above the KV capacity the engine sized its block table for at startup. Room on the card beyond that stays unassigned, or goes to other engines.
- Suggested fix: the runtime reports each engine's initial KV capacity in the snapshot (the kvcached segment's `total_size` when the engine came up, or `num_gpu_blocks` × block bytes). `planKVLimits` caps `kvLimitBytes` at it. Add a regression test where a single engine on a card gets a capped limit.
- kvcached should also clamp or reject a limit beyond `num_gpu_blocks` instead of handing out out-of-range block ids. We will report that side to ovg-project/kvcached.

### Environment

- Image `ghcr.io/ovg-project/kvcached-vllm:kvcached-v0.1.6-vllm-v0.30.0` (vLLM 0.30.0, kvcached 0.1.6), runtime built with `make docker-build-kvcached-runtime`.
- 1× NVIDIA A100-SXM4-40GB, driver 570.148.08, single-node minikube.
- Models: Qwen/Qwen3-8B-FP8 (all 4 crashes) and Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B.

### Area

Orchestration (controllers, CRDs)

items.title: Should LMCacheMPConnector honor kv_transfer_config.kv_role — or is MP mode intentionally always-kv_both?
items.author: kezboard233
items.body_excerpt:
## Context

We run a production-shaped POC on 8×V100 (two vLLM TP4 instances of Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 sharing one LMCache MP server with a CPU L1 tier) and filed #5143 with a runtime-verified repro: an engine launched with `kv_role="kv_consumer"` still stores every request's KV into the shared L1 — a single 32K-token cold request produced `168 × "Stored 784"` lines (= full prefix × 4 TP ranks), and the only engine that received any request in that window was the `kv_consumer` one.

We later found #4665 (closed by its author without maintainer response) reporting the same mechanism from the CacheBlend angle: the single-process connector honors `kv_role` / `skip_save`, the MP connector honors neither. As of today's `dev`, `lmcache_mp_connector.py` still contains no occurrence of `kv_role` / `kv_consumer` / `kv_producer` / `force_skip_save`.

## The design question

Before we contribute a patch, we want to check intent: **is MP mode intentionally "every connected engine writes"?** Two readings:

1. **Contract gap** — vLLM makes `kv_role` mandatory, documents it as "Whether this vLLM instance produces, consumes KV cache, or both", and exposes `is_kv_producer` / `is_kv_consumer` for connectors to branch on; LMCache's own single-process adapter honors it (`force_skip_save` in `vllm_v1_adapter.py`). Under this reading we'd gladly contribute a small PR that skips store-metadata generation when `is_kv_consumer` (mirroring the single-process gate), so warm-then-read-only fleets and PD-style topologies become possible on the MP path.

2. **Intentional always-kv_both** — the MP tier is a shared scratch space where every connected engine contributes. Under this reading we'd instead ask for the intent to be documented, plus ideally a one-line warning at connector init when `kv_role != "kv_both"`, so users aren't misled (we only noticed via instrumented counter evidence ourselves).

Happy to do either — a steer from maintainers decides which.

(Impact context: no correctness issue — stored content is identical — but a consumer-role engine burns D2H bandwidth and shared-L1 capacity; a 32K prefix on our model is ≈8.6 GB across 4 ranks.)

items.title: [Bug]: Grouped MLA generation cubins are registered as Dense in kernelMetaInfo.h but named and selected as Causal
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

TensorRT-LLM main, `cpp/tensorrt_llm/kernels/trtllmGenKernels/fmha/cubin/kernelMetaInfo.h` (artifacts from #19591). On release/1.3 the table is split per architecture since #20022; the same rows are in `kernelMetaInfoSm100f.h` and `kernelMetaInfoSm107.h` (see the location list below). Seen on SM107; the SM100f rows have the same pattern.

### Who can help?

@pengbowang-nv @farazkh80 (#15009)

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [x] My own modified scripts

### Reproduction

All 36 grouped MLA generation cubins (`fmhaSm100fKernel_...` and `fmhaSm107aKernel_Qkv{Bfloat16,E4m3}OBfloat16HQk576HV512{,HVPerCta128,HVPerCta256}PagedKvCausalP32...VarSeqQ64Kv128{Static,Persistent}GroupedKeepsAbForGen`; per architecture 9 with BF16 and 9 with E4M3 Q/KV, 18 for `kSM_100f`, 18 for `kSM_107`) have `Causal` in the function name, but their `mMaskType` field is `0` (`TrtllmGenAttentionMaskType::Dense`). Locations:

- main @ 13e19d6cf3, `kernelMetaInfo.h`: SM100f BF16 lines 19057-19110, SM100f E4M3 19347-19400, SM107 BF16 20903-21019, SM107 E4M3 21907-22023.
- release/1.3 @ c9d1169641 (after #20022): `kernelMetaInfoSm100f.h` lines 243-296 (BF16) and 533-586 (E4M3); `kernelMetaInfoSm107.h` lines 887-1003 (BF16) and 1835-1951 (E4M3). The values are unchanged by the split. The grouped P128 E4M3 H128 cubins added there for SM107 are registered with `mMaskType = 1` (Causal), so only the HQk576 grouped MLA rows are affected.

`mMaskType` is part of the hash that the cubin path looks up (`hashFromFmhaOptions` -> `hashID`). With `FmhaOptions::mSelectsGroupedMla = true`, the autotuner selects the grouped kernel with a causal mask for MLA generation with multiple query tokens, so the lookup fails (`Trtllm-gen kernels not found`), and the only remaining route is NVRTC. On SM107, NVRTC currently fails for these configurations (separate issue). We had to map Causal back to Dense for grouped MLA kernels in `algoFilterForCubinPath` before the cubins could be used.

With that mapping, the cubins give the expected causal result: compared with the non-grouped kernel on SM107, outputs are bit-identical for KV lengths 16 and 64, and at most 2 bf16 ulp apart from 256 up to 128K. So the kernels behave as their names say, and only the metadata is off. #15009 also mentions that its re-exported rows were changed to `maskType=Causal` "to match the shipped lib's grouped mask rewrite".

### Expected behavior

The registered mask type matches what the kernel implements and what the selector asks for, so that grouped MLA generation cubins can be found without a remapping.

### actual behavior

`mMaskType = Dense` for kernels named `...Causal...`; the cubin lookup misses them when grouped MLA selection is enabled.

### additional notes

This does not affect main today because `mSelectsGroupedMla` is never set in TensorRT-LLM. It blocks enabling it (#15009), together with the missing `cumSeqLensQ/Kv` in the MLA generation path (#20375). If the right fix is on the export side, a regenerated `kernelMetaInfo.h` (`kernelMetaInfoSm100f.h` / `kernelMetaInfoSm107.h` after #20022) would be enough; otherwise I can send the remapping as a small PR.

Related: #20375, #20377, #20382 (FP8-KV grouped MLA hang for head counts that do not divide 64).

items.title: [Bug]: FP8-KV MLA generation hangs on SM107 with the grouped trtllm-gen E4M3 kernels when heads per rank do not divide 64 (e.g. 12)
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- GPU: SM107, 8 GPUs over 2 nodes (TP8 attention)
- TensorRT-LLM main @ 69a455ae974bcf9582c9a2cc4f7fd9a5f75680fe (code and cubin list checked there), PyTorch backend, TRTLLM attention backend
- Model: MLA model with 96 query heads -> 12 heads per rank at TP8 (kv_lora_rank 512, qk_rope_head_dim 64)
- kv_cache_config.dtype: fp8, tokens_per_block 32, MTP speculative decoding with 8 query tokens per step
- Grouped (tokens x heads in one Q tile) MLA generation kernel selection enabled locally (`FmhaOptions::mSelectsGroupedMla`; main does not set it, see #15009)

### Who can help?

@pengbowang-nv @farazkh80

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [x] My own modified scripts

### Reproduction

1. Serve the model with `kv_cache_config.dtype: fp8` and grouped MLA generation selection enabled.
2. Startup never finishes: every rank stops in the first generation-shape attention call of the warmup (num_tokens=8, num_gen_requests=1, KV length 8). GPU utilization stays at 100 %, nothing is logged after `Attention workspace size is not enough, increase the size from 0 bytes to ...`. `TRTLLM_ENABLE_PDL=0` does not change it.
3. A host-side backtrace of a rank shows the main thread inside the next cuBLAS call (`cublasGemmStridedBatchedEx -> cuKernelSetAttribute`), i.e. queued behind a kernel that never completes.
4. With synchronizing checkpoints in `MLA.forward_absorption_generation`: the q_nope bmm and `mla_rope_generation` (FP8 Q quantization, FP8 KV append, bmm scales) complete; the attention op does not. A sync right after the FMHA launch in `TllmGenFmhaRunner::run` never returns. The selected cubin is `fmhaSm107aKernel_QkvE4m3OBfloat16HQk576HV512HVPerCta256PagedKvCausalP32VarSeqQ64Kv128StaticGroupedKeepsAbForGen` (grid 2x2x1, numHeadsQ 12, maxSeqLenQ 8, multiCtasKv off for this KV length).

Standalone reproduction with the FMHA runner only (no model): `TllmGenFmhaRunner(E4M3, E4M3, E4M3, BF16)`, paged KV page 32, MLA head dims 576/512, 1 KV head, generation kernel, grouped selection enabled, seqLenQ 8 (12 heads also hangs at seqLenQ 1, 4, 5, 6), seqLenKv 2048:

| numHeadsQ | 4 | 6 | 8 | 10 | 12 | 14 | 16 | 20 | 24 | 32 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FP8 (E4M3 Q/KV) grouped | ok | **hangs** | ok | **hangs** | **hangs** | **hangs** | ok | **hangs** | **hangs** | ok |
| BF16 grouped (checked: 12, 16) | — | — | — | — | ok | — | ok | — | — | — |

The FP8 kernel completes only when numHeadsQ divides the 64-row Q tile. BF16 grouped kernels with 12 heads are fine.

### Expected behavior

The FP8 grouped MLA generation kernel works for any head count, or is not selected for head counts it cannot handle.

### actual behavior

The FMHA kernel never completes; the process hangs with the GPU at 100 %.

### additional notes

**Analysis.** In `makeTmaShapeStrideQ` (`cpp/tensorrt_llm/kernels/trtllmGenKernels/fmha/trtllmGen_fmha_export/KernelParams.h`), for `mGroupsTokensHeadsQ`:

~~~
numTokensPerTileQ = numTokensPerTileQ / numGroupedHeads;   // 64 / 12 = 5
tileShapes = {clampedHeadDimQ, numGroupedHeads, 1, numTokensPerTileQ};  // 5 tokens x 12 heads = 60 rows
~~~

so the Q TMA box covers 60 of the 64 tile rows. The comment there says padding at the end of the tile is allowed. The BF16 cubins handle it; the E4M3 cubins never finish, which looks like the kernel waits for a full 64-row tile (a transaction byte count or row bookkeeping derived from tileSizeQ instead of from the box). Unchanged on current main.

**Reachability on main.** Main never sets `mSelectsGroupedMla`, so this hang is latent there today. But the precompiled SM107 E4M3 MLA generation cubins are KeepsAb only (Dense / Sliding / Sparse, plus the grouped ones above); there is no SwapsAb E4M3 MLA generation cubin. Non-grouped FP8 MLA generation on SM107 therefore goes to NVRTC and fails with `Array.cpp:376 Out-of-bound access` (#20377, case 2, including the 2048-query-token shape). I think the two are likely the same coverage gap seen from two sides: shapes without an E4M3 cubin fail in NVRTC, and the existing grouped E4M3 cubins hang when 64 % numHeadsQ != 0. The only FP8 MLA generation path that works on SM107 right now seems to be grouped selection with 4/8/16/32 heads per rank.

**Workaround** (removes the hang in our runs). In `AttentionOp::mlaGeneration` (TRTLLM-Gen path), when the selected kernel is grouped E4M3, Q is decode-size (<= 16 tokens) and `64 % numHeadsQ != 0`: copy Q into a zero-padded `[numTokens, nextPow2(numHeadsQ), 576]` FP8 buffer, run the FMHA with `mNumHeadsQ = mNumHeadsQPerKv = nextPow2(numHeadsQ)` and a padded BF16 output, then copy the real heads of O back (two small row-copy kernels; MLA heads are independent, so padded heads only produce output that is dropped). Not used when softmax stats, attention sinks or an output scale-factor buffer are requested. I have not opened a PR for it: it only matters once grouped selection is enabled (#15009, #20375, #20376), so it would be dead code on main as is; it could go in together with that change.

Possible proper fixes: (a) make the E4M3 grouped kernels handle a partial last tile like the BF16 ones; (b) build the Q TMA box from whole tokens rounded up, with OOB fill and row masking; (c) exclude such head counts from grouped selection for FP8 (on SM107 this currently lands on the NVRTC failure in #20377, so it needs that fixed too).

**End-to-end with the workaround** (one serving run, TP8 over 2 nodes, 8 query tokens per step, batch 1; the build also includes the split-KV reduction change from #20380; bf16 KV vs fp8 KV):

- Without the workaround: all ranks hang in the first generation warmup, as above. With it: startup completes, including CUDA graph capture for batch 16..1; no new errors in the logs.
- Decode step period (median, ms), bf16 KV -> fp8 KV: 2K 12.57 -> 12.64, 32K 12.87 -> 12.85, 128K 13.62 -> 13.39.
- Per MLA call (8 query tokens, 1 sequence): BF16 grouped with 12 heads vs FP8 grouped with 16 padded heads: 2K 12.16 v
