items.title: [Bug]: trtllm-gen FMHA CudaArchDecl.h numbers Sm107a as 4, but the prebuilt libTrtLlmGen archives use 4 for 105a and 5 for 107a
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- TensorRT-LLM main @ e88d19ca3b
- Affects SM107 builds (the trtllm-gen FMHA target is compiled with `TLLM_RUBIN_FEATURES`, see `cpp/tensorrt_llm/kernels/trtllmGenKernels/fmha/CMakeLists.txt`). The reproduction below is CPU-only and uses the checked-in prebuilt archives, on both x86_64 and aarch64.

### Who can help?

Related: #18518 and #19038 (enable `TLLM_RUBIN_FEATURES` for the FMHA target and refresh the archives), #18758 (maps SM107 to `Sm100f` for NVRTC), #20054 (latest archive update).

### Reproduction

`cpp/tensorrt_llm/kernels/trtllmGenKernels/fmha/trtllmGen_fmha_export/trtllm/gen/CudaArchDecl.h` declares:

```cpp
enum class CudaArch {
  Sm90a = 0,  // 0
  Sm100a,     // 1
  Sm100f,     // 2
  Sm103a,     // 3
#ifdef TLLM_RUBIN_FEATURES
  Sm107a,     // 4
#endif
};
```

The prebuilt `fmha/lib/<arch>/libTrtLlmGen.a` and `libTrtLlmGenFmhaLib.a` were compiled with an enum that also has `105a`. Value 4 is `105a` there, and `107a` is 5:

- `strings libTrtLlmGen.a` contains `90a 100a 100f 103a 105a 107a`.
- In the archive's `trtllm::gen::cudaArchToString`, the jump table covers 0..5.
- In the archive's `trtllm::gen::getMaxNumTmemCols`, values 1..3 return 512, 5 returns 576, and anything else goes to the "unsupported" error path.

Minimal CPU-only reproduction, from the repository root:

```cpp
// repro.cpp
#include "CudaArchDecl.h"
#include <cstdio>
#include <exception>
namespace trtllm { namespace gen { int getMaxNumTmemCols(CudaArch); } }
using trtllm::gen::CudaArch;
int main() {
  std::printf("header: Sm103a=%d Sm107a=%d\n", int(CudaArch::Sm103a), int(CudaArch::Sm107a));
  for (int v : {1, 2, 3, 5})
    std::printf("libTrtLlmGen getMaxNumTmemCols(%d) = %d\n", v, trtllm::gen::getMaxNumTmemCols(CudaArch(v)));
  try {
    std::printf("getMaxNumTmemCols(CudaArch::Sm107a) = %d\n", trtllm::gen::getMaxNumTmemCols(CudaArch::Sm107a));
  } catch (std::exception const& e) {
    std::printf("getMaxNumTmemCols(CudaArch::Sm107a) threw: %s\n", e.what());
  }
}
```

```bash
D=cpp/tensorrt_llm/kernels/trtllmGenKernels/fmha
g++ -std=c++17 -DTLLM_RUBIN_FEATURES -I$D/trtllmGen_fmha_export/trtllm/gen repro.cpp \
    $D/lib/$(uname -m)-linux-gnu/libTrtLlmGen.a -o repro && ./repro
```

Output (identical on x86_64 and aarch64):

```
header: Sm103a=3 Sm107a=4
libTrtLlmGen getMaxNumTmemCols(1) = 512
libTrtLlmGen getMaxNumTmemCols(2) = 512
libTrtLlmGen getMaxNumTmemCols(3) = 512
libTrtLlmGen getMaxNumTmemCols(5) = 576
getMaxNumTmemCols(CudaArch::Sm107a) threw: Unsupported CUDA arch: 105a
[E] [TmemTile.cpp:46]: Unsupported CUDA arch: 105a
```

So `CudaArch::Sm107a`, as compiled into TensorRT-LLM, is `105a` to the archive.

### Expected behavior

`CudaArch` values passed across the boundary to the prebuilt archives mean the same architecture on both sides.

### Actual behavior

On SM107, `TllmGenFmhaKernel` sets `options.mCudaArch = intToCudaArch(107) = Sm107a` (4) in `checkIfKernelExist`, `warmupOneKernel` and `run` (`fmha/fmhaKernels.h`). It then hands those `FmhaOptions` to archive code that reads `mCudaArch`:

- `fmha::FmhaAutoTuner::selectKernel()` (through `selectKernelAutotuned`), on every path;
- `fmha::FmhaInterface::generateAndCompileKernel()`, on the NVRTC path.

`run()` rewrites `mCudaArch` to `Sm100f` before NVRTC compilation for non-spcompress kernels (added in #18518). `warmupOneKernel()` does not. So the JIT warmup path, and every autotuner call, gives the archive `105a` instead of `107a`. Any SM107-specific branches in the archive are therefore not taken, and the archive's TMEM limit lookup for that value is the error path shown above.

### Additional notes

Suggested fix: make the header match the archives. The smallest change is:

```cpp
#ifdef TLLM_RUBIN_FEATURES
  // SM107. 4 is Sm105a in the prebuilt trtllm-gen archives.
  Sm107a = 5,
#endif
```

A more robust alternative is to export the archive's value (or the enum header itself) together with the archives, and add a CPU-only check. Something like the reproduction above, run as a unit test, would catch the next drift when the archives are refreshed.

The other `CudaArchDecl.h` copies (`batchedGemm/trtllm/gen/`, `batchedGemm/trtllmGen_bmm_export/trtllm/gen/`) also number `Sm107a` as 4. As far as I can tell, they do not pass the value into a prebuilt archive.

What is verified: the reproduction above, on x86_64 and aarch64 against the archives at e88d19ca3b, and the code paths listed under "Actual behavior". Our SM107 builds carry `Sm107a = 5`. I have not run an SM107 build with the unpatched value end to end, so I cannot say exactly which kernel selections change with 4.

I have the one-line fix and can open a PR.

items.title: [BUG] NVCC 13.3 cudafe++ explodes host code for structured bindings of CuTe TMA tuples
items.author: RobotGF

comments.author: RobotGF
comments.body:
Update: I retested the public reproducer with **CUDA Toolkit 13.4 Update 1**, released on 2026-09-09. Its NVCC component reports:

```
Cuda compilation tools, release 13.4, V13.4.59
Build cuda_13.4.r13.4/compiler.38657139_0
```

Using the same CUTLASS `main` commit (`147295a3d4b75f3aeff247c25b8927cea9a7006a`) and GCC 12.3.1:

| NVCC | Source form | Result | Generated `repro.cudafe1.cpp` |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: |
| 13.4.59 | structured binding | stopped after exceeding the 64 MiB safety limit in 22.24 s | >64 MiB |
| 13.4.59 | `std::get` workaround | succeeds in 36.65 s | 13,232,759 bytes |

So the `cudafe++` expansion regression is still present in CUDA 13.4 Update 1; the workaround remains effective.

comments.author: RobotGF
comments.body:
Further isolation points to the tuple-like structured-binding type printer in `cudafe++`, rather than CUTLASS/CuTe semantics or the host compiler.

I passed the exact same public repro preprocessed input (`repro.cpp4.ii`) directly to each `cudafe++` binary:

| `cudafe++` | EDG front end | Result | Generated host C++ |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: |
| 13.0.88 | 6.7 | succeeds | 13,135,720 bytes |
| 13.1.115 | 6.7 | succeeds | 13,136,458 bytes |
| 13.2.86 | 6.7 | succeeds | 13,133,760 bytes |
| 13.3.33 | 6.8 | stopped at safety limit | >64 MiB |
| 13.3.73 | 6.8 | stopped at safety limit | >64 MiB |
| 13.4.59 | 6.8 | stopped at safety limit | >64 MiB |

The first observed regression is therefore the initial CUDA 13.3 compiler build. The EDG 6.7 to 6.8 change correlates with its introduction, although this alone does not establish whether the defect is in EDG itself or NVIDIA's CUDA-specific integration.

Generated-code comparison on the identical input is particularly revealing:

* 13.2.86 emits a 2,415-byte kernel-instantiation line containing concrete `cute::TiledCopy<...>` types. The entire file contains 151 occurrences of `tuple_element`.
* 13.3.33 emits an incomplete 56,050,392-byte kernel-instantiation line beginning with `std::tuple_element<0, std::tuple<...>>`. That partial file already contains 660,490 occurrences of `tuple_element`.

Additional syntax tests with NVCC 13.4.59 and the current CUTLASS `main`:

| Form | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `std::tuple` + structured binding + `decltype(binding)` | fails / expands |
| `cute::tuple` + structured binding + `decltype(binding)` | fails / expands |
| Plain aggregate return + structured binding + `decltype(binding)` | succeeds |
| `std::apply` with deduced lambda parameters | succeeds |
| Helper function that deduces the kernel template arguments from values | succeeds |

This matches the C++ structured-binding rules: tuple-like decomposition gives each binding a referenced type based on `tuple_element<I, E>::type`, while aggregate decomposition uses the declared member type. In 13.3+, `cudafe++` appears to preserve and recursively print the former type expression instead of canonicalizing it before serializing the explicit CUDA kernel template-id.

A compiler-friendly workaround that preserves the original call-site syntax is therefore to return a plain aggregate rather than a tuple:

```cpp
template<class Q, class KV, class Y>
struct TmaBundle { Q q; KV kv; Y y; };

auto [q, kv, y] = make_tma_bundle(...);
auto kernel = probe<decltype(q), decltype(kv), decltype(y)>;
```

I also tested this form in the larger source: NVCC 13.3.73 host generation succeeds and returns to the normal ~13 MiB output size; a full NVCC 13.4.59 compile succeeds as well.

items.title: Support `bytearray` in Dynamo
items.author: guilhermeleobas
items.body_excerpt:
`bytearray` has no `VariableTracker` model in Dynamo and any attempt to use it will result in a graph break. We want to close this gap as `bytearray` seems to be used by some libraries under the hood. 

## Current state

Probed on `main` with `torch.compile(fn, backend="eager", fullgraph=True)`.
Each row is roughly `torch.compile(lambda b: <op>, backend="eager",
fullgraph=True)(bytearray(b"abc"))`.

| operation | result |
| --- | --- |
| `bytearray()` / `bytearray(3)` / `bytearray([1,2,3])` / `bytearray(b"abc")` / `bytearray("abc", "utf-8")` | `Unsupported: Failed to trace builtin operator` |
| pass a `bytearray` arg straight through | works |
| `b == b"abc"` | works |
| `isinstance(b, bytearray)` | works |
| `len(b)` | `Unsupported: C-implemented special method without VariableTracker model` |
| `b[1]`, `b[1:]`, `b[0] = 65` | same as above |
| `iter(b)` / `list(b)`, `98 in b` | same as above |
| `b.append(65)`, `b.extend(b"cd")`, `b += b"cd"` | `Unsupported: Failed to trace builtin operator` |
| `bytes(b)`, `memoryview(b)` | `Unsupported: Failed to trace builtin operator` |
| `b.decode()`, `b.hex()` | `Unsupported: Unsupported method call` |
| `b * 2` | `Unsupported: sq_repeat_impl not implemented` |
| mutating a `bytearray` passed in as an arg | `Unsupported: Unsupported method call` |
| `torch.frombuffer(b, dtype=torch.uint8)` | `Unsupported: Failed to convert args/kwargs to proxy` |
| `bytearray` subclass instantiation | `Unsupported: Unsupported function call` |

Three of the 26 probed operations work today.

## Scope of work
1. Port the CPython test suite
CPython has no `test_bytearray.py`; `bytearray` coverage lives in
`Lib/test/test_bytes.py` (~2657 lines), shared with `bytes` via a common base
class.

2. Add a `ByteArrayVariable(VariableTracker)` with support for sequence / mapping / number protocols, methods (using `tp_methods`), iteration, etc. Not everything needs to be done in the same PR and follow-ups are ok.

3. Fix the corner cases the port surfaces

items.title: [DCP] `dcp.save` silently keeps one rank's copy when values under the same key differ across ranks, e.g. RNG state
items.author: Qinyu-Xu
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.distributed.checkpoint.save` treats a value under the same key on every rank as replicated. It keeps only one rank's copy and drops the others (see #120356). When the value is per-rank state, for example Python or NumPy RNG state, every rank restores that one copy on load, and the other ranks' state is lost.

In the example below, each rank seeds Python's `random` with `1234 + rank` and saves its state under the key `rng`. After loading, all four ranks restore rank 0's state.

```python
import os, random, tempfile
import torch.distributed as dist
import torch.distributed.checkpoint as dcp
import torch.multiprocessing as mp


def run(rank, path):
    os.environ.update(MASTER_ADDR="localhost", MASTER_PORT="29513")
    dist.init_process_group("gloo", rank=rank, world_size=4)
    random.seed(1234 + rank)

    dcp.save({"rng": random.getstate()}, checkpoint_id=path)
    expected = random.random() 

    state = {"rng": random.getstate()}
    dcp.load(state, checkpoint_id=path)
    random.setstate(state["rng"])
    got = random.random()

    print(f"rank {rank}: expected {expected:.4f}  got {got:.4f}", flush=True)
    dist.destroy_process_group()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    mp.spawn(run, args=(tempfile.mkdtemp(),), nprocs=4)
```

Output:

```
rank 0: expected 0.9665  got 0.9665
rank 1: expected 0.9086  got 0.9665
rank 2: expected 0.5334  got 0.9665
rank 3: expected 0.1487  got 0.9665
```

#### Why this matters

Saving RNG state is meant to make a resumed run continue exactly like an uninterrupted one. However, when every rank's RNG state collapses to one rank's, exact continuation no longer holds. RLinf ran into this problem and fixed it in RLinf/RLinf#1570. They report that their original checkpoint "restored incorrect rank RNG streams and diverged during continuation".

Also, in some setups, ranks are seeded differently so that dropout masks or MoE router noise are independent across ranks. After the collapse, all ranks draw the same values, so this independence is lost. For example, Megatron-LM seeds its RNG per rank for independent MoE router noise. NVIDIA/Megatron-LM#6858 fixed a resume that restored other ranks' streams in its own checkpoint format, and left a TODO for the same defect in its `fsdp_dtensor` format, which saves with `dcp.save`([source](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Megatron-LM/blob/3914483fd325e053797aff3fa431d4a3141139aa/megatron/training/checkpointing.py#L573-L577)).

#### Where it happens

When building its save plan, every rank adds a write request for each value, so every rank asks to write `rng`:

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/54b9926ebf45a422247d8a72011dcbde9eb90f3d/torch/distributed/checkpoint/default_planner.py#L555-L559

The coordinator then removes duplicates in `dedup_save_plans`. It groups requests by key alone and keeps only one rank's request for each key:

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/54b9926ebf45a422247d8a72011dcbde9eb90f3d/torch/distributed/checkpoint/_dedup_save_plans.py#L36-L55

#### Expected behavior

1. Warn when values under the same key differ across ranks. Each rank could hash its non-tensor values while building its local plan. The hashes would travel with the local plans that are already gathered on the coordinator, so the coordinator could compare them cheaply.
2. Document the requirement. The documentation should state that values under the same key must be identical on every rank.

### Versions

Reproduced on torch 2.14.1 (stable) and 2.15.0.dev20260923 (nightly, 54b9926e).

items.title: Elastic c10d rendezvous reuses stale MASTER_ADDR/MASTER_PORT across rounds
items.author: digit50
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

With the c10d rendezvous backend and the shared rendezvous TCPStore (the default, `TORCH_DISABLE_SHARE_RDZV_TCP_STORE` unset), `DynamicRendezvousHandler` caches the bootstrap store info (`MASTER_ADDR`/`MASTER_PORT`) from its first round and reuses it in later rounds. This breaks two ordinary elastic cases:

1. Scale-up while rank 0 stays rank 0: the rank-0 node never writes `MASTER_ADDR`/`MASTER_PORT` under the new round's store prefix, so a node joining in a later round blocks on `store.get("MASTER_ADDR")` until the store read timeout (60 s by default for c10d) and its rendezvous fails with `DistStoreError`, while the existing nodes have already counted it in the world size.
2. The rank-0 node leaves: the new rank 0 starts a new store and publishes its own address, but every surviving non-zero rank keeps returning the old rank 0's address. The agent passes these straight to the workers as `MASTER_ADDR`/`MASTER_PORT`, so the workers of one round are pointed at two different stores, one of them on a dead node.

Repro: each node is a `DynamicRendezvousHandler` with its own loopback address and its own `TCPStore` client, run in threads of one process. Ranks are assigned by sorted node address, so node1 is rank 0 while it is alive.

```python
"""c10d rendezvous with the shared TCPStore (the default): bootstrap store info
(MASTER_ADDR / MASTER_PORT) is cached across rounds.

A: scale-up while rank 0 stays rank 0. The joining node waits for MASTER_ADDR
   under the new round's prefix, nobody writes it, and its rendezvous fails.
B: the rank-0 node dies. The new rank 0 publishes its own address, the
   surviving rank 1 keeps returning the dead node's address.

Each "node" is a DynamicRendezvousHandler with its own loopback address and its
own TCPStore client, run in threads of one process.
"""

import os
import sys
import threading
import time
from datetime import timedelta

import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
from torch.distributed.elastic.rendezvous.c10d_rendezvous_backend import C10dRendezvousBackend
from torch.distributed.elastic.rendezvous.dynamic_rendezvous import (
    DynamicRendezvousHandler,
    RendezvousTimeout,
)

STORE_TIMEOUT = timedelta(seconds=8)
master = dist.TCPStore("127.0.0.1", 0, is_master=True, multi_tenant=True, timeout=STORE_TIMEOUT)


def make_node(run_id, addr, min_nodes, max_nodes):
    store = dist.TCPStore("127.0.0.1", master.port, is_master=False, timeout=STORE_TIMEOUT)
    return DynamicRendezvousHandler.from_backend(
        run_id,
        store,
        C10dRendezvousBackend(store, run_id),
        min_nodes,
        max_nodes,
        local_addr=addr,
        timeout=RendezvousTimeout(
            join=timedelta(seconds=60),
            last_call=timedelta(seconds=1),
            heartbeat=timedelta(seconds=2),
        ),
        keep_alive_interval=1,
    )


def rendezvous_all(nodes):
    out = {}

    def run(name, h):
        t0 = time.monotonic()
        try:
            info = h.next_rendezvous()
            b = info.bootstrap_store_info
            out[name] = f"rank={info.rank} world={info.world_size} master={b.master_addr}:{b.master_port}"
        except Exception as e:
            out[name] = f"{type(e).__name__} after {time.monotonic() - t0:.1f}s: {e}"

    threads = [threading.Thread(target=run, args=(n, h)) for n, h in nodes.items()]
    for t in threads:
        t.start()
    for t in threads:
        t.join()
    return out


def scale_up():
    print("A: scale-up, --nnodes=1:2")
    h1 = make_node("a", "127.0.0.1", 1, 2)
    print("  round 0", rendezvous_all({"node1": h1}))
    h2 = make_node("a", "127.0.0.2", 1, 2)
    # node2 arrives after round 0 closed; it lands on the wait list.
    t = threading.Thread(target=lambda: res.update(rendezvous_all({"node2": h2})))
    res = {}
    t.start()
    while h1.num_nodes_waiting() == 0:
        time.sleep(0.1)
    # node1's agent sees a waiting node and re-rendezvouses, as the agent does.
    res.update(rendezvous_all({"node1": h1}))
    t.join()
    print("  round 1", dict(sorted(res.items())))
    print("  expected: node2 gets rank=1 and node1's master address")


def rank0_leaves():
    print("B: rank-0 node dies, --nnodes=2:3")
    nodes = {f"node{i}": make_node("b", f"127.0.0.{i}", 2, 3) for i in (1, 2, 3)}
    print("  round 0", dict(sorted(rendezvous_all(nodes).items())))
    # node1 dies: no more keep-alive heartbeats.
    nodes["node1"]._stop_heartbeats()
    time.sleep(4)
    out = rendezvous_all({"node2": nodes["node2"], "node3": nodes["node3"]})
    print("  round 1", dict(sorted(out.items())))
    print("  expected: node2 and node3 report the same master (node2's)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(f"python: {sys.version.split()[0]}")
    print(f"torch: {torch.__version__}")
    print(f"TORCH_DISABLE_SHARE_RDZV_TCP_STORE={os.getenv('TORCH_DISABLE_SHARE_RDZV_TCP_STORE')}")
    scale_up()
    rank0_leaves()
    sys.stdout.flush()
    # Keep-alive threads are still running; skip interpreter teardown.
    os._exit(0)
```

Output on 2.14.1:

```
python: 3.12.3
torch: 2.14.1+cpu
TORCH_DISABLE_SHARE_RDZV_TCP_STORE=None
A: scale-up, --nnodes=1:2
  round 0 {'node1': 'rank=0 world=1 master=127.0.0.1:36363'}
[W1017 20:43:03.839016103 socket.cpp:469] [c10d] waitForInput: poll for socket SocketImpl(fd=25, addr=[localhost]:40750, remote=[localhost]:34271) returned 0, likely a timeout
[W1017 20:43:03.839080599 socket.cpp:494] [c10d] waitForInput: socket SocketImpl(fd=25, addr=[localhost]:40750, remote=[localhost]:34271) timed out after 8000ms
  round 1 {'node1': 'rank=0 world=2 master=127.0.0.1:36363', 'node2': 'DistStoreError after 10.2s: wait timeout after 8000ms, keys: /torch.rendezvous.a.1/MASTER_ADDR'}
  expected: node2 gets rank=1 and node1's master address
B: rank-0 node dies, --nnodes=2:3
  round 0 {'node1': 'rank=0 world=3 master=127.0.0.1:40975', 'node2': 'rank=1 world=3 master=127.0.0.1:40975', 'node3': 'rank=2 world=3 master=127.0.0.1:40975'}
  round 1

items.title: TORCHELASTIC_ENABLE_FILE_TIMER: one expired worker timer SIGKILLs torchrun
items.author: digit50
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

With `TORCHELASTIC_ENABLE_FILE_TIMER=1`, when a worker's `expires()` timer runs out, the `FileTimerServer` kills the worker and then sends the same signal (SIGKILL by default) to its own process. That server runs as a thread inside the torchrun agent, so the agent kills itself. `--max-restarts` is ignored, the other workers are never stopped (binary workers run in their own session, so they are orphaned), no `ChildFailedError` is raised, the rendezvous is not shut down and the timer FIFO is left on disk.

Repro: 2 local workers, `--max-restarts=1`. Local rank 0 holds `expires(after=0.5)` and hangs, local rank 1 just sleeps.

```python
"""With TORCHELASTIC_ENABLE_FILE_TIMER=1, one expired worker timer SIGKILLs the
torchrun agent itself.

torchrun --nproc-per-node=2 --max-restarts=1: local rank 0 enters
expires(after=0.5) and hangs, local rank 1 just sleeps.
"""

import os
import signal
import socket
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
import textwrap
import time

import torch

WORKER = textwrap.dedent(
    """
    import os, sys, time
    from torch.distributed.elastic.timer import FileTimerClient, configure, expires

    pid_dir = sys.argv[1]
    rank = int(os.environ["LOCAL_RANK"])
    with open(os.path.join(pid_dir, f"rank{rank}.pid"), "w") as f:
        f.write(str(os.getpid()))
    if rank == 0:
        configure(FileTimerClient(file_path=os.environ["TORCHELASTIC_TIMER_FILE"]))
        with expires(after=0.5):
            time.sleep(30)  # hangs past its deadline
    else:
        time.sleep(30)
    """
)


def free_port():
    with socket.socket() as s:
        s.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0))
        return s.getsockname()[1]


def alive(pid):
    try:
        os.kill(pid, 0)
        return True
    except ProcessLookupError:
        return False


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(f"python: {sys.version.split()[0]}")
    print(f"torch: {torch.__version__}")
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
        worker = os.path.join(d, "worker.py")
        with open(worker, "w") as f:
            f.write(WORKER)
        timer_file = os.path.join(d, "watchdog_fifo")
        env = dict(os.environ, TORCHELASTIC_ENABLE_FILE_TIMER="1", TORCHELASTIC_TIMER_FILE=timer_file, LOGLEVEL="INFO")
        cmd = [
            sys.executable, "-m", "torch.distributed.run",
            "--nproc-per-node=2", "--max-restarts=1", "--monitor-interval=0.5",
            "--rdzv-backend=c10d", f"--rdzv-endpoint=127.0.0.1:{free_port()}",
            worker, d,
        ]
        log = os.path.join(d, "torchrun.log")
        t0 = time.monotonic()
        with open(log, "w") as f:
            p = subprocess.Popen(cmd, env=env, stdout=f, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT)
            p.wait(timeout=120)
        elapsed = time.monotonic() - t0
        for line in open(log).read().splitlines():
            if "reaped worker" in line or "Terminating the server process" in line:
                print("  log:", line.split("] ", 1)[-1][:160])
        print(f"observed: torchrun (pid {p.pid}) exit code {p.returncode} after {elapsed:.1f}s")
        rank1 = int(open(os.path.join(d, "rank1.pid")).read())
        print(f"observed: local rank 1 still running after torchrun exited: {alive(rank1)}")
        print(f"observed: timer FIFO left behind: {os.path.exists(timer_file)}")
        if alive(rank1):
            os.kill(rank1, signal.SIGKILL)
    print("expected: torchrun kills rank 0, restarts the worker group once (--max-restarts=1), "
          "then exits non-zero with ChildFailedError after stopping all workers")
```

Output on 2.14.1:

```
python: 3.12.3
torch: 2.14.1+cpu
  log: Successfully reaped worker=[3740272] with signal=9
  log: Terminating the server process=[3740191] because of expired timers
observed: torchrun (pid 3740191) exit code -9 after 2.3s
observed: local rank 1 still running after torchrun exited: True
observed: timer FIFO left behind: True
expected: torchrun kills rank 0, restarts the worker group once (--max-restarts=1), then exits non-zero with ChildFailedError after stopping all workers
```

Expected: the agent kills rank 0 and treats it as a worker failure, so it restarts the group once and then exits non-zero with `ChildFailedError` after stopping every worker.

Cause: in `torch/distributed/elastic/timer/file_based_local_timer.py` at 31ba9a5, after a successful reap `FileTimerServer` calls `self._reap_worker(os.getpid(), reap_signal)` (lines 354-359), added in #141060 (first in 2.7.0). `LocalElasticAgent` starts this server with `daemon=True` inside the agent process when the env var is set (`torch/distributed/elastic/agent/server/local_elastic_agent.py` 271-278), so `os.getpid()` is the agent. I think this is also why `test_get_timer_recursive` gets killed in #143965.

Proposed fix: don't kill the hosting process from inside the agent. Either make the self-kill opt-in with a constructor flag that `LocalElasticAgent` leaves off, or let the agent pick up the reaped worker through its normal monitoring so the restart and failure handling runs.

I can send a PR for this.

### Versions

```
PyTorch version: 2.14.1+cpu
Is debug build: False
CUDA used to build PyTorch: None
OS: Pop!_OS 24.04 LTS (x86_64)
GCC version: (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0
Python version: 3.12.3 (64-bit runtime)
Is CUDA available: False
```

items.title: ☂️ Deprecations and frozen components: when they started, and when the code is removed
items.author: drisspg
items.body_excerpt:
This issue tracks every deprecation, frozen component, and pending removal in PyTorch. Each one has its own tracking issue, listed as a sub-issue below, so progress is visible at a glance.

### Process

1. **Deprecate in release N.** Warn on use. The warning names the start version, the removal version, and the tracking issue, e.g. ``"`torch.foo` is deprecated since 2.15 and will be removed in 2.17. Use `torch.bar` instead. See https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/NNNN"``.
2. **Warn for at least two releases.** The earliest removal is N+2. Behavior changes become an error for one release before the new behavior is enabled.
3. **Remove** in N+2 or later, and close the tracking issue.

Frozen components (no new features, bugs closed as won't-fix) are tracked the same way, with removal target `none` until a removal is planned.

### Adding an entry

1. File a tracking issue with the [Deprecation tracking](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/new?template=deprecation.yml) form. It is labeled `module: deprecation` and `slowroll`.
2. Attach it as a sub-issue of this issue.
3. Keep its `Next step` field current (e.g. `remove in 2.17`). Milestones are assigned from it at each branch cut, following the convention that milestone X means "land right after the X branch cut".

Agents follow the same steps through the `deprecate-feature` skill (#201299).

### Needs a tracking issue

These are already deprecated or frozen but have no tracking issue yet. Main is at 2.15.0a0, so every target below has passed.

| API or component | Kind | Stated removal target | Location |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| C++ frontend (`torch::nn`, `torch::optim`, ...) | Frozen component | none | e.g. #80494 |
| `torch.ao.quantization` | Removal | 2.10 | torch/ao/quantization/utils.py |
| `torch._custom_op` | Removal | 2.6 | torch/_custom_op/impl.py |
| flex_attention `return_lse` | Removal | 2.10 | torch/nn/attention/flex_attention.py |
| cpp_extension PyBind11 ABI handling | Removal | 2.9 | torch/utils/cpp_extension.py |
| DCP `state_dict` deprecated options | Removal | 2.5 | torch/distributed/checkpoint/state_dict.py |
| `make_tensor` with `low==high` for float/complex | Behavior change | 2.3 | torch/testing/_creation.py |
| FSDP `optim_input` | Removal | 1.13 | torch/distributed/fsdp/fully_sharded_data_parallel.py |
| `torch.utils.data.graph.traverse` | Removal | 1.13 | torch/utils/data/graph.py |
| `AutoNonVariableTypeMode` | Removal | 1.10 | aten/src/ATen/core/LegacyTypeDispatch.h |
| Distribution templates warning becomes an error | Behavior change | 1.7 | aten/src/ATen/native/DistributionTemplates.h |
| C++ `Optimizer::parameters()/add_parameters()/size()` | Removal | 1.6 | torch/csrc/api/src/optim/optimizer.cpp |

### Related

- #55953: previous deprecation tracker (closed)
- #49642: turn deprecation warnings into errors in CI
- #60149: find out when an API was added or changed

items.title: CUDA SymmetricMemory: rank-local rendezvous failure leaves peer resources and stalls other ranks
items.author: jackLei0901
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

I tested the behavior when a CUDA SymmetricMemory rendezvous fails on a specific rank. By artificially injecting a peer-import or peer-map failure on Rank 0, Rank 1 returned after approximately 301 seconds, with the imported resources remaining unreleased. Although local tensor health checks passed on both ranks, the subsequent rendezvous operation within the same group failed during the metadata exchange phase. These results come from injected-fault testing, with one run per case, rather than the reproduction of a failure under a real-world workload.

#### AI-assisted technical report

AI assistance was used for the diagnostic and this report. Two processes shared one RTX 4090, using a Gloo group, the Store-exchange/POSIX-FD route, overlapping-device allowance and multicast disabled. The shim temporarily intercepts process-local DriverAPI calls; only rank 0's first peer import or map is failed.

H/R/M below denotes imported-handle references, address reservations and mappings remaining when the first call returned:

| Case | Rank 0 | Rank 1 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Normal | Success | Success; fresh same-group second rendezvous and peer-data checks also passed on both ranks |
| Import failure | Error in 0.012 s; H/R/M 0/0/0; received FD still open | `RuntimeError("Wait timeout")` after 301 s; H/R/M 1/1/1 |
| Map failure | Error in 0.012 s; H/R/M 1/1/0; received FD still open | Same 301 s wait and H/R/M 1/1/1 |

The normal resources have committed owners; they are not leaks. Fault-case leftovers were measured while processes remained alive, before teardown. FD evidence is an open descriptor with matching identity at first return, not a complete close-call trace. The map case's rank-0 reservation leak is the already-known #201091 problem, not a new finding.

With injection disabled and fresh allocations, both fault-case retries failed in about 6 s: rank 0 waited for `CUDASymmetricMemory/1/1`, while rank 1 waited for `CUDASymmetricMemory/2/0`. Neither reached a new peer import. Both ranks observed metadata keys `0/0`, `0/1`, `1/0`, `2/1` present, with `1/1` and `2/0` absent. This corroborates exchange-sequence divergence; counters were not directly instrumented. Retry was a diagnostic, not an assertion that same-group recovery is currently supported.

The Store timeout was configured and read back as 5 s. The 301 s peer wait is consistent with the PrefixStore barrier's inherited timeout; that is a separate c10d concern, not the proposed fix here.

#### Source explanation

On the audited source, rank 0 throws inside the [peer-import loop](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/74b55cafb21cf7d14bf8adc466e256ef2b994533/torch/csrc/distributed/c10d/symm_mem/CUDASymmetricMemory.cu#L1039) before reaching the [Store barrier](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/74b55cafb21cf7d14bf8adc466e256ef2b994533/torch/csrc/distributed/c10d/symm_mem/CUDASymmetricMemory.cu#L1078). Rank 1 waits there. Peer [AllocationRef owners are constructed only afterward](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/74b55cafb21cf7d14bf8adc466e256ef2b994533/torch/csrc/distributed/c10d/symm_mem/CUDASymmetricMemory.cu#L1121), leaving its imports and mappings without an owner when the barrier throws. Rank 0 also skips the barrier's exchange sequence, consistent with the divergent metadata keys observed on retry.

The diagnostic and sanitized evidence are linked below.

https://gist.github.com/jackLei0901/cf4c1ff43d39504291f084b4fc391975

#### Scope and limits

The tested library is a local build on reported pin `215856938cfe9347ea2d0a20a766577e45fa5bb8`, containing an earlier draft of #201091's local `alloc()` change. Its peer-rendezvous code, StoreExchange and Store code match `74b55cafb21cf7d14bf8adc466e256ef2b994533`; this is not a complete current-main build or the shared-helper revision in #201284.

No fix arm, two-physical-GPU run, NCCL process-group (`use_pg`) path, multicast, Fabric, ROCm, fatal CUDA error or process-loss case was tested. vLLM fallback relevance is source-based, not a serving reproduction.

#### Reporter conclusion and scope question

kapilsh, do you think it would be appropriate to use the existing `MulticastSetup` coordinated-outcome pattern to handle the subsequent processing for the peer setup phase? My goal is for the participating ranks to reach a consensus on success or failure, and—in the event of failure—to release the peer handles, mappings, and received file descriptors (FDs) they have acquired.

Should the agreed-upon behavior be limited strictly to "prompt coordinated failure handling and resource cleanup" (with the caller responsible for recreating the group or terminating the program), or should it also support "subsequent rendezvous within the same group"? This decision will determine the scope of the exchange sequence logic and the regression testing strategy. I haven't implemented the fix for coordinated failure handling yet; unless you need to support the "retry within the same group" feature, I plan to exclude it from the current implementation scope.

### Versions

PyTorch: 2.16.0a0+git2158569; reported pin: 215856938cfe9347ea2d0a20a766577e45fa5bb8.
CUDA build: 13.0; driver: 595.71.05; OS: Linux; GPU: one RTX 4090 shared by two processes.
Backend: CUDA SymmetricMemory; allocator: native, expandable segments disabled.

items.title: `get_ema_avg_fn` and `get_ema_multi_avg_fn` silently accept NaN decay, producing silently-NaN averaged parameters
items.author: muditagrawal2007
items.body_excerpt:
## Title

`get_ema_avg_fn` and `get_ema_multi_avg_fn` silently accept `NaN` `decay`, producing silently-NaN averaged parameters

## Body

### Describe the bug

`torch.optim.swa_utils.get_ema_avg_fn` and `torch.optim.swa_utils.get_ema_multi_avg_fn` are documented to require `decay` in `[0, 1]`, but they actually accept `float("nan")` at construction time and then produce `NaN` averaged tensors on every subsequent `AveragedModel.update_parameters(...)` call. There is no warning, no error, and no diagnostic.

A recent PR, #199953, fixed the same bug in `torch.optim.sgd.SGD` (the same `x < 0.0` vs. `not 0.0 <= x` NaN-comparison pitfall). `swa_utils.py` is the only place left in `torch/optim/` that still uses the broken ordered-comparison check for the EMA `decay`. Because the bug was reported and fixed elsewhere in `torch.optim` already, this is effectively a regression against the project-wide convention; the SWA factories were simply overlooked.

### Reproduction

```python
import math
import torch
from torch.optim.swa_utils import (
    AveragedModel,
    get_ema_avg_fn,
    get_ema_multi_avg_fn,
)

model = torch.nn.Linear(3, 3)
avg_model = AveragedModel(
    model,
    multi_avg_fn=get_ema_multi_avg_fn(decay=float("nan")),  # no error raised -- BUG
)
# Construct the non-multi variant too:
_ = get_ema_avg_fn(decay=float("nan"))                       # no error raised -- BUG

# Drive one update so the closure runs.
x = torch.randn(2, 3)
loss = (model(x).sum() - 0.0) ** 2
loss.backward()
avg_model.update_parameters(model)

print(torch.isnan(next(avg_model.parameters())).any().item())  # True
```

After the proposed fix, both `get_ema_avg_fn(decay=float("nan"))` and `get_ema_multi_avg_fn(decay=float("nan"))` raise `ValueError: Invalid decay value nan provided. Please provide a value in [0,1] range.` at construction time, matching what `SGD` does today for `lr`, `momentum`, and `weight_decay` (after #199953).

### Expected behavior

`get_ema_avg_fn(decay=float("nan"))` and `get_ema_multi_avg_fn(decay=float("nan"))` should both raise `ValueError` at construction time, just like they already do for negative decays (`-0.1`) and decays above `1.0` (`1.5`).

### Root cause

Both factories validate with an ordered comparison:

```python
if decay < 0.0 or decay > 1.0:
    raise ValueError(...)
```

Per IEEE-754, every ordered comparison with `NaN` evaluates to `False`, so the `or` expression is `False` for `decay=nan` and the guard is skipped. The closure then computes `decay * ema + (1 - decay) * current_param` (or `_foreach_lerp_(..., 1 - decay)`), and `1 - float("nan") == float("nan")`, so every update produces `NaN` tensors.

### Why this matters

`AveragedModel` is the canonical recipe for EMA used in PyTorch examples, in torchvision references for object detection, and in Hugging Face trainer defaults. Silent NaN averages are particularly bad in distributed/slow-fail training jobs because they corrupt the averaged checkpoint and any downstream evaluation.

### Suggested fix

```python
if not 0.0 <= decay <= 1.0:
    raise ValueError(
        f"Invalid decay value {decay} provided. Please provide a value in [0,1] range."
    )
```

This is the same idiom used by every other built-in optimizer (`Adam`, `AdamW`, `Adagrad`, `RMSprop`, `RAdam`, `Rprop`, `SparseAdam`, `ASGD`, `NAdam`, `Adadelta`, `LBFGS`, `_FunctionalOptimizer`, `Muon`, and `SGD` after #199953). NaN becomes rejected at construction; valid values (`0.0`, `0.999`, `1.0`, `-0.0`) behave exactly as before.

### Versions

Nightly `pytorch` built from `main` (HEAD ~ `ece869f8d25`). Python 3.11, CPU-only reproduction; no CUDA needed.

### Agent details (if applicable)

> Prepared with an AI coding assistant (Claude / Anthropic) and reviewed by the human reporter. The root cause (NaN ordered-comparison) was verified locally by running the validation logic directly in Python; the underlying IEEE-754 behavior is the source of the bug, not PyTorch-specific. A `git grep` confirmed `swa_utils.py` is the only file in `torch/optim/` whose `[0, 1]`-style guard still uses the `x < 0.0 or x > 1.0` form, so the fix has a clear cross-file precedent. A PR with the proposed fix and a parametrized `assertRaisesRegex` test for invalid decay (`NaN`, `-0.1`, `1.5`) plus boundary passes (`0.0`, `0.5`, `1.0`) is being prepared for review.

items.title: [RFC]: Support Encode/Prefill/Decode (EPD) Disaggregation in AIBrix Gateway
items.author: varungup90
items.body_excerpt: ### Summary This RFC proposes adding Encode/Prefill/Decode (EPD) disaggregation support to AIBrix Gateway. Today, AIBrix supports Prefill/Decode (PD) disaggregation. With growing multimodal workloads, the encoding stage can also become a significant and independently scalable part of inference. EPD disaggregation separates inference into three stages: * Encode (E): Process multimodal inputs such as image, video, or audio and generate intermediate representations. * Prefill (P): Process prompt tokens and encoder outputs and generate KV cache. * Decode (D): Perform autoregressive token generation. The Gateway should become aware of these worker roles and route requests to the appropriate Encode, Prefill, and Decode worker pools. ### Motivation Encode, Prefill, and Decode have different compute and memory characteristics. Running all stages on the same workers can lead to resource contention and makes it difficult to scale each stage independently. EPD disaggregation enables: * Independent scaling of Encode, Prefill, and Decode workers. * Better resource utilization for multimodal workloads. * Different hardware or parallelism configurations for each stage. * Isolation of expensive multimodal encoding from Prefill/Decode workloads. * Reuse of the existing AIBrix PD routing architecture for multimodal serving. vLLM has started supporting disaggregated encoder architectures, including EPD-style deployments: * https://docs.vllm.ai/projects/ascend/en/latest/user_guide/feature_guide/epd_disaggregation.html * https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/features/disagg_encoder/ ### Proposed Change Extend AIBrix Gateway’s existing PD disaggregation support to understand an additional Encode worker role. Conceptually: For multimodal requests, the Gateway should: 1. Identify compatible Encode, Prefill, and Decode workers. 2. Select workers using the existing AIBrix load-balancing framework. 3. Pass the required routing/transfer metadata to the inference engine. 4. Allow the inference engine and its connectors to handle encoder-output and KV-cache transfers. For text-only requests, the Encode stage can be bypassed and existing PD routing can continue to be used. The implementation should reuse the existing PD routing infrastructure as much as possible rather than introducing a separate routing architecture. Initial Scope * Add encode as a supported worker role alongside prefill and decode. * Discover and maintain Encode/Prefill/Decode worker pools. * Extend PD routing to select a compatible E/P/D execution path. * Support multimodal requests requiring an Encode stage. * Keep encoder-output and KV-cache transfer outside of the Gateway. * Add basic stage-level routing metrics and failure handling. Future work can explore encoder-cache-aware routing, heterogeneous hardware selection, and independent autoscaling of E/P/D worker pools. Open Questions * Should Encode workers be shared across multiple Prefill/Decode pools? * What metadata should the Gateway provide to coordinate encoder-output transfer? * Should worker selection happen in E → P → D order, or should Decode/Prefill capacity drive the selection first? * How much of the existing PD router can be generalized into an EPD stage-aware router? ### Alternatives Considered _No response_ ### Area Not sure

items.title: [Bug] A recovered Batch job past its window with no execution metadata never finishes expiring
items.author: Jackmeson1
items.body_excerpt:
## 🐛 Describe the bug

An in-progress Batch job that is already past its completion window when the metadata service recovers it, and that has no execution metadata (`status.execution is None`), never finishes expiring. It stays `in_progress` with the `expired` condition set, and clients keep seeing `in_progress`.

On recovery, `job_committed_handler` (`python/aibrix/aibrix/batch/batch_manager.py:554` at `99325e7`) does not schedule overdue work and calls `expire_job` instead. For an in-progress job, `expire_job` (line 1184) persists the expired condition and leaves finalization to the live driver it then signals. A recovered job has no driver. The orphan cleanup path that would finish it runs only when `job_expired.status.execution is not None` (line 1258). Every later expiry pass from the scheduler then returns early, because the job is already `IN_PROGRESS` with `EXPIRED` (line 1215). Nothing else owns the job, so it never becomes terminal.

The same recovery with `execution = {}` (not `None`) does finish `expired`, and an overdue `created` job finalizes `expired` as expected (`batch-api.rst:147` documents expiry after the window).

## Steps to Reproduce

From `python/aibrix` at `99325e7`, put this in `tests/batch/` and run it with `pytest`:

<details><summary>test_overdue_recovery.py</summary>

```python
import os
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

import pytest

os.environ.setdefault("SECRET_KEY", "test-secret-key-for-testing")

from aibrix.batch.batch_manager import BatchManager
from aibrix.batch.job_entity import (
    BatchJob,
    BatchJobEndpoint,
    BatchJobSpec,
    BatchJobState,
    BatchJobStatus,
    CompletionWindow,
    ConditionType,
    ObjectMeta,
    TypeMeta,
)
from aibrix.context import InfrastructureContext
from aibrix.metadata.api.v1.batch import _batch_job_to_openai_response


class _Scheduler:
    def __init__(self):
        self.appended = []

    def append_job(self, job_id):
        self.appended.append(job_id)


def _overdue_in_progress_job(job_id, execution):
    created = datetime.now(timezone.utc) - timedelta(hours=25)
    job = BatchJob(
        typeMeta=TypeMeta(apiVersion="batch/v1", kind="Job"),
        metadata=ObjectMeta(
            name=f"job-{job_id}", namespace="default", uid=f"uid-{job_id}",
            creationTimestamp=created, resourceVersion=None, deletionTimestamp=None,
        ),
        spec=BatchJobSpec(
            input_file_id=f"input-{job_id}",
            endpoint=BatchJobEndpoint.CHAT_COMPLETIONS.value,
            completion_window=CompletionWindow.TWENTY_FOUR_HOURS.expires_at(),
        ),
        status=BatchJobStatus(
            jobID=job_id, state=BatchJobState.IN_PROGRESS,
            createdAt=created, inProgressAt=created,
        ),
    )
    job.status.request_counts.total = 1
    job.status.execution = execution
    return job


@pytest.mark.asyncio
@pytest.mark.parametrize("execution", [None, {}], ids=["execution-none", "execution-empty"])
async def test_recovered_overdue_in_progress_job_expires(execution):
    manager = BatchManager(InfrastructureContext())
    scheduler = _Scheduler()
    manager.set_scheduler(scheduler)
    job = _overdue_in_progress_job(f"overdue-{execution is None}", execution)

    await manager.job_committed_handler(job)  # recovery after a restart
    await manager.expire_job(job.job_id)  # the scheduler's next expiry pass

    assert scheduler.appended == []  # overdue work is not scheduled
    current = manager._done_jobs.get(job.job_id) or await manager.get_job(job.job_id)
    assert current.status.state == BatchJobState.FINALIZED, (
        f"state={current.status.state.value} condition={current.status.condition} "
        f"client={_batch_job_to_openai_response(current).status}"
    )
    assert current.status.condition == ConditionType.EXPIRED
    assert _batch_job_to_openai_response(current).status == "expired"
```

</details>

`execution-empty` passes. `execution-none` fails with:

```text
AssertionError: state=in_progress condition=expired client=in_progress
```

The test calls the recovery handler and one more expiry pass directly; it does not restart a process against durable storage.

## Expected behavior

A recovered job past its window finishes `expired` (state `finalized`, condition `expired`, client status `expired`), the same as when it has an empty execution record or was still `created`.

## Environment

- AIBrix version: `main` at `99325e7`
- Deployment environment: Batch API, metadata service recovery; reproduced in-process on Linux, Python 3.10.12
- LLM(s) being used: none

## Area

Batch

I don't plan to send a fix for this soon, so anyone is welcome to take it. A fix probably belongs in `expire_job`: route a recovered job that has no live driver and no execution reference through the existing stopped-job finalization, without stamping `FINALIZED` directly and so bypassing output finalization.

This report was prepared with AI assistance (Claude Code); the test above was run against `main`.

items.title: [Bug] KPA panic mode never holds replicas and reports idle workloads as panic
items.author: AarnavNoble
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

KPA's panic mode doesn't behave as its code describes, and part of that code can never run. Before sending a fix I'd like to agree on which behavior is wanted, since there are two reasonable directions (below).

**1. The "no scale-down while in panic" rule is dead code.** `computeTargetReplicas` (`pkg/controller/podautoscaler/algorithm/kpa.go`) keeps the highest pod count seen during panic in `maxPanicPods` and refuses to go below it:

```go
// We do not scale down while in panic mode. Only increases will be applied.
if desiredPodCount > maxPanicPods { ... context.SetMaxPanicPods(maxPanicPods) }
desiredPodCount = maxPanicPods
```

But the context the controller passes in is `baseScalingContext`, where `GetMaxPanicPods()` returns `0` and `SetMaxPanicPods` is a no-op (`pkg/controller/podautoscaler/context/context.go`). The controller also builds a new context on every reconcile, so `InPanicMode` doesn't carry over either. Each reconcile therefore just takes `max(stable, panic)` for that reconcile, and the panic-mode recommendation can go down while still in panic. The unit tests use `mockScalingContext`, which does store `MaxPanicPods`, so they pass while production never gets this behavior.

**2. An idle workload is reported as panic.** `shouldEnterPanicMode` returns `true` whenever `StableValue <= 0`, so zero traffic (stable 0, panic 0) produces the reason `"panic mode scaling"` and the `Operating in panic mode.` log line.

**3. Panic entry doesn't use Knative's rule.** Panic is entered when `panic / stable > panicThreshold`. Knative enters panic when the panic-window pod count is at least `panicThreshold` times the ready pods (`dppc / readyPods >= panicThreshold`) and stays in it until a full stable window has passed without that. The code computes `isOverPanicThreshold` with Knative's rule but only logs it.

In practice the default 5-minute scale-down cooldown (`stabilizeRecommendation`) hides most of point 1, since it keeps the highest recommendation of the last 5 minutes anyway. With a shorter `scale-down-cooldown-window`, nothing holds replicas during a burst.

### Steps to Reproduce

Calling `KPAAlgorithm.ComputeRecommendation` the way the controller does (a fresh `NewBaseScalingContext()` per call, one `POD` metric `concurrency` with `targetValue: "10"`, default annotations):

| Call | Current pods | Stable value | Panic value | Desired | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 4 | 10 | 25 | 8 | panic mode scaling |
| 2 | 8 | 3 | 6.5 | 6 | panic mode scaling |
| 3 | 4 | 0 | 0 | 2 | panic mode scaling |

Call 2 is still in panic (6.5 / 3 > 2) but recommends fewer pods than call 1, and `GetMaxPanicPods()` is still `0` after both calls. Call 3 has no traffic and is labeled panic.

### Expected behavior

- No `panic` label (reason, log, metrics) when there is no traffic.
- One of these for panic hold, which is what I'd like your input on:
  - **A. Implement it.** Keep panic state per PodAutoscaler across reconciles (the reconciler already keeps per-PodAutoscaler state, such as the recommendation history in `stabilizeRecommendation`, and releases it on delete), enter panic with Knative's `dppc / readyPods >= panicThreshold`, and hold the peak until a stable window passes without panic.
  - **B. Remove it.** Drop `maxPanicPods`, `GetMaxPanicPods`/`SetMaxPanicPods` and the hold logic, document that KPA scales on `max(stable, panic)` while panicking, and leave holding replicas to the scale-down cooldown.

A is closer to Knative and to KPA's docs. B is smaller and keeps one mechanism for holding replicas. I'm happy to send a PR for whichever you prefer, along with the idle-panic fix.

### Environment

- AIBrix version: `main` at 177ba311
- Deployment environment: unit-level reproduction against the KPA algorithm and the real `baseScalingContext`

### Area

Orchestration (controllers, CRDs)

items.title: [Feature][ModelClaim] Lower Retry-After for a sleeping model from 10 s to 3 s; a wake takes 2.5–3.1 s
items.author: Jeffwan
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 Feature Description and Motivation

When a request names a sleeping ModelClaim, the gateway answers `503` with `Retry-After: 10` and asks the controller to wake the model. The wake itself takes 2.5–3.1 s, so a client that honours `Retry-After` waits 10 s for a model that has been ready for about 7 s.

We measured this through Envoy and the gateway on a single A100-40GB, sleeping each model with level-1 sleep and then sending one request:

| Model | Sleeping → Active | First 200, client retries every 1 s | First 200, client honours `Retry-After` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Qwen3-0.6B | 2.5 s | 3.05 s | 10.05 s |
| Qwen3-1.7B | 2.7 s | 3.05 s | 10.05 s |
| Qwen3-8B-FP8 | 3.1 s | 4.06 s | 10.05 s |

The claim stays in the `Sleeping` phase for the whole wake and then moves straight to `Active`, so every 503 in that window carries the sleeping-state value. In a 16-minute run with 12 models taking turns on one card, all 28 requests that found their model asleep had their first token at 10.0–10.1 s. Once awake, the engine answered them in about 40 ms.

The 10 s comes from the default `modelClaimRetryAfterSeconds` ([modelclaim_wake.go#L46](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/main/pkg/plugins/gateway/modelclaim_wake.go#L46)). `modelClaimRetryAfter` picks the value by the controller's reason only ([gateway_req_body.go#L428-L442](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/main/pkg/plugins/gateway/gateway_req_body.go#L428-L442)). A sleeping claim usually carries no reason, so it gets the same 10 s as a claim that is starting from scratch, which takes 40–53 s.

### Use Case

Long-tail models that sleep when idle and are woken by their next request: the first request after an idle period is the one users notice. Cutting its wait from 10 s to the time the wake actually takes makes request-triggered wake usable for interactive traffic.

### Proposed Solution

1. Choose the Retry-After by the binding's state as well as by its reason. A claim in the `sleeping` state with no reason gets 3 s. Everything else keeps today's values:

   | Case | Retry-After |
   | --- | --- |
   | `sleeping`, no reason (a wake in progress) | 10 s → **3 s** |
   | `activating` (a fresh start) | 10 s |
   | `WaitingForRoom`, `MakingRoom` | 20 s |
   | `Moving` | 30 s |

2. With 3 s, from the numbers above, a small model's first retry at 3 s finds it ready. An 8B model's first retry is a little early, so it succeeds on the second retry at 6 s. Either way the wait drops from 10 s to 3–6 s.

3. A client that retries earlier sends more requests while the model wakes. A retry that still finds the model asleep only costs a 503. The gateway does not ask for the same wake twice (`RequestWake` returns false for a wake already asked for).

4. Optionally make the value configurable, for example an environment variable on the gateway, so operators running larger models can raise it.

A gateway-side bounded hold would remove the client retry altogether. That is a larger change and could follow separately. Related: #2925 (declarative Wake policy), which keeps today's `OnDemand` request-triggered wake.

### Area

Gateway

items.title: [Gluon] async_load accepts a pointer whose element type differs from the shared memory buffer
items.author: shuyilinn
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

Gluon's `async_copy.async_load` (and `async_copy_global_to_local` in general) does not check that the pointer element type matches the shared memory element type. Copying from an fp32 pointer into an fp16 buffer compiles and copies raw bytes, and the reverse faults with a misaligned address. `smem.store` rejects the same mismatch at compile time.

```python
import torch
from triton.experimental import gluon
from triton.experimental.gluon import language as gl
from triton.experimental.gluon.language.nvidia.ampere import async_copy


@gluon.jit
def kernel(inp, out, SMEM_DTYPE: gl.constexpr, N: gl.constexpr):
    L: gl.constexpr = gl.BlockedLayout([4], [32], [4], [0])
    offs = gl.arange(0, N, L)
    smem = gl.allocate_shared_memory(SMEM_DTYPE, [N], gl.SwizzledSharedLayout(1, 1, 1, [0]))
    async_copy.async_load(smem, inp + offs)
    async_copy.commit_group()
    async_copy.wait_group(0)
    gl.store(out + offs, smem.load(L))


N = 512
inp = torch.arange(N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32) + 0.5
out = torch.zeros(N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
kernel[(1, )](inp, out, gl.float16, N)  # fp32 pointer -> fp16 smem: compiles, wrong values
print(out[:8].tolist())

inp = torch.arange(N, device="cuda").to(torch.float16)
out = torch.zeros(N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
kernel[(1, )](inp, out, gl.float32, N)  # fp16 pointer -> fp32 smem
torch.cuda.synchronize()                # RuntimeError: CUDA error: misaligned address
```

```
[0.0, 1.75, 0.0, 1.9375, 0.0, 2.28125, 0.0, 2.34375]
RuntimeError: CUDA error: misaligned address
```

The first kernel should print `[0.5, 1.5, 2.5, ...]`; instead each 8-byte copy moves the raw bytes of two fp32 values into four fp16 slots.

Expected: a compile-time error for both, like `smem.store` gives for a value whose dtype does not match the buffer.

The frontend (`python/triton/experimental/gluon/language/nvidia/ampere/async_copy.py`, and the AMD `cdna4`/`cdna5` versions) only checks the shapes, and `AsyncCopyGlobalToLocalOp::verify` only checks that the destination is mutable. The lowering sizes each copy by the shared memory element type, so a mismatch reads with the wrong stride.

### Environment details

Triton: main @ 41846bc965
GPU: NVIDIA RTX 4090 (sm_89), driver 570 / CUDA 12.8

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body:
Opened #12341, picking up where the closed #12250 left off (same verifier + frontend-check shape, extended to both AMD copy directions).

The builtins now reject the mismatch at the frontend on every NVIDIA and AMD async-copy path, and AsyncCopyGlobalToLocalOp verifies it for non-Gluon producers. The regression test is red without the frontend check and green with it on this machine (no GPU here, so the byte-level runtime repro stays as documented in the issue).

- TensorRT-LLM main @ e88d19ca3b, PyTorch backend, CUDA 13.2 toolchain, torch 2.14
- DeepGEMM at the pinned `b64107f2b9` (`3rdparty/fetch_content.json`)
- GPU with compute capability 10.7 (SM107)

### Who can help?

Upstream root cause: deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM#461 (DeepGEMM's vendored CUTLASS 4.2.1, which is also what TensorRT-LLM's pinned `b64107f2b9` ships, has no SM107 enablement; that issue asks for a CUTLASS 4.8.0 bump, and reports the same assert from vLLM). This issue is about the TensorRT-LLM side: the default FP8 block-scale `Linear` path on SM107 hits it.

Related: #18758 maps SM107 to the `sm_100f` NVRTC target for the trtllm-gen FMHA JIT for the same kind of reason. #19067 covers the build side of SM107 (`107-real` folds to `100f`).

### Reproduction

An FP8 block-scale `Linear` with default settings (DeepGEMM enabled) on SM107:

```python
import torch
from tensorrt_llm._torch.modules.linear import Linear
from tensorrt_llm.models.modeling_utils import QuantConfig
from tensorrt_llm.quantization import QuantAlgo

m, k, n = 12, 512, 1024
lin = Linear(k, n, bias=False, dtype=torch.bfloat16,
             quant_config=QuantConfig(quant_algo=QuantAlgo.FP8_BLOCK_SCALES)).cuda()
with torch.no_grad():
    lin.weight.copy_(torch.randint(-32, 33, lin.weight.shape, device="cuda").to(lin.weight.dtype))
    lin.weight_scale.fill_(1e-3)
lin.post_load_weights()
out = lin(torch.randn(m, k, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16))
torch.cuda.synchronize()
```

`Linear.forward` → `FP8BlockScalesLinearMethod.apply` → `torch.ops.trtllm.fp8_swap_ab_gemm` → `deep_gemm.fp8_gemm_nt`. The JIT-compiled `sm100_fp8_fp4_gemm_1d1d_impl` kernel hits a device-side assert:

```
.../deep_gemm/include/cute/arch/tmem_allocator_sm100.hpp:143: void cute::TMEM::Allocator2Sm::allocate(int, unsigned int *): block: [13,0,0], thread: [80,0,0] Assertion `0 && "Attempting to use TMEM allocation PTX without CUTE_ARCH_TCGEN05_TMEM_ENABLED"` failed.
...
torch.AcceleratorError: CUDA error: device-side assert triggered
```

The same happens for every shape I tried: (m, k, n) = (12, 512, 1024), (1, 7168, 2048) and (128, 7168, 2048). In the unit tests it shows up as `test_kimi_kda_fused_verify_parity.py::test_fused_vs_sequential_two_rounds[full-rank-fp8]`. That test aborts the process, so the rest of the file then fails with it.

### Expected behavior

The DeepGEMM FP8 GEMM runs on SM107, as it does on SM100/SM103. Alternatively, `Linear` does not route SM107 to DeepGEMM.

### Actual behavior

With `DG_JIT_DEBUG=1`, DeepGEMM compiles the kernel with `--gpu-architecture=sm_107f`. By default, `deep_jit::cuda::Device::get_arch()` returns `<major><minor>f` for every arch with major ≥ 10.

The CUTLASS bundled with DeepGEMM enables the tcgen05/TMEM CuTe paths only for the `100f`, `101f` and `103f` families (`CUDA_ARCH_FAMILY(1000/1010/1030)` in `cutlass/arch/config.h`, and then `CUTE_ARCH_TCGEN05_TMEM_ENABLED` in `cute/arch/config.hpp`). Under `sm_107f`, `__CUDA_ARCH_FAMILY_SPECIFIC__` is 1070, so `CUTE_ARCH_TCGEN05_TMEM_ENABLED` is not defined. The TMEM allocator then compiles to its `assert(0)` fallback. The CUTLASS used by TensorRT-LLM itself has no 1070 family either.

What I checked:

- Rewriting `--gpu-architecture=sm_107f` to `sm_100f` in the JIT compile, with an `nvcc` wrapper under a custom `CUDA_HOME`, makes all three shapes pass on SM107. The max relative error against an fp32 reference matches the non-DeepGEMM path for each shape (for example 0.0413 vs 0.0413 at 12×512×1024). TensorRT-LLM's own `.so` files also run `sm_100f` code on SM107 (see #19067).
- `Linear(..., disable_deep_gemm=True)` avoids the problem on SM107 for all three shapes.

### Additional notes

Suggested fixes, in order of preference:

1. Have the DeepGEMM JIT target `sm_100f` on SM107 until the pinned DeepGEMM carries a CUTLASS with SM107 support (deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM#461). For example, extend the existing `3rdparty/patches/deepgemm_*.patch` mechanism so that `get_arch()` maps 107 → `100f`. This matches what #18758 does for the trtllm-gen FMHA JIT, and it is the change verified above.
2. Until then, route SM107 away from DeepGEMM for FP8 block-scale `Linear`, as `disable_deep_gemm` does today. In `FP8BlockScalesLinearMethod.apply` / `transform_weights`, `is_sm_100f()` alone currently sends SM107 to `fp8_swap_ab_gemm`.

I only checked `fp8_gemm_nt`. The other SM100 DeepGEMM kernels compiled through the same JIT (BF16 GEMM, MQA logits, and so on) use the same CuTe TMEM allocator and are probably affected the same way, but I have not run them.

items.title: [Bug]: Kimi K3 / MLA unit tests on SM107: two KDA files skip SM107, a cute_dsl_mla routing case contradicts the perf table, and an indexed-pool decode test compares two code paths bit-exactly
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- TensorRT-LLM main @ e88d19ca3b, PyTorch backend
- GPU with compute capability 10.7 (SM107). Item 2 is a host-side routing test (it monkeypatches the SM version) and fails independently of the GPU.

### Who can help?

Related: #19960 (adds the `test_cute_dsl_mla` case below and extends Kimi K3 to SM107), #18599 (the `(96, 1)` entry in the FP8 perf table), #18938 (the KDA decode kernel and dispatch).

### Reproduction

Three test-only problems seen when running the Kimi K3 / MLA unit tests on SM107. They are grouped here to keep the noise down. None of them is a product bug as far as I can tell. Each item lists the fix I verified.

**1. Two KDA test files skip everything on SM107**

`tests/unittest/_torch/modules/kimi_kda/test_kda_cache_soundness.py:57` and `test_kda_prefill_state_parity.py:40` gate on

```python
torch.cuda.get_device_capability(0) in {(10, 0), (10, 3)}
```

with reason "Kimi K3 is supported only on Blackwell (SM100/SM103)". The runtime predicate `is_kda_optimized_supported()` (`_torch/modules/kimi_kda/_kda_kernels.py:66`) accepts `(100, 103, 107)`, and the neighbouring files (`test_kda_decode_op.py`, `test_kda_prefill_op.py`) already gate on it. So on SM107 these two files report 6 and 15 skips and cover nothing.

Fix: gate on `is_kda_optimized_supported()` like the other files. With `(10, 7)` added, `test_kda_cache_soundness.py` gives 5 passed and 1 skipped on SM107; the remaining skip is its own runtime condition, "could not obtain a recycled cu_seqlens tensor ID". `test_kda_prefill_state_parity.py` gives 15 passed.

Related stale comment: the `_has_supported_gpu()` comments in `test_kda_decode_op.py:33` and `test_kda_prefill_op.py:38` still say the predicate "accepts SM100/SM103 only; SM107 takes the FLA fallback".

**2. `test_cute_dsl_mla.py::test_mla_generation_routes_wide_head_fp8_verify_away_from_trtllm_gen[103-96-1-True-False-cute_dsl_mla]` fails independently of the GPU**

```
pytest tests/unittest/_torch/attention/test_cute_dsl_mla.py -k routes_wide_head
E       AssertionError: assert 'trtllm_gen' == 'cute_dsl_mla'
```

The case `(103, 96, 1, True, False, "cute_dsl_mla")` ("Single-token H=96 is unchanged (measured perf-table entry)") goes through the FP8 perf gate. `_PERF_MIN_BATCH_FP8[(96, 1)] = 8` (`attention/backends/fmha/cute_dsl_mla.py:419`), but `_select_mla_generation_fmha` always builds a decode batch of `batch_size = 4` (`test_cute_dsl_mla.py:148`). So the gate rejects CuTe DSL MLA and the selection falls through to the TRTLLM-Gen stub. The code behaves as the table says; the expectation is wrong for batch 4.

Fix: either expect `"trtllm_gen"` for that case (verified: the parametrization then gives 10/10 passed), or add a `batch_size` parameter to the helper and assert `"cute_dsl_mla"` at batch 8, which would test the table entry the comment refers to.

**3. `test_kda_decode_op.py::test_optimized_decode_updates_indexed_recurrent_state_pool_in_place` (all 3 ids) fails on SM107**

```
torch.testing.assert_close(indexed_output, local_output, rtol=0, atol=0)
E       Mismatched elements: 2154 / 21504 (10.0%)
E       Greatest absolute difference: 0.00048828125
```

The test compares two different code paths bit-exactly:

- The "local" reference calls `_run_production_decode(...)` without `ssm_state_indices`. `KimiKDALinearAttention.forward_decode` then routes to `forward_decode_fallback` (`ssm_state_indices is None`), which runs separate q/k/v/g projections.
- The indexed call passes `ssm_state_indices` and takes the optimized path with the fused `qkvg` projection.

On SM107 the two GEMM shapes round differently, by one bf16 ulp on 10% of the elements. That difference then also shows up in the fp32 recurrent state. Each path is deterministic: two local runs are bit-identical. Running the same core output through `_project_output` twice is bit-identical too.

Fix: compute the local reference on the same path with dense indices, so that the test checks only the pool addressing:

```python
dense_indices = torch.arange(batch_size, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
local_output, local_cache = _run_production_decode(
    optimized,
    hidden_states,
    copy.deepcopy(initial_cache),
    slot_indices=dense_indices.long(),
    ssm_state_indices=dense_indices,
)
```

With this, the indexed output and the indexed recurrent state are bit-identical to the reference for `many-dense-pool`, `many-strided-pool` and `compact-dense-pool`. The test then gives 3 passed on SM107. I have not checked whether the two paths happen to agree bit-exactly on SM100/SM103.

### Expected behavior

These tests run and pass on SM107 (items 1 and 3), and item 2 passes on any GPU.

### Actual behavior

On SM107, item 1 skips everything and item 3 fails as shown above. Item 2 fails independently of the GPU.

### Additional notes

All three fixes are test-only. I can put them in one PR.

items.title: [cake deslop] csrc/kda root + PTX (2): drop 20 legacy prefill files, template decode/prefill clones, retire exact-shape PTX/T1 routes
items.author: yyihuang
items.body_excerpt:
**Background.** This issue covers the Cake-generated root files of `csrc/kda` and the PTX backend in `csrc/kda/ptx`. The root files include fused decode, recurrent decode, packed T=1 decode, the generated BF16 prefill portfolio with its legacy static fallbacks, and the unbounded-softplus/affine prefill. Their loaders live in `flashinfer/jit/`, `flashinfer/kda_decode.py`, `flashinfer/kda_prefill_ptx.py` and `flashinfer/kda_kernels`, and their tests in `tests/kda`. `csrc/kda/bf16` and `csrc/kda/tf32` are tracked separately. The code serves `flashinfer.recurrent_kda(backend='cake'|'auto'|'ptx')` and KDA prefill on sm100a/sm100f/sm103a. Packed T=1 also builds for sm107a (JIT only), and PTX runs on CC 10.3 only. At main @ 3184bbea the unit is 303 files / 409,282 lines: `csrc/kda` root 228 / 299,834, `csrc/kda/ptx` 8 / 30,010, Python 36 / 52,023, tests 31 / 27,415. Every checked-in source is compiled; 35 root files are reached only through f-string loaders. The first round split this code over five sub-issues:
- #5814 (closed by #6026) made the fused-decode programs stride-taking but regenerated the 64-bit-offset twins (34 programs, 34 checked-in bindings, a 1,538-line `MODULES`).
- #5841 (#5901) deleted 7 decode instances but did not template value split or tile size.
- #5839 (#5903) unified the PTX shim but kept the four PTX blobs imported by #5665.
- #5840 (#5919) compacted the generated metadata to 2,087 lines but kept the 16 legacy static prefill bodies (41,987 lines) and the 59 per-flag generated bodies (179,129 lines).
- #5820 (#5917) dropped the manifests but did not merge the affine role bodies.

Since then only #6238 has added kernel sources here: the sm107a `early_publish` packed T=1 body.

**Findings**
- **Superseded legacy prefill fallbacks (20 files, 31,551 lines).** `flashinfer/kda_prefill.py` always tries the generated portfolio first (`_run_generated_bt16_prepare_chain`, `_run_generated_single_route`). It loads a legacy static module only on `_GeneratedFlashKDASelectorNotFoundError`.
  - No reachable vector misses into h12_short/long, tensor_state_decay, n16/n16_short, n16_checkpoint, piece_persistent, small_bh, bt16 chain s8/s9 or prepare_beta_tma. Reasons: fp32 state requires `ssm_state_indices` (778-779). Checkpoints force the serving ABI and forbid fp32. bf16 indexed/padded-slot BT16 and small_bh calls redirect to the direct family (5960-5975). The legacy BT16 stage rule equals the generated one. `_uses_measured_sm100_persistent_policy` applies to CC (10, 0) only.
  - Confidence is medium. The coverage rests on source reading plus a 3,760-vector enumeration that does not cover BT16, small_bh, piece_persistent or checkpoint vectors explicitly.
  - `aot.py:752` still AOT-builds the unreachable `m128_n16_checkpoint` module (4,092 lines) on both targets, under a stale "only legacy fallback" comment.
  - Five legacy fallbacks stay (fused m128, fused m64, persistent m128, bt16 prepare, bt16 chain s7; 13,509 lines). H=12 calls without a pair-packed beta carrier and calls with non-default scalars still fall back to them.
- **fp32 BT16 selector gap.** fp32 indexed state on the BT16 route at stage 7 or stage 9 has no generated row; the only fp32 row, `d3d65ffa34`, is stage 8. `kda_prefill.py:6440-6450` re-raises the miss for fp32. This is either an unreached contract or a latent exception on public `recurrent_kda(backend='cake')` calls. It also decides whether the legacy BT16 fallback can be removed.
- **Generated prefill flag clones.** The 38 direct + 6 vtile `csrc/kda/flashkda_generated_bf16_fused_m128_*.cu` bodies total 145,346 lines.
  - The 46 direct metadata rows differ only in the 16 booleans of `_flash_kda_generated_direct_specialization` (serving ABI, fp32 state, PDL, pair-packed beta, early_n32, register-inverse, tensor_state_decay, affine role, ...). Each combination is emitted as its own body. Sampled pairs differ by 1–7 normalized lines.
  - Clustering found 27 clusters / 57,600 redundant lines at ≤60 differing lines, and 7 / 122,340 at ≤200. These figures have not been re-run.
  - #5840 asked for runtime flags; #5919 kept the bodies.
  - Other clone sets:
    - affine main vs map: 24 of ~3,300 lines differ (~6.7K redundant).
    - generated m64: 4 bodies, 1–21 lines apart (~8K redundant).
    - persistent and small_bh: 11–202 lines apart.
- **Decode clones.**
  - Fused decode `ROUTES` is 17 schedules × {32-bit, `_wide_slot_offsets`}. The 17 twins are 12,172 kernel + 3,080 binding lines and differ from their base kernels by 12–47 lines (symbol name and `long long` casts on the slot math).
  - `wide512_regcap128_positive_f32` differs from `wide512_positive_f32` by one line (`LAUNCH_MIN_BLOCKS`).
  - The 4 `cake_kda_decode_d128_t1_unbounded_softplus_direct_split*` bodies differ by 4–8 of ~302 lines.
  - The 17 `flashkda_decode_d128_t*` bodies are 6 templates × a split constant (~7,800 redundant lines). #5841 asked for templating; #5901 deleted only 7 instances.
  - The #6238 `early_publish` packed T=1 body is selected only on SM107. Its selector comment calls it bitwise identical to the tile-64 register pipeline.
- **Checked-in bindings and tables.**
  - The 34 `cake_fused_kda_decode_*_binding.cu` files (7,088 lines) reduce to 12 normalized templates (4,554 redundant lines). They could be rendered at JIT time, as `render_kda_decode_binding` already does for the decode family.
  - `MODULES` (`flashinfer/jit/cake_fused_kda_decode.py:50-1587`) repeats an identical 24-row `arg_plan` and the same `compile_flags` in all 34 entries. Only about 150 lines are real data.
  - Kernel bodies are shared across sm_100a and sm_103a. However, `flashkda_generated_variant_metadata.json` (104 rows) repeats 45 rows that differ only in `arch`; there are also 2 sm_100a-only and 12 sm_103a-only rows.
  - Two `_POSITIVE` rules on `direct_f32` (`cake_fused_kda_decode.py:1928`) can never match.
- **Exact-shape routes and baked scalars.**
  - PTX `fixed_h64.ptx` / `fixed_h96.ptx` (11,284 lines) are

items.title: [cake deslop] sm110_xqa + sm110_gqa_decode (round 2): dedupe 15 kernel preludes, template tmem/pair, retire superseded routes
items.author: yyihuang
items.body_excerpt:
**Background.** Two Cake-generated packages serve Thor. Both target sm_110a only, so there are no per-arch copies. `flashinfer/experimental/sm110_xqa` (#5293 tcgen05 + register_mma, #5597 register_mma_split, #5658 tmem, #5674 per-ratio tmem + pair) backs `flashinfer.sm110_xqa.prepare/attention` (D128 decode, D512 tree attention). `flashinfer/experimental/sm110_gqa_decode` (#5052, plus the exact-shape prepared routes from #5302) backs `flashinfer.sm110_gqa_decode`, `prepare_sm110_gqa_decode` and `launch_sm110_gqa_decode_prepared`. Both are JIT-only and neither is in `aot.py`. Each `jit.py` names all of its `.cu` files (42 + 10), and each file is built lazily on first use. No file is left uncompiled, so the open questions are reachability and redundancy. Round 1 closed #5777 with #5872 (+8,751/−152,380). That PR cut 52 → 22 kernel files, templated the per-ratio clones on `kHeadGroupSize`, added the shared `cake_sm110_xqa_device_common.cuh`/`host_common.cuh`, and removed the manifests, RESULTS.md and the dead `decode_merge` route. Round 1 also closed #5808 with #5929, which removed the per-call syncs, merged the registries into one and moved the bindings onto `sm110_gqa_decode_launch.cuh`. Still open: the superseded `kernel='tcgen05'` default and the register families (#5777), the exact-shape prepared routes, and runtime head/split/paged-KV regeneration (#5808). No commit has touched either package since then, so nothing was re-added. Size at 3184bbea: 75 files / 68,362 lines (xqa 56,505; gqa_decode 10,031; tests 1,173; bench/examples/ledger 572; `decode.py` wrappers 107).

**Findings**
- **Private preludes in 15 kernels (15,942 lines).** These are the lines before the first `__global__`: 4 register_mma kernels at 1,041–1,322 each, 6 frozen xqa kernels in `csrc/sm110_xqa/sm_110a/` at 1,010–1,016, and 5 gqa kernels at 1,005–1,046.
  - After normalization, the 11 frozen + gqa kernels share 350 lines and the 4 register kernels share 394.
  - The register kernels already `#include "cake_sm110_xqa_device_common.cuh"` but overlap it by only 17 lines, so they need their own header. tmem, pair and the split kernel already start at lines 56–65.
- **tmem and pair are constant clones.** The 8 tmem kernels (25,474 lines) and 8 bindings (2,224) are already `template<int kHeadGroupSize>`. Between any two of them, 52–160 normalized lines differ, all paged, E4M3 or even/odd-cluster constants. Same-form bindings differ in 9–17 lines. The 2 pair kernels (5,274 kernel + 674 binding lines) differ in 53/79 lines. Unlike the frozen programs, both families have a Cake producer.
- **Superseded D512 default.** `backend.py:134` defaults to `kernel='tcgen05'`, which sends D512 tree attention to 4 frozen programs (`sm_110a/sm110_xqa_tree_{fp16,fp8}_{contiguous,paged}_*` plus their `FROZEN` entries, 8,188 lines). `'auto'` (`backend.py:308-311`) never selects them.
  - Ledger round 9 (`git show c06c901e9^:flashinfer/experimental/sm110_xqa/RESULTS.md`, Thor, B1/Q20/Hq32/Hkv4/C256): tcgen05 takes 58.9–61.5 µs vs 22.3–30.9 µs for tmem/pair on all four rows (1.97–2.64× slower).
  - #5872 states that no Cake producer exists for the 6 frozen programs, so they can only be hand-edited behind `FROZEN sources_sha256` or retired.
  - Only that one shape was measured. Small `q_len*ratio` (frozen `tile_rows` 64 vs tmem 128) is unmeasured.
- **Register families are explicit-only.** The 5 programs (`tree_*_mma__any` ×4, `tree_fp16_paged_mma_split__any`; 9,375 lines) are reachable only through `kernel='register_mma'|'register_mma_split'|'register_mma_auto'`. In-repo, only the docstring, tests and bench rows use them.
  - Ledger round 8: tmem is faster on the paged modes (fp16 29.712 vs 34.687 split / 38.112 mma µs; fp8 24.288 vs 25.760). On the contiguous modes it is within the ledger's own 3% gate (fp16 31.168 vs 31.408; fp8 23.887 vs 24.544).
  - `backend.py:253` already limits ratios to {2,4,8,16}, which tmem/pair instantiate, so retiring these programs loses no API coverage.
- **Exact-shape gqa prepared kernels survived #5929.** The 3 kernels `csrc/prepared/sm110_gqa_decode_{n32_b4_direct,n32_disjoint_s10,n64_kvlast_s10}.cu` (5,588 lines; 5,856 with bindings) are chosen only by `_select_route` (`prepared.py:48-64`). That happens when `batch:capacity` matches a `PREPARED_ROUTES` key (`4:256`, `1:1024`, `1:4096`; `jit.py:105-109`), or with `num_splits=10` at the two split shapes. Every other shape gets `long`.
  - The kernels partition at runtime, so the shape gate exists only on the host side.
  - The kernels are live code. `prepare_sm110_gqa_decode` selects them by default at those three shapes, and the defaults in `examples/experimental/sm110_gqa_decode_prepared.py` (`--batch 1 --capacity 1024`) select `n64_kvlast_s10`.
  - #5302 measured 57.22/51.87/16.58% lower latency than `long` at the three shapes. #5929 kept the kernels pending a Thor A/B. `benchmarks/bench_sm110_gqa_decode.py:30,97` calls only the convenience API, so no in-repo benchmark covers them.
- **Dead host code (46 lines).**
  - The 15 × `block`/`dynamic_smem_bytes` fields in `sm110_xqa/jit.py` are never read; the bindings hard-code both values.
  - `jit.route_module()` (:666-668) has no callers.
  - The gqa `kernel_symbol` value flows into `launch_names`, which `launch_prepared` throws away; only `test_sm110_gqa_decode.py:112,189` reads it.
  - `_ACCEPTED_SPLITS` (`prepared.py:38`) lists 2/4/8/16, but `_select_route` rejects them every time, and `decode.py:266` still advertises them.
- **Per-replay host work in all 26 bindings.** Each launch re-encodes the TMA maps (2 `cuTensorMapEncodeTiled` per generated xqa launch, 3 for pair, `EncodeQ` + 2× `EncodeKV` for gqa) and re-runs 30–80 checks.
