items.title: [Discussion] Should StormService support runtime Prefill/Decode role switching?
items.author: googs1025
items.body_excerpt:
### Background

Inference engines are starting to support changing the role of a running
instance between Prefill and Decode.

SGLang added runtime P/D role switching in v0.5.21. A running instance can
switch roles without restarting the process or reloading model weights:

- https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/releases/tag/v0.5.21
- https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/28403

vLLM is also discussing this capability and has a draft implementation:

- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/56133
- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56134

The vLLM implementation has not been merged or released yet, but both
projects appear to be moving toward an engine-level role switching
interface.

### Question

Should AIBrix provide a corresponding orchestration capability for
StormService?

StormService currently represents Prefill and Decode as separate roles.
Their capacity can be adjusted by changing replica counts, but an existing
running instance cannot be reassigned from one role to the other.

Runtime role switching could be useful when the workload changes while
the total GPU allocation remains fixed. For example, a deployment may
want to move from `2 Prefill + 2 Decode` to `1 Prefill + 3 Decode`
without deleting one instance, creating another one, and loading the
model again.

Before discussing an API or implementation, it would be useful to
understand whether this is a capability AIBrix users need.

### Topics for discussion

1. Are there production workloads where the desired P/D ratio changes
   often enough for runtime role switching to be useful?

2. Is changing role replicas through the existing StormService and
   PodAutoscaler mechanisms sufficient, or is the startup and model
   loading cost a problem?

3. Should AIBrix treat engine-level P/D role switching as a StormService
   lifecycle capability?

4. Which component should decide when a role switch is needed:
   the user, StormService, the gateway, or PodAutoscaler?

5. Should AIBrix wait for a common capability across SGLang and vLLM,
   or consider experimental SGLang support first?

6. What availability and draining guarantees would users expect while
   a role is changing?

This is related to the PD-aware autoscaling discussion in:

- https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/issues/2613

That proposal changes Prefill and Decode replica counts. Runtime role
switching may address a different case where the total capacity stays
constant and existing instances are reassigned.

At this stage, this issue is intended to collect requirements and decide
whether AIBrix should support the capability. It does not propose a
specific API or implementation.

items.title: [CI] Add label-controlled CI for external contributors
items.author: googs1025
items.body_excerpt:
Related to #3135.

This issue tracks the label-controlled CI workflow for external contributors as a separate follow-up to the broader CI runner usage reduction work in #3135.

## Summary

Add a CI approval label for pull requests opened by external contributors. Expensive CI jobs should wait until a maintainer reviews the PR and applies the label.

Repository members and trusted contributors should keep the current automatic CI behavior. The exact label name can be decided during implementation.

## Motivation

As more contributors use AI tools, we may receive more PRs and more frequent updates to each PR. Every update can start image builds, integration tests, and E2E tests, even when the PR is still under review or has basic issues.

AIBrix uses the GitHub-hosted runner pool shared by the vllm-project organization. Repeated CI runs from unfinished external PRs can use a large part of this pool.

Most AIBrix checks can also run locally because they do not require a GPU. External contributors should run local checks and address review comments before requesting the expensive CI jobs.

## Proposed behavior

- Repository members and trusted contributors continue to run CI automatically.
- External contributors can still receive lightweight checks and review feedback without starting the expensive CI jobs.
- Image builds, integration tests, and E2E tests wait for a dedicated CI approval label.
- Only maintainers with the required repository permission can approve the CI run.
- The approval is tied to the current PR HEAD SHA.
- When an external contributor pushes a new commit, the previous approval becomes invalid and the label is removed or ignored.
- A maintainer reviews the new changes and applies the label again when the PR is ready.
- Nightly and release workflows are not affected.

The implementation may use a label such as `ci-approved`, `ready-for-ci`, or another name agreed by the maintainers.

## Contributor experience

When an external PR is waiting for approval, the bot or status check should explain:

- which CI jobs are waiting;
- that the contributor should run the available checks locally;
- that a maintainer will start CI after the PR is ready;
- that pushing a new commit will require a new approval.

There should be one lightweight gate check that always reports the current state. This avoids required checks staying in an unclear Pending state because an entire workflow was skipped.

## Security requirements

A trusted workflow may check permissions, manage the label, and record the approved HEAD SHA. It must not checkout or execute code from the pull request when running with a write token or repository secrets.

The actual build and test jobs should continue to run in an unprivileged `pull_request` context without write permissions or secrets.

The workflow must also verify the PR HEAD SHA before starting CI. A label left from an older commit must not authorize a newer commit.

## Acceptance criteria

- An external PR without the CI approval label does not start expensive CI jobs.
- A maintainer can apply the label and start CI for the current HEAD SHA.
- A new commit invalidates the previous approval.
- A contributor without the required permission cannot authorize CI.
- Repository members and trusted contributors keep the current automatic behavior.
- Nightly and release CI continue to run normally.
- The PR page clearly shows whether CI is waiting for approval, running, or completed.
- No workflow with elevated permissions executes code from an external PR.

## Out of scope

This issue does not define path-based E2E selection. Component-aware test selection should be handled in a separate issue.

items.title: DGX Spark (SM121) Current Support Audit
items.author: kahyunnam
items.body_excerpt:
# FlashInfer — DGX Spark (SM121) Current Support Audit

**Date:** 2026-04-24
**Scope:** Audit of SM121 (compute capability 12.1, DGX Spark) support across FlashInfer ops, APIs, backends, and testing.
**Goal:** Improve Spark usability on FlashInfer by identifying existing gaps.

**Note: skip to "15. Consolidated Action Items" for TLDR.**

---

## Architecture Context

| Gencode | Target | CUDA Requirement |
|---------|--------|------------------|
| `compute_120a` / `sm_120a` | RTX 5090 (SM120) | CUDA 12.8 |
| `compute_120f` / `sm_120f` | SM12x family (120 + 121) | CUDA 12.9 |
| `compute_121a` / `sm_121a` | DGX Spark (SM121) | CUDA 12.9 |

### SM120 vs SM121: Implications for FlashInfer

Per the [CUDA 13.2 Programming Guide — Compute Capabilities](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/archive/13.2.0/cuda-programming-guide/05-appendices/compute-capabilities.html) (Tables 29–33), SM120 and SM121 share a single "12.x" spec column: identical shared memory (99 KB/block, 100 KB/SM), warps (48/SM), registers (64K/SM), tensor core data types (TF32, BF16, FP16, FP8, FP6, FP4, INT8), TMA, and cluster support. [Table 28](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/archive/13.2.0/cuda-programming-guide/05-appendices/compute-capabilities.html#compute-capabilities-family-specific-compatibility) confirms `compute_120f` is compatible with **both** CC 12.0 and 12.1. The chip-level differences (SM121 = aarch64 host, unified LPDDR5x, 84 SMs vs SM120's x86_64, discrete GDDR7, up to 170 SMs) do not affect kernel correctness — only SM-count-based heuristics and host toolchain.

### `f` vs `a` compilation targets: performance implications

Per the [PTX ISA 9.3](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/parallel-thread-execution/index.html) (§9.7.15.5.14 for dense `mma`, §9.7.15.6.3 for sparse `mma.sp`), `120f` (family) is a subset of `120a`/`121a` (arch-specific). Most SM12x features — including **dense** NVFP4/MXFP4 block-scaled MMA — are family-specific and available via `120f` from PTX ISA 8.8. The arch-specific restriction (requiring `sm_120a`/`sm_121a`) applies **only to sparse MMA** (`mma.sp`) with `.kind::mxf4nvf4`/`.kind::mxf4`:

| PTX Feature | `compute_120` (baseline) | `compute_120f` (family) | `compute_120a` / `compute_121a` (arch) |
|-------------|--------------------------|------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| FP4/FP6/FP8 conversions (`cvt`) | No | Yes | Yes |
| FP4/FP6 MMA, block-scaled MMA (`.kind::mxf8f6f4`) | No | Yes | Yes |
| **Dense** NVFP4 MMA (`.kind::mxf4nvf4`) | No | **Yes** (PTX ISA ≥ 8.8) | **Yes** |
| **Dense** MXFP4 MMA (`.kind::mxf4`) | No | **Yes** (PTX ISA ≥ 8.8) | **Yes** |
| **Sparse** NVFP4 MMA (`mma.sp` `.kind::mxf4nvf4`) | No | **No** | **Yes** |
| **Sparse** MXFP4 MMA (`mma.sp` `.kind::mxf4`) | No | **No** | **Yes** |

FlashInfer's b12x GEMM kernel (`dense_blockscaled_gemm_sm120_b12x.py`) uses `cute.nvgpu.warp.MmaMXF4NVF4Op` — a **dense** block-scaled MMA atom. This means `sm_120f` wheels already emit native NVFP4/MXFP4 dense MMA instructions. Only **sparse** NVFP4/MXFP4 MMA (not currently used in FlashInfer) requires `sm_120a`/`sm_121a`.

> **Correction (2026-06-12):** An earlier version of this table stated that ALL `.kind::mxf4nvf4`/`.kind::mxf4` MMA was arch-specific-only. Per [Harry-Chen's feedback](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/3170#issuecomment-4677810517) and PTX ISA §9.7.15.5.14 vs §9.7.15.6.3, the restriction is limited to the sparse (`mma.sp`) variant.

### Wheel build arch targets

The release wheel CI (`.github/workflows/release.yml`) builds the following SM12x targets:

| CUDA Version | SM12x target in `FLASHINFER_CUDA_ARCH_LIST` |
|---|---|
| < 12.9 | `12.0a` (SM120 arch-specific; no SM121 support) |
| >= 12.9, < 13.0 | `12.0f` (family; covers SM120 + SM121; includes dense NVFP4/MXFP4 MMA) |
| >= 13.0 | `12.0f` (same) |

**No `121a` target is included in any wheel build.** However, since FlashInfer's FP4 kernels use **dense** block-scaled MMA (`MmaMXF4NVF4Op`, not sparse), the `120f` wheels already emit native NVFP4/MXFP4 MMA instructions. The `121a` target would only be needed for future sparse MMA kernels. JIT compilation on SM121 still produces `121a` cubins for forward-compatibility.

### What this means for FlashInfer

- **Any kernel that runs on SM120 is architecturally compatible with SM121.** Hardcoded `sm_version == "sm_120"` or `minor == 0` checks in backend dispatch are over-restricting without justification.
- **Separate cubins matter for JIT but not for wheels.** `CompilationContext` correctly emits `sm_121a` for JIT on SM121. Since FlashInfer uses only dense block-scaled MMA (available on `120f`), the wheels do not lose FP4 GEMM performance. The `121a` JIT path provides forward-compatibility for future sparse MMA use.
- **SMEM capacity maps, tile configs, and MMA atoms are identical.** Code using `get_smem_capacity_in_bytes("sm_120")` returns the correct value for SM121 too — the only risk is `KeyError` if a map expects an `"sm_121"` key and doesn't have one.

### Key utility functions

| Function (`utils.py`) | Behavior for SM121 |
|------------------------|--------------------|
| `is_sm12x_supported` | True (CUDA ≥ 12.9) |
| `is_sm121a_supported` | True (CUDA ≥ 12.9) |
| `is_sm120a_supported` | **False** (12.0 only) |
| `device_support_pdl` | True (`major >= 9`) |
| `determine_attention_backend` | Returns `fa2` (fa3 is SM90-only) |
| `determine_gemm_backend` | Returns `sm80` (no SM12x branch) |

---

## 1. Attention

### 1.1 Decode (batch paged KV)

| Backend | CC Gate | SM121 Status | Notes |
|---------|---------|--------------|-------|
| **fa2** | Generic | **Supported** | Default via `determine_attention_backend` for non-FP8 tensor-core decode |
| **fa3** | SM90 only | **Not available** | `determine_attention_backend` returns fa3 only on SM90 |
| **xqa** | `major in {9, 10, 12}` | **Supported** | `trtllm_batch_decode` auto → xqa when `major != 10` |
| **trtllm-gen** | `major == 10` only | **Not available** | Auto selects this

items.title: [cake deslop] cake_blackwell_softmax + cake_rmsnorm_train: delete 3 unreachable softmax kernels, fold clones, slim registries (-6.8K lines)
items.author: yyihuang
items.body_excerpt:
**Background.** This issue covers the small Cake families that no other #5768 sub-issue covers. `cake_blackwell_softmax` was added in #4282 (2026-09-23) and has never been deslopped. It backs `flashinfer.sampling.softmax` on CC 10.0/10.3 through one JIT module, `blackwell_softmax` (`flashinfer/jit/cake_blackwell_softmax.py`, also registered for AOT at `flashinfer/aot.py:1066`). That module is built from 6 `csrc/cake_blackwell_softmax*.cu` files (4,165 lines, 14 `__global__` kernels) plus `include/flashinfer/cake_blackwell_softmax.cuh` (108 lines). `cake_rmsnorm_train` was added in #5741 (2026-10-05), after the first round. It serves `cake_rmsnorm_train_forward`/`_backward`/`cake_rmsnorm` on CC 10.0/10.3/10.7. #6571 moved it into `flashinfer/cake_rmsnorm_train_backend` behind a thin facade, #6584 re-rendered it with `build.json` and the shared `cake_build.py` loader (both under #6553), and #6610 added keyword-arg switches. The package has 52 files and 13,061 lines: 21 kernels (6,100 lines), 21 bindings (2,241), `cake_jit.py` (2,398, of which 1,875 are the `MODULES` literal) and `build.json` (1,124 lines, 46 libraries: 21 kernels delivered on sm_100a 15 / sm_103a 16 / sm_107a 15). `cake_deepseek_fused_routing` (`fused_topk_deepseek(backend="cake")`) was folded by #5788, closed by #5906 (+276/−7,963), into 2 templates plus 36 explicit instantiations (518 + 60 lines). Its csrc has not changed since: #6238 added CC 10.7 to the Python contract and #6171 added cross-backend tests. Line numbers below refer to main @ 3184bbea.

**Findings**
- **3 softmax kernels are compiled but never selected.** `csrc/cake_blackwell_softmax_cached_cluster.cu` (2,377 lines) defines 10 `cached_c{1,2,4,8,16}_t{4,8}` kernels. `select_cached_variant` (`csrc/cake_blackwell_softmax.cu:118-158`) never returns `(1,8)`, `(2,8)` or `(4,8)`:
  - the tiles=4 small-chunk candidate exists and wins for every vocab ≤ 65,536;
  - above that, the wide-chunk candidates start at `(8,8)`, and spreading only grows C;
  - the `any` fallback is dead because `use_cached_cluster_kernel` caps vocab at the `(16,8)` capacity (262,144).

  Enumerating every vocab multiple of 8 up to that cap, across a range of row and SM counts, returns exactly the other 7 variants. Nothing else references the 3 symbols, and `tests/utils/test_sampling.py` asserts only route id 5. The removal is 683 lines, including header declarations and dispatch cases.
- **The cluster kernels reduce to 2 bodies.** After normalising names:
  - `cX_t4` and `cX_t8` differ in 6 lines (tile loop bounds);
  - `c2`/`c4`/`c8`/`c16` differ in 10 lines (`gridDim.x / C`, `bid / C`, lane compares against `C-1`);
  - `c1` and `c2` differ in 68 lines (no cluster vs DSM exchange).

  The source headers state that the sm_100a and sm_103a payloads were byte-identical. The only arch-guarded code is 28 `#if __CUDA_ARCH__ == 1030` blocks (20 of them in the cluster file), each wrapping one `griddepcontrol` instruction.
- **Route 4 is an exact-shape route.** `csrc/cake_blackwell_softmax.cu:88-95` selects the 235-line `csrc/cake_blackwell_softmax_*_exp2.cu` kernel (hard-coded vocab 32000, 512 threads, 16 vectors/thread) only when all of these hold: SM103, vocab == 32000, no temperature, PDL off, and rows ∈ {128, 512, 1024}.
  - The default call never takes this route. `flashinfer.sampling.softmax` resolves `enable_pdl=None` to `device_support_pdl()` (`sampling.py:957-958`), which is true for major ≥ 9 (`utils.py:869-873`). Only an explicit `enable_pdl=False` reaches it. Every other shape already uses CachedCluster (route 5).
  - A dispatcher comment (73-76) says the kernel is "still measured ahead" on those rows. This has not been re-measured.
  - Pinned by `flashinfer/sampling.py:124` and by `tests/utils/test_sampling.py` lines 145-158 and 180-202 and the `(512, 32000, None, False, 4)` param at 204-236. These see route 4 because the test hook defaults `enable_pdl=False`.
- **21 rmsnorm_train bindings, 11 distinct launch configs.** The 21 bindings (17 × 101 + 4 × 131 = 2,241 lines) differ only in `dim3 block(...)` and `config.dynamicSmemBytes`. Both values are already in `MODULES[...]["launch"]` (11 distinct values), and the grid comes from Python.
  - The bindings use the package-private `cake_ffi_checks.h` plus `tvm::ffi::CUDADeviceGuard`/`TVMFFIEnvGetStream`, not `csrc/tvm_ffi_utils.h`.
  - Every binding includes `cake_rmsnorm_train_host_common.cuh` and adds a `using` line. The header's body is an empty `namespace cake_host_shim_common { }` and it only re-includes `cake_ffi_checks.h`, which every binding already includes (29 lines + 42 lines).
  - Sources are digest-bound (`cake_build.py:_verified_sources` 168-180), so any edit needs a `build.json` re-render.
- **6 rmsnorm_train kernels are constant clones (1,049 lines).** Each of the following files under `flashinfer/cake_rmsnorm_train_backend/csrc/` is 4-8 normalised lines from a sibling:
  - `308da182` vs `03bdf566`: `__launch_bounds__` min-blocks 4;
  - `2a42e5c0` and `3430e5d9` vs `7673978d`: THREADS 256/128/64, ROWS_PER_CTA 8/4/2, loop form;
  - `60f47c5d` vs `3d20ab4a`: THREADS 256/512, ROWS_PER_CTA 8/16;
  - `cf1d0554` vs `bad4db91`: `ld.global.L2::cache_hint` vs plain load;
  - `c5a8099e` (sm_103a only) vs `b44107e0`: an `#if __CUDA_ARCH__ == 1000` loop branch plus the cache hint.
- **Hard-coded hidden sizes.** `HIDDEN_SIZES = (512, 2048, 6144)` (`cake_jit.py:2035`). Residual routes exist only for 6144, so `cake_rmsnorm(x, w, residual=u)` with H = 512 or 2048 raises `ValueError` (`__init__.py:364-374`). The kernels hard-code the width (`obase = row64 * 512`).
- **Generated registries.**
  - `MODULES` (`cake_jit.py:52-1926`) has 31 records over 21 libraries. 10 of them are `__wide`/`__quad`/... aliases that change only `select_rule`/`grid_rule`, and `arg_plan` and `logical` have only 2 distinct values each. No record is dead, and the row bands have no gaps or overlaps.
  - In `build.json`, each of the 46 entries (23 lines) repeats 10 i

items.title: [Bug]: Qwen3-VL: rewriting video_metadata.total_num_frames without rescaling fps makes default HF frame sampling keep only min_frames and produces wrong `<t seconds>` timestamps
items.author: john-liu-dev
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- TensorRT-LLM 1.3.0rc25 (`785c948`); transformers 5.5.4 (the version pinned in `requirements.txt`, also on `main`).
- Re-checked on `main` at `760a584` (2026-10-12): `_decide_do_sample_frames` and `Qwen3VLInputProcessorBase._preprocess` are identical to rc25 (main L169-221 and L349-425).
- Model: `Qwen/Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct` (the 8B model goes through the same code path).
- Seen end-to-end through the NVIDIA Dynamo TensorRT-LLM backend (`7e8b9fc2`) in aggregated multimodal mode; the reproduction below is CPU-only and needs only the HF processor.

### Who can help?

_No response_

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [x] My own modified scripts

### Tasks

- [ ] An officially supported task in the `examples` folder (such as GLUE/SQuAD, ...)
- [x] My own task or dataset (give details below)

### Reproduction

`Qwen3VLInputProcessorBase._preprocess` (`tensorrt_llm/_torch/models/modeling_qwen3vl.py`, L400-412 in rc25, L402-414 on `main`) forwards `VideoData.metadata` to the HF processor with `total_num_frames` rewritten to `len(vd.frames)`, so that HF's `sample_frames` (`np.linspace(0, total_num_frames - 1, num_frames)`) stays in range. The metadata `fps` (source video fps) and `frames_indices` are left untouched. When the IO layer has already subsampled the clip (e.g. 40 frames out of a 10 s / 24 fps / 240-frame video), HF's `Qwen3VLVideoProcessor` therefore believes the video is 40/24 = 1.67 s long and, with its class defaults (`fps=2`, `min_frames=4`), samples `int(40/24*2) = 3 -> 4` frames. This is the default path: when the caller passes no `do_sample_frames` / `num_frames` / `fps`, `_decide_do_sample_frames` (L167-219 in rc25, L169-221 on `main`) turns sampling on to match HF's class default. Two consequences:

1. Only 4 of the 40 decoded frames reach the ViT (1760 visual tokens instead of 11880). Any caller that does not pass `mm_processor_kwargs={"do_sample_frames": False}` (or an exact `num_frames`) silently gets a 4-frame summary of the video, regardless of clip length (a 30 s clip decoded to 40 frames gives the identical 4-frame result).
2. The `<t seconds>` timestamp tokens inserted by the processor are computed from the resampled indices over the rewritten `total_num_frames` divided by the *source* fps, so they are compressed by (decoded frames / source frames): for the 10 s clip the model sees `<0.3 seconds>` and `<1.4 seconds>` for frames that are actually at about 0 s, 3.3 s, 6.7 s and 10 s.

With `do_sample_frames=False` the processor uses `frames_indices / fps`, and both the frame count and the timestamps are correct, which shows the frame list itself is fine; only the sampling-path metadata is inconsistent. For comparison, HF sampling the 240-frame source itself at the default fps=2 would keep `int(240/24*2) = 20` frames with timestamps in source seconds, so the rewrite also makes the default path diverge from stock HF, which `_decide_do_sample_frames` intends to match.

Reproduction (CPU only, HF processor only):

- Decode a 10 s, 24 fps, 1280x720 H.264 clip into 40 uniformly spaced RGB float32 `(C, H, W)` tensors in [0, 1], metadata = `{"fps": 24.0, "total_num_frames": 240, "duration": 10.0, "frames_indices": linspace(0, 239, 40)}`.
- Apply the same rewrite as `_preprocess` (`total_num_frames := 40`) and call `AutoProcessor.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct")(text=[chat_template_text], videos=[frames], video_metadata=[meta], do_sample_frames=True, do_rescale=False, padding=True, return_tensors="pt")`.
- Observe `video_grid_thw == [2, 44, 80]`, 1760 `<|video_pad|>` tokens, timestamps `<0.3 seconds>`, `<1.4 seconds>`.
- Same call with `do_sample_frames=False`: `video_grid_thw == [20, 36, 66]`, 11880 tokens, timestamps `<0.1 seconds>`, `<0.6 seconds>`, `<1.1 seconds>`, `<1.6 seconds>`, ... (one per 0.5 s across the clip).
- Without the rewrite (original `total_num_frames=240`) HF raises `IndexError: index 50 is out of bounds for axis 0 with size 40`, which confirms why the rewrite exists.
- End-to-end: the Dynamo TensorRT-LLM worker's `/metrics` reports `trtllm_prompt_tokens_total = 1789` (= 1760 visual + 4 vision markers + 12 timestamp tokens + 13 text) for this request.

### Expected behavior

Either (a) when rewriting `total_num_frames` to the decoded count, also rescale `fps` to `len(frames) / duration` and reset `frames_indices` to `range(len(frames))`, so HF's duration and timestamps stay consistent with the frames it receives, or (b) default `do_sample_frames` to False whenever the caller passes an already-subsampled frame list with `frames_indices` (the IO layer has done the sampling), and only sample when the caller explicitly asks for `num_frames` / `fps`.

### actual behavior

With default `mm_processor_kwargs`, 4 of 40 decoded frames reach the ViT and the timestamps are compressed by 40/240 (details under Reproduction).

### additional notes

**Impact.** Silent quality loss for every video request that relies on defaults (temporal reasoning over a ~2 s window of a longer clip, wrong timestamps), plus misleading throughput numbers (the prompt is ~7x shorter than intended).

**Workaround.** Pass `mm_processor_kwargs={"do_sample_frames": False}` per request (the frame count is then whatever the IO layer decoded, e.g. `DYN_MM_VIDEO_NUM_FRAMES` in Dynamo).

The metadata rewrite and `_decide_do_sample_frames` were introduced in #15598.

**Related:** #20138 (Qwen3-VL video over the E/PD handoff; its reproduction passes `do_sample_frames=False` to get all decoded frames into the ViT, i.e. the workaround above).

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and checked the [documentation](https://nvidia.github.io/TensorRT-LLM/) and [examples](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/tree/main/examples) for answers to frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Performance]: DFlash TRTLLM backend: non-causal block attention runs as context FMHA and scales poorly with context length at batch 1
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

With `attention_backend="TRTLLM"`, a DFlash / DSpark draft layer that is non-causal and has no sliding window runs its block attention through `trtllm_batch_context_with_kv_cache` (`DFlashForCausalLM.dflash_forward`, `causal=False` branch). At batch 1 the query is a single block of `block_size` tokens, so the context kernel launches only a few CTAs per (request, KV head) and each of them walks the whole context. The causal branch already uses `trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache`, which splits the KV across CTAs.

With no mask, every block query attends exactly the same keys (all `seq_lens_after` tokens of its request). So the same attention can be expressed as `B * block_size` single-token decode requests that share the request's page table and sequence length (`q_len_per_req=1`, `block_tables` / `seq_lens` repeated `block_size` times). The decode kernel then gets its multi-CTA split-KV across the context. No new kernel is needed; the workspace and the multi-CTA counter buffer have to be sized for `B * block_size` requests.

Measured with Kimi K3 + a GQA DSpark drafter (non-causal, no sliding window, block size 7, TRTLLM DFlash backend), 8 GPUs over 2 nodes, SM107, single request. Change in the decode step time versus the context-FMHA path:

| context | 2K | 32K | 64K | 96K | 128K |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| step time | -0.15 ms | -1.05 ms | -2.21 ms | -3.12 ms | -4.21 ms |

Acceptance length was unchanged within noise (4.31 vs 4.35 over the whole run), and our accuracy and long-context needle checks gave the same results.

Trade-off: each decode row reads its request's whole KV, so this form reads `block_size` times more KV than the context kernel. That is the right trade at batch 1, where the context kernel leaves most SMs idle, but it would cost more at large batches. I only measured batch 1, so the proposal limits the decode-row form to batch 1 and leaves the context path in place above that. The limit is a single constant and can be raised once someone has batch sweeps.

PR to follow.

cc @jhaotingc @dc3671

items.title: [BUG] 02_dump_reg_shmem faults on sm_120: Fragment is 2-byte aligned but accessed through a 16-byte-aligned pointer
items.author: random25160765-collab
items.body_excerpt:
> **Correction (2026-09-13).** My original report framed this as an `nvcc` codegen bug specific to
> `sm_120`. That framing was wrong, and I have rewritten this issue. Further testing showed the
> codegen is identical on `sm_80`/`sm_90`/`sm_100`/`sm_120`, and that the underlying defect is on the
> CUTLASS side: the iterators access `Fragment` through a type that requires 16-byte alignment, while
> `Fragment` itself is only 2-byte aligned. Details and a verified fix below.

## Summary

`examples/02_dump_reg_shmem` aborts on `sm_120` with `cudaErrorMisalignedAddress` (error 716); the
example prints `Failed` and exits `255`. Reproduced on `main` @ `147295a3` with the stock example.

Root cause: `PredicatedTileIterator` reinterprets its `Fragment` (a plain `cutlass::Array`, 2-byte
aligned for `half_t`) as a 16-byte-aligned `AlignedArray` and accesses it 128 bits at a time. When the
compiler homes that fragment in local memory, it allocates the frame slot using the *declared*
alignment (2 → offset `+0xc`) but emits the stores using the *cast-implied* alignment (16 →
`STL.128`). The slot ends up at `12 (mod 16)`, so the 16-byte store is misaligned and the kernel
faults. Aligning the fragment moves the slot to `+0x10` and the example completes.

## Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| GPU | NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060, compute capability 12.0 (`sm_120`), driver 591.86 |
| Toolkit | CUDA 13.3 — nvcc V13.3.73 (`cuda_13.3.r13.3/compiler.38244171_0`) |
| OS | Linux (Ubuntu 26.04 LTS under WSL2), x86_64 |
| CUTLASS | `main` @ `147295a3`, unmodified (`git status` clean) |

## Where the alignment requirement comes from

The example itself is not at fault — `examples/02_dump_reg_shmem/dump_reg_shmem.cu:85` only declares

```cpp
typename GmemIterator::Fragment frag;
```

The requirement is imposed by the iterator
(`include/cutlass/transform/threadblock/predicated_tile_iterator.h`):

| Line | Code | Alignment |
|---|---|---|
| [181](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/main/include/cutlass/transform/threadblock/predicated_tile_iterator.h#L181) | `using AccessType = AlignedArray<Element, AccessSize, (AccessSize * sizeof_bits<Element>::value / 8)>;` | **16 bytes** (for `half_t`, `AccessSize == 8`) |
| [191](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/main/include/cutlass/transform/threadblock/predicated_tile_iterator.h#L191) | `using Fragment = cutlass::Array<Element, ThreadMap::Iterations::kCount * ThreadMap::kElementsPerAccess>;` | **2 bytes** — `cutlass::Array` has no `alignas` (`include/cutlass/array.h:101`; only `AlignedArray` at `array.h:2867` declares one) |
| [327](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/main/include/cutlass/transform/threadblock/predicated_tile_iterator.h#L327) | `AccessType *frag_ptr = reinterpret_cast<AccessType *>(&frag);` | casts the 2-byte-aligned object to the 16-byte-aligned type |

So the library relies on an alignment its own `Fragment` type does not declare. That dependency is
invisible to a caller who simply declares `typename GmemIterator::Fragment frag;`, which is the
documented idiom — and it is the reason the example breaks without any misuse on the caller's side.

## Evidence

**SASS of `kernel_dump` (`cuobjdump -sass`), stock example — the local slot is at `+0xc`:**

```sass
STL.128 [R1+0xc], R52 ;
STL.128 [R1+0x1c], R48 ;
STL.128 [R1+0x2c], R44 ;
STL.128 [R1+0x3c], R40 ;
STL.128 [R1+0x4c], R36 ;
STL.128 [R1+0x5c], R32 ;
STL.128 [R1+0x6c], R28 ;
STL.128 [R1+0x7c], R24 ;
```

Every offset is `≡ 12 (mod 16)`; `STL.128` requires a 16-byte-aligned address, and the kernel faults
at the first one.

**With the fragment aligned, the slot moves and the fault disappears:**

| | fragment slot | `STL.128` offsets | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| stock | `+0xc` | `0xc, 0x1c, … 0x7c` (all `≡12 mod 16`) | fault, exit 255 |
| `alignas(16)` | `+0x10` | `0x10, 0x20, … 0x80` (all 16-byte aligned) | **completes, exit 0** |

**Not architecture-specific.** Compiling the reproducer below for `sm_80`, `sm_90`, `sm_100` and
`sm_120` produces the identical 8 × `STL.128` at `[R1+0xc … R1+0x7c]`. The codegen is
architecture-independent; whether it faults depends on the runtime frame base, and on `sm_120` it
does. (I could only *execute* on `sm_120` — other architectures were compile-only.)

## Proposed fix

Minimal, verified on `sm_120`:

```cpp
// examples/02_dump_reg_shmem/dump_reg_shmem.cu:85
alignas(16) typename GmemIterator::Fragment frag;
```

However this only protects the example. Since `AccessType` is 16-byte aligned for every user of
`PredicatedTileIterator` (and the other iterators with the same pattern), the more principled fix
would be to declare the alignment on the `Fragment` typedef itself — e.g. make it an `AlignedArray`,
or add `alignas` — so that any caller declaring `Fragment frag;` is safe. That is a wider change, so
I'd rather leave the choice to the maintainers.

## Exposure (why this is not caught elsewhere)

A fragment that never has its address taken stays in registers and never touches local memory. Real
GEMM kernels therefore don't hit this. The fault needs the fragment's address to escape to a
non-inlined function — which is exactly what the dump/debug path does (`cutlass::debug::dump_fragment`,
`printf`). That is consistent with it showing up in this example and seemingly nowhere else.

## Note on the compiler side

I filed this with NVIDIA's compiler team as well. Their assessment was that the
`reinterpret_cast` to a 16-byte-aligned type is a source-level alignment promise that the object does
not satisfy, and therefore source-level UB rather than a codegen defect. I accept that reading — it
is why I have rewritten this issue rather than insisting on a compiler bug. The remaining point for
CUTLASS is narrower: the library should not depend on an alignment guarantee its own type does not
make.

<details>
<summary>Minimal reproducer (no CUTLASS)</summary>

The program below reproduces the same codegen and fault on `sm_120`. Note that the `Frame` layout is
deliberately constructe

items.title: [cake deslop] cake_mxfp4_situ_moe: drop 16 unreachable stages, fold 9 _nopdl twins, share the cake/cake_cute plan, slim the manifests
items.author: yyihuang
items.body_excerpt:
**Background.** `csrc/fused_moe/cake_mxfp4_situ_moe` is the Cake-generated Kimi-K3 W4A8 MXFP4 SiTU routed MoE. It ships as two JIT-only backends, `flashinfer.fused_moe.cake.CakeMxfp4MoEWrapper` (CUDA) and `flashinfer.fused_moe.cake_cute.CakeMxfp4MoEWrapper` (CuTe DSL), for sm_103a only. It serves 896 experts, top-16, H 7168, I 3072 on EP8 (112 local experts) and TP8 (shard 384). Neither wrapper is exported from `flashinfer.fused_moe`. `fused_moe(backend="cake")` routes to the NVFP4 sibling `cake_kimi_k3_situ` (`core.py:1523`) instead, and inside the repo only the two test files import these packages. #5783 added the family (+345K lines). Later PRs extended it: #6154 added the TP8 mixed192 long-prefill chain, #6320 re-rendered it, #6411 added the device-side `gemm2_gate`, #6452 shipped every route layout (62 modules) and #6577 (merged 2026-10-17) added the swap-AB cluster split-K `_cs` forms. At 3184bbea the family is 600 files / 543,846 lines: cuda 152 modules (175,605 kernel + 43,418 binding lines), cute 140 modules (188,766 + 21,889), two manifests (43,342 + 49,145 lines), 2 × (4,727-line plan + ~450-line loader) and 2 × 1,552 test lines. No earlier sub-issue covers it; the NVFP4 sibling was #5800, closed by #6135. Every re-render exported the full registry, so the dead forms below have existed since #5783, and #6320, #6452 and #6577 each re-rendered them.

**Findings**
- **16 unreachable stages.** 32 modules / 64 files (54,241 source + 9,380 manifest lines). `compile_all()` builds them, but no executable chain in `cake_mxfp4_situ_moe_plan.py` (identical in both packages) selects them. This was established by reading the source; the host sweep in step 1 has not been run.
  - Constant levers. `SWAP_MIXED=False` and the only `DispatchConfig` using `all_lists=False` (:3460) rule out `dispatch_mixed_lists`, `routing_cluster8` and `routing_ep8_decode`. `DENSE_GEMM1_A_TMA=False` rules out `token_index_top8`. `SWAP_WIDE192_LISTS='sort'` rules out `dispatch_mixed192_dual`. `SWAP_WIDE192_ZERO_FILL='dense'` rules out `gemm1_dense_situ_m256_n256_2cta_rowgroup`. Because `SWAP_PDL` and `SWAP_SPLIT_EARLY_TRIGGER` are `True`, the split chain always takes the `_early` dense forms, and TP8 mixed192 always uses raster `auto`. That leaves `gemm1_dense_situ_m128_n128_rowgroup` and `gemm2_dense_finalize_n256_rg` unused. No tactic entry has N=128, so `gemm2_dense_finalize_n128` is never chosen. `find_kernel` has no builder for kinds `token_index` or `dispatch_mixed`.
  - Placements that no chain produces: `gemm2_swapab_finalize_n64` and `_n128` (`late_dep_wait=False`), `gemm2_swapab_finalize_n192_2cta` (mixed192 always uses `_cm4`), and `finalize_top8` (the only `FinalizeConfig`, at :3363, uses `accumulate=True` with top_k 16).
  - Refused path. The dp-on `gemm2_swapab_partial_n8_m2`, `_n16_m2` and `_n32_m2` are used only by the `two_stage` path (TP8, T 17..127), which `plan()` refuses (:3973-3975). The split chain uses only `_nodp` partials. `finalize_top8` and `partial_n8_m2` are marked `plan_selected=True` only because that refused path names them.
  - Do not use the manifests' 25-entry `unlaunched_registry_forms` as a disable list. It includes `gemm2_dense_finalize_n192_c12_rg_rauto`, which TP8 selects for T in [14337, 16383], and it omits the two forms above.
- **11 off-contract forms.** 20 modules / 40 files (31,261 source + 5,968 manifest lines) are reachable only outside Kimi-K3 EP8/TP8:
  - `gemm1_swapab_situ_n16` and `_n32` need H/128 odd.
  - `gemm2_swapab_finalize_n8`, `_n16` and `_n32` need a shard > 512 that is not a multiple of 256 or 384.
  - The static-raster `gemm2_dense_finalize_{n256_c12,n256_2cta,n192_c12}_rg` need a TP shard in (512, 1024).
  - The cuda-only `moe_sort_init_t384` and `moe_sort_coop_t384_dual_mixed` need 257..384 experts.
  - `finalize_top8_split` needs top_k 8.
  
  The wrapper accepts these inputs because it only checks `% 128` and top_k (:3864-3867). The same geometries also need forms that are not shipped (for example, single layout at T 17..128 needs `gemm1_swapab_situ_n16_cs`), so they fail at `find_kernel`. Confidence is medium, and removing them is a policy decision.
- **`_nopdl` twins.** After hash normalisation, the 9 cuda `_nopdl` dense GEMM kernels (4 `gemm1_dense_situ_*`, 5 `gemm2_dense_finalize_*`; 16,339 lines) are identical to their PDL twins. Their bindings differ only in the `cudaLaunchAttributeProgrammaticStreamSerialization` block. The 9 cute twins differ by one `use_pdl=True,` compile option and have identical bindings (18,893 lines). Both twins are reachable through `enable_pdl`, so the fix is to share the source, not delete it. The 4 moe_sort `_nopdl` modules really differ (`griddepcontrol.wait`) and stay.
- **Copied and dead host code.**
  - `cake_cute/cake_mxfp4_situ_moe_plan.py` (4,727 lines) differs from the `cake/` copy in 4 lines (docstring, `PACKAGE_BACKEND`, `SIBLING_MODULE`), although the plan already parameterises the backend (:4573-4590). The `_cute` test differs from the `cake/` test in 6 lines, and the two loaders share ~350 of 441 lines. Together these copies are 6,629 lines.
  - The `tma_workspace` / `'workspace'` arg kind is dead: no record sets `tma_workspace_bytes`, and every module uses `tma_abi='grid_constant'`.
  - `build_launch_module` (:4705-4717) is only called from tests.
  - The mixed192 `'dense'`/`'alt'` GEMM2 branches are unreachable: `swap_mixed192_gemm2` returns `'gate'` first because both thresholds are 16384. The constant-off mixed chain also remains (83 lines reference it).
- **Constant clones.** The 56 routing modules per backend (37,646 cuda device lines) are one ~600-line program plus an ~840-line split variant, instantiated over mode × cluster × split × single-tile × max_routes. For example, `routing_packed_c2` and `_c3` differ in 33 of ~571 lines. Together with sort_coop (9), route_preprocess (6), dispatch (2) and finalize (3), that is about 91K redundant lines across both backends. This number is estimated fro

items.title: [Performance] XQA generic launcher on SM12x: the split leaves a near-empty second wave and over-splits short sequences
items.author: waynehacking8
items.body_excerpt:
On SM12x every non-MLA XQA decode runs the generic launcher, `launchMHAFlashInfer` in `csrc/xqa/mha.cu` (the SM90 FP8 kernel is capability 9 only), which sets `nbSubSeqPerSeq = min(max(1, SMs / (batch * nbKHeads)), divUp(maxSeqLen, 256))` at one CTA per SM. Two cases lose on an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q (188 SMs; FlashInfer 0.7.2, FP8 KV, page 16, vLLM's `xqa_batch_decode_with_kv_cache` calls, KV larger than L2, CUDA-graph timing, 5 rounds).

When batch x KV heads is just above the SM count, the second wave is nearly empty: Qwen3-4B (8 KV heads) at batch 24 is 192 CTAs, 4 of them in a second wave, and split 6 is 12 to 13% faster from 4K to 64K tokens (level at 1K). Short sequences are over-split, because the length bound is the block-table width (max_model_len in vLLM): with a 64K table, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (2 KV heads) at batch 1 runs split 94, and split 4 is 2.5x faster at 1K tokens, split 16 2.1x at 4K.

End to end on vLLM main `153a17166e` (Qwen3-4B, FP8 KV, 16K context), forcing only batch 24 to split 6 cuts decode ITL from 31.4 to 28.5 ms over four interleaved boots, with batch 8 and 1 unchanged.

vLLM captures one decode graph per batch size, so a context-blind rule trades short contexts against long ones (split 8 at batch 32 is 35% slower at 1K). #5998 traced its SM90 case to this launcher, and #4904's `computeNbSubSeqPerSeq` is the natural template, its `max_kv_len` bound helping callers that know the length at launch. Would a split that changes only when the last wave is partial be acceptable here? I have the sweep and can open a PR.

cc @bkryu

items.title: [Core/Auth] Detect auth mode mismatch in the jobs and state API clients
items.author: MortalHappiness
items.body_excerpt:
The HTTP side of #67052. The dashboard must not reject requests on the `Authorization` header: reverse proxies in front of a disabled dashboard can send their own (the former `kuberay-auth.md` guide put kube-rbac-proxy in front of the dashboard; also ray-project/kuberay#1824, #42606). The check goes on the client instead.

Change:

- Before the first request, the client reads `GET /api/authentication_mode` and raises the AuthModeMismatch error when the cluster is disabled and the client is in token mode.
- Jobs SDK: in `SubmissionClient._check_connection_and_version`.
- State API: `StateApiClient` (`util/state/api.py`) doesn't call that method today, so it needs the same check.
- The AuthModeMismatch error is an `AuthenticationError` with the message from #67052, so `AuthenticationError.__str__` doesn't append `TOKEN_AUTH_FIX_MESSAGE` (#67051) to it.
- Test: jobs and state clients against a disabled cluster, with and without `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled`.

Parent: #67047
PRs must keep the rules in #67047.
Depends on: #67051
Blocks: #67055

items.title: [Bug] Console-created deployments are not discoverable by the AIBrix data plane
items.author: Jeffwan
items.body_excerpt:
A deployment created from the Console can reach `Ready`, and its generated Service can handle requests directly, but the AIBrix Gateway does not discover it.

The generated Pod template currently has only the Console/application labels ([code](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/a40be9ba404730e4be2d2a0820942bca79275dc6/apps/console/api/deployment/provider/kubernetes.go#L633-L642)). It is missing the AIBrix model labels defined in [`pkg/constants/model.go`](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/a40be9ba404730e4be2d2a0820942bca79275dc6/pkg/constants/model.go#L23-L37), such as `model.aibrix.ai/name` and `model.aibrix.ai/port`. The [mocked app manifest](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/a40be9ba404730e4be2d2a0820942bca79275dc6/development/app/config/templates/deployment/deployment.yaml#L6-L23) shows the expected shape.

To reproduce:

1. Create a deployment in Console with the dev [`mock-vllm` template](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/a40be9ba404730e4be2d2a0820942bca79275dc6/apps/console/api/store/demo.go#L569-L590).
2. Wait for it to become ready.
3. Inspect the Pod labels with `kubectl get pods --show-labels`.
4. Port-forward the generated Service: `/v1/chat/completions` works.
5. Send the same request through the AIBrix Gateway: the model has no discovered backend.

A Console deployment reported as ready should also be callable through the AIBrix data plane.

The fix will likely need to map the Console Model's `serving_name`, the effective container port, and the template engine to the canonical AIBrix labels. Please reuse the existing label constants. If a different model-name mapping is intended, it should be documented as part of the change.

This is complete when the mock model can be deployed from Console and reached through the Gateway, with a small rendering test plus an end-to-end check.

items.title: [Bug]: EAGLE-3 latency penalty on Hopper with TensorRT-LLM 1.3.0rc29
items.author: dtemraz
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info


- **Primary hardware:** single H100 SXM 80 GB, same pod for the cross-engine tests
- **Runtime:** TensorRT-LLM `1.3.0rc29`, PyTorch backend; comparison with vLLM `0.31.0`
- **Serving:** `trtllm-serve --backend pytorch`, `--kv_cache_free_gpu_memory_fraction 0.85`
- **Environment:** CUDA toolkit 12.8; Python 3.12; TensorRT-LLM installed from NVIDIA PyPI wheels
- **Host controls:** 22.1-core cgroup CPU quota, with no additional CPU-throttling events observed during the load tests; `OMP_NUM_THREADS=8`, `MKL_NUM_THREADS=8`, `TOKENIZERS_PARALLELISM=false`


### Who can help?

_No response_

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [x] My own modified scripts

### Tasks

- [ ] An officially supported task in the `examples` folder (such as GLUE/SQuAD, ...)
- [x] My own task or dataset (give details below)

### Reproduction

- **Target:** `Qwen/Qwen3-4B` (BF16) or `Qwen/Qwen3-4B-FP8` (official block-scaled FP8 checkpoint)
- **Draft head:** `AngelSlim/Qwen3-4B_eagle3`, one-model EAGLE-3, `max_draft_len: 2`
- **Requests:** approximately 1,040 shared prefix tokens, ~50 request-specific tokens; outputs average 10.5 tokens (p95 18), max_tokens: 24, greedy sampling, thinking disabled
- **Traffic:** open-loop Poisson, 20 requests/sec, 400 requests per run
- **Measurement:** request arrival to completed response, p50/p95 in milliseconds; first run after boot discarded; reported measurements taken from warmed runs
- **Repeatability:** quoted latency cells were checked against a second consecutive warm run, typically agreeing within approximately 10%.

The workload used a shared, byte-stable prefix and a ~50 request-specific tokens. 
Requests were sent at open-loop Poisson arrival times. Latency was measured from scheduled arrival through response completion. The first benchmark run after each server restart was excluded.

EAGLE configuration:

```yaml
enable_in_graph_sampling: true
speculative_config:
  decoding_type: Eagle3
  max_draft_len: 2
  speculative_model: AngelSlim/Qwen3-4B_eagle3
```

The one-model EAGLE-3 path (`eagle3_one_model=True`) was confirmed in startup logs. The request-level comparisons were run without iteration performance statistics enabled.


### Expected behavior

Enabling EAGLE-3 with draft acceptance of ~2 output tokens per iteration (out of a maximum 3) should reduce, or at worst not increase, request latency. Just as it does in vLLM 0.31.0 on the same host and in TensorRT-LLM on RTX PRO 6000.


### actual behavior

On H100 SXM, enabling one-model EAGLE-3 in TensorRT-LLM 1.3.0rc29 increases request latency for our short-output workload, despite draft acceptance of ~2 output tokens per iteration out of a maximum 3. The same draft checkpoint improves latency in vLLM 0.31.0 on the same host, and EAGLE-3 also helps TensorRT-LLM on RTX PRO 6000 (−14% p50, −32% p95).

### H100 results: same FP8 checkpoint and EAGLE head

| Engine | FP8 without EAGLE (p50 / p95) | FP8 with EAGLE-3 (p50 / p95) |
|---|---:|---:|
| vLLM 0.31.0 | ~78 / 121 ms | **67.1 / 102.0 ms** |
| TensorRT-LLM 1.3.0rc29 | **68.6 / 98.7 ms** | 100.6 / 165.2 ms |

Within vLLM, EAGLE-3 improves p50 by about 14% and p95 by 16%. Within TensorRT-LLM, it worsens p50 by about 47% and p95 by 67%.

The TensorRT-LLM EAGLE configuration takes about **50% longer at p50** and **62% longer at p95** than vLLM's EAGLE configuration.

Both engines use the same target and draft checkpoint, GPU, traffic shape, and draft length.

### Draft acceptance

The draft head is producing useful predictions in both engines:

| Engine | Measured acceptance |
|---|---|
| TensorRT-LLM | `acceptanceLength` 2.03–2.04 output tokens per iteration; approximately 52.5% of drafted tokens accepted |
| vLLM | 1,984 / 4,168 drafted tokens accepted (47.6%); 59.6% at draft position 0 and 35.7% at position 1 |

The TensorRT-LLM acceptance metric was collected with `enable_iter_perf_stats`. That instrumentation affects latency on this workload, so we do **not** use instrumented runs for the end-to-end comparison above. 

### Fixed-batch experiment

To remove ongoing request admission from the test, we sent bursts of 1, 4, or 16 simultaneous requests, with no further arrivals until completion. The figures below are medians across five warmed bursts using the BF16 target, with iteration statistics disabled.

Each cell gives **median request latency / slowest request / burst makespan** in milliseconds.

| Simultaneous requests | BF16 without EAGLE | BF16 + EAGLE-3 |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1 | 66.4 / 66.4 / 66.6 | 75.5 / 75.5 / 75.6 |
| 4 | 105.9 / 139.2 / 143.5 | 133.6 / 138.1 / 142.5 |
| 16 | 150.5 / 213.6 / 217.9 | 186.5 / 205.4 / 211.1 |

EAGLE increases median request latency at every tested burst size, although the slowest-request latency and makespan are close between configurations at 4 and 16 requests. 

### Version comparison

Results from the same H100 pod, using BF16:

| TensorRT-LLM version | Without EAGLE (p50 / p95) | With EAGLE-3 (p50 / p95) |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1.2.1 | 143.8 / 261.7 ms | 137 / 248 ms |
| 1.3.0rc29 | 76.3 / 110.8 ms | 98.3 / 158.8 ms |

The non-speculative path improved far more between these releases than the EAGLE path. As a result, EAGLE moves from a small net benefit in 1.2.1 to a substantial regression in 1.3.0rc29. 

### Cross-GPU results

TensorRT-LLM 1.3.0rc29, BF16 target, same model family and draft head:

| GPU | Without EAGLE (p50 / p95) | With EAGLE-3 (p50 / p95) |
|---|---:|---:|
| RTX PRO 6000 (SM120) | 89.0 / 144.0 ms | **76.3 / 97.5 ms** |
| H100 (SM90) | **76.3 / 110.8 ms** | 98.3 / 158.8 ms |
| H200 (SM90) | **52.7 / ~80 ms** | 81 / 149 ms |

EAGLE helps on RTX PRO 6000 but hurts on both tested Hopper GPUs.


Please investigate why enabling one-model EAGLE-3 in TensorRT-LLM 1.3.0rc29 increases request latency on the tested Hopper systems despite comparable draft acceptance, while the same checkpoint improves latency in vLLM on H100 and in TensorRT-LLM on RTX PRO 6000.

items.title: [CI] AIBrix CI takes a large share of vllm-project's shared GitHub-hosted runners
items.author: Jeffwan
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

AIBrix's GitHub Actions workflows take a large share of the GitHub-hosted runners that every vllm-project repo shares. The org is on GitHub's Free plan, so all repos draw from one pool of about 20 concurrent jobs. AIBrix starts up to ~32 jobs on every merge to main and up to ~23 on every PR push, so a single AIBrix event can fill the whole pool, and jobs from other vllm-project repos wait for a runner.

This issue records the numbers and tracks changes to cut AIBrix's footprint.

## How the pool is shared

- GitHub-hosted runner concurrency is set per organization, not per repo. On the Free plan, all vllm-project repos share about 20 concurrent jobs. We observed a ceiling of 20–22.
- vllm's main CI runs on other infrastructure, but vllm and several other vllm-project repos still run some jobs on GitHub-hosted runners. Those jobs wait whenever the pool is full.

## Measurements

### Org-wide, two 2-hour samples

All GitHub-hosted jobs across vllm-project, counting only jobs that got a runner.

| Window (UTC) | Org concurrency (median / max) | AIBrix share | AIBrix jobs running (avg / max) | Median queue, vllm | Median queue, AIBrix |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Oct 16 19:00–21:00 | 17 / 20 | 51% (largest) | 7.8 / 20 | 25 min | 42 min |
| Oct 17 01:00–03:00 | 14 / 22 | 25% (second largest) | 3.6 / 11 | 2 min | 12 min |

In the first window, there were minutes when all 20 runners were running AIBrix jobs.

### AIBrix, 24 hours (Oct 16 04:00Z – Oct 17 04:00Z)

361 workflow runs, 20 merges to main, about 8,160 GitHub-hosted job-minutes. That keeps about 5.7 of the org's ~20 runners busy on average, around the clock.

| Workflow | Jobs per run | Job-minutes | Share | Triggered by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Docker Push Images | 12 | 3,571 | 44% | every merge |
| Installation Tests | 8 | 1,834 | 22% | PRs and every merge |
| Linter and Unit Tests | 6 | 1,285 | 16% | PRs and every merge |
| Installation Smoke | 7 | 948 | 12% | PRs |
| Code Quality (CodeQL) | 3 | 159 | 2% | every merge |
| Docker Push kvcached-runtime | 1 | 151 | 2% | every merge |
| Others (Python tests, StormService E2E, Helm chart, docs, bot) | – | ~215 | 3% | – |

**62% of these minutes (5,083) come from merges to main, not from PRs.**

## Problems in AIBrix's workflows

1. **Every merge rebuilds and pushes every image.** Docker Push Images builds 6 images twice, once for Docker Hub and once for GHCR. Each build covers amd64 and arm64 through QEMU and takes 15–25 minutes. That is 12 long jobs per merge, about 20 times a day. These jobs themselves waited a median of 114 minutes for a runner.
2. **Every merge re-runs tests that already passed on the PR.** Installation Tests and Linter and Unit Tests run again on every push to main: about 1,150 job-minutes a day.
3. **Many small jobs per run.** Before its one e2e job, Installation Tests runs 5 image-build jobs (1–4 minutes each), a mock-app auth test (under 1 minute) and an artifact cleanup job. Installation Smoke builds 5 images again in its own jobs. Each small job takes its own runner and its own wait in the queue.
4. **Linter and Unit Tests uses 6 jobs**, including a coverage check that runs for about 20 seconds.

## Proposed changes

| Change | Jobs per merge | Jobs per PR push |
|---|---|---|
| Build and push images nightly, plus a manual trigger (release builds unchanged); one build pushes to both registries | −13 | – |
| Stop re-running Installation Tests and Linter and Unit Tests on push to main; keep them on `release-*`; add one nightly full run on main | −14 | – |
| Fold the image builds, mock-app auth test and artifact cleanup into the Installation Tests e2e job | – | 8 → 1 |
| Fold the image builds into the two Installation Smoke jobs | – | 7 → 2 |
| Merge lint and verify into one job; fold coverage into unit tests | – | 6 → 4 |
| **Total** | **~32 → ~3** | **~23 → ~9** |

Expected result: the number of jobs each AIBrix event starts drops by more than half, and AIBrix's job-minutes drop by about 55–60%.

Trade-offs:

- Docker Hub and GHCR no longer get a `:<commit-sha>` image for every merge, and `nightly` updates once a day. The manual trigger builds images on demand.
- If two PRs each pass but break main when combined, the nightly run catches it, up to a day later.
- The Installation Tests e2e job takes a few minutes longer, but it waits in the queue only once instead of after every build job.

## Alternatives considered

Moving the heavy e2e jobs to self-hosted or third-party runners. We deferred this: AIBrix's CI load is bursty (heavy around PRs and merges, idle most of the day), and billing for a runner service is hard to separate from vllm-project. The changes above cost nothing, don't add infrastructure to maintain, and are easy to revert.

## Method

Data from the GitHub Actions REST API (`/actions/runs` and `/actions/runs/{id}/jobs`), counting only jobs that ran on GitHub-hosted runners (`runner_group_name == "GitHub Actions"`). For each sample window, runs created in the hour before the window are included, so jobs already running when the window starts are counted. The script is available on request.

items.title: [Bug] sm12x MoE CuTe-DSL kernels are never disk-cached — cute.compile hardcodes no_cache=True, so every fresh engine re-pays 15–40 s MLIR compiles per kernel shape
items.author: jhsmith409
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

The Blackwell sm12x fused-MoE path compiles all of its CuTe-DSL kernels through explicit
`cute.compile(...)`, which unconditionally disables the DSL's file cache. The only caching
layer is three in-process Python dicts, so **every engine start re-pays the full MLIR JIT
cost for every kernel specialization it touches** — measured at **~40 s** for the dynamic
kernel's first hit and **~15–18 s per small-`m` micro-kernel specialization**. In a serving
context (vLLM `--moe-backend=flashinfer_b12x`) these compiles land mid-request and freeze
the whole engine (vllm#47458: ~17.5 s stop-the-world stalls, all in-flight requests frozen
including mid-decode).

`CUTE_DSL_CACHE_DIR` / `CUTE_DSL_DISABLE_FILE_CACHING` have no effect on this path — the
gate that would consult them is short-circuited before they are read.

## Environment

- flashinfer 0.6.12, 0.6.13, and **0.6.15.post1** (all verified; `moe_dispatch.py` cache
  structure unchanged across them)
- nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.5.0 and **4.6.0** (both verified)
- SM120: RTX 5070 Ti (×2, TP/PP), RTX 5090 (unsharded), RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell — reproduced
  on all three in the vllm#47458 thread
- Model: `nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4` via vLLM `--moe-backend=flashinfer_b12x`

## Mechanism (exact code paths)

1. **The DSL hardcodes `no_cache=True` for explicit compiles.**
   `CompileCallable._compile` sets `kwargs["no_cache"] = True` unconditionally:
   - nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.5.0: `base_dsl/compiler.py:604-605`
   - nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.6.0: `base_dsl/compiler.py:1319`

2. **The file cache is gated behind `if not no_cache`** — both the load and the dump —
   so the env vars are never even consulted for explicit compiles:
   - 4.5.0: `base_dsl/dsl.py:1645` (load), `:1736` (dump)
   - 4.6.0: `base_dsl/dsl.py:2004` (load), `:2105` (dump); in-memory `jit_cache` lookups
     likewise skipped under `no_cache` at `:2012`, `:2293`

3. **The sm12x MoE dispatch only ever compiles through `cute.compile`,** with plain
   in-process dicts on top — nothing reaches disk:
   - 0.6.12/0.6.13: `blackwell_sm12x/moe_dispatch.py:676/912/1675` (compile sites);
     `_STATIC/_MICRO/_DYNAMIC_KERNEL_CACHE`
   - 0.6.15.post1: compile sites at `:697/:942/:1723`; caches at `:486/:733/:1524`

4. Compounding factor (tracked separately as #3836): the micro-kernel `cache_key`
   includes both `m` and `workspace.max_rows` (0.6.15.post1 `moe_dispatch.py:770-791`,
   fields at `:774`/`:778`), so workspace growth invalidates already-compiled small-batch
   entries even *within* a process lifetime. With no disk layer underneath, each
   invalidation is a full 15 s+ recompile, not a reload.

## Verification

Behavioral check from the vllm#47458 thread (credit @waynehacking8, on 0.6.12 / DSL 4.5.0):

- `cute.compile` of a trivial `@cute.jit` function leaves `CUTE_DSL_CACHE_DIR` **empty**.
- Calling the same jit function **directly** (implicit compile path) writes
  `cute_dsl_<hash>.mlir`, and a fresh process then logs `JIT cache hit IN-FILE`.
- Only the implicit direct-call path caches; flashinfer's MoE dispatch never uses it.

Source-level re-verification on 0.6.15.post1 / DSL 4.6.0 (2026-08-02, inside the
`vllm/vllm-openai` nightly image): every line cite in the Mechanism section above was
confirmed against the installed packages — the hardcoded `no_cache=True`, the
`if not no_cache` gates around both file-cache load and dump, the three `cute.compile`
sites, the three in-process dicts, and `m`/`max_rows` still present in the micro-kernel
cache key.

Measured first-hit compile costs (RTX PRO 6000, synthetic MoE E=32/topk=4 driving
`B12xMoEWrapper.run` exactly as vLLM's `FlashInferB12xExperts` does):

| kernel path | first hit | subsequent (same key) |
|---|---|---|
| dynamic (m-independent key) | ~40 s | 1–3 ms |
| micro m=1 | 14.9 s | ms |
| micro m=2 | 15.2 s | ms |
| micro m=64 | 18.3 s | ms |

Production symptom: vllm#47458 — py-spy captured 16 consecutive samples over 8.35 s pinned
in `b12x_fused_moe (flashinfer/fused_moe/cute_dsl/b12x_moe.py:166)` during a live
~17.5 s engine-wide stall; `perf` showed `_cutlass_ir.cpython-312.so` frames present only
during stalls.

## Why this deserves a disk layer even after #3836

#3836 stops *rekeying* (recompiles within one process). But serving engines restart —
deploys, config changes, crash recovery, autoscaling — and each fresh process re-pays the
entire compile set: ~40 s dynamic + 15–18 s per small-shape class. For a model like
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B this is 1–2 minutes of mid-serving stalls per engine lifetime that a
disk cache would reduce to milliseconds. The artifacts are deterministic products of
(kernel source, shape/config tuple, DSL version, arch) — exactly what file caches are for.

## Suggested fix directions

Either would resolve it; the first is contained entirely in flashinfer:

1. **flashinfer grows its own disk layer for sm12x MoE kernels**: serialize the compiled
   artifact keyed by the existing `cache_key` tuples + flashinfer version +
   nvidia-cutlass-dsl version + SM arch, under `FLASHINFER_WORKSPACE_DIR` (or a new env),
   loading into `_STATIC/_MICRO/_DYNAMIC_KERNEL_CACHE` on miss. The DSL's own
   `compile_and_cache` machinery demonstrates the artifact is serializable (the implicit
   path already writes/reads `.mlir` + compiled objects).
2. **Upstream: nvidia-cutlass-dsl honors its file cache under explicit `cute.compile`**
   (stop hardcoding `no_cache=True`, or add an opt-in kwarg flashinfer can pass).

A third, cheaper-but-partial option is an official warm-up API (the attempt in
vllm#47599 was closed unmerged): it moves the cost to boot but still re-pays it every
process start, and needs the largest-workspace-first ordering to avoid #3836 rekeying —
a disk cache composes with, rather than replaces, that.

## Cross-references

- vllm#47458 — serving-stall report this splits from (mechanism established in-thread by
  @waynehacking8; py-spy confirmation by me)
- flashinfer#3836 — the workspace-rekeying half (open)

items.title: [cake deslop] cake_dsv4 SM120: fold nvfp4 and rope kernel clones into templates, drop 16 planner-dead ht1 prefill kernels (~202K lines)
items.author: yyihuang
items.body_excerpt:
**Background.** `csrc/cake_dsv4/sm_120a` is the Cake-generated SM120/SM121 backend for RTX PRO 6000, RTX 5090 and GB10. It sits behind `trtllm_batch_decode_sparse_mla_dsv4(backend="cake")` (`flashinfer/mla/_core.py:451-524`), `SparseMLASm120Wrapper(backend="cake")` and the lazy exports in `flashinfer/mla/__init__.py:44-82`. It serves DeepSeek-V4 NVFP4-cache sparse-MLA decode/prefill, DeepSeek-V4.1 mixed-cache (`fp8_dsv41_fp4_ca`) decode, and the NVFP4 RoPE quantize-insert writers. The tree was added by #5914 (nvfp4 decode, +102,994), #5959 (nvfp4 prefill, +99,098), #5983 (dsv41, +228,599) and #6033 (rope insert, +15,539). #5949 and #6000 extended it (GB10 planners, batched merge). Three PRs regenerated it: #6004 (prefill, +103,600/−36,600), #6027 (decode for CUDA 12.9, +11,176/−11,178) and #6071 (replaced the #5983 dsv41 export wholesale, +286,168/−223,681). The tree is now 74 files / 564,752 lines: nvfp4 decode 9 TUs 101,877, nvfp4 prefill 8 TUs 163,212, dsv41 47 TUs 283,070, rope insert 1 TU 12,809, bindings/headers/manifests 3,784. Three JIT specs compile all 68 `.cu` files (18/48/2 sources, appended in `flashinfer/aot.py:1212-1220`), so no file goes uncompiled. No earlier sub-issue covers this tree: #5794 (closed by #5920) only cleaned up `sm_100a`/`sm_103a`. #6071 already exports dsv41 as `template<int kHeads, bool kPow2Pages, bool kNoMul>` fold TUs with SASS-identical proofs, but the nvfp4 and rope exporters never adopted that form. In `flashinfer/mla/_sparse_mla_sm120`, only `cake_dsv41_mixed.py`, `_cake_dsv4_nvfp4.py` and `_cake_dsv4_nvfp4_rope_insert.py` are in scope; the other 7 files are the hand-written SM120 sparse backend. `flashinfer/experimental/deepseek_v41` (SM100 CuTe-DSL decode) and `tests/mla/test_cake_dsv4_hardening.py` (SM100/SM103) do not touch this tree.

**Findings**
- **nvfp4 decode: per-head clones.** The 9 files `cake_sparse_mla_dsv4_nvfp4_h{8,16,32,48,64,80,96,112,128}.cu` (101,877 lines, 44 `__global__`) contain only 3 forms: h8 (6,777 lines), one-tile h16/48/80/112 (7,255 each) and two-tile h32/64/96/128 (16,520 each). h16 differs from h48/80/112 by 215 lines (`token*16` → `token*48`, `(1) ? 16 : 48`, namespace, kernel name), h32 from h64/96/128 by 603, and h8 from h16 by 976 (the `(0) ? 16 : 8` mask). The head literal explains every differing line. 30,552 unique lines → 71,325 redundant.
- **nvfp4 prefill: per-head clones.** The 8 files `cake_sparse_mla_dsv4_nvfp4_prefill_h*.cu` (163,212 lines, 44 `__global__`) contain 3 tile forms: ht1 only (h16/48/80/112, 12,727 lines each), ht1+ht2 (h32/96, 20,887) and ht1+ht2+ht4 (h64/128, 35,265). Within each form the files differ by 39/61/83 lines, all head literals. 68,879 unique lines → 94,333 redundant, or 69,037 after the ht1 removal below. A single `template<int kHeads>` TU holding every tile form (35,265 lines) would remove 127,947.
- **Planner-dead ht1 prefill kernels.** For 32/64/96/128 heads, the 4 ht1 kernels (`*_ht1_qr2_io72_ru`, `_dual_ru`, `_s3_ru`, `_s3_dual_ru`) occupy lines 158–12805 of each TU: 12,648 × 4 = 50,592 lines.
  - `cake_sparse_mla_sm120_dsv4_nvfp4_plan_prefill` (`_cake_dsv4_nvfp4.py:594-611`, `wide_heads=64` at :425) returns 2 for 32 heads and 2 or 4 for 64/96/128. It returns 1 only for 16/48/80/112.
  - `functional_run` (:1437-1451) and `wrapper_run` (:1586-1599) never pass `head_tiles`. The three-stage kernels exist only for ht1 (`kernels.h:54`).
  - The kernels are still reachable through the documented `head_tiles=1` kwarg (`docs/api/attention.rst:242`, README :152-154) and the GPU prefill tests. Removing them turns that override into a `ValueError` (host :1249-1252, binding :398).
  - They are also clones of the h16 TU's 4 kernels, so the prefill fold covers most of this reduction even if the knob stays.
- **rope insert: 34 kernels, 4 bodies.** `cake_dsv4_nvfp4_rope_insert_kernel.cu` (12,809 lines) instantiates 5 padded head counts {8,16,32,64,128} × {qkv, noqrope, inplace} × {i32, i64} slots, plus 2 compress ratios × 2 slot dtypes. Pairs differ by 4–9 lines out of 300–433: the padded-head literal, and `slot_mapping_i64[tok]` vs `(long long)slot_mapping_i32[tok]`. The unique text is ~1,441 kernel + 68 header + ~150 launch lines, so ~11,100 lines are redundant.
- **dsv41 `tl+ip+e2f` toolchain fallback.** 7 of the 97 decode bodies (dual, 32–128 heads) live in `cake_sparse_mla_dsv41_mixed_dual_tl_ip_e2f_heads_h32_64_96_128_fold.cu` (5,563 lines) and `..._h48_80_112_fold.cu` (5,587), 11,150 lines in total. No rule selects them. `_table_variant` (`cake_dsv41_mixed.py:454-460`) takes them only when `_direct_cvt_toolchain()` (nvcc ≥ 13.2, :473-481) is false. `ci/cuda-versions.json` runs 12.9/13.0/13.4, so on 2 of the 3 CI toolchains these bodies are the production dual two-tile path. They are also reachable via `variant=`.
- **dsv41 per-SKU table.** `plan_variant` has 21 rules, 7 each for SM counts 48 (CC 12.1 unified memory), 170 and 188. Any other card (RTX 5080 84 SMs, 5070 Ti 70, RTX PRO 5000 110) runs only the 18 `default` bodies. The 97 decode bodies split into 18 default, 12 multi-card, 20 each sm188-/sm170-/sm48-only, 7 CUDA<13.2-only and 0 unreachable. 29 of them exist only as non-pow2 page twins, which `dispatch_from_manifest` (:238-243) requires. The TUs that hold only single-card bodies total 159,812 lines: sm188 8 files 56,683, sm170 9 files 49,629, sm48 7 files 53,500. All variants compute the same result, so pruning is a performance decision.
- **Host overhead.** `cake_sparse_mla_sm120_dsv4_nvfp4_format_info` (`_cake_dsv4_nvfp4.py:88-124`) is uncached and rebuilds a 15-key dict 5× per decode call and 6× per prefill call (8 call sites). `functional_run`/`wrapper_run` run `_normalize_indices` + `_resolve_plan`, then the entry repeats `_prepare_inputs`/`_resolve_plan` (:1056, :1069). `_num_sms` is already `@functools.cache`d (:412). The nvfp4 (:118-176) and dsv41 (:69-128) bindings each define `CheckDevice`/`CheckDtype`/`CheckRows`/`CheckLse`/`CheckIndices`/`CheckCache`/`LengthP

items.title: [Gateway] Add routing support for the SGLang /v1/score API
items.author: googs1025
items.body_excerpt:
Parent issue: #2989

## Background

SGLang v0.5.21 adds and extends `POST /v1/score` for pointwise and setwise scoring.

References:

- https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/releases/tag/v0.5.21
- https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/38965

AIBrix Gateway supports related endpoints but does not currently register or parse `/v1/score`.

## Proposed behavior

The Gateway should:

1. accept `POST /v1/score`;
2. parse its JSON request;
3. require a non-empty `model`;
4. require a non-empty `items` field;
5. preserve all request fields;
6. use existing non-PD routing;
7. process token usage when present;
8. preserve the upstream score response without transforming score matrices.

AIBrix must require `model` even when SGLang can use a server-side default, because the Gateway needs it for backend selection.

## Validation

Add a focused validator such as:

```go
func validateScoreRequest(
    requestID string,
    requestBody []byte,
) (model, message string, errRes *extProcPb.ProcessingResponse)
```

Validate only Gateway requirements:

- JSON object root;
- non-empty string `model`;
- present, non-null, non-empty `items`;
- no streaming response.

Forward model-specific fields such as `score_extraction_token`, `apply_softmax`, `return_pooled_hidden_states`, and `item_first` without duplicating SGLang validation.

## Routing text

- Prefer a non-empty textual `query`.
- Otherwise use the first textual item when available.
- If neither is textual, leave the routing message empty.
- Do not stringify token-ID arrays.
- Do not concatenate all items.

## Response handling

The endpoint is non-streaming. Preserve nested score matrices, `pooled_hidden_states`, and upstream errors. Extract `prompt_tokens`, `completion_tokens`, and `total_tokens` when present.

## Routing changes

Add `/v1/score` to path constants, request validation dispatch, ModelRouter default paths, the shared reserved HTTPRoute, and Gateway documentation. Follow the existing structure without adding a central endpoint registry.

## Testing

Cover pointwise and setwise requests, tokenized items, optional query, routing-text selection, unknown fields, invalid model/items, malformed JSON, unsupported streaming, query strings, usage extraction, nested responses, upstream errors, and reserved/model route presence.

## Non-goals

- Do not implement scoring in AIBrix.
- Do not reproduce the complete SGLang scoring schema.
- Do not add PD support.
- Do not transform score matrices.
- Do not change Rerank or Classify semantics.

## Acceptance criteria

- Valid score requests route to an eligible SGLang Pod.
- Gateway-required fields receive bounded validation.
- Pointwise and setwise payloads remain intact.
- Nested responses remain intact.
- Usage is accounted for when present.
- Both reserved and model routes expose the endpoint.

Is LinearCombination fully supported for OpClassTensorOp in 3D convolutions?

What is the correct way to pass the Bias vector?

items.title: [CAKE] Long-term CAKE-generated Kernel Progress Tracker
items.author: yyihuang
items.body_excerpt:
To track multi-platform kernels generated from CAKE 🍰 harness + claude/codex agent. 

We are more than happy to take any new kernel challenges!

**Feel free to reach out/leave your comments/create sub-issues here to submit your customized CAKE kernel request. And we will bake it for you!**

**We know many of you have been asking for training kernels—and we heard you.** You have had your CAKE going forward; now it is time to take it **back**! Follow the dedicated forward & backward tracker at #4642, bring us your toughest training bottleneck, and let us bake the full pass together. 🍰🔥

And we recommend using agent to index the kernels you need. 😜

## Kernel categories

Pull requests are tracked in the category sub-issues below, with detailed sections and links to each PR. Please add new PRs to the corresponding category.

### Communication

Sub-issue: #6593

MoE all-reduce/finalize and residual-add/RMSNorm/combine fusion; MNNVL, Ulysses and DCP all-to-all; all-gather matmul and sequence parallelism; QKV/Norm/RoPE and MiniMax ICP exchange; FP8 GEMM + all-reduce; NVFP4-transport TP all-reduce with residual + RMSNorm fusion; Kimi-K3 TP12 tails, SM120 PCIe communication and MoK.

### Attention

Sub-issue: #6594

FMHA variants (paged/DCP/GQA, MiniMax sparse, NVFP4, Sage/VSA, and MiniMax-H3 dense/packed-varlen); MLA K concatenation, decode and sparse MLA, including DSA forward/backward. Also covers fused pre-attention/output projection, QKV quantize-and-pack, QK RMSNorm/RoPE/KV append, Kimi-K3 AttnRes, and DSA indexer logits/top-k.

### Linear Attention & State Space

Sub-issue: #6595

Recurrent KDA prefill, decode and training; Gated Delta Rule context-parallel and non-CP prefill, FP32-state paths and the source-only Blackwell backend; Mamba SSDCombined and selective state update.

### GEMM / BMM

Sub-issue: #6596

BF16 BMM, BF16 x FP4/NVFP4/FP8 and grouped GEMM, DeepGEMM/TinyGEMM2, all-gather matmul and router GEMM. Includes SVDQuant, runtime BF16 LoRA, per-token quantize + GEMM, projection gradients, MiniMax-H3 FC1 + SwiGLU/full-MLP fusion, and Kimi-K3 FP8 projection.

### MoE & Routing

Sub-issue: #6597

Fused MoE, AlphaMoE, MegaMoE and BGMV MoE; DeepSeek fused routing; Kimi-K3 Stable LatentMoE and fused router; warp-decode kernels.

### Activation & Quantization

Sub-issue: #6598

MXFP8 quantization, fused SwiGLU + MXFP8 quantization, softmax, and RMSNorm training kernels for forward and backward passes.

### LM-head & Loss

Sub-issue: #6599

Chunked LM-head with fused cross-entropy or policy loss, including memory-bounded backward for training.

### Sampling

Sub-issue: #6600

Fused radix top-k/top-p sampling, architecture qualification, kernel and dispatch optimizations, source/loader refactoring, and CUDA graph replay tests.

### Vision Encoder

Sub-issue: #6601

Kimi-K3 vision tower kernels for MoonViT-3D and PatchMergerV2.

### Cross-family Support

Sub-issue: #6602

Rubin/SM107 support and tuning across GDN, KDA, routing, BGMV MoE and MLA K concatenation; MiniMax-H3 SM120 shared kernels/helpers.

### Standalone Build of CAKE Packages

Sub-issue: #6553

The seven CAKE packages (`cake_rmsnorm_train`, `cake_dsa_train`, `cake_dsa_indexer`, `cake_lm_head_loss`, `dense_projection_gemm`, `cake_moe_grouped_gemm`, `cake_mok_bf16`) build and test outside flashinfer without patches: `build.json` manifests and a shared loader, header-free bindings, behaviour switches as keyword arguments, and backend test suites that import only the package.

- #6571
- #6584
- #6610
