items.title: [cake deslop] cake_vsa round 2: keep one SM90 build (-120K lines), fold the 14 SM90 bindings and manifest, drop dead stages and ABI
items.author: yyihuang
items.body_excerpt:
**Background.** The Cake VSA kernels serve three explicit backends. All three are JIT-only: none is in `flashinfer/aot.py`, and `backend="auto"` never selects any of them.
- SM100/SM103 `BlockSparseAttentionWrapper(backend="cake")`: `csrc/cake_vsa`, 11 files / 16,932 lines, 10 profiles × {sm_100a, sm_103a}.
- SM90 `VariableBlockSparseAttentionWrapper(backend="cake")`: the CUDA C++ build in `csrc/cake_vsa_sm90`, 31 / 52,833.
- SM90 `backend="cake_cute"`: the CuTe DSL build in `flashinfer/experimental/cake_vsa_sm90_cute`, 19 / 120,187. It was added in #5596, and #5687 added the queue stage.

Including Python, JIT and tests, the family is 72 files / 198,004 lines at 3184bbea.

Round one was #5826 and #5827:
- #5826 was closed by #5926 (+1,587/−22,072). It removed the 10 byte-identical sm_103a copies and replaced 10 host shims with one `cake_vsa_binding.cu`. It deferred the fp16 dtype clone and kept the ultrasparse/longseq gates as hard errors. No per-arch copies remain.
- #5827 was closed by #5923 (+49,949/−52,950). It flattened the SM90 CUDA layout behind thin launchers (14/14 kernels SASS-identical) and retired `small_k1s`/`small_k3s`, but only from the CUDA build.

#5827 was closed with four items still open: "Keep one build", "Template the small kernels and bindings", "Pass the plan as a buffer / precompute TMA metadata" and "Drop the debug buffers". No later PR re-added material to any of the three directories.

**Findings**
- **Two SM90 builds of one planner.** `flashinfer/sparse.py:1856-1878` sends `cake` and `cake_cute` to the same `create_plan`, passing `engine="cuda"` or `"cute"`. `tests/experimental/test_cake_vsa_sm90_cute.py:138` asserts that the two builds are bit-exact per stage. #5923's body records:
  - CuTe/CUDA GPU time of 0.98..1.01 over four shape families;
  - about 11 us of extra host time per CuTe call;
  - a prepared keep-CUDA removal commit that keeps `cake_cute` as an alias of `cake`.

  Per call, the CuTe path converts about 440 Python ints (`slot_words`, `__init__.py:304-323`) and re-walks the manifest's TMA expression trees (`_eval_dim`).
- **`cake_cute` works only from a source checkout.** `pyproject.toml:59` sets `include-package-data=false`, and `[tool.setuptools.package-data]` (lines 78-150) has no entry for the CuTe package. As a result, `cake_vsa_sm90_cute_manifest.json` (4,548 lines) is missing from wheels, and `__init__.py:101` raises `FileNotFoundError` on the first plan. This has not been confirmed against a built wheel. Separately, `sparse.py:1705` calls `nvidia-cutlass-dsl` optional, but `requirements.txt:49` pins it as a hard dependency.
- **Retired CuTe stages still ship.** `small_k1s.py` (2,898 lines), `small_k3s.py` (6,305) and their two 290-line manifest entries total 9,783 lines. No route can reach them:
  - The `s` suffix is built only at `cake_vsa_sm90.py:1320-1325`.
  - `plan_small` raises for a split `kmax` outside `SPLIT_KMAX_VARIANTS=(4, 6)` (lines 486-489).
  - `split_kmax` iterates only over (4, 6) (line 204).
  - `compile_all` has no caller.

  The CUDA manifest's `contract.retired_stages` already lists both stages.
- **SM90 manifest is mostly unread.** `flashinfer/jit/cake_vsa_sm90.py` reads only 382 of the 2,201 lines in `cake_vsa_sm90_manifest.json`; the other 1,819 are never read. `modules[].launch` is read only by `cake_vsa_sm90_launch`, which has no caller. All 14 `compile_flags` are `['--use_fast_math']`. `_source_path` computes a SHA-256 of every source again each time a spec is created.
- **14 SM90 bindings with 3 ABI shapes.** The 14 `*_binding.cu` files (4,176 lines) use three ABIs: 10 × 11 parameters (plan), 2 × 14 (split: `small_k4s`/`small_k6s` add `Wo/Ws/Wc`) and 2 × 15 (persistent: `attention`, `attention_queue`). After normalization, pairs differ in 8-83 lines: namespace, dynamic SMEM, block size and export. `csrc/cake_vsa/cake_vsa_binding.cu` (580 lines) already serves 10 profiles and 3 ABIs through `-D` defines.
- **Dead debug ABI.** `tl` appears only in the kernel signatures (`cake_vsa_sm90_7bffc3d851bf002de78f_kernel.cu:70`, `cake_vsa_sm90_efbb759a1ac3a01e0317_kernel.cu:73`). `dbg` is used only by the queue kernel (`dbg[62]`, `dbg[63]`). Even so, `cake_vsa_sm90.py:1248-1249` allocates both buffers for every plan and passes them on every launch.
- **SM90 near-duplicate kernels.** `attention_queue` (3,458 lines) differs from `attention` (3,412) in 192-194 normalized lines, so they are 94% identical. The 12 small-selection kernels (39,378 CUDA lines, about 90K CuTe lines) are one schedule instantiated per (KMAX, split, cluster). #5923 notes that because KMAX is unrolled, a literal-template fold does not work.
- **SM100 dtype clone.** `cake_vsa_blk128_fp16_compact.cu` and `cake_vsa_blk128_compact.cu` (1,519 lines each) differ in 38 normalized lines:
  - the kernel symbol;
  - four smem typedefs;
  - the conversion intrinsics;
  - four tcgen05 instruction-descriptor immediates.

  The `CAKE_VSA_FP16` define already exists (`flashinfer/jit/cake_vsa.py:90`, `cake_vsa_binding.cu:85-91`). head64 and head96 differ in 149 lines, so they are not a clone.
- **Dead SM100 parameters and paths (about 600 lines).**
  - Temperature-LSE: `_run_standard` always passes `(1.0, int(return_lse), 0)` for the three temperature-LSE parameters (`cake_vsa.py:585-589`). This leaves dead device code in 8 kernels.
  - `fp16_direct`: `cake_vsa_fp16_direct.cu` (2,167 lines, 29 arguments) is called only by `_run_fp16`, always with batch 1, no paging, `causal=0` and unit FP8 scales. Its five `if (causal != 0)` branches and its paged and scale paths are therefore dead.
- **Exact-shape gates.**
  - `ultrasparse_bsr` (1,529 lines) runs only when `mb >= 625`, `Hq == Hkv == 8`, the BSR pattern is shared across heads, and exactly 6 blocks are selected uniformly (`cake_vsa.py:776-802`, `cake_vsa_binding.cu:334-335`). That is exactly the `benchmarks/bench_cake_vsa.py` deployment row `(128, bf16, 8, 8, 128, 80000, 80000, 6)`. No device test reaches it. Any ot

items.title: [RLlib] Potential infinite Env Runer sampling loop with non default algorithm parameters
items.author: corentinlger
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

Hi ! While investigating algo configs leading to silently discarded env runners results (https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/63302), I ran into a rare but weird case where RLlib training can hang forever without any error. It probably almost never happens, but it still seems a bit weird it's possible, so I'm still posting an issue in case it can help.

The issue: with a synchronous algo on the new API stack (e.g. PPO), if every `sample()` call takes longer than `sample_timeout_s`, each sampling round returns nothing. If `min_sample_timesteps_per_iteration > 0`, the iteration can never reach its minimum, so `train()` loops forever without crashing.

RLlib already warns while this happens and gives a useful advice to fix it, but can still keeps running the training indefinitely.

```
2026-10-01 12:54:33,281 WARNING rollout_ops.py:122 -- No samples returned from remote workers. If you have a slow environment or model, consider increasing the `sample_timeout_s` or decreasing the `rollout_fragment_length` in `AlgorithmConfig.env_runners().
2026-10-01 12:54:35,290 WARNING rollout_ops.py:122 -- No samples returned from remote workers. If you have a slow environment or model, consider increasing the `sample_timeout_s` or decreasing the `rollout_fragment_length` in `AlgorithmConfig.env_runners().
. . .
```

Do you think it would make sense to add a simple safeguard (e.g if no new samples are collected for N consecutive training steps, raise an error and crash the training) ? If so, I can open a quick PR for this (: (but idk if it's worth it as this bug is likely very rare)

### Versions / Dependencies

- Ray 2.58.0
- Python 3.11.13

### Reproduction script

```python
# Toy env whose episodes take ~10s (longer than sample_timeout_s)
class SlowEnv(gym.Env):
    def __init__(self, config=None):
        self.observation_space = spaces.Box(-1.0, 1.0, (2,), np.float32)
        self.action_space = spaces.Discrete(2)
        self._t = 0
        self.n_resets = 0

    def reset(self, *, seed=None, options=None):
        print(f"{self.n_resets = }")
        self.n_resets += 1
        super().reset(seed=seed)
        self._t = 0
        return self.observation_space.sample(), {}

    def step(self, action):
        time.sleep(0.2)          # 50 steps * 0.2s = ~10s per episode
        self._t += 1
        print(f"{self._t = }")
        done = self._t >= 50
        return self.observation_space.sample(), 0.0, done, False, {}

# algo config with low sample timeout + non null min_sample_timesteps_per_iteration
config = (
        PPOConfig()
        .environment(SlowEnv)
        .env_runners(
            num_env_runners=2,
            batch_mode="complete_episodes",
            sample_timeout_s=2.0,          # too low: episodes take ~10s
        )
        .reporting(min_sample_timesteps_per_iteration=100)  # the gate that causes the hang
    )

algo = config.build_algo()
result = algo.train()  # infinite env runner sampling loop
```

### Issue Severity

None

comments.author: lindicaphxag-tech
comments.body:
I put together a draft implementation in #66687 to explore the no-progress safeguard described here. It detects a successful training-step loop that repeatedly makes zero sampling progress while `min_sample_timesteps_per_iteration > 0` and `sample_timeout_s` is finite, and covers both the old counters path and the new lifetime-metrics path.

I have intentionally kept it draft because one design point deserves maintainer input: the current prototype uses `num_consecutive_env_runner_failures_tolerance` as the retry budget, which avoids a new config knob but couples EnvRunner failure tolerance to sampling-timeout/no-progress tolerance. If a separate internal/default budget or dedicated config is preferred, I can adjust before review.

Also happy to defer/close the draft if the original reporter would prefer to implement the fix.

comments.author: corentinlger
comments.body: Hi, I'd be happy in implementing a PR for this issue if needed , but before doing so it would be good to even know if RLlib maintainers think it's worth fixing (which is not sure)

comments.author: lindicaphxag-tech
comments.body: Update on my draft fix in [PR #66687](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/66687): I rebased the change onto current `master` and separated the no-progress budget from `num_consecutive_env_runner_failures_tolerance`. The new `num_consecutive_sample_no_progress_tolerance` defaults to 100 and is independently configurable through `AlgorithmConfig.fault_tolerance(...)`. This avoids changing the worker-failure retry behavior when users tune the sampling-stall safeguard. Added tests for both independence directions, and retained coverage for old/new API stacks, env/agent counters, progress reset, finite vs blocking timeouts, NaN retired-agent metrics, and invalid infinite counters. Current-head CI is now the gate; I am not claiming merge-ready until the required Ray checks pass.

items.title: [Bug] An unhealthy remote tokenizer is re-probed on every prefix-cache request, adding up to 5s each
items.author: AarnavNoble
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

With the remote tokenizer enabled (`AIBRIX_PREFIX_CACHE_USE_REMOTE_TOKENIZER`, or KV event sync, which turns it on), `TokenizerPool` (`pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/prefixcache/tokenizer_pool.go`) keeps one remote tokenizer per model, and a background health check marks an entry unhealthy when its endpoint stops answering.

From then on, every prefix-cache request for that model misses the fast path in `GetTokenizer` and goes to `createOrUpdateTokenizer`. That builds a new remote tokenizer for the same endpoint and runs a health probe with a 5s timeout. Only when the probe fails does the request fall back to the default tokenizer. Nothing remembers that the endpoint just failed, so the next request does it all again.

- Against an endpoint that hangs (an overloaded engine, a network partition), each routed request waits the full 5s before routing continues.
- Concurrent requests each send their own probe, so the slow endpoint gets one extra request per routed request on top of its load.
- This lasts until the endpoint recovers, not just for one health-check period.

The fallback to the default tokenizer is the right outcome. It just costs 5s per request to get there.

### Steps to Reproduce

Unit level on `main` (065e50f7): a `ModelServiceMap` endpoint backed by an `httptest` server that never answers, and an existing entry for the model already marked unhealthy.

| | Result on main |
|---|---|
| 3 sequential `GetTokenizer` calls | 5.0s each, default tokenizer each time |
| 20 concurrent `GetTokenizer` calls | slowest 5.0s, 20 probes sent to the endpoint |

### Expected behavior

- Only one request at a time probes for a model's tokenizer; concurrent requests wait for that result instead of each probing.
- After an endpoint fails creation or its probe, requests use the default tokenizer at once for a while (one health-check period) instead of probing it again. The background health check already re-probes existing entries and brings them back when the endpoint recovers.

I have a fix with tests and can open a PR.

### Environment

`main` at 065e50f7, `prefix-cache` routing with the vLLM remote tokenizer.

### Area

Gateway (prefix-cache routing)

items.title: [Performance]: SM107 trtllm-gen MLA decode: the pre-selection cap mMaxNumCtasPerSeqKv = 16 / max(clusterDimX, 2) limits split-KV at low batch
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

On SM107, `TllmGenFmhaKernel::selectKernelAutotuned` (`fmhaKernels.h`) caps `options.mMaxNumCtasPerSeqKv` at `16 / max(clusterDimX, 2)` = 8 for every GmemReduction + Static request before the autotuner runs, so that a later promotion to `CgaSmemReduction` stays within the 16-CTA cluster limit. That is the generation path. #18945 removed the same cap on SM100 because it took most of the split-KV parallelism away from low-batch MLA decode; #19038 kept it for SM107. On SM107 we see the effect that #18945 describes.

Kimi K3 MLA decode, per-rank TP8 shape (16 heads, one latent KV head, HQk 576 / HV 512, BF16, 64 tokens per page, 8 query tokens from MTP, batch 1, multi-CTA KV with the static scheduler, as `AttentionOp` issues it). `TllmGenFmhaRunner` microbenchmark on SM107, us per call, with the pre-selection cap replaced by the value in the first column:

| cap | 2K | 32K | 128K | kernel picked at 32K |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 (current) | 8.50 | 37.88 | 209.9 | HVPerCta256 ... MultiCtasKvCga |
| 12 | 8.48 | 51.72 | 253.3 | HVPerCta256 ... MultiCtasKvCga |
| 16 | 8.59 | 27.08 | 122.6 | HV512 ... MultiCtasKvCga |
| 24 | 8.58 | 28.58 | 94.7 | HV512 ... MultiCtasKv (gmem reduction) |
| 32 | 8.47 | 27.80 | 88.7 | HV512 ... MultiCtasKv |
| 64 | 8.44 | 27.86 | 88.7 | same as 32 |

From a cap of about 24, the autotuner leaves CGA reduction and picks the gmem-reduction kernel with more KV splits. Above 32 nothing changes. Against the current cap, 2K output is bit-identical (same kernel), and 32K / 128K differ by at most 1 bf16 ulp (different split), with no NaN/Inf.

End to end (Kimi K3 + MTP, 8 GPUs over 2 nodes, single request), cap 32 vs the current cap: decode step unchanged at 2K, -0.64 ms at 32K, -2.51 ms at 128K. Cap 16 gives -0.35 / -1.67 ms. Accuracy and long-context needle checks were unchanged.

One side effect: with a cap above `16 / clusterDimX`, the post-selection `limitCgaSmemReductionCtasKv` clamps the shapes where the autotuner still picks CGA reduction. It logs "CGA reduction is not supported when numCtasPerSeqKv * clusterDimX > 16 ..." for each of them, which comes to many thousands of lines per rank during warmup and graph capture. Nothing is logged during graph replay.

Questions / proposal:
- Is the pre-selection cap still needed on SM107, or is the post-selection `limitCgaSmemReductionCtasKv` enough? If the cap only guards a CGA promotion that would otherwise be illegal, raising it on SM107 to 32 (or removing it, as #18945 did on SM100) keeps the clamp where it matters and lets the gmem-reduction kernels get their split-KV.
- If maintainers prefer a knob for now, the change is a few lines: an override of the pre-selection cap, with the current value as the default. I can send either version, plus a downgrade of that warning to debug level.

I only measured MLA decode; the cap also applies to SM107 GQA generation, so a check there would be good too.

cc @yifeizhang-c (#19038) @kris1025 (#18945)

items.title: [Bug]: Nemotron 3.5 Super VL NVFP4 with --tool_parser qwen3_coder emits arguments "" (not "{}") for no-argument tools; echoing the call back in history then fails with HTTP 400 "arguments must be valid JSON"
items.author: satishalluri
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary
When serving `nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL-120B-A12B-NVFP4` with `trtllm-serve` (`--tool_parser qwen3_coder --reasoning_parser nemotron-v3`), the model sometimes calls a tool that has no required parameters (`run_tests`) and the response returns `function.arguments` as an empty string `""` instead of `"{}"`. An OpenAI-style agent appends that assistant message to history, and the next request is rejected by the same server:

`HTTP 400 {"object":"error","message":"tool_calls[0].function.arguments must be valid JSON.","type":"BadRequestError"}`

The server produces output it then refuses to accept as input.

## Environment
- Model: nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL-120B-A12B-NVFP4
- TensorRT-LLM 1.3.0rc29 (nvcr.io/nvidia/tensorrt-llm/release:1.3.0rc29), PyTorch backend, CUDA 13.0
- Hardware: 2x DGX Spark (GB10), TP=2 across the two nodes (mpirun, 1 rank per node)
- Launch: `trtllm-serve <model> --tp_size 2 --backend pytorch --max_batch_size 16 --max_num_tokens 8192 --max_seq_len 131072 --trust_remote_code --tool_parser qwen3_coder --reasoning_parser nemotron-v3 --extra_llm_api_options nemotron-tp2.yaml`
- Extra options: kv_cache dtype fp8, enable_chunked_prefill true, moe backend CUTEDSL, guided_decoding_backend xgrammar
- Requests: /v1/chat/completions, stream=true, max_tokens 1500, `chat_template_kwargs: {"enable_thinking": true}`

## Tool schema (the no-arg tool)
```json
{"type":"function","function":{"name":"run_tests","description":"Run the test suite, optionally filtered",
 "parameters":{"type":"object","properties":{"pattern":{"type":"string"}},"required":[]}}}
```
Also offered in the same request: read_file(path), write_file(path, content), search_code(query).

## Prompt pattern
System: "You are a coding agent. Use the provided tools to inspect and modify the repository. When done, reply with a short summary."
User (one of): "The function parse_config in src/config.py crashes on empty files. Find and fix it, then make sure tests pass." / "Add input validation to src/api/handlers.py so negative quantities are rejected; update tests." / "tests/test_cache.py::test_expiry is flaky. Investigate and fix the root cause."
The agent loops up to 5 turns, appending each assistant tool_calls message plus a role=tool result. Bad calls occur mostly at turns 4-5, often as the second parallel call (tool_calls[1]).

## Repro
1. Serve as above; run several concurrent multi-turn coding-agent loops with the tools and prompt above.
2. Inspect each response's accumulated `tool_calls[i].function.arguments`: occasionally `name="run_tests", arguments=""`.
3. Append that assistant message to history and request the next turn: HTTP 400 "tool_calls[i].function.arguments must be valid JSON."
4. Minimal server-side check (no generation needed), history containing a run_tests call:
   - `arguments: ""` -> 400 "must be valid JSON"
   - `arguments: "{}"` -> 200
   - `arguments: "\"{}\""` or `"[]"` -> 400 "must be a JSON object"

## Expected vs actual
- Expected: no-argument tool calls are emitted as `arguments: "{}"`, or the server accepts/normalizes `""` in history.
- Actual: `arguments: ""` is emitted and then rejected by the server on the next turn.

## Observed rates (20-minute mixed load, 10 concurrent agents)
- Without a workaround: 5 of 559 requests (0.9%) failed with this 400.
- With a client-side strict `json.loads(arguments)` check plus retry (discard bad response, re-request the same turn at temperature 0.3): 11 bad calls caught out of 689 tool calls, all `run_tests` with `arguments=""`, all fixed on the first retry; 0 of 527 requests failed.

## Workaround
Client-side: replace `""` with `"{}"` before appending to history, or discard and retry.

## Suggested fixes
1. Tool parser (`qwen3_coder` path): emit `"{}"` when a call has no parameters.
2. Server request validation: accept `""` as `{}` for tool_calls arguments in history, consistent with what the server itself emits.
3. Optionally constrain tool-call argument generation (e.g. xgrammar JSON schema) so arguments are always a JSON object.

items.title: [QST] SM120 FP8 MMA with FP32 accumulate, plain form against block-scaled form with unit scales
items.author: emre570
items.body_excerpt:
**What is your question?**

On an RTX 5080, the plain FP8 MMA with FP32 accumulate runs at half the rate of the block-scaled FP8 MMA with FP32 accumulate. When all scale bytes are `0x7F` (UE8M0 1.0), the two forms give equal bits.

My FP8 attention kernel in CuTe DSL used `MmaFP8Op`. I changed it to `MmaMXF8Op` with constant unit scales and no other change. The kernel time went from 123.6 ms to 83.6 ms and the output is byte-equal (sgl-project/sglang#43390). So a user can do this today. My question is about the default.

1. Is there a reason to keep the plain form for E4M3 x E4M3 with FP32 accumulate on SM120?
2. If there is no reason, do you want `MmaFP8Op` and `rr_op_selector_sm120` to emit the block-scaled form with unit scales for this case? I can send a PR.

### Related report

The same behavior is reported in flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#5963 for the FlashInfer SM120 FP8 attention kernel, with RTX 5090 numbers and a bit-identity check. That issue also points to the MXFP8 attention work in flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#3628 and flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#4149. The numbers below add an RTX 5080 and a CUTLASS GEMM measurement to that report.

### Scope

E4M3 x E4M3, FP32 accumulate, one RTX 5080 (driver 595.99.02, CUDA 13.3, CUTLASS `ffa119a12`). I did not measure other types or other cards.

### Raw MMA rate

Independent MMA chains, no memory access, 84 SMs. The rate is the same from 4 to 32 warps per SM.

| instruction | TFLOP/s |
|---|---:|
| `kind::f8f6f4.m16n8k32 ... f32.e4m3.e4m3.f32` | 246 |
| `kind::mxf8f6f4.block_scale.scale_vec::1X.m16n8k32 ... f32.e4m3.e4m3.f32.ue8m0` | 489 |

### Bit equality

- Random finite inputs. 0 of 704,643,072 accumulator registers differ.
- Negative control with scale 2.0. 704,643,071 registers differ.
- Edge cases (subnormal, ±448, NaN bytes, accumulator start at zero, FLT_MAX, subnormal, infinity, NaN). 30 classes, 176,160,768 registers each, 0 bits differ.

### CUTLASS GEMM

I used the SM120 `CollectiveBuilder` with `OpClassTensorOp`, pingpong schedule, tile 128x128x128, FP32 output. Then I changed only the instruction in `SM120_16x8x32_TN<float_e4m3_t, float_e4m3_t, float>` to the block-scaled form. The scale `0x7F7F7F7F` stays in a register. There is no scale factor tensor and no additional load. The patch is 34 lines.

I measured 30 shapes from real models. All 30 give 0 different output words. Five examples:

| shape source | M x N x K | plain | patched | speedup |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Wan 2.2 14B, `to_q` | 32760 x 5120 x 5120 | 236.1 | 398.6 | 1.69x |
| Llama 3.3 70B, MLP up | 4096 x 28672 x 8192 | 234.7 | 398.1 | 1.70x |
| FLUX.1-dev, FFN up | 4608 x 12288 x 3072 | 231.8 | 393.3 | 1.70x |
| MiniMax-H3, FFN up | 30272 x 14336 x 5376 | 234.6 | 363.5 | 1.55x |
| Gemma 3 27B, MLP up | 128 x 21504 x 5376 | 195.8 | 203.4 | 1.04x |

TFLOP/s. The speedup is 1.55x to 1.72x for the 22 shapes with M of 4096 or more. It is 1.04x to 1.82x for the 8 shapes with M = 128, where the low end is DRAM-bound.

Nsight Compute on the stock plain kernel shows the tensor pipe 96% busy. The MMA instruction rate is 47.9% of the peak.

One caution. These numbers use `max_swizzle_size = 8`. With the default of 1, three large shapes become DRAM-bound and the patched kernel is slower than the plain kernel (0.88x). I can open a different issue for that with the data.

### Where the plain form is used

- CuTe DSL `MmaFP8Op`
- `rr_op_selector_sm120` in `sm120_mma_builder.inl`, `sm120_array_mma_builder.inl` and `sm120_blockwise_mma_builder.inl`

cuBLASLt on the same card uses `QMMA.SF.16832.F32.E4M3.E4M3.E8` in its FP8 GEMM kernel and no plain `QMMA`.

I can share the benchmark source, the patch and the raw results if they are useful.

items.title: [BUG] sm120 GEMM hangs when K = 0 (grouped and non-grouped) after can_implement(), initialize() and run() return success
items.author: vera-rubin
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

On sm120, a CUTLASS 3.x GEMM with K = 0 passes `can_implement()`, and `initialize()` and `run()` return `kSuccess` in the tested release builds. The records show zero-K kernels not completing within 10, 15 or 60 seconds.

- **Grouped GEMM, where K = 0 is documented as supported.** With the sm120 ptr-array kernel, the recorded K = {128, 0, 256, 0} and {0, 0, 0, 0} groups do not complete within the recorded timeouts, while {128, 128, 128, 128} and {256, 512} pass. The mainloop source indicates that one K = 0 group is sufficient. CHANGELOG 4.3.0 says ([CHANGELOG.md L715](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/CHANGELOG.md?plain=1#L715)):

  > Enable GEMM_K = 0 in grouped gemm.

  The same case was fixed for Hopper in #2547 and for sm100 grouped GEMM in #2746.
- **Non-grouped GEMM, a validation gap.** The docs don't say whether K = 0 is supported, and a debug build stops at `assert(gmem_prob_shape[0] >= 1)` in `make_tma_copy_desc` ([copy_traits_sm90_tma.hpp L957](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cute/atom/copy_traits_sm90_tma.hpp#L957)). A release build (`-DNDEBUG`, as the examples use) prints `Error: Failed to initialize the TMA descriptor 1` to stderr, `initialize()` still returns `kSuccess`, and the launched kernel does not complete before the recorded timeout. With M = 0 or N = 0, the same kernel's `run()` returns `Error Internal` instead. Upstream examples 79a (NVFP4) and 79c (MXFP8 x MXFP6) time out at `--k=0`. Our own tests time out the same way with FP8 (cooperative and pingpong) and NVFP4 cooperative kernels at 128x128, and with FP8 at 300x392 with L = 2 and with beta = 0. They use real (non-null) A/B buffers.

A caller whose K can be 0 at run time (for example a weight-gradient GEMM for an MoE expert that received no tokens) is an illustrative scenario. This makes reachability plausible, not demonstrated for a deployed SM120 framework, product, or protected workload.

The submitted computation does not complete within the recorded timeout. Software waiting for it can lose availability; recovery and impact on other GPU users were not assessed. No confidentiality or integrity failure was demonstrated.

**Cause (our reading):**

1. The producer issues TMA loads only inside `for ( ; k_tile_count > 0; --k_tile_count)` ([sm120_mma_tma.hpp L400](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm120_mma_tma.hpp#L400), [sm120_blockscaled_mma_tma.hpp L665](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm120_blockscaled_mma_tma.hpp#L665)), so at K = 0 it loads nothing.
2. The consumer `mma()` clears the accumulators and then calls `pipeline.consumer_wait(smem_pipe_read)` unconditionally ([sm120_mma_tma.hpp L526](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm120_mma_tma.hpp#L526), [sm120_blockscaled_mma_tma.hpp L848](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm120_blockscaled_mma_tma.hpp#L848)). No TMA transaction ever completes that barrier. The array mainloops have the same first wait ([sm120_mma_array_tma.hpp L516](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm120_mma_array_tma.hpp#L516), [sm120_blockscaled_mma_array_tma.hpp L934](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm120_blockscaled_mma_array_tma.hpp#L934)).
3. The collectives' `can_implement()` checks only TMA alignment ([sm120_mma_tma.hpp L278](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm120_mma_tma.hpp#L278), [sm120_blockscaled_mma_tma.hpp L399](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm120_blockscaled_mma_tma.hpp#L399)). items.title: Expert Parallelism (EP) roadmap for SM12x b12x MoE kernel (b12x_fused_moe / B12xMoEWrapper)
items.author: ItamarTerem
items.body_excerpt:
Hi flashinfer team,
We're deploying a large MoE model (384 experts, top_k=8) on 8x RTX PRO 6000 (SM120/Blackwell workstation) using the b12x_fused_moe CuteDSL kernel via TensorRT-LLM's pytorch backend, and have hit the Expert Parallelism restriction:

b12x_fused_moe does not yet support Expert Parallelism
(num_local_experts={X} != num_experts={Y}).
Use a different MoE backend for EP configurations.

This comes from the explicit guard in flashinfer/fused_moe/cute_dsl/b12x_moe.py (both in the free function b12x_fused_moe and in B12xMoEWrapper.__init__), confirmed in flashinfer version 0.6.12.
Context on why this matters for us specifically: without EP, every GPU must retain workspace/routing capacity sized for the full state_E (all 384 experts), even though tensor parallelism already shards each expert's weights across GPUs. This is a meaningful, measured memory cost — in our case, the dynamic workspace's packed_input buffer alone accounts for roughly 7–11GB/GPU across a 60-MoE-layer model, purely from having to size for the worst-case "all experts active" scenario rather than a num_experts/ep_size subset.

What we're asking:

1. Is EP support for the SM12x b12x kernel family (static/dynamic/micro backends) on the roadmap, even at a preliminary stage?
2. Is there a rough timeline or tracking issue we could follow?
3. Are there known architectural blockers specific to SM120 (vs. SM100/SM103, where other kernels like MegaMoE already support EP) that make this a harder problem here?

We also note that vLLM's FlashInferB12xExperts (_supports_parallel_config) explicitly declines to use this backend when EP is requested, for the same underlying reason — so this appears to be a shared, cross-framework limitation rather than something specific to our integration.
Happy to provide more detail on our exact shapes/config if useful. Thanks for your work on this — the b12x kernel has otherwise been the only correctness-verified MoE path we've found for SM120 (CUTLASS produces silently incorrect output on this architecture in our testing).

items.title: [Core/Auth] Enable token authentication by default for all clusters in Ray 2.61
items.author: MortalHappiness
items.body_excerpt:
Since Ray 2.59, token authentication is on by default only for local clusters. Every other cluster (started by hand, by `ray up` and the autoscaler, by KubeRay, or by the Anyscale platform) still runs with auth disabled, so anyone who can reach its ports can run arbitrary code. Ray 2.61 makes token auth the default for every cluster. `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` stays the opt-out.

Goals:

- Every newly started cluster, local or remote, has token auth on unless the user sets `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled`.
- Local development stays zero-config, and every tool in this repo works with auth on.
- The local-cluster special cases are deleted, with no dead branches left.

Design:

- `AUTH_MODE` defaults to `"token"` in `src/ray/common/ray_config_def.h`. The local-cluster special cases added in #64755, #66467 and #66778 are deleted, since every path is already in token mode.
- One place creates the token: `Node(head=True)`. Connecting nodes and clients never create one; without a token they fail fast with an error that names `ray get-auth-token` and the `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` opt-out.
- The token never goes on a command line. `ray up` ships it to the head node as a file mount, the head ships it to the worker nodes it launches, and `image_uri`/`container` workers get it as a read-only file mount.
- A client in token mode talking to a cluster that opted out gets an error instead of silent success. gRPC servers in disabled mode reject requests that carry a token. HTTP clients check `GET /api/authentication_mode` instead, because reverse proxies in front of a disabled dashboard can send their own `Authorization` header (the former `kuberay-auth.md` guide set one up with kube-rbac-proxy; also ray-project/kuberay#1824, #42606).
- Ray's Prometheus metrics endpoints (nodes, autoscaler, dashboard head) require the token when auth is on. Ray's own Prometheus reads it from `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN_PATH` or `~/.ray/auth_token`; Ray writes no new copy of the token.


How users use it in 2.61. Every sub-issue PR must keep these flows working as shown:

1. Local development, no setup. The head creates `~/.ray/auth_token`, and everything in the same HOME reads it.

```bash
ray start --head
ray start --address=127.0.0.1:6379   # a second node on the same machine
python -c "import ray; ray.init()"   # a driver
```

A bare `ray.init()` needs no setup: it connects to the running local cluster if there is one, and otherwise starts a new one.

2. A cluster built by hand across machines. The token file must be copied from the head to each machine; the token never goes on a command line.

```bash
# head machine
ray start --head
# worker machine, after the head's ~/.ray/auth_token is copied here
ray start --address=<head-ip>:6379
```

Without the copy, `ray start --address` fails at once with an error that says to run `ray get-auth-token` on the head and copy the token.

3. `ray up`. No token steps: `ray up` creates the token on the operator's machine if needed and ships it to the head node. The head ships it to every worker node it launches, including ones the autoscaler adds later.

```bash
ray up cluster.yaml
ray dashboard cluster.yaml &
ray job submit --address http://127.0.0.1:8265 -- python script.py
```

4. A client on another machine. Clients on the head machine, or on the machine that ran `ray up`, already have the token. Any other machine needs the token file copied to it.

```bash
# after the head's ~/.ray/auth_token is copied to this machine
ray job submit --address http://<head-ip>:8265 -- python script.py
```

`RAY_AUTH_TOKEN_PATH` is only needed when the token file lives somewhere other than `~/.ray/auth_token`.

5. Opting out. Every node and every client sets `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled`. The head logs a warning that auth is disabled.

```bash
RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled ray start --head
RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled ray start --address=<head-ip>:6379
RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled ray job submit --address http://<head-ip>:8265 -- python script.py
```

A node or client that leaves out `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` fails with an error telling it to set it: AuthModeMismatch if it has a token, the missing-token error if it doesn't. For `ray up`, put `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` in the cluster YAML's start commands.

6. Mismatches never fall back to auth off. A worker or client with no token, a different token, or a different auth mode than the head fails right away with an error that names the fix. It does not hang or connect without auth.

7. Prometheus scraping. `ray metrics launch-prometheus` works with no change when the token is in `~/.ray/auth_token` or `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN_PATH` is set in its shell. With only `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN`, it fails with an error saying to use a file. An external Prometheus adds the token to each scrape job that targets Ray, with the token file copied to the Prometheus host:

```yaml
authorization:
  type: Bearer
  credentials_file: /path/to/auth_token
```

Without it, the Prometheus Targets page shows Ray targets down with 401; with a wrong token, 403. With `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled`, every scraper works as today.

Rules every sub-issue PR must keep:

- Auth is on unless `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` is set. No code decides auth on or off from whether a cluster is local, new, or started by a particular entry point.
- A head node started with `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` logs a warning once, from `Node(head=True)`, saying auth is disabled and anyone who can reach the cluster's ports can run code. Worker nodes, drivers and clients don't warn.
- Only a head node (`Node(head=True)`) creates a token. Worker nodes, drivers, `ray://` clients, the CLI and the SDKs never create one, because a token made on a client can't match the cluster's. The one exception is `ray up`, which creates the cluster and ships its token to the head node, which ships it to the worker nodes it launches.
- Token creation is atomic and never overwrites a non-empty token file. When several processes create the token at once in one HOME (a head start, or `ray up` on the operato

In the VM deployment guide, note that existing `ray up` clusters update their worker nodes once after upgrading to a Ray version with the auth token file mount (#67050): each worker reruns its setup commands and restarts Ray, and in Docker mode its container restarts. Instances aren't relaunched.

Also document metrics scraping in `doc/source/cluster/metrics.md`: how an external Prometheus sends the token (`authorization` with `credentials_file`), and that `ray metrics launch-prometheus` needs the token in a file.

Also say in the docs and the release notes that an auth rejection now raises `AuthenticationError` at once, where `ray.init(address=...)` used to raise `ConnectionError` after retrying. `AuthenticationError` subclasses `ConnectionError`, so existing handlers still catch it.

items.title: [Core] Metrics endpoints listen on IPv4 only, so IPv6-only nodes can't be scraped
items.author: MortalHappiness
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

Ray's Prometheus metrics servers bind to IPv4 addresses only, unless the node IP is localhost. On an IPv6-only node, Prometheus can't reach the node, dashboard or autoscaler metrics endpoints. I expected them to listen on `::` on IPv6 hosts, the way `get_all_interfaces_ip()` already does.

The affected servers:

- Dashboard head ([`head.py#L362`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/f178b1887d2f9bb43a323678dc54c14aae7378be/python/ray/dashboard/head.py#L362)) and autoscaler v1 ([`monitor.py#L207`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/f178b1887d2f9bb43a323678dc54c14aae7378be/python/ray/autoscaler/_private/monitor.py#L207)) and v2 ([`v2/monitor.py#L130`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/f178b1887d2f9bb43a323678dc54c14aae7378be/python/ray/autoscaler/v2/monitor.py#L130)) call `prometheus_client.start_http_server` and pass `addr` only when the node IP is localhost. Otherwise `prometheus_client` defaults to `0.0.0.0`, which accepts IPv4 only.
- The node metrics exporter passes `address=""` for non-localhost nodes ([`reporter_agent.py#L560`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/f178b1887d2f9bb43a323678dc54c14aae7378be/python/ray/dashboard/modules/reporter/reporter_agent.py#L560)) to `wsgiref.simple_server.make_server` ([`prometheus_exporter.py#L329`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/f178b1887d2f9bb43a323678dc54c14aae7378be/python/ray/_private/prometheus_exporter.py#L329)), whose default server class is `AF_INET`. It also can't bind `::1` at all: `make_server("::1", ...)` raises `gaierror: [Errno -9] Address family for hostname not supported`. So on a host where `localhost` resolves only to `::1`, the exporter should fail to start.

I measured the bind behavior directly on a dual-stack Linux host, but haven't reproduced it on an IPv6-only Ray cluster.

Likely fix: bind to `get_all_interfaces_ip()` ([`network_util.cc#L284`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/f178b1887d2f9bb43a323678dc54c14aae7378be/src/ray/util/network_util.cc#L284)), which returns `::` on IPv6 hosts, and give the exporter's server an address family that matches the bind address.

### Reproduction script

```python
import socket, threading, requests
import prometheus_client
from prometheus_client import CollectorRegistry, make_wsgi_app
from wsgiref.simple_server import make_server

def free_port():
    with socket.socket(socket.AF_INET6) as s:
        s.bind(("", 0))
        return s.getsockname()[1]

def reach(port):
    out = []
    for host in ("127.0.0.1", "[::1]"):
        try:
            out.append(requests.get(f"http://{host}:{port}/metrics", timeout=2).status_code)
        except requests.exceptions.ConnectionError:
            out.append("refused")
    return out

for addr in ("0.0.0.0", "::"):
    p = free_port()
    prometheus_client.start_http_server(port=p, addr=addr, registry=CollectorRegistry())
    print(f"start_http_server addr={addr!r}:", reach(p))

p = free_port()
httpd = make_server("", p, make_wsgi_app())
threading.Thread(target=httpd.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()
print('make_server address="":', reach(p))

make_server("::1", free_port(), make_wsgi_app())  # raises socket.gaierror
```

Output:

```
start_http_server addr='0.0.0.0': [200, 'refused']
start_http_server addr='::': [200, 200]
make_server address="": [200, 'refused']
socket.gaierror: [Errno -9] Address family for hostname not supported
```

### Versions / Dependencies

Ray master at f178b1887d2f9bb43a323678dc54c14aae7378be, prometheus_client 0.25.0, Python 3.12, Linux.

items.title: [Gateway] Gate raw request body logging behind verbose log levels
items.author: googs1025
items.body_excerpt:
Parent issue: #2989

## Problem

Several Gateway validators log the complete request body when JSON parsing fails. Other request-processing logs include parsed prompts or messages at `V(4)`.

These diagnostics are useful, but request bodies can contain user prompts, tool arguments, conversation history, or large encoded data. Request contents should not appear at normal production log levels.

## Proposed behavior

At normal log levels, parsing failures should record only:

- request ID;
- endpoint;
- sanitized parse reason;
- request body size.

Raw JSON content may be logged only at `klog.V(6)`.

Verbose logging must:

- include at most 4 KiB of the request body;
- record whether the value was truncated;
- never log multipart file contents, filenames, or form values;
- apply the same policy to parsed prompt or message fields;
- require no new environment variable.

Example normal log:

```go
klog.ErrorS(nil, "error to unmarshal request",
    "requestID", requestID,
    "endpoint", requestPath,
    "reason", jsonParseReason(err),
    "requestBodyBytes", len(requestBody))
```

Example verbose diagnostic:

```go
if klog.V(6).Enabled() {
    klog.V(6).InfoS("request body parse failure details",
        "requestID", requestID,
        "requestBody", truncateRequestBodyForLog(requestBody, 4096),
        "requestBodyTruncated", len(requestBody) > 4096)
}
```

## Scope

Apply this policy to the Gateway validators for Chat Completions, Responses, Completions, Embeddings, image and video generation, Tokenize, Pooling, Decisions and SystemOne where applicable, and new Score and Audio Speech validators.

Move parsed prompt/message logging from `V(4)` to the same bounded `V(6)` behavior.

## Testing

Cover:

1. Default verbosity: metadata is logged; raw body and prompt are absent.
2. `V(6)`: JSON content is present; values longer than 4 KiB are truncated; truncation is reported.
3. Multipart: file contents, filenames, and form values remain absent at every level.
4. Compatibility: existing HTTP validation responses remain unchanged.

## Non-goals

- Do not completely remove verbose request diagnostics.
- Do not add per-field redaction rules.
- Do not add a request-body logging environment variable.
- Do not log multipart contents at any verbosity.
- Do not change parsing or routing behavior.

## Acceptance criteria

- Raw JSON is absent from normal logs.
- Raw JSON is available only at `V(6)`.
- Verbose bodies are capped at 4 KiB.
- Multipart contents are never logged.
- Parsed prompt/message logging follows the same policy.
- Client-visible behavior remains unchanged.

items.title: [cake deslop] cake_gdn (non-CP) round 2: merge 20 mask-only sm_107a prefill copies, drop dead files, template the 227 host shims
items.author: yyihuang
items.body_excerpt:
**Background.** The Cake non-CP GDN backend (`csrc/gdn/cake`, dating to #4581) serves `gated_delta_rule_decode_pretranspose` / `gated_delta_rule_decode` and `chunk_gated_delta_rule` on sm_100a/sm_103a/sm_107a (B200/B300/R200). For decode, `backend="auto"` tries Cake first and falls back to CuTe on `CakeGDNUnsupportedError`. Prefill reaches Cake only with `backend="cake_gdn"`: `auto` never selects non-CP Cake prefill (`gdn_prefill.py:1687-1710`). The first round, #5816 (closed by #5939, +2,391/−327,042), collapsed 112 constant-clone kernels, merged the SM100/SM103 copies and slimmed the manifest. About 205K lines have come back since 2026-10-06:
- #6131 (+23,736): Qwen3.5 BF16 T=1 bands vec8/vec8occ/vec8r56 and 5 prefill head splits.
- #6238 (+12,393): sm_107a routing and the first sm_107a bodies.
- #6323 (+3,769): FP64-free q-scale sm_107a re-renders and splitv8_tilev32.
- #6478 (+43,008): FP32-state TP2/TP4/TP8 prefill records.
- #6519 (+121,867/−30,022): host-free launch ABI v2. It regenerated every prefill body, which produced the 20 per-arch sm_107a copies and the 227-shim host tree.

The directory is now 315 files / 285,233 lines: 82 `.cu` (209,618), 227 host `.cc` (62,204), and a 12,052-line `manifest.json` with 227 records (84 decode, 143 prefill). On top of that come `csrc/gdn/cake_gdn_common.cuh` (735 lines) and 2 of the 79 shared `csrc/cake_device_helpers` headers. The backend is JIT only, with no AOT entry. The manifest is the only registry, and a record is compiled only when the resolver selects it.

**Findings**
- **Per-arch prefill copies (75,548 lines).** 89 records carry two outputs: an sm_100a+sm_103a body and an sm_107a body.
  - In 20 of the 26 distinct pairs, the two bodies are the same size, export the same `__global__` symbol and differ only in 17–18 smem-descriptor lines: `(addr >> 4) & 0x3FFF` vs `& 0x7FFF`. Example: `cake_gdn_prefill_initial_b04a60d33f1a.cu` vs `cake_gdn_prefill_initial_3c4e0ac632be.cu`, 3,658 lines each. All 20 were created by #6519.
  - The other 6 pairs are old- vs new-generation decode bodies (59–141 normalised diff lines), not per-arch copies.
  - The 4 three-arch single-output prefill bodies (e.g. `cake_gdn_prefill_dvsplit_685c10d5e83a.cu`) guard the mask with the opposite polarity (`#if __CUDA_ARCH__ == 1030` → 0x3FFF, else 0x7FFF). So sm_100a already runs 0x7FFF there, and the two masks may not be SASS-distinct.
- **Orphan record (936 lines).** `decode_gdn_decode_pretranspose_mtp_t4_bf16state_wide128_843a6f975145` (H16/HV32, T_STEPS=1, TILE_V_WIDE=32) consists of manifest lines 309–354, `cuda/cake_gdn_decode_pretranspose_mtp_t4_bf16state_wide128_ad39ffcf85b6.cu` and `host/cake_gdn_decode_pretranspose_mtp_t4_bf16state_wide128_843a6f975145.cc`. The resolver never asks for this combination:
  - The BF16 T=1 path (`cake_gdn.py:1073-1089`) passes TILE_V_WIDE from `cake_gdn_bf16_t1_route`, and every band table ends with `(None, 'wide', 128)`.
  - The T>1 path passes T_STEPS ≥ 2.

  The #6131 band tables orphaned it. Overall, 226/227 records are selectable, and 43 of the 514 (record, arch) listings are never selected.
- **Dead headers and helpers.**
  - `cuda/gdn_prefill_generated.cuh` (729 lines) has had 0 includers since #6519 (26 before). Its 61 functions are byte-identical to `cake_gdn_common.cuh`, but it is still listed in the manifest `cuda_headers`, so its sha256 enters every compile digest, and README.md:44 still names it.
  - `cake_gdn_host_common.cuh` (50 lines, added by #6131) has 0 includers; the shims use `host/cake_gdn_host_common.h`.
  - Five helpers from #6323/#6478 are referenced nowhere (138 lines): `cake_mul_f32x2_e8f6ec24fd2e329c`, `cake_sub_f32x2_04ff45cfde4607c2`, `cake_sub_f32x2_inplace_e1d43df9dc0e8fb1`, `cake_tma_5d_gmem2smem_71f59b0935752442` and `cake_tmem_ld_x32_a8bcbefdae2ace77` (`.cuh`).
  - The 14 bodies that include `csrc/gdn/cake_gdn_common.cuh` use only `approx_rcp`, `fma_f32x2_rn_ftz` and `make_warp_uniform`. The other 59 of its 62 device functions (~603 lines) are never called.
- **Constant clones (4 decode bodies, 2,892 lines).** Each pair below differs only in one constant and the kernel symbol:

  | Clone | Kept body | Difference |
  |---|---|---|
  | `cake_gdn_23b1dd923d28be021748_99d46896cfe6.cu` | `cake_gdn_eaf1e8b244cd4ba498be_7f3845a33c38.cu` | `TILE_V_WIDE` 64 vs 32 |

  | `cake_gdn_3c946c068a265505fc87_d757178e68b0.cu` (vec8occ) | `dbf9…` (vec8) | `__launch_bounds__` form |

- **Shadowed listings.**

items.title: [cake deslop] cake_moe_grouped_gemm: fold fp32 dtype clones, hoist shared helpers, drop dead host code (-3.8K lines); A/B k512/tail routes
items.author: yyihuang
items.body_excerpt:
**Background.** `flashinfer/experimental/cake_moe_grouped_gemm` is the Cake-generated bf16 MoE grouped GEMM (fwd, dgrad, wgrad; wgrad can also write fp32) for sm_100a, sm_103a and sm_107a. It is reached through:
- `grouped_gemm_{fwd,dgrad,wgrad}` and `prepare_grouped_gemm_*` / `GroupedGemmLaunch`;
- the `cake_grouped_mm` autograd function, with custom ops `flashinfer::cake_moe_grouped_gemm_{fwd,dgrad,wgrad}`;
- fwd only, through `grouped_mm_bf16(..., backend="cake")` (`flashinfer/grouped_mm/core.py` 147-154).

It reads no env vars and is never picked automatically; it is JIT-only, with no `flashinfer/aot.py` entry. #5751 added it as 58 files / 31,041 lines, including per-arch copies. No #5768 sub-issue covers this family yet. #6017 (part of #5768) re-exported it with deduplicated sources and thin launchers, leaving 22 files / 8,646 lines: it removed the per-arch copies and the k256/k512 tail-reduce constant clones and replaced `MODULES` with `PROGRAMS`/`ROUTES`, but kept the fp32 output-dtype clones. Since then:
- #6572 (fix for #6570) added a tensor-map slot ring to the 4 wgrad kernels (+34 net lines each);
- #6584 (#6553 steps 2-4) added 977 lines of loader infrastructure (`build.json` 580, `cake_build.py` 324, `csrc/cake_ffi_checks.h` 73);
- #6610 added `tests/experimental/test_cake_moe_grouped_gemm_api.py`.

At main @ 3184bbea the package is 26 files / 9,662 lines (16 `.cu` = 6,831; 5 `.py` = 2,006; `build.json` 580). Tests add 530 lines and the benchmark 325.

**Findings**
- **Every compiled source is reachable.** The 26 `build.json` entries (sm_100a 10, sm_103a 10, sm_107a 6) name all 16 `.cu` files (8 kernel/binding pairs). Dispatch goes `cake_jit.PROGRAMS` (8) → `ROUTES` (6) → `cake_build.load_library(f"{library}{tag}_{arch}")`, and every route can be called from a public API. No per-arch copies remain (each main kernel has one `#if __CUDA_ARCH__ == 1000`), and no PTX/cubin is tracked. Nothing can be deleted just because it is unreachable.
- **fp32 output-dtype clones (2,619 lines).** 05498a (tail-reduce), 7ac85a (wgrad k256) and d77aff (wgrad k512) differ from their bf16 twins bc774d, ed9a74 and 611af0 only in the `C` pointer type and the epilogue store (`float4` vs `__floats2bfloat162_rn` + `st.global.v8.b32`).
  - With hash-named symbols normalised, the kernel diffs are 37 lines / 2 hunks, 72 / 3 and 72 / 3. Each binding differs in 12 lines / 6 hunks: the `kDLFloat32` check, the pointer cast and the error text.
  - The tail-reduce kernels already get `-DWGRAD_TILE` from `build.json` `nvcc_flags`, so an output-dtype define can use the same mechanism.
- **Shared kernel preamble and binding boilerplate (~1,080 lines).**
  - Kernels: 105 preamble lines are verbatim in all 6 main kernels and 46 in all 8. One header that keeps the per-kernel `#define`s saves ~630 lines.
  - Bindings: they repeat `EncodeTma_A` (2 variants × 51 lines), `EncodeTma_B` (63/51/51) and `CakeSetMaxDynamicSmem` (19 identical lines × 6), about 450 lines at a conservative estimate.
  - The two tail kernels define `CakeTensorMap64`, `CUtensorMap`, `NUM_MAIN_STAGES`, `BLOCK_M` and `cta_rank` and include `cuda_fp8.h`, but never use them.
- **Dead host code and unread registry fields (134 lines).**
  - `cake_backend.py` (25 lines): `_Launch.__call__` (337-338), `.stage`/`.module`, `GroupedGemmLaunch.stage_launchers` (378-389) and `.stage_modules` (391-393). These are dead because `launch()` calls `item.entry(*item.arguments)` directly. `GroupedGemmLaunch.stages` is public (in `__all__` and the docstring) but nothing in the repo reads it.
  - `cake_jit.py` (8 lines): `specs_for_arch` and `registered_arches`. Every caller targets another package's copy.
  - Exporter-written keys that nothing reads (87 lines): `ROUTES[*]['host_plan']` (60 lines), `public_helper`, `out_dtype`, `tile_k`, `PROGRAMS[*]['kernel']` and `HOST_PLAN_CONSTANTS['block_m']`.
  - Unreachable "registry not filled" scaffolding (14 lines, medium confidence): the `host_plan_constants()` `NotImplementedError` (`cake_backend.py` 72-77), the `not HOST_PLAN_CONSTANTS` guard in `generated_program_available`, the str-key branch of `_cycles_per_step` and the test helper's `_constants()` skip.
- **No GPU test launches 18 of the 26 builds.**
  - k512 (611af0/d77aff, 8 builds): `wgrad_tile_k` (`cake_backend.py` 134-146) picks them only when `K % 512 == 0`, the arch is in `k512_archs` (sm_100a, sm_103a) and the average is at least 20,480 rows/group.
  - Split-K tail (05498a/bc774d, 10 builds): runs only when `plan_wgrad` finds `num_tail != 0` and `wgrad_tail_plan` picks splits > 1.
  - Every GPU wgrad test shape averages at most 6,145 rows/group. Planner arithmetic at 148/160/212 SMs gives splits = 1 for all of them; this has not been observed on a GPU. `test_wgrad_long_reduction_selects_a_valid_tile` asserts only `tile_k in (256, 512)`. The CPU `test_plan_invariants` reaches k512 and tail splits inside the planner but never launches a kernel.
  - The benchmark does reach both paths. All 16 E=4 wgrad rows pick k512 on sm_100a/sm_103a. The tail runs on 20, 11 and 17 of the 22 wgrad rows on sm_100a, sm_103a and sm_107a.
  - These programs contain the same tensor-map slot ring that #6570 fixed, with no GPU coverage.
- **Neither path has an A/B measurement.**
  - #5751 justified k512 by wall time measured in isolation. Its interleaved protocol showed ~6% more cycles than the 256×256 tile on the E8-E32 rows, and the lowest row scored 0.971. #5751 says the no-tail arm was "not expressible under the frozen protocol".
  - The planner constants (`cake_jit.py` 404-424) come from one design point: the 20,480-row threshold matches the E≤4 GLM-5.2 rows, and the tail cost model assumes 1.8 GHz / 6 TB/s / 5 µs, B200-class figures. They apply unchanged to sm_103a and sm_107a, so the split count varies with SM count alone (`wgrad_down_e4`, N=6144, K=2048: 5 / 1 / 4 splits at 148 / 160 / 212 SMs).
- **Host path.**
  - Each wgrad prepare allocates a slot ring (340,992 B at grid 1

items.title: [Core] RESCHEDULING placement group retry storm saturates the GCS main thread
items.author: dancingactor
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

If scheduling a placement group in the `RESCHEDULING` state fails, `GcsPlacementGroupManager` keeps retrying scheduling it(~90k retry/s), which saturates the GCS main thread. Every retry is guaranteed to fail the same way until the next resource sync update arrives, so retrying before then is unnecessary and only blocks the GCS main thread.

Here is the issue in detail:

- Placement group P is already scheduled successfully on nodes A and B, with one bundle on each node.
- Node A dies, so P needs to be rescheduled elsewhere, and P enters the `RESCHEDULING` state.
- `GcsPlacementGroupManager` treats a `RESCHEDULING` placement group as top priority, so it inserts P at the front of the queue.
- The cluster doesn't currently have available resources for P, so `GcsPlacementGroupManager` fails to schedule P.
- `GcsPlacementGroupManager` immediately reinserts P at the front of the queue and retries scheduling it. The cluster resources haven't been updated yet, so it fails again.
- This retry loop keeps running and busy-spins the GCS main thread, starving other tasks. It only stops when a resource sync update finally provides enough available resources for P.

### Proposed Change

To avoid the retry storm, remove the immediate retry. A failed `RESCHEDULING` placement group would then be retried only on `Tick()` and the existing scheduling triggers (a new placement group registered, a node event). This can add a small recovery latency (0–1s), but that's much better than saturating the GCS main thread for a possibly long time.

|                             | Retries while stuck (5s) | GCS CPU | PG Recovery latency |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------ | ------- | ----------------------------- |
| Original (retry storm)      | ~459k                    | 75%     | 0.11s                         |
| **Don't immediately retry** | **5**                    | **1%**  | **0.59–0.94s**                |


### Versions / Dependencies

- Ray: 3.0.0.dev0, built from source at commit a1a2cc64ee

### Reproduction script

``` python
import time

import psutil

import ray
from ray.cluster_utils import Cluster
from ray.util.placement_group import placement_group, placement_group_table

# Head node with 0 CPUs and two 1-CPU workers, both filled by a placement group.
cluster = Cluster(initialize_head=True, head_node_args={"num_cpus": 0})
workers = [cluster.add_node(num_cpus=1) for _ in range(2)]
ray.init(address=cluster.address)
pg_a = placement_group([{"CPU": 1}])
pg_b = placement_group([{"CPU": 1}])
ray.get([pg_a.ready(), pg_b.ready()])

# Remove pg_a's node. pg_a becomes RESCHEDULING: it's feasible, but pg_b holds the
# only remaining CPU.
node_id = placement_group_table(pg_a)["bundles_to_node_id"][0]
cluster.remove_node(next(w for w in workers if w.node_id == node_id))
while placement_group_table(pg_a)["state"] != "RESCHEDULING":
    time.sleep(0.1)
time.sleep(1)

# Nothing in the cluster changes from here on.
gcs = psutil.Process(cluster.head_node.all_processes["gcs_server"][0].process.pid)
start = placement_group_table(pg_a)["stats"]["scheduling_attempt"]
gcs.cpu_percent()
time.sleep(5)
end = placement_group_table(pg_a)["stats"]["scheduling_attempt"]
print(f"pg_a scheduling attempts in 5s: {end - start}, GCS CPU: {gcs.cpu_percent():.0f}%")
```

After discussing with the core team in the Ray Core community sync, we concluded that "retry when a resource sync update arrives" adds too much code complexity. Instead, we'll just remove the immediate retry. It's the smallest change (2 lines), and it only adds a small PG recovery latency (0–1s), since the retry then depends on `Tick()` and the existing scheduling triggers (a new PG registered, a node event).

I'll implement the immediate retry removal. It has a significant benefit:

| Original (retry storm)      | ~459k                    | 75%     | 0.11s                         |

items.title: [Performance]: trtllm-gen fmhaReductionKernel walks all KV partials serially per thread; low-batch decode pays a fixed ~6-13 us per call
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

Multi-CTA-KV generation kernels with a separate reduction (`KeepsMmaAbForGeneration` kernels with gmem reduction) finish with `fmhaReductionKernel` (`cpp/tensorrt_llm/kernels/trtllmGenKernels/fmha/fmhaReduction.cu`). At low batch its grid is tiny: for Kimi K3 MLA decode at batch 1, it is 8 x 2 CTAs for the target model and 2 x 4 for the drafter. Each thread then merges all `numCtasKv` partials of its row one after another. The kernel costs about 6.5 us per call at 2K context and 13.5 us at 128K with 64 KV splits, which is a large share of the attention time at batch 1. #15009 saw the same thing on B300 ("the only remaining gap is the generic fmhaReductionKernel, ~9.2 us flat").

Proposal: an extra template parameter `KvSplit`. The 512 threads of a CTA form `KvSplit` groups. Group g merges partials g, g + KvSplit, ... of the same rows (the same online-softmax update as today), and group 0 then merges the per-group (max, sum, O) through shared memory. Each CTA covers `1/KvSplit` of the rows, so the grid grows by `KvSplit` within the existing `2 x SMs` CTA budget, and every thread walks `KvSplit` times fewer partials. `KvSplit = 1` keeps the current kernel.

Measured on SM107 with the grouped Q64 MLA generation kernels (Kimi K3 shapes, 32 tokens per page, causal, up to 64 KV splits), p50 us per MLA call including the reduction, batch 1:

| config | 2K | 8K | 32K | 128K |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| target, 16 heads, KvSplit 1 | 14.20 | 24.56 | 29.13 | 55.81 |
| target, 16 heads, KvSplit 4 | 12.01 | 18.02 | 22.70 | 49.81 |
| target, 16 heads, KvSplit 8 | 12.30 | 17.28 | 21.74 | 49.27 |
| target, 16 heads, KvSplit 16 | 13.26 | 17.02 | 21.60 | 49.17 |
| drafter, 8 heads, KvSplit 1 | 12.80 | 22.76 | 26.77 | 50.51 |
| drafter, 8 heads, KvSplit 8 | 11.06 | 15.59 | 19.63 | 44.38 |

Outputs match KvSplit 1 to about 1e-5 in output sum and absolute sum at batch 1, 2 and 4. End to end (Kimi K3 + MTP, 8 GPUs over 2 nodes, single request, two cold starts that agree within 0.04 ms), KvSplit 8 changes the decode step by -0.10 ms at 2K, -0.23 ms at 32K and -0.21 ms at 128K, with unchanged accuracy.

PR to follow. Because I could only measure this on SM107 with the grouped MLA kernels, the PR makes it opt-in (`TLLM_FMHA_REDUCTION_KV_SPLIT`); if someone can check SM100/SM103, a default of 8 (still limited by the CTA budget) looks like the right end state.

items.title: [Serve] [RFC] Computed Retry-After for backpressure rejections
items.author: vinay7373
items.body_excerpt:
## Motivation

PR #65193 added `BackpressureConfig`. Deployments can now reject backpressured requests with a 429 and a static `Retry-After` header. Each caller (proxy or `DeploymentHandle`) has its own request queue, and at the time of a backpressure rejection a static `Retry-After` value can be incorrect in both directions. If the queue is deep and the static value is too short, clients retry into another rejection, adding load exactly when the system is trying to shed it. If the queue drains fast and the value is too long, capacity sits idle while clients wait.

This proposal computes the `Retry-After` value from observed load. This makes the header a reliable estimate of when capacity will be available, instead of a number the operator guessed. This was the original shape of the production request behind #65193 and it fits the discussion there about making 429 the default at some point.

No OSS inference server does this today (TGI, Triton, NVIDIA Dynamo and TorchServe all reject without a retry hint). The closest prior art is cloud-side (Azure OpenAI's `retry-after-ms`, AWS's `x-amz-retry-after`) and per-client rate limiters, where the value can be exact because a rate window is a clock. Capacity recovery is not a clock, so here the value is an estimate at any layer.

## Goals

- An opt-in `BackpressureConfig` policy that computes `Retry-After` from load signals the rejecting component already has.
- Keep the rejection path as cheap as it is today. No RPCs, locks or extra work on reject-and-respond.
- Degrade gracefully: computed, else static, else no header. Never fail or delay a rejection.

## Non-goals

- Changing when requests are rejected. Admission control is a separate discussion.
- Guaranteeing admission at the suggested time. The header is a hint, not a reservation.
- Changing the default rejection status code. Tracked separately.
- Implementing any further policy, such as the cluster-informed one (see "Future policies").

## Proposed API

```python
from ray.serve.config import BackpressureConfig

@serve.deployment(
    max_queued_requests=64,
    backpressure_config=BackpressureConfig(
        status_code=429,
        retry_after_policy="queue_drain_rate",   # NEW: "static" (default) | "queue_drain_rate"
        retry_after_s=5,                         # static value; also the fallback for computed policies
    ),
)
```

`retry_after_policy` is a named policy instead of a bare `"auto"` so future strategies can be added without changing what existing configs mean.

## Proposed design

This design adds a new field to `BackpressureConfig` called `retry_after_policy`, and one new policy named `queue_drain_rate` that computes `Retry-After` from the rejecting component's observed queue depth and drain rate.

The overall mechanism has 3 basic aspects: (i) how to compute the `Retry-After` value (what the `queue_drain_rate` policy implements), (ii) where to compute it, and (iii) who stamps the header and emits it to the client.

These boil down to emission and estimation. Emission answers (iii) and is fixed: the rejecting component stamps the header. Estimation covers (i) and (ii): one shared implementation, invoked at the two places Serve rejects today, each feeding its own local signals.

### The `queue_drain_rate` policy (this proposal)

```
retry_after = ceil(observed_queue_depth / drain_rate)
```

- **The numerator is the depth observed at rejection.** It is at least `max_queued_requests`, since a rejection only fires once the queue has reached the cap, and occasionally a little above it: the router's check is not atomic, and replica-rejected requests re-enter the queue behind new arrivals. The raise site already holds this number (it is in the `BackPressureError` message today), so using the observed value costs nothing and is exact.
- **`drain_rate` is the live signal**: how fast the queue empties, updated at the end of every interval as `drain_rate = 0.3 * rate_over_last_interval + 0.7 * previous_drain_rate`. `rate_over_last_interval` is the fresh measurement: requests drained during the interval that just ended. `previous_drain_rate` is this same formula's output from the previous update, so it carries the whole history with older intervals fading out. The 70% weight on the trend keeps lumpy traffic from whipping the value around (completions land in bursts, so a single interval can read 0 or 3x the true rate), and the 30% on the fresh measurement keeps the estimate chasing real load changes within a few intervals. The split, the interval length and the warmup threshold are implementation constants with environment-variable overrides, like Serve's other internal tunables, not new `BackpressureConfig` fields. The update runs on a lightweight background timer in the component's existing metrics machinery (default 1s). An interval with zero completions counts as a real observation when work is in flight, since that is what slow drain looks like, but idle intervals (nothing running or queued) skip the update instead of decaying the rate. The rate counts as warm after a configurable minimum number of counted intervals; until then the fallback applies.
- **Two call sites, one implementation.** On the proxy path the router rejects; its drain rate is its own assignment throughput, from a monotonic counter added at the existing send event (the current per-replica counter is an in-flight gauge, so it can't provide a rate). The rate is fleet-blended: faster replicas take more assignments, so mixed hardware is priced in. On direct ingress the replica rejects; its drain rate is its own completion rate, and its queue is drained only by itself. Same formula, different local inputs, different values, each describing its own queue. A replica's value is a conservative upper bound, since a retry may be re-balanced to a replica that frees up sooner.
- **Clamp to [1, 60] seconds.** Common client SDKs ignore `Retry-After` above 60s.
- **Jitter (for example +/-20%) is applied in the shared heade

comments.author: johntaylor-cell
comments.body:
My main concern is how this RFC and direct-ingress work together.  Serve is moving toward direct-ingress with HAProxy as the default, and on that path the router is no longer the module that rejects the request.  HAProxy will sit between the client and Serve, and it already has retry-after functionality (as does Envoy).  Both implement it very differently from what the RFC proposes.  Their calculation is time-based so it is more exact than the proposed prediction.  It is also per-client, and HAProxy exposes queue-based metrics so the limit can fire only under real back pressure.  I suggest we provide a way to enable that functionality in HAProxy, which Serve already generates config for but does not use today.

If we also want retry-after on the router path (when direct-ingress is disabled), I would try to duplicate HAProxy's time-based functionality, rather than use a forecast. That is a larger change than this RFC scopes, since admission control is listed as a non-goal, but I think it is worth deciding explicitly rather than estimating.

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
Thanks for the review. Breaking it down into where we agree and where we don't.

**Where we agree:**

1. The RFC did not cover the direct-ingress path. That was a real gap and I updated the RFC. Short version: on direct ingress the same policy runs at the replica, using its own queue depth divided by an EWMA of its own completion rate. Same formula, one shared estimator implementation, two call sites. A replica's queue is drained only by itself, so that vantage is even simpler than the router's.

2. Per-client rate limiting at the HAProxy layer is valuable. It answers "this client exceeded its quota", and its Retry-After can be exact because a rate window is a clock. That is complementary to this RFC, which answers "the deployment is out of capacity, here is when to come back". I would support that as a separate proposal and am happy to file it.

**Where we don't agree, and why:**

1. "HAProxy will sit between the client and Serve" as the rejector. Not for backpressure today. On the direct-ingress path the replica rejects the request (see the "Request dropped due to backpressure" emission sites in [replica.py on the ray-2.58.0 tag](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/ray-2.58.0/python/ray/serve/_private/replica.py)). HAProxy passes the replica's response through, and its errorfiles only rewrite HAProxy-generated errors. #65193 shipped 429 + Retry-After on this path, tested with `RAY_SERVE_ENABLE_DIRECT_INGRESS=1`.

2. "Functionality Serve already generates config for but does not use". I checked `haproxy_templates.py`: no stick-tables, no track-sc, no deny rules, no Retry-After anywhere in the generated config. Enabling this would be new work, not switching on something dormant.

3. "Their calculation is time-based so it is more exact than the proposed prediction". I checked the [HAProxy docs](https://www.haproxy.com/documentation/haproxy-configuration-tutorials/security/traffic-policing/) on this. HAProxy's computed Retry-After is `http-after-response set-header Retry-After %[src,table_expire(...)]`: the time until the client's stick-table rate-limit record expires. That is per-client policing, and it is exact because a rate window is deterministic. For capacity overload (server maxconn queue full, `timeout queue` expiring) the docs show no Retry-After computation: that 503 ships without a hint. The queue timer measures elapsed wait, not time until capacity returns. When capacity frees depends on service completions and arrivals, and no layer can know that exactly, including HAProxy, which cannot see how long the inference ahead of a request will take. Any capacity Retry-After is an estimate at every layer. That is why the RFC ships an acceptance criterion and telemetry to measure the estimate, instead of claiming exactness.

Rate limiting and capacity backpressure are different problems. An exact time-based Retry-After exists for the first and cannot exist for the second. This RFC is scoped to the second, now explicitly works on both ingress paths, and leaves room for a HAProxy rate-limiting proposal alongside it.

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
@johntaylor-cell 

My thoughts on your a HA Proxy based admission control and what I see as limitations:

- As you mentioned the HAProxy queue resets on every reload and Serve reloads HAProxy on every replica-set change. So the primary queue evaporates exactly during autoscaling churn (your own finding).
- Composition traffic never passes HAProxy, so the Serve backstop must stay. That means 3 admission systems with 3 threshold vocabularies to keep coherent.
    - Users configuring three queueing layers instead of one: per-server `maxconn` plus timeout queue in HAProxy, `max_queued_requests` at handles, `max_ongoing_requests` at replicas. Three knobs at three levels in different units (connections vs requests, per instance vs per caller vs per replica) that all have to be sized against each other and re-sized as the cluster scales. Mis-size any pair and you get double queueing or shedding while replicas sit idle. That is more error prone, not simpler.
- The default proxy path gets nothing from it.
- Per-deployment BackpressureConfig granularity would have to be re-expressed in generated HAProxy config.
- Moving where queueing happens is an admission-control redesign, which this RFC explicitly scopes out as a non-goal.
- On jittered-static vs computed: 
    - jitter only spreads retries around a center, it cannot make the center reliable. With `retry_after_s` we already ship the option to set a fixed, guessed value at config time, so a jittered constant is not a new proposal, it is [#65193](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/65193) plus jitter. Drain rate moves 10-100x across load regimes, so the constant is wrong exactly when it matters. A 5s center against a 60s real drain means every jittered retry comes back early and gets refused again. Guessing that constant is the problem this RFC exists to remove. So a computed value using drain rate is more reliable. And @suppagoddo 's suggestion for A/B against a jittered-static baseline will show it under real workloads and make this measurable.
