With `retry_after_s` we already ship the option to set a fixed, guessed value at config time, so a jittered constant is not a new proposal, it is [#65193](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/65193) plus jitter. Drain rate moves 10-100x across load regimes, so the constant is wrong exactly when it matters. A 5s center against a 60s real drain means every jittered retry comes back early and gets refused again. Guessing that constant is the problem this RFC exists to remove. So a computed value using drain rate is more reliable. And [@suppagoddo](https://github.com/suppagoddo) 's suggestion for A/B against a jittered-static baseline will show it under real workloads and make this measurable.

I have one last set of comments, but I think I have explored an HAProxy centric solution enough at this point.    A less invasive change as proposed in your RFC is likely the safest approach.  I do have two comments about the estimation calculation as presented below in #6 and #7.
1. The reload is really a gap.  There is no reason to wipe out the HAProxy state unless there is a configuration change that requires such a drastic step.  HAproxy can add/remove servers dynamically of course
2. If HAProxy did perform admission control (set per-server maxconn), composition traffic would become indirectly visible, since it slows the replica and HAProxy's queue fills behind it, at least while the replica holds the overflow rather than fast-rejecting it.
3. Yes, an HAProxy approach doesnt work if there is no HAProxy :slightly_smiling_face: Hopefully that path is rare as direct-ingress will become the default very soon
4. Yes, but entirely doable and not difficult
5. No reason to not explore admission control even though the RFC mentions it as a non-goal.  Seems limiting if we are trying to find best long-term soln
6. The estimator has three inputs and I do not think any of them hold up.  Queue depth is not an observation, a rejection only fires once depth has reached `max_queued_requests`, so it is always the configured cap.  Occupancy is zero for LLM deployments, where `max_ongoing_requests` defaults to a billion.  And I could not find any signal behind the backoff term.  That leaves the drain rate, which the RFC agrees carries the estimate, but the router has no counter for it today and the code that raises the rejection cannot reach the router state it would need.
7. Regarding adding jitter, today's static path has none, `retry_after_s` is emitted verbatim by every path through one helper.  That makes the A/B @suppagoddo suggested a comparison bet

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
@johntaylor-cell took your 6 and 7 into the RFC:

On 6: you are right that queue depth is the configured cap at rejection, and right about occupancy. I checked: `serve.llm` sets `DEFAULT_MAX_ONGOING_REQUESTS = int(1e9)` (python/ray/llm/_internal/serve/constants.py), so occupancy against configured capacity reads zero. The saturation factor is dropped entirely and the formula is now `ceil(max_queued_requests / drain_rate)`. 

One clarification on the drain rate, since implementability was questioned: the router already counts assignments per replica (num_requests_sent_to_replicas, router.py:152) and the rejection is raised from a method on the same `RouterMetricsManager` that owns those counters, so the EWMA is a derivation over state the raise site already holds, not new plumbing.

On 7: agreed and adopted. Jitter moves into the shared header helper, so the static retry_after_s path gets it too, which both fixes today's verbatim emission and keeps the A/B fair. Good catch, credited in the RFC.

Separately, your reload observation (HAProxy state wiped on replica-set changes when dynamic server updates would do) is a real standalone improvement to the HAProxy ingress, worth its own issue regardless of this RFC.

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
@suppagoddo thanks for your review, all of your points are in the updated RFC:

1. Renamed to queue_drain_rate, since the same policy runs at the router or the replica, whichever rejects.
2. On a local saturation factor for direct ingress: we ended up dropping the saturation factor everywhere instead. From @johntaylor-cell 's finding `serve.llm` defaults `max_ongoing_requests` to `1e9`, so occupancy measured against configured capacity reads zero for the main workload class, and the backoff term had no existing signal behind it. It isn't gone forever though: if the A/B data shows the simple formula consistently errs in a way a saturation signal would fix, that data is the justification to bring one back. Evidence first, term later.
3. EWMA warmup is configurable as an implementation constant with an environment-variable override, alongside the smoothing split and the interval length, same as Serve's other internal tunables. Deliberately not a new BackpressureConfig field, to keep the public API at two fields plus the policy name.
4. Adopted your measurement point: since retries can't be reliably correlated (new request IDs, different proxy, or no retry at all), the primary measure is suggested delay vs the locally observed queue drain time, with admitted-retry rate secondary where correlation does exist.
5. Your A/B against a jittered-static baseline is now the acceptance test itself.

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
@abrarsheikh to summarize the whole review thread and the current state of RFC:

Updated the RFC based on the review so far and it came out simpler. 
One policy, `queue_drain_rate` which computes `retry_after` on rejection using below formula:
```
retry_after = ceil(max_queued_requests / drain_rate)
```
Where:
- `max_queued_requests`: the numerator is the configured cap (depth at rejection is always the cap) and 
- `drain_rate` is a smoothed measure of how fast the rejecting component's queue empties which is assignment throughput at the router, completion rate at the replica. 

The value is clamped to [1, 60]s and jittered in the shared header helper so the static path gets jitter too, falls back to the static retry_after_s when the rate isn't warm, and the acceptance test is an A/B against a jittered-static baseline measured on suggested delay vs observed local drain time.

comments.author: JerryChaox
comments.body:
hello guys, some information and test for this RFC.

I tested the proposal on Ray 2.58.0 and found two implementation details worth checking before coding it.

First, num_requests_sent_to_replicas is an in-flight gauge: it increments on send and decrements on completion. It cannot directly provide assignment throughput, so the router likely needs a monotonic counter at the accepted-assignment event.

Second, router queue depth is not always equal to max_queued_requests at rejection. Internal replica rejection can cause requests to re-enter after new requests occupy temporarily freed slots. With a cap of 8, 1,418 of 17,270 router rejection events had an observed depth of 9–11. I did not observe this on the direct-replica path.

I also compared the computed policy with a tuned jittered-static baseline over 90 held-out distributed runs. Conditional local-drain header MAE was 1.865s for the computed policy and 1.141s for static 2s. The computed policy generated fewer attempts, so this looks like a precision versus retry-cost tradeoff rather than a clear winner.

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
@JerryChaox Thanks for testing the approach and for those valuable findings. Here are my thoughts on each of them:

1. Agree (and my earlier comment was wrong on this) that `num_requests_sent_to_replicas` is an in-flight gauge, increments on send (`router.py:404`) and decrements on completion (`router.py:412`). I will fix this by adding a new monotonic assignment counter at the same send event. So the raise site and the counters live on the same object and the drain rate is still a derivation over local state.

2. This is a great find. Agreed. This finding makes the formula better: use the observed depth at rejection as the numerator instead of the configured cap. The raise site already holds that number, it is in the BackPressureError message today.

3. On your third observation, the A/B test: I see how a static value wins on a homogeneous workload, where a good constant like your 2s can be guessed or tuned in advance. But the whole purpose of this RFC is the case where the constant cannot be guessed in advance, because load regimes vary and move the drain rate. I'd like to know: a) Did drain time vary across your 90 runs? b) Was the 2s tuned per workload or once overall?

Your fewer attempts observation is the most interesting part. MAE weighs a 1s early and a 1s late suggestion equally, but the costs are not equal: early means a wasted attempt plus more load on a system that is already shedding, late means idle wait. So I think we should use a asymmetric or composite metric that penalizes wasted attempts (penalize early more than late).

comments.author: vinay7373
suppagoddo

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
Acceptance criteria spec:

1. Ground truth: Each rejection records the observed depth D and the drain counter value at that moment. Ground truth T is the wall time until the counter advances by D: assignments at the router, completions at the replica on direct ingress. This measures what the header claims, that the observed backlog clears. It does not measure whether a specific retry gets admitted, since that depends on other clients' arrivals. T stays measurable under continuous overload because the counter keeps advancing even when the queue never dips below the cap.
2. Metric: An asymmetric loss between the suggested delay `s` and `T`: `0.75 * max(T - s, 0) + 0.25 * max(s - T, 0)`. One second too early costs 3x one second too late, because an early retry wastes an attempt and adds load while the system is shedding and a late one only waits, bounded by the clamp. The minimizer of this loss is the 75th percentile of the drain time distribution, so the estimator gets a concrete target. MAE is reported as secondary for comparability. Scoring is offline over logged pairs, on the pre-jitter post-clamp value.
3. Baseline: The comparison arm is jittered static, with the constant tuned only on calibration runs disjoint from the evaluation set (rule: 75th percentile of calibration drain times, one global constant). A per-scenario tuned static is also reported. Runs are open loop (clients ignore the header) with autoscaling off and a pinned replica set.

@suppagoddo For me to run the above acceptance test I'll need one structured record per rejection with `policy id, fallback rung used, observed depth, drain rate estimate and warm flag, pre-jitter and post-jitter values, and the counter value at rejection`. Plus the counter itself readable by a test harness at sub-second granularity. Everything already exists at the raise site or in estimator state; the cost is one log line on a path that already logs a warning today. Please make sure this record emission is part of your implementation.

Pass bar (proposal): 
- Computed beats the static baseline on the primary loss by at least 20% in aggregate across the scenarios
- is never more than 10% worse in any single scenario
- the undershoot rate lands at 25 +/- 10 points
- and cold start falls back to the static value cleanly.

cc. @JerryChaox @abrarsheikh @johntaylor-cell

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
**AI serving regimes for the acceptance runs**

Now that the implementation is up for review (#66798), here are the regimes the acceptance runs will cover. The runs collect the metrics defined in my acceptance comment above. The scenarios its pass bar refers to are drawn from these regimes. I'm deriving the regimes from real-world AI serving, using two characteristics: load and completion.

What a regime is: An AI serving regime is a recurring pattern of load and completion at the component that rejects requests. Load is how requests arrive. Completion is how they finish: how long each one runs, how many run at once, and whether they finish one at a time or in batches.

**Why these two (load and completion)?**
Ground truth in the acceptance spec is the time for the drain counter to advance by the observed depth: assignments at the router, completions at the replica on direct ingress. Both count the completion process, seen from each vantage, since the router hands a queued request to a replica when one finishes. So completion sets the drain time directly. Load decides when the queue overflows and what the estimator sees between rejections, such as idle gaps. Latency is an outcome of both, not an input.

Completion is the important half in AI serving, because processing time is not known when a request arrives. A generative model decides its output length while it generates, and in production "the remaining output length of an LLM request is not conditioned on the generated length so far" [1]. Drain speed cannot be computed from what is in the queue. It has to be measured from completions.


**Completion regimes:** 
The estimator samples once per second, so what matters is how far apart completions arrive at that scale.

| Regime | Examples | Completions | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| W1 Real-time predictive | vision, ranking, LLM code completion | Dense: many per second | Latency bounds of 15 to 250 ms [2]. Code completion has a median output of 13 tokens [3] |
| W2 Batched execution | `@serve.batch`, dynamic batching | Grouped: a batch finishes together | Each response returns once its whole batch is evaluated [4] |
| W3 Interactive LLM | chat on continuous batching | Dense to moderate: seconds each, many at once | A median of 129 output tokens [3] at 20 to 50 tokens/s [5] |
| W4 Long-running LLM | reasoning, long context, agent steps | Sparse: minutes each, few at once | A mean of 3,880 output tokens [6]. Long contexts limit how many run at once [7] |

**Load regimes:**

| Regime | Arrivals | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| L1 Steady | A constant rate. The runs use fixed-interval schedules so repeated runs are comparable | MLPerf's Server scenario models online load with Poisson arrivals [2] |
| L2 Bursts and idle gaps | High-rate bursts separated by silence | API traffic is "aperiodic... characterized by burstiness" [8]. Short-term arrivals are "often bursty (CV > 1)" [1] |
| L3 Mix shift | A steady rate, but the request mix changes, so completions speed up or slow down | Services have "widely different prompt and token distributions" [3]. In one 48-hour window, 29 of 2,412 clients sent 90% of requests [1] |

**Scenarios:** 
|# | Cell | Completions | Expected drain time | Load |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | W1, L1 | every 0.25 s | 2 s | 2x drain |
| S2 | W3, L1 | every 2.5 s | 20 s | 2.5x drain |
| S3 | W1 to W3, L3 | every 0.25 s, then every 1 s | 4 s, then 16 s | 2x drain |
| S4 | W1, L2 | every 0.25 s during bursts | 4 s | 3x drain for 20 s, then idle for 25 s |
| S5 | W3, L1, mixed fleet | every 0.4 s, from one fast and one 4x slower replica | 10 s | 2.4x drain |
| S6 | W4, L1, beyond cap | every 8 s | 240 s | 4x drain |
| S7 | W1, L1, cold start | every 0.25 s | 4 s | 3x drain from the first second |
| S8 | W3, L1, pipeline | every 1 s at the inner deployment | 8 s | 3x drain |
| S9 | W2, L1 | 8 at once every 4 s | about 8 s | 2x drain |
| S10 | W4, L1 | every 8 s | about 48 s | 2x drain |

[1] ServeGen, NSDI'26: https://

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
From the above clearly EWMA's loss is 74% lower overall than static jitter. Though the results above show a clear gain, it falls short when completions are seconds apart:
1. Long requests, one completion every 8 s: never early, but clients waited 15 to 17 s longer than needed on average.
2. Batched, 8 requests finishing together every 4 s: early only 2 to 3% of the time, and clients waited about 6 s longer than needed.
3. Steady slow, one completion every 2.5 s: the estimate swings both ways. On the proxy path it was early 45% of the time. On both paths, when it was late, clients waited 9 to 12 s longer than needed.
4. Beyond cap, one completion every 8 s with 30 requests waiting: the true wait is 240 s. Without the 60 s cap, the EWMA would have sent a median of 382 s, and up to about 2,400 s (40 minutes). These are rejections from the first 180 s of each run, while the drain held at one every 8 s.

**Main cause for the above limitation:** The EWMA counts drains in each one-second sample and divides the depth by that rate. When completions are seconds apart, most samples count zero. The rate falls at every empty second and dividing by a small rate gives a long wait. When the next completion comes, the rate jumps back up. So the estimate follows the time since the last completion, not the real drain speed. For example, with one completion every 4 s and 8 requests ahead, the true wait is 29 to 32 s, but the EWMA's estimate moves between 20 and 59 s.

Lets take LLM serving as an example. After bit research on how requests complete in LLM serving, I found that what matters is not just how long each request runs, but how far apart completions are at the component that rejects. That gap is about how long one request runs, divided by how many requests run at the same time. For example, if a replica runs 40 requests at once and each takes 20 s, one finishes every 0.5 s or if it can run only 2 at once, one finishes every 10 s. LLM requests run for seconds to minutes. Memory for long contexts limits how many run at once on a replica and batched work finishes in groups. So in Batched execution (W2), Long-running LLM (W4) and Interactive LLM (W3) when a replica runs only a few requests at once, completions at the rejecting component are seconds apart or come in groups. These patterns are common in LLM serving and they are where a per-second rate breaks down. So we want to measure the drain in a way that does not depend on completions landing inside each one-second sample.

To address the above, I would like to propose **The busy clock**:
The PR already keeps one running total for each component, the drain counter. The busy clock adds a second running total: busy seconds.
- A drain is one step of the drain counter: an assignment at the router, or a completion at a replica.
- A busy second is a second in which the component had work pending or saw a drain. These are the seconds the PR's sampler already counts. Idle seconds, which the PR skips, are not added, so the busy clock stops when the component is idle.
- Seconds per drain is busy seconds divided by drains over a recent window. It is the average time the component needs for one drain while it is working.
- The window is the most recent stretch of busy time that holds at least 8 drains and at least 10 busy seconds. Each limit protects one kind of workload:
  - When completions are seconds apart, the 8 drains matter. They keep the estimate from resting on one or two gaps. With one completion every 8 s, the window stretches to about 64 s.
  - When there are many completions per second, 8 drains can pass in a fraction of a second. The 10 busy seconds keep the estimate from jumping with every small burst.
  - The window only sets how far back the estimate looks. The estimate is still updated every second and every rejection is answered at once. Until 10 busy seconds have passed, the window is all the busy time so far, so warmup still takes 3 counted seconds. If the last 10 minutes of busy

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
@suppagoddo, 
Following up on your uneven jitter range idea (for example -5% to +15%, so fewer clients come back early).

The tables above score the value before jitter. Clients see the header after jitter and rounding up to whole seconds. So I replayed the final acceptance round the way the PR builds the header: jitter, round up, then clamp to [1, 60] (cap enforced only to keep the experiment consistent with previous ones here, I still prefer no cap with busy clock implementation) for computed values. Same rejections and measured drain times as before. The numbers are the average loss, with the share of clients told to come back early:

| Jitter range | Busy clock | EWMA |
|---|---|---|
| None (rounding up only) | 0.687 (15% early) | 1.321 (12% early) |
| ±5% | 0.722 (12%) | 1.309 (12%) |
| **±10%** | **0.759 (14%)** | 1.298 (13%) |
| ±20% (current default) | 0.882 (20%) | 1.302 (17%) |
| -5% to +15% | 0.834 (8%) | 1.384 (9%) |
| 0% to +20% | 0.948 (4%) | 1.464 (6%) |

**Why the uneven range does not help.** Compare it with ±10%, which has the same spread. -5% to +15% does cut early clients, from 14% to 8%. But its loss is 10% higher (0.834 against 0.759), and it is worse in all 15 scenario and path pairs. The EWMA shows the same pattern (1.384 against 1.298).
- An early second costs three times a late one, so the loss is lowest when about a quarter of clients are early. Below that, everyone else waits longer than needed, and that costs more than the early retries it saves.
- The busy clock already sits close to that point before jitter: 24% of its values are early.
- Rounding up to whole seconds already makes every header later by up to 1 s. Shifting the jitter range up adds more of the same.

**I prefer ±10% instead of ±20%:**
- It lowers the busy clock's loss on the wire from 0.882 to 0.759. The EWMA barely changes, because its own errors are larger than the jitter.
- It keeps most of the spreading. Headers are whole seconds, so for waits up to about 5 s, ±10% and ±20% give nearly the same headers: a 4 s estimate becomes 4 or 5 s either way. For longer waits, ±10% still spreads a 30 s wait over 27 to 33 s.

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
@suppagoddo, regarding the busy clock's history that we discussed offline, so it is on record here.

**Change:** keep the busy clock's history by drains, not by time. My first version kept the last 10 minutes of history of busy time. This change keeps at least the last 8 drains, however long ago they were. The window rule itself stays the same: at least 8 drains and at least 10 busy seconds.

**Why:** with a 10 minute history, a component that finishes a request less often than once every 75 s (600 / 8) cannot hold 8 drains in its window. Past one completion every 10 minutes, it cannot even see one full gap, so the estimate comes out too low. This happens with very long requests, such as LLM research or agent tasks that run for about 15 minutes, when a replica runs only a few at a time.

**Other benefits:**
- It removes a jump during long stalls. With a 10 minute history, once the last 8 drains are out of history, the estimate jumps to D x 600 s (5 hours for D = 30). With this change it keeps growing steadily, by D / 8 for each stalled second.
- For very slow workloads the window gets long, about 2 hours for 15 minute requests, so it follows changes slowly. There is no way around this: a request's length can only be learned by watching such requests finish.
- Memory stays small.

comments.author: suppagoddo
comments.body:
@vinay7373 - In both the EWMA and Busy second we are considering the current load on the system, shall we also include the number of incoming requests too in the calculation? Imagine this scenario:
```
T0:
 -> Queue Depth is full and We cannot take a new Request.
 -> Request R1 comes: We calculate the retry after and return xx sec
 -> Request R2 comes: We calculate the retry after and return xy sec
 -> The only difference between xx and xy is jitter-delta

T0 + xx:
 -> R1 retry occurs and we let it in. Queue depth have 1 empty slot.

T0 + xy:
 -> R2 retry occurs and we reject it as Queue depth is full because R1 got it.
```

Basically the current estimator is predicting backlog-clear time, which might not be 100% equal to future admission time, which I think seems reasonable as it is a hint. But I think we should make this distinction clear.

items.body_excerpt:
Under a token default, every head must be able to create the token. Today only `ray.init()` creates one: `ray start --head` with no token fails with `AuthenticationError`, and `ray.cluster_utils.Cluster()` builds `Node(head=True)` directly, so its GCS crashes on `Check failed: has_token || ignore_auth_mode` (`authentication_token_loader.cc:115`) and the user only sees `Timed out waiting for file .../gcs_server_port_...`.

Change:

- `Node.__init__` with `head=True` calls `ensure_token_if_auth_enabled(create_token_if_missing=True)` before starting the GCS. This covers `ray start --head`, `ray.init()`, C++/Java drivers and `Cluster()`.
- Remove the token-creation calls in `worker.py` (new-cluster path) and `scripts.py` (`ray start --head`).
- Connecting paths keep `create_token_if_missing=False`.
- `generate_and_save_token` writes the token to a temp file and links it into place, so heads that start at the same moment in one HOME end up with the same token. It never overwrites a non-empty token file; an empty one is replaced.
- Test: `ray start --head` with an empty HOME creates `~/.ray/auth_token` with mode 0600.
- Test: `ray.cluster_utils.Cluster()` with an empty HOME starts with auth on.
- Test: several processes creating the token at once in an empty HOME all end up with the token on disk.
- Test: a C++ driver that starts its own cluster gets a token (`//cpp:metric_example`). Java drivers start the head through the same `ray start --head` (`RunManager.startRayHead`), so the `ray start --head` test covers them.
- Test: `ray start --address` and `ray.init(address=...)` never create a token file.

No behavior change while the default is still `disabled`.

items.title: [Core/Auth] Reject gRPC requests that carry a token on clusters with auth disabled
items.author: MortalHappiness
items.body_excerpt:
A server with an empty token accepts every request (`server_call.h`), so a client in token mode talking to a cluster with `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` succeeds silently. The client should be told to opt out too.

Change:

- A server in disabled mode rejects any request that carries a token with `UNAUTHENTICATED` and "AuthModeMismatch: cluster has RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled; set it on the client too". Apply it in `ServerCall::ValidateAuthenticationToken` and in the Python gRPC server interceptor in `grpc_utils.py`, which is then always installed. Both keep the Kubernetes token exception (`ENABLE_K8S_TOKEN_AUTH`).
- `AuthenticationError.__str__` doesn't append `TOKEN_AUTH_FIX_MESSAGE` (`authentication_constants.py`) to this message.
- Test: a disabled cluster with a driver that also sets `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` and has a token file works; a driver that doesn't set it gets the AuthModeMismatch error.
- Test: `ray start --address` in token mode against a head with `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` fails with AuthModeMismatch, without hanging or timing out. #67051 stops `Node._init_gcs_client` and the Ray Client connect loop from retrying `AuthenticationError`; without that, this fails only after 20 retries.

HTTP is out of scope here (see #67053).

items.title: [KubeRay][Core/Auth] Verify KubeRay clusters work with token auth on by default
items.author: MortalHappiness
items.body_excerpt:
From 2.61, Ray nodes and clients need the token unless `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` is set. Check KubeRay and report any gaps:

- Head, worker and autoscaler containers get the token as a file (for example a Secret mounted with `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN_PATH` pointing at it), not on a command line.
- Clusters that opt out set `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` on every pod.
- Health probes and job submissions send the token.
- Prometheus monitors (PodMonitor or ServiceMonitor) send `Authorization: Bearer <cluster token>` when scraping Ray's metrics endpoints.
- With `ENABLE_K8S_TOKEN_AUTH`, the Prometheus configs Ray generates (the dashboard's `prometheus.yml` and the one `ray metrics launch-prometheus` uses) point `credentials_file` at `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN_PATH` or `~/.ray/auth_token`, never at the service-account token in `/var/run/secrets/ray.io/serviceaccount/token`, so check whether KubeRay users rely on those configs and, if they do, point them at the service-account token (raised on #67128).
- With Kubernetes service-account tokens, which rotate, a node or `ray://` client keeps working across a rotation. Auth rejections are no longer retried, so a rotated token must be picked up before a request is rejected.

Related: #66561, #66716 (`image_uri` workers under Kubernetes token auth).

items.title: [Autoscaler][v2] max_concurrent_launches (default 10) splits a gang scale-up into multiple steps, wasting nodes with Kueue
items.author: kevin85421
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

Autoscaler v2 launches at most `AUTOSCALER_MAX_CONCURRENT_LAUNCHES` (default **10**) instances at a time, so a scale-up that needs more than 10 nodes at once is split into multiple steps. For workloads that need all of their nodes before they can start (e.g. a placement group), this can leave a partially scaled-up cluster holding resources that can never be used.

**Example with Kueue:**

1. A user has a RayCluster with only a head Pod and wants to run SFT on 16 GPU nodes, so they create a placement group with 16 bundles (one per node).
2. The scheduler correctly decides to launch 16 worker nodes, but the reconciler only launches 10 of them in the first step. The worker group is scaled `0 -> 10`, and only later `10 -> 16`.
3. The Kubernetes cluster has 10 free GPU nodes, so Kueue admits the first scale-up.
4. When the second scale-up (`10 -> 16`) comes, fewer than 6 GPU nodes are left, so Kueue can't admit it and it's stuck.
5. SFT can't start without all 16 nodes, so the 10 admitted nodes are wasted, and they also block other workloads that could have used them.

If the autoscaler had requested all 16 nodes in a single step, Kueue would have either admitted all of them or none of them, and no resources would be wasted.

**Where the limit comes from:**

- `Reconciler._compute_to_launch` caps the number of instances in flight (`REQUESTED`) by `max_concurrent_launches`: https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/3e2f0b5c2aa2caa01cf6c08268325bb9a9c62048/python/ray/autoscaler/v2/instance_manager/reconciler.py#L920-L924
- `AutoscalingConfig.get_max_concurrent_launches()` always returns `AUTOSCALER_MAX_CONCURRENT_LAUNCHES`, which defaults to 10 and can only be changed with an env var on the autoscaler container: https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/3e2f0b5c2aa2caa01cf6c08268325bb9a9c62048/python/ray/autoscaler/_private/constants.py#L51-L53
- For KubeRay, the default `upscalingMode` sets `upscaling_speed = 1000` with the comment "i.e. big, no rate-limiting by default", but the global cap of 10 still applies, so there is rate limiting by default after all: https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/3e2f0b5c2aa2caa01cf6c08268325bb9a9c62048/python/ray/autoscaler/_private/kuberay/autoscaling_config.py#L119

**Expected:** a scale-up needed by a single resource demand (at least a gang request such as a placement group) is requested in one step, so that admission systems like Kueue see the full size up front.

**Possible directions** (open to discussion):

- Don't split the instances launched for the same gang resource request across steps.
- For KubeRay, a launch is just one patch of the worker group's `replicas`, so the concurrent launch cap mainly adds latency. Consider not applying it (or a much higher default) on KubeRay.
- Make the cap configurable from the RayCluster CR (e.g. via `autoscalerOptions`), not only through an env var.

### Versions / Dependencies

- Ray: master (`3e2f0b5c2a`), autoscaler v2
- KubeRay: v1.7.0
- Kueue

### Reproduction script

1. Create a RayCluster with autoscaler v2, only a head Pod, and a worker group with `minReplicas: 0`, `maxReplicas: 16` (or more), and 1 GPU per worker.
2. Manage the RayCluster with Kueue, with a ClusterQueue whose quota fits 10 workers but not 16.
3. Create a placement group that needs 16 workers, e.g. `ray.util.placement_group([{"GPU": 1}] * 16, strategy="STRICT_SPREAD")`.
4. Observe that the worker group's `replicas` goes to 10 first and only then to 16, and that the cluster gets stuck with 10 admitted workers that the placement group can't use.

### Issue Severity

Medium: It causes significant difficulty or wasted resources, but there is a workaround (setting `AUTOSCALER_MAX_CONCURRENT_LAUNCHES` on the autoscaler container).

items.title: [Autoscaler][KubeRay] Autoscaler can patch worker group replicas below minReplicas
items.author: kevin85421
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

When the autoscaler terminates a worker Pod on KubeRay, it can patch the worker group's `replicas` below `minReplicas`. KubeRay itself never runs fewer than `minReplicas` Pods (it clamps `replicas` to `[minReplicas, maxReplicas]`), so the RayCluster spec then disagrees with what is actually running. Other controllers that read `replicas` from the spec can act on the wrong number.

This caused a real problem with Kueue: https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kueue/pull/16884

1. A worker group has `minReplicas=maxReplicas=2` and `replicas=2`, and both worker Pods are scheduling-gated by Kueue.
2. One Pod can't get resources within `RAY_AUTOSCALER_RECONCILE_ALLOCATE_STATUS_TIMEOUT_S`, so autoscaler v2 moves its instance to `ALLOCATION_TIMEOUT` and terminates it.
3. The termination patches `replicas` from 2 to **1** (below `minReplicas`) and adds the Pod to `workersToDelete`.
4. KubeRay still keeps 2 worker Pods because of `minReplicas`.
5. Kueue sizes the worker PodSet from `replicas`, so it only accounts for 1 worker and the other Pod stays scheduling-gated. In some Ray versions the autoscaler never restores `replicas` to 2, so it's stuck indefinitely, even once capacity is available.

Kueue worked around it on their side by clamping to the replica bounds when computing PodSet counts, but the root cause is that the autoscaler writes a `replicas` value KubeRay won't honor.

**Expected:** the autoscaler never patches `replicas` outside `[minReplicas, maxReplicas]`, for both scale-up and scale-down, so the spec always matches what KubeRay will actually run.

**Current behavior in the code** (permalinks to master `3e2f0b5c2a`):

- Autoscaler v2 `KubeRayProvider._initialize_scale_request` starts from `max(replicas, minReplicas) * numOfHosts` and subtracts one per Pod to delete, only asserting the result is `>= 0`. Nothing keeps it at or above `minReplicas`:
  - https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/3e2f0b5c2aa2caa01cf6c08268325bb9a9c62048/python/ray/autoscaler/v2/instance_manager/cloud_providers/kuberay/cloud_provider.py#L319-L321
  - https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/3e2f0b5c2aa2caa01cf6c08268325bb9a9c62048/python/ray/autoscaler/v2/instance_manager/cloud_providers/kuberay/cloud_provider.py#L357-L358
- `_submit_scale_request` already caps the target at `maxReplicas`, but has no matching lower bound: https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/3e2f0b5c2aa2caa01cf6c08268325bb9a9c62048/python/ray/autoscaler/v2/instance_manager/cloud_providers/kuberay/cloud_provider.py#L404-L412
- The autoscaler v1 KubeRay node provider has the same pattern (caps at `maxReplicas`, no `minReplicas` bound): https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/3e2f0b5c2aa2caa01cf6c08268325bb9a9c62048/python/ray/autoscaler/_private/kuberay/node_provider.py#L619-L626
- For reference, KubeRay's `GetWorkerGroupDesiredReplicas` (v1.7.0) clamps `replicas` to `[minReplicas, maxReplicas]`: https://github.com/ray-project/kuberay/blob/v1.7.0/ray-operator/controllers/ray/utils/util.go#L389-L407

**Proposal:** clamp the target `replicas` to `[minReplicas, maxReplicas]` in the KubeRay providers before patching, next to the existing `maxReplicas` cap. When the autoscaler deletes a Pod while the group is at `minReplicas`, keep `replicas` at `minReplicas` and still list the Pod in `workersToDelete`; KubeRay deletes it and creates a replacement, which is what it does today anyway.

One thing to check while fixing this: when the group is at `minReplicas`, both KubeRay (to keep `minReplicas` Pods) and the autoscaler (to satisfy `min_worker_nodes`) may create a replacement for the deleted Pod. If so, the group could temporarily get one more worker than needed until idle termination removes it.

### Versions / Dependencies

- Ray: reported on 2.55.1; the unclamped code path is still on master (`3e2f0b5c2a`)
- KubeRay: v1.7.0
- Kueue: before https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kueue/pull/16884

### Reproduction script

1. Create a RayCluster with autoscaler v2 and a worker group with `minReplicas: 2`, `maxReplicas: 2`.
2. Make one of the two worker Pods unschedulable (e.g. not enough capacity, or gated by Kueue without quota), and lower `RAY_AUTOSCALER_RECONCILE_ALLOCATE_STATUS_TIMEOUT_S` on the autoscaler container to make it time out sooner.
3. After the timeout, observe the worker group's `replicas` being patched to 1 while `minReplicas` is 2, and KubeRay still running 2 worker Pods.

### Issue Severity

Medium: It causes significant difficulty, e.g. workers stuck scheduling-gated with Kueue, but Kueue now has a workaround on its side.

items.title: [Core] `ray metrics launch-prometheus` doesn't pick up new scrape targets for up to 5 minutes
items.author: MortalHappiness
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

Prometheus started by `ray metrics launch-prometheus` keeps scraping the targets that were in the service discovery file when it started, and ignores later updates until its file_sd refresh interval (5 minutes by default). I expected it to pick up new targets within seconds, as Prometheus file_sd does when it gets a file change event.

Measured on one machine: starting Prometheus right after a 2-node cluster comes up, Prometheus listed only 1 target (the autoscaler) for 60 seconds, while the service discovery file listed 4 (two nodes, the autoscaler and the dashboard). This happened in 9 of 9 runs, on Prometheus 2.48.1 and 3.15.0. Waiting until the file listed all 4 targets before starting Prometheus passed 2 of 2 runs, and so did pointing the config at the real file in the session directory with no wait.

The [static config](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/f178b1887d2f9bb43a323678dc54c14aae7378be/python/ray/dashboard/modules/metrics/export/prometheus/prometheus.yml#L12) that `launch-prometheus` uses reads `/tmp/ray/prom_metrics_service_discovery.json`. That path is a symlink into the current session directory, created by [`PrometheusServiceDiscoveryWriter.write`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/f178b1887d2f9bb43a323678dc54c14aae7378be/python/ray/_private/metrics_agent.py#L828-L863), which rewrites the real file in the session directory every few seconds through a temp file and `os.replace`. Prometheus watches the directory of the configured path, `/tmp/ray`, so the rewrites in the session directory never trigger a reload. That is the cause.

I inferred, but haven't verified on an autoscaling cluster, that nodes added after `launch-prometheus` starts, such as autoscaled workers, aren't scraped for up to 5 minutes. The config the dashboard writes ([`_create_default_prometheus_configs`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/f178b1887d2f9bb43a323678dc54c14aae7378be/python/ray/dashboard/modules/metrics/metrics_head.py#L430)) uses the real session path and isn't affected.

Possible fixes:

- Point the static config at `/tmp/ray/session_latest/prom_metrics_service_discovery.json`. `session_latest` is a directory symlink, so the watch should resolve to the real directory; I haven't verified this.
- Have `launch-prometheus` write its config with the resolved session path.
- Set a short `refresh_interval` under `file_sd_configs`.

### Versions / Dependencies

Ray master (f178b1887d), Linux, Prometheus 2.48.1 and 3.15.0.

### Reproduction script

```bash
ray start --head
ray metrics launch-prometheus  # start it right away, before the file lists every target
# then add a node in another shell
ray start --address=127.0.0.1:6379
sleep 30
cat /tmp/ray/prom_metrics_service_discovery.json  # lists the new node
curl -s localhost:9090/api/v1/targets | python -c "import json,sys; print([t['scrapeUrl'] for t in json.load(sys.stdin)['data']['activeTargets']])"  # doesn't
```

### Issue Severity

Low: It annoys or frustrates me.

items.title: Illegal memory access in triton kernel and non-determinism codegen
items.author: xw285cornell
items.body_excerpt:
Hi team, we seem to identified an issue that triton is generating non-deterministic codegen results, and in certain cases (small chances) it seems to have illegal memory access due to out of bound access in shared memory. 
The triton code is fairly simple (shown below). We run the code many times (disabled pytorch's codegen cache) and it seems it produced different shared memory: 
Most of times: 
{"name": "triton__0d1d2d3d4", "shared": 2560, "num_warps": 4, "num_stages": 1}
Sometimes: 
{"name": "triton__0d1d2d3d4", "shared": 544, "num_warps": 4, "num_stages": 1}

So sometimes it only asks for 544 bytes for shared memory space which might lead to out of bound access to shared mem. We checked and ttir is the same across the two runs, but llir is different. Wondering if you can shed some lights on this (and whether the codegen is deterministic. Also this is still on llvm IR - not sure if it repros in MLIR. 

```
from torch._inductor.triton_ops.autotune import pointwise

@pointwise(
    size_hints=[262144, 64],
    tile_hint=TileHint.DEFAULT,
    filename="notebook",
    meta={
        "signature": {0: "*bf16", 1: "*fp32", 2: "*bf16", 3: "i32", 4: "i32"},
        "device": 0,
        "constants": {},
        "mutated_arg_names": [],
        "configs": [instance_descriptor(divisible_by_16=(0, 1, 2, 3), equal_to_1=())],
    },
)
@triton.jit
def triton_(
    in_ptr0,
    in_ptr1,
    out_ptr0,
    xnumel,
    ynumel,
    XBLOCK: tl.constexpr,
    YBLOCK: tl.constexpr,
):
    xnumel = 262144
    ynumel = 62
    xoffset = tl.program_id(0) * XBLOCK
    xindex = xoffset + tl.arange(0, XBLOCK)[:, None]
    xmask = xindex < xnumel
    yoffset = tl.program_id(1) * YBLOCK
    yindex = yoffset + tl.arange(0, YBLOCK)[None, :]
    ymask = yindex < ynumel
    x0 = xindex % 512
    x1 = xindex // 512
    y2 = yindex
    x3 = xindex
    tmp0 = tl.load(
        in_ptr0
        + (
            512
            + x0
            + (1536 * x1)
            + (786432 * y2)
            + (786432 * (((x0 + (512 * x1)) // 262144)))
        ),
        xmask & ymask,
    ).to(tl.float32)
    tmp1 = tl.load(in_ptr1 + (512 + x0), xmask)
    tmp2 = tmp1.to(tl.float32)
    tmp3 = tmp0 + tmp2
    tmp4 = 2.8284271247461903
    tmp5 = tmp3 / tmp4
    tl.store(
        out_ptr0 + (y2 + (62 * x3) + tl.zeros([XBLOCK, YBLOCK], tl.int32)),
        tmp5,
        xmask & ymask,
    )
```

items.title: [CI] Installation E2E test step grew from ~9 min to ~41 min since July
items.author: Jeffwan
items.body_excerpt:
**Area:** Testing (E2E)

## Summary

In the `Installation Tests` workflow, the `Run installation e2e tests` step went from 9m15s in mid-July to 40m36s now, and the whole workflow from about 20 minutes to 54. The `installation-test` job has a 75-minute timeout.

Measured on two runs of the same workflow:

- July 13: https://github.com/Jeffwan/aibrix/actions/runs/29281096831/job/86923371188
- October 8, `a228471` (main at #2930): https://github.com/Jeffwan/aibrix/actions/runs/37735233267/job/113174859334

## Numbers

| | Jul 13 | Oct 8 |
|---|---|---|
| Whole workflow | 20.5 min | 54 min |
| `Run installation e2e tests` step | 9m15s | 40m36s |
| Test packages | 1 (`./test/e2e`) | 13 |
| Top-level tests | 44 | 180 |
| Sum of test time | 486s | 2,123s |
| Compile time before the first test | 47s | 3m08s |

October 8 time per package. All packages run one after another (`go test -p 1`):

| Package | Time |
|---|---|
| gateway/routing | 527s |
| controller/roleset | 360s |
| controller/stormservice | 257s |
| gateway/pd | 218s |
| controller/podset | 206s |
| controller/modeladapter | 169s |
| controller/modelclaim | 163s |
| controller/raycluster | 117s |
| controller/modelwarmup | 46s |
| gateway/api | 32s |
| controller/modelrouter | 25s |
| controller/autoscaling (+ external-metrics) | ~5s |

## Why it grew (about +31 min)

### 1. New controller lifecycle E2E tests: about +19 min

Controller tests went from about 204s (only `TestRoleSetInPlaceUpdate`) to 1,348s. Every new package runs on the same kind cluster, one after another, so each one adds its full time to the step.

| Change | Package time now |
|---|---|
| StormService E2E (#2733, Sep 16) | 257s |
| PodSet lifecycle E2E (#2751, Sep 20) | 206s |
| ModelAdapter E2E no longer skipped (#2657, Sep 3) | 169s |
| ModelClaim E2E (#2460 Jul 18, expanded through #2929 Oct 8) | 163s |
| RayClusterFleet lifecycle E2E (#2753, Sep 20) | 117s |
| ModelWarmup E2E (#2769, Oct 2) | 46s |
| ModelRouter lifecycle E2E (#2743, Sep 19) | 25s |
| RoleSet historical-node (#2628) and drain (#2736) tests enabled in CI | roleset 202s → 360s |

### 2. Gateway tests: about +8 min

Gateway tests went from about 282s to 777s.

- **Each request to the mock is about 3.3× slower (#2383, Jul 14).** That change turned on capacity-aware latency in the mock by default. A request with no `max_tokens` now sleeps about 0.03s + 2ms × `randint(10, 500)` output tokens. That averages about 0.55s, where it used to be a fixed 0.2s.
  - 30 pod-discovery requests: 6.3s → 20.8s.
  - The 8 routing tests present in both runs: 163s → 351s in total. `TestRandomRouting` went 21s → 67s; the VTC tests went from about 21s to 52–61s.
- **New tests:**
  - power-of-two routing: 137s
  - PD failure, bucketing and watchdog tests: `gateway/pd` is 218s now
  - backend-request and API endpoint tests

### 3. Build overhead: about +4 min

#2676 (Sep 8) split the suite into packages and added `go test -p 1`. The `-p` flag limits concurrent compile actions as well as test binaries, so all compilation is now serial:

- compile time before the first test: 47s → 3m08s
- about 5–9s of compiling and linking before each of the 13 packages

items.title: [cake deslop] cake_warp_decode (2): drop 47K lines of unread clamped-E256 JSON, dead FFI/manifest plumbing; retire 26 low-row kernels
items.author: yyihuang
items.body_excerpt:
**Background.** `csrc/fused_moe/warp_decode` is the Cake-generated warp-decode expert GEMM behind `CakeWarpDecodeConfig(backend="cake")`. It is opt-in, never a default backend, and is served by `CakeWarpDecodeRunner` in `flashinfer/fused_moe/runners.py`. It requires exactly SM100 or SM103, 1 ≤ T ≤ 32, `enable_pdl=True` and no EP, and supports 16 `(activation, H, I, E, K)` geometries. It was added by #4855 (SM103), #5036 (SM100 + standalone SiLU), #5134, #5574 and #5593. The first round, #5785, was closed by #5908 (merged 2026-10-03, +465/−152,444). That PR deleted 66 per-module and 55 per-sequence never-compiled bindings (97,836 lines) and the import-time hash-checked `cake_warp_decode_inventory.json` (35,171 lines). It also moved the 17 byte-identical sm_103a kernels into `generated/common` and added the GPU parity test. It left kernel templating, a shared helper header, cached TMA descriptors with a table-driven launcher, stride-aware descriptors and shape-bucketed selection open. Since then, #6067 added 4 sharded-TP geometries with 12 fused route-pack kernels. #5558 (+73,547/−34) added the clamped DeepSeek-V4-Flash H4096/I2048/E256/K6 route for SM100 as a second generation with its own host framework and 47K lines of JSON, bringing back the import-time metadata pattern #5908 had removed. The directory is now 71 files / 137,938 lines, against 52 / 72,845 right after #5908: 64 kernel `.cu` (71,052), two generated host manifests (17,674), two JSON files (47,039), the binding (1,017) and the contract header (1,129). Counts at 3184bbea.

**Findings**
- **Unread clamped-E256 JSON.** `generated/dsv4_clamped_e256/route_metadata.json` (41,611 lines, 1.06 MB) and `module_manifest.json` (5,428 lines) have one reader: `_load_clamped_e256_sources` in `flashinfer/jit/cake_fused_moe_warp_decode.py` (207–291). It uses 653 + 141 lines' worth of fields and raises on any mismatch.
  - Dispatch is hard-coded in `dsv4_clamped_e256_manifest.cuh::ForEachLaunch`, a 32-case switch on `num_tokens`. Its device→T sets equal the JSON launch sets.
  - All 15 modules use `--use_fast_math`, `pdl=True` and `cooperative=False`, so a static tuple like `_SM100A_SOURCES` gives the same result.
  - Nothing in `flashinfer/`, `tests/`, `benchmarks/`, `docs/`, `csrc/` or `pyproject.toml` reads either file, and neither has a digest field.
- **Dead FFI exports.** `cake_fused_moe_warp_decode_prepare_workspace_with_inputs` / `_with_partials` / `_with_inputs_and_partials` and the `run` alias (binding 1003–1008, 1014) have no caller in this repo; the runner calls six other FFI names. Their support code is inert because the Python path passes empty owners (173 host-only lines):
  - `PreparedWorkspaceState` owner tensors with their memsets and overlap checks;
  - `UsesOwnedInputScratch` / `UsesOwnedPartialScratch` and `Invocation.prepared_*` in the contract;
  - the `prepared_*` overrides in both `ForEachLaunch` halves.
- **Dead host code in `generated/cake_warp_decode_generated_manifest.cuh`.**
  - 19 hard-wired-false predicate blocks (116 lines, including `sharded_evict_first = fused_pack && false`) and their 24 `? -1` ternary arms.
  - `kGeneratedSourceSha256` and `kMaximumAuthoredDynamicSharedMemoryBytes` are each defined twice and never read; the `KernelSpec` fields `kind`, `tensor_map_abi` and `grid` are never read either.
  - `NeedsNonPortableSmem` calls `cudaGetDevice` and takes `DeviceMutex` from every `VisitKernel_N` (68 call sites, 3–4 per forward). It only fills `KernelLaunch.allow_oversized_smem`, which the binding discards at line 547.
- **All 64 kernels are reachable, but 26 serve ≤4 rows.** sm100a compiles 19 common + 15 `sm_100a` + 15 clamped sources; sm103a compiles 19 + 15. Enumerating `SelectSm100aSchedule`/`SelectSm103aSchedule`, both `ForEachLaunch` halves and the clamped switch over 16 geometries × T=1..32 gives 480 rows per target, 34/34 kernels selected and no row at index −1.
  - 26 sources (33,123 lines) serve ≤4 (geometry, T) rows each.
  - 12 of them (13,967 lines) serve exactly one row per target. Examples: sm100 `b451f69a` + `6aee17fe` at M3 (H6144/I3072/E128/K4) T=1, `f5eac8f9` at Q30 (H2048/I768/E128/K8) T=18, sm103 `5304d683`/`c5afe5ba` at Q30 T=11/21, `common/514c77f6` at E192 SiLU T=1, and clamped `device_10`/`12`/`14` at T=10/9/8.
  - Every one of them has a neighbouring kernel 1–103 normalised lines away. sm103 already routes M3 T=1 to Persistent/K256 (contract 231–235).
  - These row counts come from the source selectors, not from a compiled build.
- **The parity test skips the low-row rows.** `_GPU_GEOMETRIES` in `tests/moe/test_cake_warp_decode.py` (1131–1165) runs Q30 at T ∈ {1,2,8,9,10,16,32} and Q35/M3 at {1,2,32}. As a result, pytest never launches `f5eac8f9`, `5304d683`, `c5afe5ba`, `57d9c60c`, `common/8acc0c77` or sm100 `5312a738`, and never runs `ebcaf3ae`/`2355e317` at T=18/19. Only the benchmark's full-range modes reach these.
- **Constant-clone clusters.** About 43.9K of the 71K kernel lines are copies that differ in a single knob:
  - `#pragma unroll 1`→`2` (`510ad9e9`↔`5304d683`) and unroll 4→16;
  - `a_tma_merged` (`7d6f9437`↔`6b5216f2`) and a moved early-SFB `mbarrier_arrive`;
  - `THREADS`, inline L2 evict_first asm, `valid_k64` guards, padded SFC and fixed top_k.

  The 43.9K total was spot-checked on 18 pairs, not recomputed. The clamped kernels (`kernel_trtllm_moe_bmm_tile_n8_*`/`kernel_dsv4_*`) are a separate generation and do not dedupe against the rest.
- **Unrolled host manifests.** The two generated host files total 17,701 lines, against the 1,017-line binding.
  - `cake_warp_decode_generated_manifest.cuh` (10,549 lines) has an sm100 half (5,237) and an sm103 half (5,268) that share 4,075 identical lines. It holds 184 `EncodeTensorMap_*` functions (8 distinct bodies after digit normalisation) and 68 each of `KernelArgs_N`, `PrepareKernel_N`, `SubmitKernel_N` and `VisitKernel_N`, all derivable from `kKernelSpecs`.
  - `dsv4_clamped_e256_manifest.cuh` (7,125 lines) consis

items.title: Five conv filter tile access iterators invert the byte scaling in add_pointer_offset (8/sizeof_bits instead of sizeof_bits/8)
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

Five conv filter tile access iterators invert the byte scaling in `add_pointer_offset`: they compute `pointer_offset * 8 / sizeof_bits<Element>::value` where every sibling iterator uses `pointer_offset * sizeof_bits<Element>::value / 8`.

Affected sites:

- include/cutlass/conv/threadblock/conv2d_fprop_filter_tile_access_iterator_analytic.h:194
- include/cutlass/conv/threadblock/conv2d_fprop_filter_tile_access_iterator_fixed_channels.h:165
- include/cutlass/conv/threadblock/conv2d_fprop_filter_tile_access_iterator_few_channels.h:167
- include/cutlass/conv/threadblock/conv3d_fprop_filter_tile_access_iterator_analytic.h:160
- include/cutlass/conv/threadblock/depthwise_fprop_filter_tile_access_iterator_direct_conv_optimized.h:162

For fp32 (32 bits) the inverted form is a silent no-op multiplier of 8/32 vs the correct 4; for fp16 it scales offsets by 1/2 instead of 2. All 30+ sibling iterators (activation/dgrad/wgrad variants) use the correct form, e.g. conv2d_dgrad_filter_tile_access_iterator_analytic.h:187.

Currently latent: no in-tree caller passes nonzero element-granularity pointer offsets into these mainloop A/B iterators (kernels call `add_pointer_offset` on the epilogue D iterator only). The defect surfaces for any external user advancing these public iterators manually.

items.body_excerpt:
### Description

`SparseGemmSplitKParallel`-style serial split-K in `include/cutlass/gemm/kernel/sparse_gemm.h` offsets the E (metadata) operand by the wrong amount for slices beyond the first:

```cpp
// sparse_gemm.h:237
cutlass::MatrixCoord tb_offset_E{
  threadblock_tile_offset.m() * Mma::Shape::kM,
  threadblock_tile_offset.k() * params.gemm_k_size / kSparse,   // missing / kElementsPerElementE
};
```

The E iterator's extent is expressed in packed element-E columns and divides twice (`sparse_gemm.h:269`, `problem_size_k / kSparse / kElementsPerElementE`), and the sibling kernel `gemm_sparse_universal.h:622` divides twice as well when offsetting:

```cpp
cutlass::MatrixCoord tb_offset_E{
  threadblock_tile_offset.m() * Mma::Shape::kM,
  offset_k / kSparse / kElementsPerElementE,
};
```

With the missing division, every K-slice `>= 1` of a split-K sparse GEMM starts its metadata reads far past the end of the packed E tensor; all accesses are predicated off and the slice runs on zero-filled (invalid) metadata.

Concrete numbers: fp16 (`kElementsPerElementE == 2`), K=128, `split_k_slices = 2`: slice 1 has an E extent of 4 columns while its offset column is 32. Zero valid accesses.

The same formula is duplicated in two more copies of this kernel body:
- `sparse_gemm_with_absmax.h:322`
- `sparse_gemm_with_visitor.h:153`

Reachability note: nothing in-tree exercises it (`device::SparseGemm` with `split_k_slices > 1`; example 15 uses one slice), so this is latent, but the wrapper accepts split-K (`device/sparse_gemm.h` passes `args.batch_count` through).

### Suggested fix

Divide by `kElementsPerElementE` in the offset at all three sites, matching `gemm_sparse_universal.h`:

```cpp
threadblock_tile_offset.k() * params.gemm_k_size / kSparse / kElementsPerElementE,
```

items.title: [BUG] CuTe DSL: export_to_c fails for a --gpu-arch other than the current GPU's
items.author: hwanseoc
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CuTe DSL

### Bug Report

**Describe the bug**

`export_to_c` fails on the plain C path (no `--enable-tvm-ffi`) when the function was compiled for a different arch than the current GPU. For example, `--gpu-arch sm_90a` on a B200:

```text
JIT session error: Symbols not found: [ _cuKernelGetAttribute, _cudaDeviceGetAttribute, _cudaFuncSetAttribute, _cudaGetDevice, _cudaKernelSetAttributeForDevice, _cudaLaunchKernelEx, _cudaLibraryGetKernel, _cudaLibraryLoadData ]
error: Error dumping object file: Failed to dump object file with PIC relocation
```

The same export works for the native arch, and it also works if I load the runtime libraries `RTLD_GLOBAL` first. My guess is that no execution engine gets built for an arch the GPU can't run, so `libcute_dsl_runtime.so` never gets loaded before the object dump.

**Steps/Code to reproduce bug**

```python
import ctypes, sys, tempfile

import cuda.bindings.driver as cuda
import cutlass
import cutlass.cute as cute
from cutlass.cute.runtime import make_fake_stream


@cute.kernel
def noop_kernel(x: cutlass.Int32):
    pass


@cute.jit
def noop(x: cutlass.Int32, stream: cuda.CUstream):
    noop_kernel(x).launch(grid=(1, 1, 1), block=(32, 1, 1), stream=stream)


if "--preload" in sys.argv:
    for lib in cute.runtime.find_runtime_libraries(enable_tvm_ffi=False):
        ctypes.CDLL(lib, mode=ctypes.RTLD_GLOBAL)
fn = cute.compile(noop, cutlass.Int32(0), make_fake_stream(), options="--gpu-arch sm_90a")
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    fn.export_to_c(tmp, "noop", function_prefix="noop")
print(f"cutlass-dsl {cutlass.__version__}: exported", flush=True)
```

```console
$ python repro.py
JIT session error: Symbols not found: [ _cuKernelGetAttribute, ... ]
$ python repro.py --preload
cutlass-dsl 4.8.0: exported
```

**Expected behavior**

`export_to_c` works for any `--gpu-arch` the compiler accepts, with no manual preloading.

**Environment details (please complete the following information):**
 - Environment location: Bare-metal
 - nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.8.0 and 4.7.0 (cu13), cuda-python 13.4.1
 - B200, driver 580.159.03, Ubuntu 22.04, Python 3.12

**Additional context**

#2859 had the same error on the TVM-FFI path and was fixed in 4.3.3; the TVM-FFI path does export cross-arch now. The plain C path still fails. Workaround: preload `cute.runtime.find_runtime_libraries()` with `RTLD_GLOBAL`.

items.title: [Store] Does Mooncake store plan to support awareness of layers, chunk ordering, and TP?
items.author: Hadigan
items.body_excerpt:
It looks like the current Mooncake store does not have awareness of layer granularity, chunk order (earlier vs. later chunks), or TP ranks. This can cause problems during cache eviction:

1. The store might evict KVs for only some layers, forcing prefill to recompute all layer KVs for those tokens.
2. The store might evict the KVs corresponding to the earliest chunk(s) of a token sequence, forcing prefill to recompute KVs for all chunks/tokens.
3. The store might evict KVs produced by some TP ranks, forcing all TP ranks to recompute KVs.

I think the Mooncake store should be aware of layers, chunk ordering, and TP. On eviction, it should evict a token’s KV caches for all layers and for all TP ranks together (i.e., keep KV state complete per token). 
From the chunk-order perspective, eviction policies should prefer removing KVs for later chunks first rather than evicting early-chunk KVs that make prefill expensive.

items.title: [Core/Auth] Distribute the auth token to ray up and autoscaler nodes via file_mounts
items.author: MortalHappiness
items.body_excerpt:
`ray up` clusters need the token on the head and every worker, without putting it on a command line. Passing it as an env var in the start commands puts it in `ps` on both ends of the SSH command and twice in the `ray up` console log.

Change:

- In `_set_up_config_for_head_node` (`autoscaler/_private/commands.py`), before the file mounts are rewritten, add a file mount for `~/.ray/auth_token` unless `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` is set locally or the YAML already mounts that path. The source follows token precedence: `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN` written to a 0600 temp file, else `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN_PATH`, else `~/.ray/auth_token` (created with `generate_and_save_token` if missing). The autoscaler reuses `file_mounts` for workers.
- `ray up` creates a missing token with the same atomic write that #67049 adds, and never overwrites a non-empty token file.
- Opting out: the user sets `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` on the nodes in the cluster YAML. `ray up` never copies the local auth mode to the nodes.
- Existing `ray up` clusters update their worker nodes once after upgrading: the new file mount changes the autoscaler's runtime hash, so each worker reruns its setup commands and restarts Ray. Instances aren't relaunched; in Docker mode the container restarts to pick up the new mount. Call this out in the PR so it reaches the release notes.
- Also cover `--no-monitor-on-head`, which skips `_set_up_config_for_head_node`.
- The fake multi-node docker provider skips worker `file_mounts` (`disable_node_updaters`), and the head's `ray start` runs at container start, before `ray up` syncs files. So add the token file to the shared `node_spec["volumes"]` in `fake_multi_node/node_provider.py`, mounted read-only at `/home/ray/.ray/auth_token`. The fake command runner must then skip `ray up`'s `~/.ray/auth_token` upload, because `docker cp` can't overwrite a read-only single-file mount.
- Test: a fake-provider cluster with `RAY_AUTH_MODE=token` scales up a worker that joins. It runs in the "core: HA integration tests" CI job (tag `ha_integration`).

Checked: `rsync -avz` keeps mode 0600. In Docker mode, file mounts are rsynced to the host and bind-mounted into the container at the expanded `~/.ray/auth_token`; this comes from reading `command_runner.py` and hasn't been run on a real cluster.

items.title: [Core/Auth] Require the auth token on Ray's Prometheus metrics endpoints
items.author: MortalHappiness
items.body_excerpt:
With token auth on, Ray's Prometheus metrics endpoints (each node's metrics port, the autoscaler and the dashboard head) serve metrics to anyone who can reach them. That discloses job, actor and deployment names, node IPs and resource use.

Change:

- Each metrics endpoint checks the token the way the dashboard does, accepting `Authorization`, `X-Ray-Authorization` or the `ray-authentication-token` cookie. With auth on, a missing token gets 401 with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer` and a wrong one gets 403. With auth off, the check is skipped.
- Ray's generated Prometheus configs (the dashboard's template and the config `ray metrics launch-prometheus` uses) add an `authorization` block with `type: Bearer` only when auth is on. The `credentials_file` is `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN_PATH` if set, else `~/.ray/auth_token`. With auth off, the config is unchanged. Ray writes no new copy of the token.
- With auth on and no token file, or with `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN` set and the token file holding a different token (`RAY_AUTH_TOKEN` takes precedence over any file), `ray metrics launch-prometheus` exits with an error saying to put the token in a file and set `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN_PATH`.
- In the same case, the dashboard logs a warning with that fix and writes its prometheus.yml without the `authorization` block; it still starts.
- Metrics tests send the token when auth is on (`fetch_raw_prometheus`).
- Test: with auth on, each endpoint returns 401 without a token, 403 with a wrong one, and 200 with each accepted form. With auth disabled, it returns 200 without a token.
- Test: with auth on, `ray metrics launch-prometheus` on a multi-node cluster shows every target up.
- Test: with auth disabled, the generated Prometheus config is unchanged.

Local clusters have run with token auth on by default since 2.59, so their metrics endpoints require the token as soon as this merges.

items.title: [Data] `Dataset.join` fails with "unjoinable types" when one input is an empty pandas-backed block
items.author: 400Ping
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

Any `Dataset.join` whose left or right input contains only empty pandas-backed blocks fails with:

```
ray.exceptions.RayTaskError(ValueError): ray::JoinShuffleReduce(num_partitions=2)()
  ...
  File "ray/data/_internal/execution/operators/join.py", line 462, in _preprocess
ValueError: Cannot join on columns with unjoinable types. Left join key columns {'k'} have unjoinable types (map, union, list, struct, etc.) which cannot be used for join operations.
```

It happens for `inner`, `left_outer`, `right_outer` and `full_outer`, whether the empty side is the left or the right input. The easiest way to get such an input is `ray.data.from_pandas(...)` followed by a `filter` that matches no rows, which is exactly what the optimizer's predicate pushdown produces when it moves a filter below a join (so a plain `join(...).filter(...)` on pandas-backed data can hit this too without the user ever writing the filter before the join).

The same join with an empty **Arrow**-backed input works and returns the correct result:

```python
empty = ray.data.from_arrow(pa.table({"k": pa.array([], pa.int64()), "lv": pa.array([], pa.int64())}))
empty.join(right, "inner", num_partitions=2, on=("k",)).take_all()  # -> []
```

**Expected**

An empty input side should behave like an empty Arrow table: `inner` returns no rows, `left_outer` / `right_outer` / `full_outer` return the rows of the non-empty side with nulls for the other side's columns.

**Root cause**

`PandasBlockAccessor.to_arrow()` (`python/ray/data/_internal/pandas_block.py`) coerces every column with no non-null value to Arrow's `null` type, to work around pandas turning all-null columns into `double`:

```python
if not col.notna().any():
    null_coerced_columns[(idx, col_name)] = pa.nulls(len(col), type=pa.null())
```

For a 0-row DataFrame that condition is true for every column, so the dtype pandas still carries (`int64` here) is thrown away:

```python
>>> df = pd.DataFrame({"k": pd.Series([], dtype="int64")})
>>> BlockAccessor.for_block(df).to_arrow().schema.types
[DataType(null)]
```

The join then rejects the key because `JoinOperator._is_pa_join_not_supported` treats `pa.null()` as unjoinable (`python/ray/data/_internal/execution/operators/join.py`, `_split_unsupported_columns` / `_preprocess`).

A possible fix is to skip the null-type coercion for 0-row columns (there is nothing to coerce, and the pandas dtype is the right Arrow type), or to have the join tolerate a null-typed key on a 0-row table.

**Related issues**

- #60013 / #60520 / #61507: empty blocks *produced by* a join losing their schema. This report is about an empty *input* to a join.
- #66125: anti joins with an empty unknown-schema side (shuffle V2 schema broadcast).
- #65539: `to_pandas()` on an empty dataset dropping columns.


### Versions / Dependencies

- Ray: master (reproduced at 6cf3af8020, with the Python layer from master on a 2.58.0 core)
- Python 3.12
- pyarrow 25.0.1, pandas 3.0.5, polars 1.44.2 (also reproduced with the repo-pinned polars 1.40.0)

### Reproduction script

```python
import pandas as pd
import ray
from ray.data.expressions import col

ray.init()

left = pd.DataFrame({"k": [1, 2, 3], "lv": [1, 2, 3]})
right = pd.DataFrame({"k": [3, 4], "rv": [3, 4]})

for join_type in ("inner", "left_outer", "right_outer", "full_outer"):
    for empty_side in ("left", "right"):
        l = ray.data.from_pandas(left)
        r = ray.data.from_pandas(right)
        if empty_side == "left":
            l = l.filter(expr=col("k") == 999)
        else:
            r = r.filter(expr=col("k") == 999)
        try:
            rows = l.join(r, join_type, num_partitions=2, on=("k",)).take_all()
            print(f"{join_type} empty {empty_side}: OK, {len(rows)} rows")
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"{join_type} empty {empty_side}: RAISED {type(e).__name__}")
```

Output on master:

```
inner empty left: RAISED RayTaskError(ValueError)
inner empty right: RAISED RayTaskError(ValueError)
left_outer empty left: RAISED RayTaskError(ValueError)
left_outer empty right: RAISED RayTaskError(ValueError)
right_outer empty left: RAISED RayTaskError(ValueError)
right_outer empty right: RAISED RayTaskError(ValueError)
full_outer empty left: RAISED RayTaskError(ValueError)
full_outer empty right: RAISED RayTaskError(ValueError)
```

### Issue Severity

Medium: It is a significant difficulty but I can work around it.

items.title: [Core] Add versioning to the GCS resource load pull to avoid re-fetching unchanged data
items.author: dancingactor
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

## Description 
GCS periodically pulls cluster resource data (resource availability and demand) for autoscaler usage. However, even for idle nodes whose resource data remains unchanged, GCS currently pulls this data redundantly.

In contrast, Ray Syncer avoids redundant resource view reports using a versioning system: Raylet returns nothing when a node's `version_ <= after_version`. In other words, Ray Syncer reports only when a node's resource state changes.

**I want to implement the same versioning system for GCS periodic pulls. On an idle cluster, this will significantly reduce the workload on both the GCS main thread and the pull thread.**
### Benchmark

Test configuration:
- Resources per node: 6
- Pending demand shapes per node: 10
- Cluster idle, which means no resources or demand change

| Nodes | Thread | Current | Versioned pull (proposed) | Reduction |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 100 | main | 1.82 | 0.006 | ~300× |
|  | pull | 0.78 | 0.25 | 3.1× |
| 1,000 | main | 15.90 | 0.006 | ~2,600× |
|  | pull | 7.15 | 2.43 | 2.9× |
| 5,000 | main | 79.03 | 0.007 | ~11,000× |
|  | pull | 35.73 | 12.94 | 2.8× |
| 10,000 | main | 158.58 | 0.009 | ~17,000× |
|  | pull | 72.24 | 26.54 | 2.7× |



### Use case

items.title: ModelWarmup target stays Running until the job timeout when Pod Security rejects its Pods
items.author: vjsairam
items.body_excerpt:
In a namespace enforcing Pod Security `restricted`, an image-only ModelWarmup is accepted and its Job is created, but Pod Security rejects every Pod the Job tries to create. The target keeps reporting "warmup job is running" until the job timeout, then fails with `DeadlineExceeded`. The rejection details are in the Job's `FailedCreate` events and in an API warning in the controller log, but not in the ModelWarmup status.

`samples/modelwarmup/README.md` already says the generated Job template has to be allowed by Pod Security admission, so the failure itself is expected. What's missing is the diagnostics: model-warmup.rst covers the API server rejecting the Job, but not an accepted Job whose Pods are rejected.

**Reproduce** (AIBrix v0.8.0, kind v0.27.0, Kubernetes v1.31.12, containerd 2.1.3)

```sh
kubectl create namespace mw-restricted
kubectl label namespace mw-restricted resource-pool.aibrix.ai/name=latency-pool \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted
kubectl label node <worker> resource-pool.aibrix.ai/name=latency-pool \
  model.aibrix.ai/warmup-enabled=true
kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: model.aibrix.ai/v1alpha1
kind: ModelWarmup
metadata:
  name: psa-image-only
  namespace: mw-restricted
spec:
  mode: Once
  targets:
  - nodes:
      names: ["<worker>"]
  imagePreload:
    images:
    - image: busybox:1.36
      command: ["sh", "-c", "exit 0"]
      imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
  policies:
    parallelism: 8
    jobTimeoutSeconds: 90
    retryLimit: 2
    ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 3600
EOF
kubectl -n mw-restricted get modelwarmup psa-image-only -o yaml
kubectl -n mw-restricted get events --field-selector reason=FailedCreate
```

**Observed**

20 s after creation, in a repeat run of the same manifest named `psa-image-only-midrun`, with no Pods in the Job:

```yaml
status:
  phase: Running
  activeNodes: 1
  targets:
  - nodeName: aibrix-test-worker2
    phase: Running
    message: warmup job is running
```

The original `psa-image-only` run recorded these Job events:

```
FailedCreate ... violates PodSecurity "restricted:latest": unrestricted capabilities (container "image-0" must set securityContext.capabilities.drop=["ALL"]), runAsNonRoot != true ...
```

At 90 s the original run's ModelWarmup ended with `phase: Failed` and condition `Degraded=True` (reason `NodeFailed`), and the target reason was `DeadlineExceeded` ("Job was active longer than specified deadline"). I only ran it with a 90 s timeout. With the sample's `jobTimeoutSeconds: 1800` I'd expect it to report Running for the full 30 minutes.

**Expected**

The target status says the Job can't create Pods, ideally with the `FailedCreate` reason. Failing that, the troubleshooting note in model-warmup.rst could cover Pod-level rejection as well as Job rejection.

**Notes**

- Image entries have no `securityContext` field, so an image-only warmup can't pass `restricted`. The same preload written as a custom container with `runAsNonRoot: true`, `runAsUser: 65534`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, capabilities `drop: ["ALL"]` and `seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault` succeeded in about 3 s in the same namespace.
- Found while testing for #3100.

items.title: feat: Add AIBrix Chat - a frontend demo portal for LLM inference
items.author: Jeffwan
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 Feature Description and Motivation

AIBrix provides powerful infrastructure for LLM inference, but we lack a user-facing demo to showcase its capabilities. Currently, users need to interact with AIBrix through API calls, or third-party clients, which creates friction when:

- Live demos — Presenting AIBrix at conferences, meetups, or internal reviews requires a polished UI
- End-to-end validation — Testing the full stack (gateway routing, model serving, load balancing) benefits from a real frontend client
- Onboarding — A working chat UI makes it easier for new contributors to understand the user-facing value of the infrastructure

### Use Case

Add a lightweight chat portal under apps/chat/web/ that serves as both a demo and a functional frontend for AIBrix-managed LLM endpoints.

What it includes:
- Chat interface with conversation management (create, search, delete, move)
- Project organization for grouping related conversations
- Model selector supporting multiple backends
- Sidebar navigation with chat history
- Dark-themed, responsive UI built with React + Vite + Tailwind CSS


Architecture:
```
  apps/
  ├── chat/
   │   ├── web/          # React frontend
   │   └── api/          # Backend proxy for LLM endpoints (planned)
```

### Proposed Solution

Why in-repo (not a separate project)?

1. Dogfooding — The chat portal consumes AIBrix gateway APIs directly, validating routing algorithms, model selection, and streaming behavior from a real client
2. Faster iteration — Co-locating with infrastructure code means API and frontend changes can land together
3. Visibility — Contributors are more likely to maintain something that lives alongside the core project
4. Demo-ready — A single repo clone gives users everything needed for a complete demo

### Task break down

#### Models and vLLM adaptatio

> Note: we do not necessarily need to host every model, each model endpoint should be fully replaced by cloud api. that means if we find some model are not supported in vllm-omni, we just use openai endpoint as replacement.

- [x] Test some ASR models (e.g.Qwen3-ASR) and make sure vLLM or vLLM-omni support it.
- [x] Test some TTS models and make sure vLLM or vLLM-omni support it.
- [x] Test Image Edit or Image Generation model  and make sure vLLM or vLLM-omni support it.
- [x] Test Video Generation model  (e.g. WAN-2.1) and make sure vLLM or vLLM-omni support it.
- [ ] Enable tool search/web search for LLM models.

#### Platform
- [x] Build lightweight frontend framework (nodejs)
- [x] Build python backend skeleton (python)
- [x] Make sure endpoint is compatible with OpenAI API
- [ ] Make sure endpoint is compatible with self-hosted models (via vllm directly).
- [ ] Make sure endpoint is compatible with self-hosted models (via aibrix directly - test with standalone, faster).
- [ ] Build applications -> CI, Docker, Deployment
- [ ] Prepare AIBrix deployment yaml for all the demo @Jeffwan 

#### Features
- [ ] Support reasoning model, UI shows thinking etc.
- [ ] Make sure streaming, reasoning are working well with the web UI.
- [ ] Enable user Login using github or simple login
- [ ] Enable user - level token based rate limiting
- [ ] P2: Finish Job Queue for near real time submission
- [ ] P2: Support object storage uploads if user configure the backend storage
- [ ] P2: Introduce SQLite to persist the conversation dat
- [ ] P2: Add intent router or intent classification component
